Proposition 6 (circulation estimates for the limit). |Gamma_U| <= (G/gamma_*)(1 - (1 + aR) e^{-aR}) with a = K gamma_*; sup_{Z, tau} int_0^infinity q_U^2 R dR <= 1 + log((KG)^2/2), and (KG)^2 > 2 holds automatically in Case 1. For every member of LL, sup Gamma (if positive) is not attained and is approached only as R -> infinity; along sequences escaping to radial infinity, Cartesian translates have subsequences converging to constant vectors, and along such sequences with Gamma -> sup Gamma the correspondingly translated circulations converge to sup Gamma locally uniformly.

Proof. Let U be the limit of Theorem 2, V its meridional part (|V^R| <= K), G' = G/gamma_*, a = K gamma_* and q_U = U^theta/R. Gamma = Gamma_U = R U^theta solves d_tau Gamma + V.grad Gamma = nu_* L Gamma on {R > 0} x (-infinity, 0], with |Gamma| <= G' and |Gamma| <= R (since |U^theta| <= 1). (a) Barrier. phi := G' phi_a, phi_a(R) = 1 - (1 + aR) e^{-aR}, satisfies phi' = G' a^2 R e^{-aR} >= 0 and phi'' - phi'/R = -a phi', so nu_*(phi'' - phi'/R) = -K phi'. For w = Gamma - phi, d_tau w + V.grad w - nu_* L w = -(V^R + K) phi' <= 0 on {R > 0}. Also w <= G'(1 + aR) e^{-aR} -> 0 as R -> infinity, and w <= Gamma <= R. Suppose m := sup w > 0. Points with w -> m have R in [m/2, R_1], where G'(1 + aR_1) e^{-aR_1} = m/2. Translating U in Z and tau and passing to a limit (compactness, stated in Theorem 3, viscosity nu_*) gives U~ with the same bounds |U~| <= K, |U~^theta| <= 1, |Gamma~| <= G', so w~ = Gamma~ - phi is again a subsolution, w~ <= m, and w~(R_infty, 0, 0) = m for some R_infty in [m/2, R_1]. The operator d_tau - nu_*(d_RR + d_ZZ) + (V~^R + nu_*/R) d_R + V~^Z d_Z has locally bounded continuous coefficients on {R > 0}, so Nirenberg's strong maximum principle [Nir] gives w~ = m on {R > 0} x (-infinity, 0], contradicting w~ <= R near the axis. Hence Gamma <= phi, and likewise -Gamma <= phi. (b) Slice integral. q_U^2 R = Gamma^2/R^3, and by (a) with 1 - (1 + x) e^{-x} <= x^2/2, |Gamma| <= min(G' a^2 R^2/2, R, G'); note G' a = KG. If (KG)^2 >= 2, split at rho_1 = 2/(G' a^2) <= rho_2 = G': the regions R < rho_1, rho_1 < R < rho_2 and R > rho_2 contribute at most (G' a^2/2)^2 rho_1^2/2 = 1/2, log(rho_2/rho_1) = log((KG)^2/2) and G'^2/(2 rho_2^2) = 1/2, so the integral is at most 1 + log((KG)^2/2). If (KG)^2 < 2, splitting min(G' a^2 R^2/2, G') at sqrt2/a gives at most (KG)^2/2 < 1. In Case 1 only the first alternative occurs: at the normalized record 1 = Gamma_U(e_1, 0) <= G' phi_a(1) < G' a^2/2, because phi_a(1) = int_0^a s e^{-s} ds < a^2/2, and G' >= 1 because sup |Gamma_U| >= 1; hence (KG)^2 = G'^2 a^2 >= G' a^2 > 2. (c) Members of LL. Let W be in LL, K_0 = ||W||_infty, G_0 = ||Gamma_W||_infty and G_+ = sup Gamma_W > 0. If sup_{R <= R_1, Z, tau} Gamma_W = G_+ for some R_1, near-maximizing points have R bounded below (|Gamma_W| <= ||grad W||_infty R^2); their translated limit in (Z, tau) attains G_+ at an interior point, and since Gamma_W solves the same equation with viscosity 1, [Nir] makes it equal to G_+ on {R > 0} x (-infinity, 0], impossible because it vanishes on the axis. So sup_{R <= R_1} Gamma_W < G_+ for every R_1, and G_+ is approached only as R -> infinity. Now let R_k -> infinity, W_k = W(. + R_k e_1 + Z_k e_3, . + tau_k) and rho_k = ((R_k + x_1)^2 + x_2^2)^{1/2}. The second Cartesian component satisfies |W_k^2| <= K_0 |x_2|/rho_k + G_0/rho_k -> 0 locally uniformly; W_k is the rotation by an angle O(1/R_k) of W written in the meridional coordinates (rho_k, x_3), so the uniform gradient bounds make every subsequential limit independent of x_2, of the form (v_1, 0, v_3)(x_1, x_3, tau). Integrating the three-dimensional kernel of e^{h Delta} Pi div in x_2 (absolutely convergent by the kernel bound of Theorem 2) gives the two-dimensional kernel, so (v_1, v_3) is a bounded mild ancient planar solution; [KNSS, Theorem 5.1] makes it constant in space, and the mild formula for a spatial constant makes it constant in time. The limit is a constant vector a_0 e_1 + c_0 e_3. If moreover Gamma_W(R_k, Z_k, tau_k) -> G_+, then Gamma_k(x_1, x_3, tau) := Gamma_W(R_k + x_1, Z_k + x_3, tau_k + tau) solves d_tau Gamma_k + V_k.grad Gamma_k = Delta_{x_1,x_3} Gamma_k - (R_k + x_1)^{-1} d_1 Gamma_k, V_k the translated meridional field, with |Gamma_k| <= G_0 and coefficients bounded in C^m locally uniformly in k (smoothing estimate for bounded mild ancient solutions), so interior Schauder estimates give local C^{2+alpha,1+alpha/2} bounds (some alpha in (0, 1)) through the terminal time; every subsequential limit is a bounded ancient solution of d_tau g + (a_0, c_0).grad g = Delta g in the plane attaining its maximum G_+ at the origin, hence equal to G_+ by [Nir].

Theorem 7 (pressure Hessian under (A); Riccati bound). For s <= t < T_*, with historical M, D, H at time t and the canonical pressure,
  ||grad^2 p(s)||_infty <= C_0 D(t)^2 [1 + log_+(M(t) H(t)/D(t)^2)],
with an absolute C_0. Under (A) this is at most C_0(1 + log_+ C_*) D(t)^2, and D is locally Lipschitz with 0 <= D' <= C_2 D^2 a.e. for late t, C_2 = 1 + C_0(1 + log_+ C_*); hence D(t) >= 1/(C_2 (T_* - t)) for late t.

Proof. Fix s <= t, write M, D, H for M(t), D(t), H(t), let c denote absolute constants (depending only on the choice of tensor norms), and assume u is not identically 0. Put f := d_i u_j d_j u_i (s); by incompressibility -Delta p = d_i d_j(u_i u_j) = f, and ||f||_infty <= c D^2, ||grad f||_infty <= c D H. Since u(s) is smooth with u(s), grad u(s) in L^2, f lies in L^1, L^infty and C^1, and the canonical pressure p = R_i R_j(u_i u_j) equals N * f with N = 1/(4 pi |x|) (both have Fourier transform -xi_i xi_j (u_i u_j)^(xi)/|xi|^2, so there is no harmonic ambiguity). Hence
  d_k d_l p(x_0) = -(1/3) delta_kl f(x_0) + lim_{eps -> 0} int_{|y| > eps} K_kl(y) f(x_0 - y) dy,   K_kl(y) = (3 y_k y_l - delta_kl |y|^2)/(4 pi |y|^5),
where K_kl has zero mean on spheres and |K| <= c|y|^{-3}, |grad K| <= c|y|^{-4}, |grad^2 K| <= c|y|^{-5}. Split the integral at radii 0 < a <= b. Near field (|y| < a): by the zero mean the integrand can be replaced by K(y)(f(x_0 - y) - f(x_0)), which gives at most c a ||grad f||_infty <= c D H a. Intermediate annulus (a < |y| < b): at most c ||f||_infty log(b/a) <= c D^2 log(b/a). Far field (|y| > b): write f(x_0 - y) = d_{y_i} d_{y_j} F_ij(y) with F_ij(y) = (u_i u_j)(x_0 - y), |F| <= M^2, |grad F| <= 2 M D, and integrate by parts twice on {b < |y| < Lambda}; the terms on |y| = Lambda are at most c(M D/Lambda + M^2/Lambda^2) -> 0, the inner sphere |y| = b contributes at most 4 pi b^2 (c b^{-3} M D + c b^{-4} M^2), and the volume term is at most c M^2 int_{|y| > b} |y|^{-5} dy = c M^2/b^2. Altogether
  ||grad^2 p(s)||_infty <= c (D^2 + D H a + D^2 log(b/a) + M D/b + M^2/b^2),   0 < a <= b.
Choose b = M/D and a = min(D/H, M/D). If a = D/H the bound is c D^2 (1 + log(M H/D^2)). If a = b = M/D < D/H, then M H < D^2, the annulus is empty and the bound is c D^2. This proves the first inequality; under (A), M H/D^2 <= C_* at late t.
Riccati step. Let J = grad u (Frobenius norm) and a(t) := ||J(t)||_infty, continuous in t. From d_t J + u.grad J + J^2 + grad^2 p = Delta J,
  (d_t + u.grad - Delta)|J|^2 = -2|grad J|^2 - 2 J:J^2 - 2 J:grad^2 p.
The spatial maximum of |J(t)|^2 is attained (J(t) decays), and there grad|J|^2 = 0, Delta|J|^2 <= 0 and |J:J^2| <= |J|^3; the maximum-point argument gives for the upper Dini derivative D^+ a(t) <= a(t)^2 + ||grad^2 p(t)||_infty. Passage to the running maximum D: where a(t) < D(t), D is constant near t; at a contact point a(t) = D(t), D(t + h) - D(t) <= max(0, sup_{t <= t' <= t + h} (a(t') - a(t))), so D^+ D(t) <= max(0, D^+ a(t)) <= D(t)^2 + C_0(1 + log_+ C_*) D(t)^2 = C_2 D(t)^2, using the first part with s = t and (A). Thus for late t the continuous nondecreasing function D has upper Dini derivative at most C_2 D^2 at every point; hence it is locally Lipschitz with 0 <= D' <= C_2 D^2 a.e., so d(1/D)/dt >= -C_2 a.e. and 1/D(t) - 1/D(b) <= C_2 (b - t) for late t < b < T_*. Since D(b) -> infinity as b -> T_* [BKM], D(t) >= 1/(C_2 (T_* - t)). The coefficient 1 in C_2 refers to the Frobenius norm.

Proposition 8 (normalized form of (A); gradient-record rescaling; abstract obstructions).
 (a) At the swirl record, m_n = M(t_n)/S_n, d_n = r_n D(t_n)/S_n, h_n = r_n^2 H(t_n)/S_n satisfy m_n >= (1 + gamma_n^{-2})^{1/2}, d_n >= 1, h_n >= 2, and (A) reads m_n h_n <= C_* d_n^2. These are global historical numbers whose maximizers need not lie near the record; passing (A) with its constant C_* to the limit U has not been justified.
 (b) Every W in LL satisfies the ancient shape inequality Q(W) := sup|W| sup|grad^2 W|/sup|grad W|^2 < infinity. If LL is nonempty, Q is unbounded on LL (axial Galilean transforms increase sup|W| without changing the derivatives).
 (c) Rescaling at a gradient record s >= max(t_A, t_P) (length M/D, time 1/D, velocity M, all at time s) gives fields V on R^3 x [-s D(s), 0], the whole past, with |V| <= 1, |grad V| <= 1 = |grad V(0, 0)|, |grad^2 V| <= C_* and viscosity kappa = D/M^2 <= C_P (historical mild smoothing). (A) is used only at s. Along gradient records s_n -> T_*, after passing to subsequences: if kappa -> kappa_infinity > 0, the limit is, after the viscosity normalization W(y, tau) = kappa_infinity^{-1} V(y, tau/kappa_infinity) and a horizontal translation taking its axis to the x_3 axis, a member of LL when the axis stays at bounded distance, and it is planar, hence constant by [KNSS, Theorem 5.1], contradicting |grad V(0, 0)| = 1, when the axis recedes. If kappa -> 0 the limit is an ancient swirl-free Euler field, axisymmetric about a fixed line or planar.
 (d) (O1) A smooth bounded divergence-free axisymmetric drift (stream function R^2 Z (1 + R^2 + Z^2)^{-1/2}) admits a bounded nonconstant steady solution of the circulation equation tending to 0 at the axis; so bounded drift alone does not make the circulation equation rigid. This drift is not a Navier-Stokes field and violates the hypotheses of Theorems 4 and 5.

Key estimates. (a) m_n >= 1 since M >= S. Since u^theta/r is, up to sign, an entry of grad u in the frame (e_r, e_theta, e_z), |u^theta|/r <= |grad u|, so d_n >= 1. With the record point rotated to (r_n, 0, z_n), g(rho) := u_2(rho e_1 + z_n e_3, t_n) has g(0) = 0, |g(r_n)| = S_n and g'(r_n) = d_r u^theta(r_n, z_n, t_n) = 0 (|u^theta(t_n)| is maximal there); Taylor's formula on [0, r_n] gives H(t_n) >= 2 S_n/r_n^2, i.e. h_n >= 2. Theorem 1 gives r_n |u^r| >= 1 at the record point, so M(t_n)^2 >= S_n^2 + r_n^{-2}, i.e. m_n >= (1 + gamma_n^{-2})^{1/2}. Multiplying (A) at t_n by r_n^2/S_n^2 gives m_n h_n <= C_* d_n^2.
(b) sup|grad^2 W| < infinity by the smoothing estimate for bounded mild ancient solutions (sec. 1.1), and sup|grad W| > 0 since W is not constant. For c in R, W_c(x, tau) := W(x - c tau e_3, tau) + c e_3 is again in LL, and Q(W_c) >= (|c| - ||W||_infty) ||grad^2 W||_infty/||grad W||_infty^2 -> infinity as |c| -> infinity (||grad^2 W||_infty > 0, as a bounded field with vanishing Hessian is constant).
(c) With D = D(s), M = M(s) and, by axial symmetry, a maximizer x(s) = (r(s), 0, z(s)) of |grad u(s)|, V(y, tau) := u(x(s) + (M/D) y, s + tau/D)/M solves NS with viscosity kappa on R^3 x [-s D, 0], and s D(s) -> infinity. Monotonicity of M, D gives |V| <= 1, |grad V| <= 1 = |grad V(0, 0)|; (A) at s alone gives |grad^2 V| <= M H/D^2 <= C_*, and Theorem 7 gives |grad^2 P| <= C_0(1 + log_+ C_*) for the rescaled pressure P; kappa <= C_P for s >= t_P. The rescaled circulation is Gamma D/M^2, so |V^theta| <= min(R, G kappa/R) <= (G kappa)^{1/2}, where R is the rescaled distance to the axis, which passes at distance a := r(x(s)) D/M from the origin. Along records s_n -> T_* take kappa_n -> kappa_infinity in [0, C_P] and a_n bounded or a_n -> infinity. Viscous case (kappa_infinity > 0): the smoothing estimate and the convergence argument of Theorem 2 without its far-field part give C^infinity_loc convergence to a bounded mild ancient V with |grad V(0, 0)| = 1. For bounded a_n, V is axisymmetric about a fixed line, |Gamma_V| <= G kappa_infinity, and V^theta is not identically 0 (otherwise V is constant by [KNSS, Theorem 5.2 and Remark 6.1]), so the horizontal translate of W taking its axis to the x_3 axis is in LL. For a_n -> infinity, |V_n^theta| <= G kappa_n/R -> 0 locally and the limit is planar, V = (v_1, 0, v_3)(y_1, y_3, tau), a bounded ancient mild 2D solution (the 3D kernel integrated in the inactive variable is the 2D kernel), hence constant by [KNSS, Theorem 5.1 and Remark 6.1]. Inviscid case (kappa_infinity = 0): ||V_n^theta||_infty <= (G kappa_n)^{1/2} -> 0; ||grad P_n||_infty <= C (grad N is integrable on the unit ball, and outside it two derivatives move onto the kernel), so ||d_tau V_n||_infty <= C(1 + C_*), and interpolation with the Hessian bound makes grad V_n equicontinuous in time. A subsequence converges in C^1 in space, locally uniformly in time, to a weak ancient swirl-free Euler flow V with |V| <= 1, |grad V| <= 1 = |grad V(0, 0)| and ||grad^2 V||_infty <= C_*, axisymmetric about a fixed line or planar. Off the axis Omega_n := omega^theta(V_n)/R solves d_tau Omega_n + div(B_n Omega_n) = kappa_n (Delta + (2/R) d_R) Omega_n + d_Z(|V_n^theta|^2/R^2), B_n the meridional part; against test functions phi supported in {R >= delta} the viscous term is at most sqrt2 C_* kappa_n int (|Delta phi| + 2 delta^{-1} |grad phi|) (as |Omega_n| <= sqrt2 |grad^2 V_n|) and the source at most G^2 kappa_n^2 delta^{-4} ||d_Z phi||_{L^1}, so the continuous limit Omega solves d_tau Omega + div(B Omega) = 0 weakly off the axis. Characteristics do not reach the axis since |V^R| <= ||grad V||_infty R. In the planar case the planar vorticity is weakly transported.
(d) Psi is the Stokes stream function; with rho := (1 + R^2 + Z^2)^{1/2}, V^R = -R^{-1} d_Z Psi = -R(1 + R^2)/rho^3 and V^Z = R^{-1} d_R Psi = Z(2 + R^2 + 2Z^2)/rho^3, so |V^R| <= 1 and |V^Z| <= 2. The steady circulation equation nu L Gamma = V.grad Gamma reads A Gamma = 0, A := nu(d_RR + d_ZZ) - (nu/R + V^R) d_R - V^Z d_Z. Upper barrier: beta := R/sqrt(nu) has A beta = -(nu/R + V^R)/sqrt(nu) <= 0 for R^2 <= nu (as -V^R <= R). Lower barrier: for eps in (0, 1] and R_1 := max(1, 1.0001 nu (11 + 2/eps^2)(2 + eps^2)^{3/2}) (so R_1 >= sqrt(nu)), w := 1 - R_1/R - Z^2/(eps^2 R^2) is positive only on the horn O_eps := {w > 0}, contained in {R > R_1, |Z| < eps R}; there nu L w = -nu(3 R_1/R^3 + 8 Z^2/(eps^2 R^4) + 2/(eps^2 R^2)) >= -nu(11 + 2/eps^2) R^{-2}, -V^R >= (2 + eps^2)^{-3/2}, w_R >= R_1/R^2 and -V^Z w_Z >= 0, so R^2 A w >= (2 + eps^2)^{-3/2} R_1 - nu(11 + 2/eps^2) > 0. Existence: on Omega_k := (1/k, k) x (-k, k), k > max(R_1, 2), solve A Gamma_k = 0 with boundary values min(1, R/sqrt(nu)) by [GT, Theorem 6.13]. The maximum principle gives 0 <= Gamma_k <= 1, Gamma_k <= beta on {R < sqrt(nu)} and Gamma_k >= w on O_eps (where O_eps meets the boundary of Omega_k, Gamma_k = 1). Interior Schauder estimates uniform in k and a diagonal argument give Gamma in C^infinity({R > 0}) with A Gamma = 0 and max(w, 0) <= Gamma <= min(1, R/sqrt(nu)): bounded, nonconstant, and -> 0 at the axis. Not a Navier-Stokes field: eta = Z(7 + 4R^2 + 4Z^2) rho^{-5}, and along Z = R/2, V.grad eta = (384/125) R^{-3} + o(R^{-3}), while nu Delta_5 eta and d_Z(q^2) = 2 Gamma d_Z Gamma/R^4 are O(R^{-4}) (interior estimates give d_Z Gamma = O(1)), so the steady eta equation fails at large R. Also V^R(R, 0) = -R(1 + R^2)^{-1/2} -> -1, which violates the envelope condition of Theorem 5 and the C/R bound of [KNSS, Theorem 5.3].

In the inviscid case of (c), the time bound for V_n and the Hessian bound give ||grad V_n(t + h) - grad V_n(t)||_infty = O(|h|^{1/2}) by interpolation, which is the time equicontinuity used. The viscous passage is the convergence argument of Theorem 2 (with globally bounded tails), and for receding axes the three-dimensional kernel integrated in the inactive variable is the two-dimensional mild kernel. These routine steps are indicated rather than written out in full.

Theorem 9 (Type I gradient growth is impossible under (A)). Assume (A). Then limsup_{t -> T_*} (T_* - t) D(t) = infinity. Equivalently, (A) together with D(t) <= C_I/(T_* - t) on late times is contradictory. The proof uses neither (K), (TAIL) nor the swirl records.

Key estimates. Assume (A) and D(t) <= C_I/(T_* - t) on [t_I, T_*); fix t_0 >= max(t_A, t_I) so late that the Riccati bound of Theorem 7 holds on [t_0, T_*). With delta := T_* - t, 1/(C_2 delta) <= D <= C_I/delta, so A_0 := C_2 C_I >= 1. Put l := delta M and f := delta M^2 = l^2/delta. Leray's lower bound [Ler] gives ||u(t)||_infty >= c_L delta^{-1/2} (c_L > 0 absolute), so f >= c_L^2. The interpolation ||g||_infty <= c ||g||_2^{2/5} ||grad g||_infty^{3/5} and ||u||_2^2 <= E_0 give M <= c E_0^{1/5} C_I^{3/5} delta^{-3/5}, so l <= c' delta^{2/5} -> 0. Call tau a running-minimum time if l(tau) = min_{[t_0, tau]} l; the largest minimum point of l on [t_0, t] is one and tends to T_*. For late tau, D(tau) is attained at a gradient record s in [t_0, tau] with delta(s) <= A_0 delta(tau); as M is nondecreasing, l(t) >= l(s)/A_0 on [t_0, s], f(s) >= f(tau)/A_0 and delta(s) D(s) >= 1/C_2. Either (E) f(tau_n) -> infinity along running-minimum times tau_n -> T_*, or (P) f <= F at all late running-minimum times.
Case (E). Local notation (differs from sec. 1.1): s_n the gradient records attached to tau_n, T_n := T_* - s_n, M_n := M(s_n), l_n := T_n M_n, nu_n := T_n/l_n^2 = 1/f(s_n) <= A_0/f(tau_n) -> 0. Rotate the gradient maximizer to x_n = (r_n, 0, z_n); along a subsequence r_n/l_n stays bounded (finite axis, a_n := (0, 0, z_n)) or tends to infinity (receding axis, a_n := x_n). V_n(y, sigma) := u(a_n + l_n y, T_* + T_n sigma)/M_n, sigma in [-(T_* - t_0)/T_n, -1], solves NS with viscosity nu_n. Write V_n = B_n + Z_n with B_n the meridional part and Z_n := V_n^theta e_theta the swirl part with respect to the original axis; R_n(y) := |a_n' + l_n y'|/l_n (y' = (y_1, y_2)) is the rescaled distance to that axis, Theta_n := T_n omega^theta and Omega_n := Theta_n/R_n. With t = T_* + T_n sigma, the historical and Type I bounds and (A) at each t give on R^3: |V_n| <= 1, |grad V_n| <= C_I/|sigma|, |grad^2 V_n| <= T_n l_n C_* D(t)^2/M(t) <= C_* C_I^2 (l_n/l(t))/|sigma| <= A_0 C_* C_I^2/|sigma| (and <= C_H := C_* C_I^2 at sigma = -1), R_n |Z_n| = |Gamma|/(l_n M_n) <= G nu_n, and |grad V_n(y*_n, -1)| = T_n D(s_n) >= 1/C_2 at the bounded points y*_n := (x_n - a_n)/l_n. By [CIV, Lemma 2.1], |grad^j V_n|^2 = |grad^j B_n|^2 + |grad^j Z_n|^2, |Theta_n| <= sqrt2 |grad B_n| and |Omega_n| <= sqrt2 |grad^2 V_n|. Swirl gradient: with rho := nu_n^{1/3}, where R_n >= 2 rho one has |Z_n| <= G nu_n/rho on B(y, rho), and |phi'(0)| <= sup|phi|/rho + (rho/2) sup|phi''| gives |grad Z_n| <= 3(G nu_n/rho^2 + rho C_H/2); closer to the axis one moves by at most 2 rho; hence ||grad Z_n(., -1)||_infty <= 4(G + C_H) nu_n^{1/3} and |grad B_n(y*_n, -1)|^2 >= C_2^{-2} - 16 (G + C_H)^2 nu_n^{2/3}. Compactness: by the meridional equation, d_sigma curl B_n is bounded in L^infty_sigma W^{-2,p}(B) on balls B; with the Lipschitz bounds, interpolation and Arzela-Ascoli give Theta_n -> Theta locally uniformly on R^3 x (-infinity, -1] (and Omega_n -> Omega off the axis for a finite axis), and B_n -> B weak-star with div B = 0, |B| <= 1 and ||grad B(sigma)||_infty <= C_I/|sigma|. Transport: for a finite axis, d_sigma Omega_n + div(B_n Omega_n) = nu_n (Delta + (2/R_n) d_{R_n}) Omega_n + d_Z(|Z_n|^2/R_n^2); against test functions phi supported in {R_n >= delta} the viscous term is O(nu_n) and the source at most G^2 nu_n^2 delta^{-4} ||d_Z phi||_{L^1}, so Omega solves d_sigma Omega + div(B Omega) = 0 weakly off the axis. For a receding axis, d_sigma Theta_n + div(B_n Theta_n) = (B_n)_r Theta_n/R_n + R_n^{-1} d_Z |Z_n|^2 + nu_n (Delta - R_n^{-2}) Theta_n, whose right side tends to 0 since R_n -> infinity on compact sets, so the planar vorticity Theta is weakly transported. Backward decay: the characteristic X' = B(X, sigma), X(-1) = y_0, has |X(sigma)| <= |y_0| + |sigma + 1| and, for a finite axis, distance to the axis at least |y_0'| |sigma|^{-C_I} (as |B^R| <= C_I R/|sigma|). By [CIV, Lemma 2.3] Omega (respectively Theta) is constant along it, so |Omega(y_0, -1)| <= sqrt2 A_0 C_* C_I^2/|sigma| -> 0 (respectively |Theta(y_0, -1)| <= sqrt2 C_I/|sigma| -> 0) as sigma -> -infinity. Thus Theta(., -1) = 0. Since B_n(., -1) is bounded in C^{1,1}, it converges in C^1_loc to B* with div B* = 0, curl B* = 0 and |B*| <= 1; B* is bounded and harmonic, hence constant, contradicting liminf |grad B_n(y*_n, -1)| >= 1/C_2.
Case (P). Excursion lemma: for late t let tau be the largest minimum point of l on [t_0, t], m := l(tau), and tau' := min{s >= t : l(s) = m}; if tau = t then tau' = t, and otherwise l(t) > m and tau' exists by continuity, since l(s) -> 0. Both are running-minimum times, so (T_* - tau)/(T_* - tau') = f(tau')/f(tau) <= F/c_L^2, and M(t) <= M(tau') = m/(T_* - tau') gives f(t) <= f(tau')(T_* - t)/(T_* - tau') <= F^2/c_L^2. Hence ||u(t)||_infty <= (F/c_L)(T_* - t)^{-1/2} on some [t_1, T_*). [CSTY2, Theorem 1.1] applies on (t_1, T_*) (u(t_1) in H^1, contained in H^{1/2}; Gamma(t_1) bounded; pressure in L^{5/3} since u is in L^{10/3}) and bounds u on B_R x [t_1, T_*) for every R. For |x_0| large, u in L^{10/3} and p in L^{5/3} make rho_0^{-2} int_Q (|u|^3 + |p|^{3/2}) smaller than eps_0 on the backward parabolic cylinders Q = B_{rho_0}(x_0) x (s - rho_0^2, s) with t_1 + rho_0^2 <= s < T_* (fix rho_0^2 < (T_* - t_1)/2; on [0, t_1 + rho_0^2] the solution is smooth and bounded), and the epsilon-regularity criterion [ESS, Lemma 2.2], applied to rho_0 u(x_0 + rho_0 ., s + rho_0^2 .), which leaves this quantity invariant, gives |u| < c_{01}/rho_0 on B_{rho_0/2}(x_0) x (s - rho_0^2/4, s). So u stays bounded up to T_*, contradicting Leray's bound.

The spatial Lipschitz bounds and the W^{-2,p} time bound give local uniform compactness of Theta_n by interpolation (as in [CIV, proof of Lemma 3.2, Step 1]); the displayed transported equations and characteristic bounds handle the finite-axis and planar cases; and the L^{10/3} velocity and L^{5/3} pressure tails make the epsilon-regularity quantities at a fixed radius uniformly small outside a large ball. The rescaled vorticity equations follow by the change of variables and are not written out.

Status: proof with key estimates (routine steps indicated, not written out in full); source: own derivation (an adaptation of [CIV, Theorem 1.2]); verification: adversarial audit rounds 3, 5, 21, 22; checked by a computer calculation (numerical sanity check of the excursion lemma only).

Proposition 10 (exact 5D identities and the Hardy threshold). With dmu = r^3 dr dz, b the meridional velocity and phi the 5D stream potential: div_5 b = -2 phi_z, div_5(phi b) = 0, and for p >= 2 (for positive classical times, with the integrability needed for the integrations by parts; at an initial endpoint impose the corresponding integrability or use cutoff inequalities)
  (1/p) d/dt int |q|^p dmu = -(p - 1) int |q|^{p-2} |grad q|^2 dmu + 2(1 - 1/p) int |q|^p phi_z dmu;
  (1/2) d/dt int eta^2 dx = -int |grad eta|^2 dx - 2 pi int eta(0, z, t)^2 dz + int eta d_z(q^2) dx.
If c > 0, -r u^r <= c on a time interval and 2 <= p <= 2/c, then int |q|^p dmu is nonincreasing there. At the critical exponent p = 5/2 this needs c <= 4/5, while every swirl record has -r_n u^r >= 1, so this absorption criterion cannot exclude Case 1. Also ||q(t)||_{L^4(dx)}^4 <= 4 E_0 H(t)^2.

Proof. With b = -r phi_z e_r + (2 phi + r phi_r) e_z, div_5 b = d_r u^r + 3 u^r/r + d_z u^z = div_3 b + 2 u^r/r = 2 u^r/r = -2 phi_z, and div_5(phi b) = phi div_5 b + b.grad phi = -2 phi phi_z - r phi_z phi_r + (2 phi + r phi_r) phi_z = 0. Here dmu = r^3 dr dz is the R^5 measure of axisymmetric functions up to the factor 2 pi^2, and q, eta, phi are smooth functions of (r^2, z), hence smooth on R^5. The swirl and vorticity equations read q_t + b.grad q = Delta_5 q + 2 q phi_z and eta_t + b.grad eta = Delta_5 eta + d_z(q^2). Multiply the first by |q|^{p-2} q and integrate in dmu: the transport term is -(1/p) int |q|^p div_5 b dmu = (2/p) int |q|^p phi_z dmu, and the diffusion term gives -(p - 1) int |q|^{p-2} |grad q|^2 dmu; this is the q^p identity, with coefficient 2 - 2/p. At positive classical times the integrals are finite: |q| <= |grad u| gives int |q|^p dmu = (2 pi)^{-1} int |u^theta|^2 |q|^{p-2} dx <= E_0 D(t)^{p-2}/(2 pi), and int |grad q|^2 r^3 dr dz <= C ||grad u||_2^2 since r q_r = d_r u^theta - q and r q_z = d_z u^theta; smoothness and decay of the classical solution justify the integrations by parts (with cutoffs) and the axis trace. Multiply the eta equation by eta and integrate in dx = 2 pi r dr dz: div_3 b = 0 removes the transport term, Delta_5 = Delta_3 + (2/r) d_r, and 2 eta eta_r/r = div_3(eta^2 r^{-1} e_r), whose integral over {r > eps} is -2 pi int eta(eps, z)^2 dz -> -2 pi int eta(0, z)^2 dz. Hardy threshold: if -r u^r <= c then phi_z = -u^r/r <= c/r^2. The Hardy inequality on R^4, int f^2 |x'|^{-2} dx' <= ((4 - 2)/2)^{-2} int |grad' f|^2 dx' = int |grad' f|^2 dx', applied to f = |q|^{p/2} on each slice z = const, gives int |q|^p r^{-2} dmu <= (p^2/4) int |q|^{p-2} |grad q|^2 dmu, hence 2(1 - 1/p) int |q|^p phi_z dmu <= (p - 1)(c p/2) int |q|^{p-2} |grad q|^2 dmu, which the dissipation absorbs when c p <= 2. The exponent 5/2 is critical (int |q|^{5/2} dmu is invariant under the NS scaling, q having dimension length^{-2}), and p = 5/2 <= 2/c means c <= 4/5, while Theorem 1 gives -r_n u^r(r_n, z_n, t_n) >= 1 at every record. L^4 bound: on the half-line {(r, 0, z): r > 0}, q = -d_{x_2} u_1 and q_r = -d_{x_1} d_{x_2} u_1, so |q_r| <= H(t). For a.e. z, I := int_0^infinity q^4 r dr = -2 int_0^infinity q^3 q_r r^2 dr <= 2 H(t) I^{1/2} (int_0^infinity q^2 r^3 dr)^{1/2}, so I <= 4 H(t)^2 int_0^infinity (u^theta)^2 r dr, and integration in 2 pi dz gives ||q(t)||_{L^4(dx)}^4 <= 4 H(t)^2 ||u^theta(t)||_2^2 <= 4 E_0 H(t)^2 (the boundary terms vanish by smoothness at the axis and decay).

Status: proved here; source: own derivation (the L^4 bound: supplied in adversarial audit round 4 and checked by the author); verification: adversarial audit rounds 4, 21, 22; checked by a computer calculation

Proposition 11 (the Type II regime is an obstruction for the method of Theorem 9). Let g = 1/D. Say that the backward window W(c, A, s) holds if g(t) >= c(g(s) + s - t) on [s - A g(s), s]; in gradient time this is exactly the historical ratio bound D(s + sigma/D(s))/D(s) <= [c(1 + |sigma|)]^{-1} on [-A, 0]. (i) Type I bounds imply W(c, A, s) for all A and late s, with c = 1/(C_I max(1, C_2)). (ii) For every C_2 > 0 there are continuous nonincreasing histories g -> 0 with |g'| <= C_2 (so D = 1/g is monotone, satisfies D' <= C_2 D^2 and the Riccati lower bound, and is Type II) for which W(c, A, s) fails at every late s once c(1 + A) > 2, while the rescaled histories g(s + sigma g(s))/g(s) stay in [1, 2] on [-A, 0]. This is a scalar construction; it does not show that the Navier-Stokes equations, (A) or the swirl records fail to imply windows. (iii) The class of normalized inviscid limit bounds of Proposition 8(c) contains a nonconstant steady Euler flow: V = e^{-|y'|^2} e_3 has sup|grad V| = sqrt(2/e), sup|grad^2 V| = 2 sqrt2 and shape constant sqrt2 e; after the change of variables y -> V(b y) with b = sqrt(e/2) and a translation of a gradient maximum point to the origin it satisfies all of those bounds, provided C_* >= sqrt2 e. It says nothing about C_* < sqrt2 e, has infinite energy and is not a Navier-Stokes blow-up limit. (iv) For every C_* > 1/2 the same class contains a nonconstant smooth steady columnar jet V = f(R) e_3 whose axis is at finite distance from the origin, and for C_* >= 1/2 a C^{1,1} steady planar shear (the class admits C^{1,1} fields, Proposition 8(c)); for C_* < 1/2 it contains no columnar jet f(R) e_3 and no planar shear (g(y_3), 0, 0). (v) For every C_* >= sqrt7/8 (= 0.3307...) the class contains a nonconstant steady planar radial vortex, C^{1,1} at C_* = sqrt7/8 and smooth for C_* > sqrt7/8; it contains no planar field when C_* < sqrt7/8, so sqrt7/8 is the exact threshold for planar members: every bounded C^{1,1} map F from R^2 to R^m satisfies the sharp planar inequality sup|grad F|^2 <= (8/sqrt7) sup|F| ess sup|grad^2 F| (Frobenius norms; equality for the vortex below, for every m >= 2). It contains no swirl-free axisymmetric field when C_* < c_3'' := 1/K_sf = 0.3281269215..., where B_2' := 8/sqrt7 = 3.0237157840..., K_sf := B_2' + t_sf^2 = 3.0476012002..., d_sf := (2^{1/2} - 1)/2, z_sf := (4 - B_2')/2^{3/2}, A_sf := (79/14) B_2' - 320/21 + (200/21) z_sf, and t_sf = 0.1545490736... is the unique positive root of (22/3) t^4 - (28 d_sf/3) t^3 + A_sf t^2 - z_sf^2; so it is empty for C_* < c_3''. This improves the swirl-free constant obtained first, c_3' := 1/(B_2' + t_0'^2) = 0.3203357565..., where t_0' = 0.3130635395... is the unique positive root of 144 t^4 - 112 2^{1/4} t^3 + (32 B_2' - 40) t^2 - 3 (B_2' - 4)^2. These thresholds improve the constants obtained first by weak majorization, c_2 := 1/B_2 = 0.3234... with B_2 := 2 + (4 7^{-1/4} - sqrt2)^2 = 3.0918..., and c_3 := 1/(B_2 + t_0^2) = 0.3158... with t_0 = 0.2723... the positive root of the same quartic with B_2 in place of B_2'; B_2 and c_2 are used, as valid constants, in Propositions 11(viii), 14 and 28 (see the remark after Proposition 28). All these swirl-free thresholds are superseded by the sharp swirl-free inequality, proved below: every bounded divergence-free axisymmetric swirl-free C^{1,1} field U on R^3 satisfies sup|grad U|^2 <= (8/sqrt7) sup|U| ess sup|grad^2 U|, so the class contains no swirl-free axisymmetric field when C_* < sqrt7/8, the threshold for planar members; c_3' and c_3'' remain valid weaker constants. Without any equation, the infimum of the quotient sup|V| ess sup|grad^2 V|/sup|grad V|^2 over the nonconstant bounded swirl-free axisymmetric divergence-free C^{1,1} fields equals sqrt7/8 = 0.330718... (the sharp swirl-free inequality gives the lower bound and the fields U_R below the upper bound). Without any equation, every bounded C^{1,1} map F from R^n to R^m, n >= 2, satisfies the sharp inequality sup|grad F|^2 <= (4n/(3n + 1)^{1/2}) sup|F| ess sup|grad^2 F| (Frobenius norms; for n = 2 this is the planar inequality, and for m >= n equality holds for a radial field g(|x|) x). In particular every bounded C^{1,1} field V on R^3 satisfies sup|grad V|^2 <= (12/sqrt10) sup|V| ess sup|grad^2 V| with 12/sqrt10 = 3.7947331922..., so (A) at a time t with D(t) > 0 forces C_* >= sqrt10/12 = 0.2635231383..., and no inequality between these three suprema valid for all bounded C^{1,1} fields on R^3 gives a larger lower bound for C_*. For divergence-free fields the constant is smaller: every bounded divergence-free C^{1,1} field V on R^3 satisfies sup|grad V|^2 <= B_div'' sup|V| ess sup|grad^2 V|, where theta_dv := arcsin (2/3)^{1/2}, p_dv := (7^{1/2}/112)(11 + 19 theta_dv/2^{1/2}) = 0.5630420133..., q_dv := (7^{1/2}/24)(5 theta_dv/2^{1/2} - 3) = 0.0416214487... and B_div'' := 4 ((7 p_dv + 50 q_dv)^3/(6125 q_dv))^{1/2} = 3.7025345862... < 3703/1000; since the velocity is divergence free, (A) at a time t with D(t) > 0 forces C_* >= 1/B_div'' = 0.2700852555.... These inequalities improve the constant 1/6 of Theorem 13(e), which is used elsewhere as stated, and the constants obtained first, which are retained in the proof as valid weaker constants: by weak majorization of the singular values, B_3 := B_2 + (6 10^{-1/4} - 4 7^{-1/4})^2 = 3.9289... (1/B_3 = 0.2545..., used by Proposition 28 as stated); with the planar inequality for the two largest singular values, B_3' := B_2' + (6 10^{-1/4} - 2^{1/2} - (B_2' - 2)^{1/2})^2 = 3.9225069643...; and, for divergence-free fields, B_div := 2 + (4 7^{-1/4} - 2^{1/2})^2 + (C_div - 4 7^{-1/4})^2 = 3.830187... and B_div' := B_2' + (C_div - 2^{1/2} - (B_2' - 2)^{1/2})^2 = 3.8200737122..., where C_div := (18 kappa_div/5)^{1/2} = 3.318390... and kappa_div := (814/87)^{1/2} = 3.058810... are such that sigma_1 + sigma_2 + sigma_3 <= C_div (sup|V| ess sup|grad^2 V|)^{1/2} for the singular values of the gradient of a bounded divergence-free C^{1,1} field V at any point. Since 12/sqrt10 < B_ax, the sharp inequality supersedes Proposition 28(a), (c) and the first statement of Proposition 28(d), and the hypothesis C_* < 1/B_ax of its second statement never holds under (A). Conversely, there is a bounded divergence-free C^{1,1} field on R^3, axisymmetric with swirl, with sup|V| sup|grad^2 V|/sup|grad V|^2 = 94^{1/2}/(6(2 + 10^{1/2})) = 0.313019...; so no inequality between these three suprema valid for all bounded divergence-free fields, or for all axisymmetric ones with swirl, can exclude C_* > 0.313019.... This field has swirl, so it is not a member of the class above; it has unbounded circulation and infinite energy and is not a Navier-Stokes or Euler solution. The extremal fields g(|x|) x of the sharp inequality are not divergence free, and over the nonconstant bounded divergence-free C^{1,1} fields on R^3 the infimum of the quotient lies in [1/B_div'', 94^{1/2}/(6(2 + 10^{1/2}))] = [0.270085..., 0.313019...]; its value is not known. Hence, by the sharp planar and swirl-free inequalities and the planar radial vortices, the class is empty if and only if C_* < sqrt7/8. The steady Euler examples of (iii)-(v) have infinite energy and are not known to be Navier-Stokes blow-up limits; the compactly supported fields U_R in (v) have finite energy and serve only as kinematic examples. (vi) (Energy at the gradient scale.) At a gradient record s >= max(t_A, t_P) (the thresholds of Proposition 8(c); the upper bound on epsilon(s) below holds at every gradient record) put epsilon(s) := M(s)^5/D(s)^3. Then epsilon(s) <= 24 E_0/pi, the rescaled fields of Proposition 8(c) satisfy ||V(tau)||_{L^2(R^3)}^2 <= E_0/epsilon(s) for -s D(s) <= tau <= 0, and int_{|x - x(s)| < M/(2 C_* D)} |u(s)|^2 dx >= c(C_*) epsilon(s) with c(C_*) = pi (2/15 - 1/28) (2 C_*)^{-5}. Consequently, if an inviscid gradient-scale limit V is taken along records with liminf epsilon(s_n) > 0, then V has finite energy at every time and is axisymmetric about a line at finite distance (it is not planar), and a fixed amount of physical energy concentrates in balls of radius M/(2 C_* D) -> 0 along these records; planar limits and limits with infinite energy, such as the steady Euler examples of (iii)-(v), can only arise as limits along records with epsilon(s_n) -> 0 (apply the preceding statement to a subsequence on which epsilon is bounded below). (vii) (Energy atoms.) As t -> T_*, |u(t)|^2 dx converges weakly-* to a finite measure mu with mu(R^3) = lim_{t -> T_*} ||u(t)||_2^2. If epsilon(s_n) >= delta > 0 along gradient records s_n -> T_*, then mu has an atom of mass at least c(C_*) delta at a point x_* of the axis, u is unbounded in every neighbourhood of (x_*, T_*), and the weak L^2 limit u_* of u(t) satisfies lim_{t -> T_*} ||u(t)||_2^2 - ||u_*||_2^2 >= c(C_*) delta, so energy equality fails at T_*. Conversely, mu has no atom, and therefore epsilon(s_n) -> 0 along every sequence of gradient records s_n -> T_*, if int^{T_*} ||u(t)||_infty^{5/3} dt < infinity or ||u(t)||_infty = o((T_* - t)^{-3/5}); neither condition follows from the hypotheses, and by Theorem 7 epsilon(s_n) >= delta forces M(s_n) >= (delta C_2^{-3})^{1/5} (T_* - s_n)^{-3/5}. (Atom radius.) If mu has an atom of mass at least m > 0, then rho_m(t) := inf{rho > 0 : sup_y int_{B_rho(y)} |u(t)|^2 dx >= m/2} is positive and measurable, tends to 0 as t -> T_*, and satisfies int_{t_m}^{T_*} rho_m(t)^{-2} dt <= C_S E_0/m for some t_m < T_* and an absolute constant C_S; so for every C the set of t > t_m with rho_m(t) <= C (T_* - t)^{1/2} has logarithmic measure int dt/(T_* - t) at most C^2 C_S E_0/m. In the situation above, with m = c(C_*) delta, rho_m(s_n) <= M(s_n)/(2 C_* D(s_n)). If moreover a limit V as in (vi) (with liminf epsilon(s_n) > 0) satisfies ||grad V(-sigma)||_infty <= C (1 + sigma)^{-a} for all sigma >= 0 and some a > 5/13, then V is constant, which is excluded; Proposition 12 requires decay o(sigma_n^{-1/2}) along some sigma_n -> infinity. (viii) (Rotational packing; separation of the two record families.) At every late gradient record s, (1 + a(s)) epsilon(s) <= C(C_*) E_0 and r(x(s)) + M(s)/D(s) = (1 + a(s)) epsilon(s) kappa(s)^2 <= C(C_*) E_0 kappa(s)^2, with C(C_*) = (1 + C_*)/(C_* c(C_*)); so in branch (II) of Theorem 13 the gradient maximizers converge to the axis in physical variables, although this bound allows a(s) to be unbounded when epsilon(s) -> 0 (when C_* < 1/B_2 = 0.3234..., Proposition 28(d) gives a(s) <= (1 - B_2 C_*)^{-1/2} at all late gradient records). In Case 1 let s_n be as in Theorem 13(d), x_n := x(s_n), a_n := a(s_n), epsilon_n := epsilon(s_n) and Lambda_n := ((1 + a_n) epsilon_n r_n^3)^{1/4}. Along every sequence of swirl records in branch (II) of Theorem 13(d), max{(t_n - s_n)/T_n, |x_n - z_n e_3|/Lambda_n} -> infinity, and M(s_n)/D(s_n) = o(Lambda_n). If moreover epsilon_n >= epsilon_0 > 0 and (t_n - s_n)/T_n stays bounded, then |z(x_n) - z_n|/Lambda_n -> infinity, where z(x_n) is the axial coordinate of x_n and Lambda_n >= (epsilon_0 r_n^3)^{1/4} (when C_* < 1/B_2, the hypothesis epsilon_n >= epsilon_0 is needed only for the lower bound on Lambda_n; Proposition 28(d)). This is a necessary condition, not an exclusion: neither the historical ordering of the records nor energy and Theorem 7 bound (t_n - s_n)/T_n from above (on the plateau D = D(t_n) of [s_n, t_n] the swirl equation and |u^r/r| <= D(t_n) give only log(S_n/S(s_n)) <= D(t_n)(t_n - s_n), which is a lower bound on t_n - s_n), and an exclusion of branch (II) along this route would need an upper bound on (t_n - s_n)/T_n and a bound |x_n - z_n e_3| = O(Lambda_n) for infinitely many n.

Proof. Fix a late time t_0 after which (A) and the Riccati bound of Theorem 7 hold, so g = 1/D is continuous and nonincreasing, g -> 0 and 0 <= -g' <= C_2 a.e.; windows are considered for c in (0, 1], A >= 1 and s - A g(s) >= t_0. With g_s(sigma) := g(s + sigma g(s))/g(s), W(c, A, s) says g_s(sigma) >= c(1 + |sigma|) on [-A, 0], and D(s + sigma/D(s))/D(s) = 1/g_s(sigma), which is the stated equivalence. (i) The Riccati bound gives T_* - s >= g(s)/C_2, so for t <= s, g(t) >= (T_* - t)/C_I = ((T_* - s) + (s - t))/C_I >= (g(s)/C_2 + s - t)/C_I >= (g(s) + s - t)/(C_I max(1, C_2)); the two-sided bound 1/(C_2 (T_* - t)) <= D <= C_I/(T_* - t) gives C_I C_2 >= 1, so c <= 1. (ii) Let a_1 = 0, let g = 2^{-k} on the flat [a_k, b_k], b_k - a_k = k 2^{-k}, and let g decrease linearly with slope -C_2 from 2^{-k} to 2^{-k-1} on the drop [b_k, a_{k+1}], a_{k+1} - b_k = 2^{-k-1}/C_2 (k >= 1). Then T_* = sum_k (k 2^{-k} + 2^{-k-1}/C_2) < infinity, |g'| <= C_2, g(t) <= C_2 (T_* - t) (the Riccati lower bound for D), and (T_* - a_k)/g(a_k) >= (b_k - a_k) 2^k = k, so the history is Type II. Let k_A := ceil(A) + 1 and s >= a_{k_A}. Then s lies in [a_{k+1}, a_{k+2}) for some k >= A, and 2^{-k-2} <= g(s) <= 2^{-k-1}. Since s - a_k >= k 2^{-k} >= A g(s), the point t := s - A g(s) lies in [a_k, s], where g <= 2^{-k}. If s lies on the flat [a_{k+1}, b_{k+1}], then g(s) = 2^{-k-1} and g(t) <= 2 g(s). If s lies on the drop [b_{k+1}, a_{k+2}), then s - a_{k+1} >= (k + 1) 2^{-k-1} >= A g(s), so t lies in [a_{k+1}, s], where g <= 2^{-k-1} <= 2 g(s). In both cases g(t) <= 2 g(s) < c(1 + A) g(s) = c(g(s) + s - t) when c(1 + A) > 2, so the window fails at its left endpoint; the same estimate on [s - A g(s), s] and monotonicity give 1 <= g_s <= 2 on [-A, 0]. The sharp swirl-free inequality. (7) (The planar inequality with the value retained.) Let F be a C^{1,1} map from R^2 to R^m with |F| <= 1 and |grad^2 F| <= 1 almost everywhere. Then |grad F(x)| <= B_2'^{1/2} (1 - |F(x)|^2/14) for every x. Proof: as in the proof of the sharp planar inequality we may assume F smooth (the mollified maps satisfy the same bounds, and F and grad F converge locally uniformly), x = 0, and we keep its notation, now with A <= 1 and C <= 1. Put a_0(r) := <F(r e)>, the projection onto the constant mode, and E_0(r) := |a_0''(r)|^2 + |a_0'(r)|^2/r^2; then a_0(0) = F(0) and a_0'(0) = 0. The constant mode and the first mode are orthogonal, so (a) improves to |a_0(r)|^2 + (r^2/2)|M(r)|^2 <= 1. The three frame operators of (c) also commute with the projection onto the constant mode, on which they act as d_r^2, 0 and d_r/r, so (d) improves to E_0 + (1/2)(|2M' + r M''|^2 + 3|M'|^2) <= 1, and (e) to (r^{7/2} y)' <= r^{5/2} (1 - E_0); integration gives y(r) <= k_7^2 - r^{-7/2} int_0^r s^{5/2} E_0(s) ds with k_7 := (2/7)^{1/2}, and the subtracted term lies in [0, k_7^2] since y >= 0. Since a_0(r) - a_0(0) = int_0^r (r - s) a_0''(s) ds, |a_0''|^2 <= E_0 and W(s) >= 1 - s/r on [0, r], the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives |a_0(r) - a_0(0)|^2 <= (int_0^r W E_0 ds)(int_0^r (r - s)^2 W(s)^{-1} ds) <= (r^3/2) int_0^r W E_0 ds. With |M(r)| <= 2^{1/2} r^{-1} (1 - |a_0(r)|^2)^{1/2} <= 2^{1/2} r^{-1} (1 - |a_0(r)|^2/2), (f) becomes |grad F(0)| <= 2^{1/2}/r + k_7 r - |a_0(r)|^2/(2^{1/2} r) - 2 |a_0(r) - a_0(0)|^2/(5 k_7 r^3). At r = 7^{1/4} one has k_7 r^2 = 2^{1/2}, 2^{1/2}/r + k_7 r = B_2'^{1/2} and 2/(5 k_7 r^3) = 2^{1/2}/(5 r), and the minimum of |X|^2 + (2/5)|X - Y|^2 over X is (2/7)|Y|^2 (at X = 2Y/7), so the subtracted terms are at least 2^{1/2} |F(0)|^2/(7 r) = B_2'^{1/2} |F(0)|^2/14. (8) (The field.) Let U be a bounded divergence-free axisymmetric swirl-free C^{1,1} field. Keep the normalization M = H = 1, the radial mollification and the notation of the two preceding paragraphs (a = u_r, b = u_z, c = u/r >= 0 after a change of sign, d = w_r, E = a + c, v = c r = u, S = R_1 + T_1, |grad U|^2 = S + c^2), and suppose S + c^2 > B_2' at a point with r > 0. By (7) for the planar map (y_1, y_3) -> (U_1, U_3)(y_1, 0, y_3), whose gradient at the point has squared norm S and whose value has squared norm u^2 + w^2 >= v^2, S^{1/2} <= B_2'^{1/2} (1 - v^2/14); so S <= B_2', hence c > 0, and v^2 <= 14 (1 - (S/B_2')^{1/2}) = 14 (B_2' - S)/(B_2' + (B_2' S)^{1/2}). From (2), (3) and (4): v >= c G, v <= 1 - R_1/2 <= 2 - S/2, T_1 <= 2, E <= 2^{1/4}, G^2 = (8/3) S - (5/3) T_1 - (28/3) E c + 12 c^2 and T_1 <= 250/117 - (6/13) E^2, hence G^2 >= (8/3) S - 1250/351 + (10/13) E^2 - (28/3) E c + 12 c^2 >= (8/3) S - 1250/351 - (734/45) c^2 (minimum over E). First, c < 1/2: otherwise G^2 >= (8/3) S - 10/3 + 12 c^2 - (28/3) 2^{1/4} c and c G <= 2 - S/2 give f(S) <= 0 for the function f of the first swirl-free argument, which is increasing in S < 4, so S > B_2' - c^2 gives P_{B_2'}(c) = 12 f(B_2' - c^2) < 0; but P_{B_2'} is increasing for c > 0 (as B_2' > 3) and P_{B_2'}(1/2) > 7413/10^6 > 0 (by B_2' > 3023/1000, 2^{1/4} < 119/100, and since P_K(1/2) increases with K < 4). Second, G^2 > 237/100: if c <= 1/5, then G^2 > (8/3) B_2' - 1250/351 - (854/45) c^2 >= (8/3) B_2' - 1250/351 - 854/1125 > 8 - 1250/351 - 854/1125 = 161444/43875; if 1/5 <= c < 1/2, the function E -> (10/13) E^2 - (28/3) c E is decreasing on E <= 2^{1/4} (its derivative there is at most (20/13)(6/5) - 28/15 = -4/195), so G^2 > (8/3) B_2' - 1250/351 + (10/13) 2^{1/2} + (28/3)(c^2 - 2^{1/4} c) >= (8/3) B_2' - 1250/351 + (10/13) 2^{1/2} + 7/3 - (14/3) 2^{1/4} > 3201677/1350000 (by B_2' > 3023/1000, 2^{1/2} > 14142/10^4 and 2^{1/4} < 118921/10^5); both bounds exceed 237/100. Third, c^2 G^2 <= v^2 and B_2' - S < c^2 < 1/4 give G^2 < 14/(B_2' + (B_2' S)^{1/2}) < 14/(B_2' + (B_2' (B_2' - 1/4))^{1/2}) < 237/100, since p_0 := 3023/1000 satisfies p_0 (p_0 - 1/4) - (2895/1000)^2 = 877/500000 > 0 and p_0 + 2895/1000 - 1400/237 = 1283/118500 > 0. This contradicts the second step. Hence |grad U|^2 <= B_2' off the axis, by continuity everywhere, and the mollification limit and the scaling give the sharp swirl-free inequality. (The two lower bounds for G^2 are 3.6796... and 2.37354..., the upper bound is 2.36497...; every rational comparison above is exact, and the polynomial identities were checked symbolically.) Upper end for the swirl-free class. Let v_c(rho) = rho - rho^2/2 for rho <= 1, 1/2 for 1 <= rho <= 2, (1 - 3 tau^2 + 2 tau^3)/2 with tau = (rho - 2)/2 for 2 <= rho <= 4, and 0 for rho >= 4, and let V_c = v_c(rho) e_theta be the planar vortex with this profile in a (xi, zeta)-plane. On [2, 4], v_c' = (3/2)(tau^2 - tau) lies in [-3/8, 0], |v_c''| <= 3/4 and v_c/rho <= 1/4, so there |grad V_c|^2 <= 13/64 and |grad^2 V_c|^2 <= 9/16 + 3 (5/8)^2/4 < 7/4; v_c and v_c' are continuous at rho = 2 and rho = 4, so with the computation for the vortex above V_c is C^{1,1}, sup|V_c| = 1/2, sup|grad V_c|^2 = 2 (at the centre) and ess sup|grad^2 V_c| = sqrt7/2. For R > 4 let U_R be the swirl-free axisymmetric field whose radial and axial components at (r, z) are (R/r) times the two components of V_c at (xi, zeta) = (r - R, z). It is supported in {(r - R)^2 + z^2 <= 16}, it is C^{1,1}, and it is divergence free, since (1/r) d_r(r U_R^r) + d_z U_R^z = (R/r) div V_c = 0. At (R, 0, 0) it vanishes and its Cartesian gradient has the entries of grad V_c(0) and a zero (2, 2) entry, so sup|grad U_R|^2 >= 2; sup|U_R| <= R/(2(R - 4)); and by the identity of Proposition 28(e) (with v = 0), |grad^2 U_R|^2 is the sum of the squared r- and z-derivatives of second order of the two components, which differ from (R/r)^2 |grad^2 V_c|^2 by O(1/R) because d_r(R/r) = O(1/R) and d_r^2(R/r) = O(1/R^2) on the support, and of [3(a - c_0)^2 + 2 b^2 + d^2]/r^2 = O(1/R^2). So the quotient of U_R is at most (1 + O(1/R)) sqrt7/8, and the infimum over the class is at most sqrt7/8. The time-independent fields U_R solve neither the Euler nor the positive-viscosity Navier-Stokes equations. Indeed, on 1 < rho < 2, where rho := ((r - R)^2 + z^2)^{1/2}, their components are U_R^r = -R z/(2 r rho) and U_R^z = R (r - R)/(2 r rho). Thus eta_R := (d_z U_R^r - d_r U_R^z)/r = -R^2/(2 rho r^3), U_R . grad rho = 0, and U_R . grad eta_R = -3 R^3 z/(4 rho^2 r^5), which is nonzero when z != 0 and contradicts steady swirl-free Euler transport. A steady Navier-Stokes solution with viscosity nu > 0 would, by testing its equation against the compactly supported divergence-free field U_R, satisfy nu int |grad U_R|^2 dx = 0, contradicting U_R != 0. Divergence-free fields. Let U be a bounded divergence-free C^{1,1} field on R^3 with M = sup|U|, H = ess sup|grad^2 U|, and let sigma_1 >= sigma_2 >= sigma_3 be the singular values of grad U(x_0); we show sigma_1 + sigma_2 + sigma_3 <= C_div (M H)^{1/2}. Then <K(e_1), grad^2 W(r e_1)> = 2h + 6b, and since K is built from delta and omega, R K(e_1) = K(R e_1) for R in O(3) (R acting on all three indices); differentiating under the average therefore gives 2h + 6b = E <O K(omega), grad^2 U(x_0 + r omega)>, where omega is uniformly distributed on the unit sphere and (O K)_{gamma i j} := O_{gamma beta} K_{beta i j}. On tensors T symmetric in the last two indices put (D T)_j := sum_alpha T_{alpha alpha j}; then D D^* = 2 I, so the orthogonal projection Pi onto the kernel of D satisfies |Pi T|^2 = |T|^2 - |D T|^2/2, and D grad^2 U = grad div U = 0. Hence <O K, grad^2 U> = <Pi(O K), grad^2 U> >= -H |Pi(O K)|, and 2h + 6b >= -H (E |Pi(O K(omega))|^2)^{1/2}. A direct computation gives D(O K(omega)) = (t_O - q) omega + 2 S omega with S = (O + O^T)/2, t_O = tr O and q = omega^T S omega, so |D(O K)|^2 = t_O^2 + 2 t_O q - 3 q^2 + 4 |S omega|^2, and the sphere moments E q = t_O/3, E q^2 = (t_O^2 + 2 tr S^2)/15 and E |S omega|^2 = tr S^2/3 give E |Pi(O K)|^2 = 10 - (11 t_O^2 + 7 tr S^2)/15. (With the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and |K|^2 = 10 in place of the projection, the same argument gives the case k = 3 of the bound for general fields.) With the cases k = 1, 2 of that bound, the decreasing vector (2^{1/2}, 4 7^{-1/4} - 2^{1/2}, C_div - 4 7^{-1/4}) (M H)^{1/2} weakly majorizes (sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3), so |grad U(x_0)|^2 <= B_div M H. Let F be a bounded C^{1,1} map from R^n to R^m, n >= 2, A = sup|F| and C = ess sup|grad^2 F|; we show |grad F(0)|^2 <= (4n/(3n + 1)^{1/2}) A C, which by translation gives the inequality at every point. Let omega range over the unit sphere S^{n-1}, let <.> denote the normalized average over S^{n-1}, and for r > 0 put M(r) := (n/r) <F(r omega) omega^T>, an m x n matrix; since <omega omega^T> = I/n, F_1(r omega) := r M(r) omega is, componentwise, the orthogonal projection of omega -> F(r omega) in L^2(S^{n-1}) onto the spherical harmonics of degree one. (b) The constant and quadratic Taylor terms of F(r omega) are invariant under omega -> -omega, so their products with omega^T average to zero, and M(r) = grad F(0) + O(r^2); the expansion of d_r F(r omega) in the differentiated average gives M'(r) = O(r) as in the planar case. (c) For a smooth scalar function f write f = sum_l f_l on each sphere, with f_l(r omega) a spherical harmonic of degree l in omega. In the orthonormal frame (omega, tau_1, ..., tau_{n-1}) at r omega the Hessian of f consists of the entry f_rr, the mixed vector grad_S(f_r/r - f/r^2) and the tangential block (f_r/r) I + Hess_S f/r^2, where grad_S, Hess_S and Delta_S are taken on the unit sphere, and |grad^2 f|^2 is the sum of the squared norms of the first and third blocks and twice the squared norm of the second. For l != k the sphere averages of the products of the corresponding blocks of f_l and of g_k vanish: <f_l g_k> = 0 and <grad_S f_l . grad_S g_k> = -<g_k Delta_S f_l> = 0 settle the first two blocks; in the third, <f_l Delta_S g_k> = 0 and, by the Bochner identity on the unit sphere (whose Ricci curvature is n - 2 times the metric) in integrated polarized form, <Hess_S f_l : Hess_S g_k> = <Delta_S f_l Delta_S g_k> - (n - 2) <grad_S f_l . grad_S g_k> = 0. (For n >= 3, individual tangential entries need not be orthogonal across degrees; the integrated Frobenius inner products of complete blocks vanish. For n = 2, the sole tangential entry is orthogonal across Fourier degrees.) Since the expansions of f and of its derivatives converge in L^2(S^{n-1}), <|grad^2 f|^2> = sum_l <|grad^2 f_l|^2> >= <|grad^2 f_1|^2>, and summing over the components, <|grad^2 F_1|^2> <= <|grad^2 F|^2> <= C^2 on every sphere. For n = 2 these are the steps of the planar inequality. On tensors T_{alpha ij} symmetric in (i, j) put (DT)_j := sum_alpha T_{alpha alpha j} and (D^* xi)_{alpha ij} := (delta_{alpha i} xi_j + delta_{alpha j} xi_i)/2; D^* is the adjoint of D and D D^* xi = ((n + 1)/2) xi, so the orthogonal projection onto ker D is Pi T = T - (2/(n + 1)) D^* D T, and |Pi T|^2 = |T|^2 - (2/(n + 1)) |DT|^2. B omega> = r m/n, contracting the frame blocks of the Hessian of each component (as in (c)) with those of K_B, the mixed blocks counted twice, and using Hess_S v = -v I and <grad_S v . grad_S f> = -<f Delta_S v> = (n - 1) <v f> for v = (B omega)_alpha, one finds <grad^2 F(r omega) : K_B(omega)> = 2 phi'' + 3 (n - 1)(phi'/r - phi/r^2) = (1/n)(2 r m'' + (3n + 1) m'). The example with swirl. Let S_e = diag(-1/2, -1/2, 1) and let J_e be the rotation generator of the (x_1, x_2)-plane (J_e e_1 = e_2, J_e e_2 = -e_1, J_e e_3 = 0); write r = |x|, u_e = x_3^2/r^2 and q_e = x^T S_e x/r^2 = (3 u_e - 1)/2, and put t_e := (3 10^{1/2}/8)^{1/2} and beta_e := t_e/3^{1/2}. Let f_e(r) = 1 - 2r/3 and h_e(r) = r/6 for r <= 1, f_e(r) = 1/(3 r^2) and h_e(r) = 2/(3 r^2) - 1/(2 r^3) for r >= 1, m_e(r) = 1 - beta_e r for r <= 1/(2 beta_e) (= 0.7952...) and m_e(r) = 1/(4 beta_e r) for r >= 1/(2 beta_e), and, for x != 0, U_e = V_e + Z_e with V_e(x) = f_e(r) S_e x + h_e(r) q_e x and Z_e(x) = t_e m_e(r) J_e x. Set V_e(0) = Z_e(0) = U_e(0) = 0. The profiles and their first derivatives are continuous at r = 1 and at r = 1/(2 beta_e), grad U_e(x) = S_e + t_e J_e + O(r) at the origin, and the second derivatives are bounded in each region, so U_e is C^{1,1}. Since tr S_e = 0 and x . grad q_e = 0, div V_e = (r f_e' + r h_e' + 3 h_e) q_e, which vanishes in both regions, and div Z_e = 0. S_e and J_e commute with the rotations about e_3, so U_e is axisymmetric, with swirl t_e m_e(r) (x_1^2 + x_2^2)^{1/2} > 0 off the axis. The reflection in the meridional plane through a point x maps V_e to itself and Z_e to its negative, so V_e . Z_e = 0, grad V_e : grad Z_e = 0 and grad^2 V_e : grad^2 Z_e = 0 at x. Velocity: |U_e|^2 = r^2 [f_e^2 (1 + 3 u_e)/4 + (2 f_e h_e + h_e^2)(3 u_e - 1)^2/4 + t_e^2 m_e^2 (1 - u_e)] is convex in u_e (f_e, h_e >= 0) and takes the values (r g_e)^2 at u_e = 1 and (r g_e)^2/4 + t_e^2 (r m_e)^2 at u_e = 0, with g_e := f_e + h_e; since 0 <= r g_e <= 1/2 and t_e r m_e <= 3^{1/2}/4, both are at most 1/4, with equality at x = e_3, so sup|U_e| = 1/2. Gradient: |grad Z_e|^2 = t_e^2 [2 m_e^2 + r m_e' (2 m_e + r m_e')(1 - u_e)] <= 2 t_e^2, since r m_e' (2 m_e + r m_e') equals -beta_e r (2 - 3 beta_e r) <= 0 and -m_e^2 in the two regions. In the core grad V_e is affine in r along each ray, so |grad V_e|^2 <= max{|grad V_e(0)|^2, (1 + 8 u_e - 9 u_e^2)/8} = 3/2 there (the second value is at most 25/72); in the tail grad V_e = r^{-2} B_e + r^{-3} C_e with B_e and C_e depending only on x/r, B_e + C_e equal to grad V_e at r = 1 and |B_e|^2 = (4 + 32 u_e - 24 u_e^2)/8 <= 11/6, so with y = 1/r, |grad V_e| <= y^2 (1 - y) 2^{1/2} + y^3 2^{-1/2} <= 2^{-1/2}. Hence sup|grad U_e|^2 = |S_e + t_e J_e|^2 = 3/2 + 2 t_e^2 = 3/2 + 3 10^{1/2}/4, attained at the origin. Hessian: |grad^2 V_e|^2 = (33 u_e^2 - 18 u_e + 17)/8 in the core and [(192 r^2 - 360 r + 225) u_e^2 + (24 r^2 - 48 r - 18) u_e + 104 r^2 - 168 r + 81]/(8 r^8) in the tail; both are convex in u_e, with the values 4 and 17/8 at u_e = 1 and u_e = 0 in the core, and 4(10 r^2 - 18 r + 9)/r^8 <= 4 and (104 r^2 - 168 r + 81)/(8 r^8) <= 17/8 in the tail (both decrease for r >= 1); and |grad^2 Z_e|^2 equals 4 beta_e^2 t_e^2 (2 - u_e) for r < 1/(2 beta_e) and t_e^2/(4 beta_e^2 r^4) beyond, so it is at most (4/3) t_e^4 (2 - u_e). So |grad^2 U_e|^2 <= u_e (4 + 4 t_e^4/3) + (1 - u_e)(17/8 + 8 t_e^4/3) = 47/8 (as t_e^4 = 45/32), with equality for r < 1/(2 beta_e) at u_e = 0 and at u_e = 1, and the quotient is (1/2)(47/8)^{1/2}/(3/2 + 3 10^{1/2}/4) = 94^{1/2}/(6(2 + 10^{1/2})). The circulation t_e m_e(r)(x_1^2 + x_2^2) equals 3^{1/2} R/4 on the equatorial tail, where R = (x_1^2 + x_2^2)^{1/2}, and is unbounded. For r > 1, |Z_e|^2 = 3(1 - u_e)/16, whose integral over the unit sphere is pi/2. Orthogonality therefore gives int_{R^3} |U_e|^2 dx >= (pi/2) int_1^infinity r^2 dr = infinity. The time-independent field solves neither the Euler nor the Navier-Stokes equations. Indeed, at (R, 0, 0), R > 1, its cylindrical components are U_e^theta = 3^{1/2}/4, U_e^R = -1/(2R) + 1/(4R^2) and U_e^Z = 0. The azimuthal pressure derivative would be independent of angle and hence zero by single-valuedness of pressure. The steady equation would require nu = 1/4 - 1/(8R) for every R > 1, which is impossible for a constant viscosity, including nu = 0 for Euler.
