Hence |Gamma| <= Psi + G eps' + psi on [0, infinity) x R x [s_0, sigma]. Let eta -> 0 and then eps' -> 0 (Psi(r, sigma) does not depend on s_0): |Gamma(r, z, sigma)| <= G (1 - exp(-r^2 w_1(sigma))). Finally let s_1 decrease to sigma - h: by monotone convergence (the integrals are improper if sigma - h = 0), 1/w_1(sigma) = 4 int_{s_1}^{sigma} exp(-2 int_tau^sigma k) dtau tends to 4 int_{sigma - h}^{sigma} exp(-2 int_tau^sigma k) dtau = 1/w (substitute tau = sigma - v). This proves (33.1). Since 1 - e^{-x} <= min{1, x}, |u^theta(r, z, sigma)| = |Gamma|/r <= G min{1/r, w r} <= G w^{1/2} (the minimum is largest at r = w^{-1/2}) and |q| = |Gamma|/r^2 <= G w; and I(v) <= I(h) gives w <= e^{2 I(h)}/(4 h).
Step 2 (proof of (b)). For 0 <= v <= h, I(v) <= int_{sigma - v}^{sigma} C_a/(T_* - t) dt = C_a log((delta + v)/delta), so e^{-2 I(v)} >= (delta/(delta + v))^{2 C_a} and int_0^h e^{-2 I} >= J; the closed forms of J are the elementary antiderivatives of delta^{2 C_a} x^{-2 C_a} on [delta, delta + h]. Hence w <= 1/(4 J), and (a) gives the two bounds. If h >= delta: for C_a > 1/2, (1 + h/delta)^p <= 2^p = 2^{1 - 2 C_a}, so J >= delta (1 - 2^{1 - 2 C_a})/(2 C_a - 1); for C_a = 1/2 the bound is the formula for J; for C_a < 1/2, f(x) := (x + h)^p - x^p is nonincreasing in x > 0 (p <= 1), so (delta + h)^p - delta^p >= f(h) = (2^p - 1) h^p and delta/J = p delta^p/f(delta) <= p (delta/h)^p/(2^p - 1). This gives (33.2).
Step 3 (proof of (c)). Let delta := T_* - sigma and apply (b) with t_a := sigma - delta = 2 sigma - T_* > 0, h = delta and C_a := theta(sigma) >= 1: then J = delta (1 - 2^{1 - 2 theta})/(2 theta - 1) >= delta/(2 (2 theta - 1)), since 2^{1 - 2 theta} <= 1/2, so G^2/(4 J) <= G^2 (theta - 1/2)/delta and G/(4 J) <= G (theta - 1/2)/delta. This is (33.3). If limsup (T_* - t) k(t) < infinity, there are C and t_2 in (0, T_*) with (T_* - t) k(t) <= C on [t_2, T_*); for sigma >= sigma_0 := (t_2 + T_*)/2 one has 2 sigma - T_* >= t_2, so theta(sigma) <= max{1, C} and (T_* - sigma) ||u^theta(sigma)||_infty^2 <= C' := G^2 (max{1, C} - 1/2). For t >= sigma_0, S(t)^2 <= max{S(sigma_0)^2, sup_{sigma_0 <= s <= t} C'/(T_* - s)} <= C_I/(T_* - t) with C_I := max{C', (T_* - sigma_0) S(sigma_0)^2}.
Step 4 (proof of (d)). Under Proposition 29(b)(i), G > 0, since G = 0 would give u^theta = 0, hence S = 0, contradicting M <= C_S S on a singular trajectory. Suppose the bracket is bounded above for some m >= 3 (m = 3 being the displayed case): there are B >= 0 and t_0 in (0, T_*) with G^2 C_S^2 (T_* - t) k(t) <= psi(T_* - t) for t in [t_0, T_*), where psi := L_2 + (5/2) L_3 + L_4 + ... + L_m + B. Choose v_0 in (0, 1) so small that on (0, v_0] all L_k (k <= m) are positive and increasing as v decreases, so that psi is decreasing, and psi >= G^2 C_S^2. Put phi_0 := psi/(G^2 C_S^2), which is >= 1 and decreasing on (0, v_0]. Let sigma be so late that delta := T_* - sigma <= v_0/2, and 2 sigma - T_* >= t_0 (so sigma > T_*/2). For t in [2 sigma - T_*, sigma], T_* - t lies in [delta, 2 delta], so (T_* - t) k(t) <= phi_0(T_* - t) <= phi_0(delta), and theta(sigma) <= phi_0(delta). By (33.3), delta ||u^theta(sigma)||_infty^2 < G^2 phi_0(delta) = psi(delta)/C_S^2. Let sigma_1 be the earliest such sigma. Since psi(v)/v is decreasing on (0, v_0], for sigma_1 <= s <= t we get ||u^theta(s)||_infty^2 < psi(T_* - t)/(C_S^2 (T_* - t)), while ||u^theta(s)||_infty <= S(sigma_1) for s <= sigma_1 and psi(T_* - t)/(T_* - t) -> infinity. Hence C_S^2 (T_* - t) S(t)^2 <= psi(T_* - t) for t near T_*, so the bracket of Proposition 31(d) in its form with C_S^2 S(t)^2 in place of g(t)^2 (with the same iterated logarithms L_4 + ... + L_m) is bounded above by B near T_*, which contradicts Proposition 31(d) under Proposition 29(b)(i).
Step 5 (proof of (e)). Write sigma_n := t_n + T_n tau for fixed tau < 0, delta_n := T_* - sigma_n = T_n (tau_n + |tau|), and recall T_n = r_n/S_n, gamma_n = r_n S_n = r_n^2/T_n, T_n -> 0 and t_n -> T_* (Theorem 1). Normalized quantities: U_n^theta(y, tau) = u^theta(r_n y', z_n + r_n y_3, sigma_n)/S_n and Gamma_{U_n}(y, tau) = R U_n^theta = Gamma(r_n R, z_n + r_n y_3, sigma_n)/gamma_n, and these converge pointwise to U^theta and Gamma_U (Theorem 2). (i) At the record time, S_n^2 (T_* - t_n) <= C_I, i.e. tau_n <= C_I/(S_n^2 T_n) = C_I/gamma_n. For fixed tau < 0 and large n, sigma_n >= t_1, so |U_n^theta(y, tau)|^2 <= C_I/(S_n^2 delta_n) = C_I/(gamma_n (tau_n + |tau|)); let n -> infinity. For the translates, let (z_k, s_k) with s_k -> -infinity; U(. + z_k e_3, . + s_k) are bounded ancient mild axisymmetric solutions with viscosity nu_* (the axis is unchanged), with |U| <= K, defined at least on R^3 x (-infinity, 0] once s_k <= 0; by the compactness statement at the beginning of the proof of Theorem 3 (smoothing estimate [KNSS, sec. 4], Arzela-Ascoli and dominated convergence in the mild formula) a subsequence converges in C^infty_loc(R^3 x (-infinity, 0]) to a bounded mild ancient solution V, axisymmetric about the same axis, and V^theta = 0 because |U^theta(y, tau + s_k)|^2 <= C_I/(gamma_* |tau + s_k|) -> 0. By [KNSS, Theorem 5.2 and Remark 6.1], V is constant, and an axisymmetric constant field is a multiple of e_3. (Restricting to tau <= 0 is enough for the statement, since the times s_k + tau with tau <= 0 still tend to -infinity.) If sup{|grad U(y, tau)| : |y'| <= R_0} did not tend to 0, there would be eps > 0, s_k -> -infinity and y_k with |y_k'| <= R_0 and |grad U(y_k, s_k)| >= eps; the translates by (y_k)_3 e_3 and s_k have a subsequence converging in C^1 on compact sets to a constant, while their gradients at the points (y_k', 0, 0), which lie in a compact set, have modulus at least eps; this is a contradiction. (ii) Theorem 1 gives -r_n u^r(r_n, z_n, t_n) >= 1, so k(t_n) >= (u^r/r)^-(r_n, z_n, t_n) >= 1/r_n^2, and k(t_n) <= C_a/(T_* - t_n); hence C_a > 0, T_* - t_n <= C_a r_n^2 and tau_n <= C_a r_n^2/T_n = C_a gamma_n. Fix tau < 0 and y. For large n, sigma_n >= t_a; put h_n := sigma_n - t_a and X_n := h_n/delta_n. Then h_n -> T_* - t_a > 0 and delta_n -> 0 (tau_n is bounded), so X_n -> infinity. By (a) and Step 2, |Gamma(r, z, sigma_n)| <= G (1 - exp(-r^2/(4 J_n))) with J_n = delta_n P(X_n), P(X) := int_0^X (1 + b)^{-2 C_a} db. With r = r_n R and r_n^2 = gamma_n T_n this reads
 |Gamma_{U_n}(y, tau)| <= (G/gamma_n) (1 - exp(-gamma_n R^2/(4 (tau_n + |tau|) P(X_n)))).
If C_a <= 1/2, P(X_n) -> infinity, so Gamma_U(y, tau) = 0 for all y and tau < 0; by continuity of U up to tau = 0, U^theta(e_1, 0) = 0, contradicting U^theta(e_1, 0) = 1. So C_a > 1/2, P(X_n) -> 1/(2 C_a - 1), and the limit gives (33.4). From (33.4) and 1 - e^{-x} <= min{1, x}, |U^theta| = |Gamma_U|/R <= (G/gamma_*) min{1/R, gamma_* (2 C_a - 1) R/(4 (tau_* + |tau|))}, which gives the bound for |U^theta|^2. If tau_* > 0, (33.4) extends to tau = 0 by continuity of Gamma_U, and at (e_1, 0), where Gamma_U = U^theta = 1, it gives 1 <= (G/gamma_*) (1 - exp(-gamma_* (2 C_a - 1)/(4 tau_*))), i.e. gamma_* (2 C_a - 1)/(4 tau_*) >= l_*; this is the bound for tau_* (trivial if tau_* = 0), and the second form follows from l_* >= gamma_*/G. For sigma >= (t_a + T_*)/2 one has h = sigma - t_a >= T_* - sigma = delta, so (33.2) gives (T_* - sigma) ||u^theta(sigma)||_infty^2 <= G^2 c(C_a), which is the hypothesis of (i). The last sentence of (ii) is the case C_a <= 1/2.

Step 6 (proof of (f)). (i) If int_{t_0}^{T_*} k = I_infty < infinity for some t_0 in (0, T_*), put h := (T_* - t_0)/2; (a) gives ||u^theta(sigma)||_infty^2 <= G^2 e^{2 I_infty}/(4 h) for sigma in [t_0 + h, T_*), and S(t_0 + h) <= M(t_0 + h) < infinity, so S is bounded, contradicting the first statement of Theorem 1. (ii) If G = 0 there are no records; let G > 0. If t_n = 0, put epsilon := sign(u^theta(r_n, z_n, 0)); at this positive-radius spatial maximum of |u^theta(., 0)|, d_r(epsilon Gamma) = S_n > 0 at (r_n, z_n, 0), so gamma_n < G, and the range 0 < h <= t_n is empty. Assume t_n > 0. By (33.1) at (r_n, z_n, t_n) with sigma = t_n and 0 < h <= t_n, gamma_n = |Gamma(r_n, z_n, t_n)| <= G (1 - exp(-r_n^2 w)) with w < infinity; hence gamma_n < G, exp(-r_n^2 w) <= 1 - gamma_n/G, i.e. r_n^2 w >= l_n, and w <= e^{2 I(h)}/(4 h) gives (33.5); the second form uses l_n >= gamma_n/G and r_n^2/gamma_n = T_n. (iii) The proof of (a) applies to V on [s_1, sigma] subset (-infinity, 0] with the following changes. Smoothness and boundedness of all derivatives of V on R^3 x (-infinity, 0] follow from the smoothing estimate quoted in the proof of Theorem 3; in particular grad V is Lipschitz in tau with values in the bounded functions, so k_V is continuous, B := ||grad V||_infty < infinity and |Gamma_V| <= min{G_V, B R^2}. With the operator L_nu := d_tau + V^R d_R + V^Z d_Z - nu (d_RR - R^{-1} d_R + d_ZZ), which annihilates Gamma_V, phi' = 4 nu - 2 k_V phi, w_1' = 2 k_V w_1 - 4 nu w_1^2 and Psi = G_V (1 - exp(-R^2 w_1)) give L_nu Psi >= 0; the barrier is psi = eta e^{lambda (s - s_0)} rho with lambda := ||V||_infty + nu + 1, for which L_nu psi >= eta e^{lambda (s - s_0)} (lambda rho - ||V||_infty - nu) > 0, since rho >= 1, |grad rho| <= 1 and rho_RR - rho_R/R + rho_ZZ = rho^{-3} <= 1. The maximum principle argument is unchanged (|Gamma_V| <= G_V, Psi >= 0 and psi -> infinity at spatial infinity, uniformly in s). This gives |Gamma_V(R, Z, sigma)| <= G_V (1 - exp(-R^2/(4 nu int_0^h exp(-2 int_{sigma - v}^{sigma} k_V) dv))) for every h > 0, and h -> infinity gives the bound at sigma = 0. At a time sigma = -a < 0, int_{-a-v}^{-a} k_V <= int_{-a-v}^0 k_V, so int_0^infinity exp(-2 int_{-a-v}^{-a} k_V) dv >= int_a^infinity exp(-2 int_{-v}^0 k_V) dv, which is infinite if Pi_V is. Hence Pi_V = infinity gives Gamma_V = 0 on R^3 x (-infinity, 0], so V^theta = 0, and V is constant by [KNSS, Theorem 5.2 and Remark 6.1], a multiple of e_3 by axisymmetry. Since k_V >= 0, E_V(v) := exp(-2 int_{-v}^0 k_V) is nonincreasing in v; if Pi_V < infinity, then (v/2) E_V(v) <= int_{v/2}^v E_V(u) du -> 0 as v -> infinity, i.e. 2 int_{-v}^0 k_V - log v -> infinity. In each of the following two cases the liminf in (iii) is strictly less than +infinity: if int_{-infinity}^0 k_V = I < infinity, then int_{-v}^0 k_V - (1/2) log v <= I - (1/2) log v -> -infinity; if k_V <= 1/(2 |tau|) for tau <= -tau_0, then int_{-v}^0 k_V <= c_0 + (1/2) log(v/tau_0) for v >= tau_0, with c_0 := int_{-tau_0}^0 k_V, so the difference is bounded above. (iv) U is a bounded mild ancient axisymmetric solution with viscosity nu_* = 1/gamma_* and |Gamma_U| <= G/gamma_* (Theorem 2), and Gamma_U(e_1, 0) = U^theta(e_1, 0) = 1. By (iii), 1 <= (G/gamma_*) (1 - exp(-gamma_*/(4 Pi_U))). This forces gamma_* < G and gamma_*/(4 Pi_U) >= l_*, i.e. the first inequality in (33.6); the second follows from l_* >= gamma_*/G, and the last statement from Pi_U >= int_0^v exp(-2 int_{-u}^0 k_U) du >= v exp(-2 int_{-v}^0 k_U), since the inner integral is nondecreasing in u; as Pi_U < infinity, (iii) gives int_{-v}^0 k_U - (1/2) log v -> infinity. Finally B_U := ||grad U||_infty is finite (smoothing estimate) and positive (U is not constant), k_U <= B_U by the formula of the preamble, so Pi_U >= int_0^infinity e^{-2 B_U v} dv = 1/(2 B_U), and the first inequality in (33.6) gives l_* <= gamma_*/(4 Pi_U) <= gamma_* B_U/2, which is the gap bound. Under the hypothesis of (e)(i) (in particular under that of (e)(ii)), given eps > 0 put R_0 := K/eps. For R <= R_0, |U^R/R| <= sup{|grad U(y', y_3, tau)| : |y'| <= R_0, y_3 in R} by the formula of the preamble applied to U, and this is < eps for tau <= tau_eps by (e)(i); for R > R_0, |U^R/R| <= K/R_0 = eps. So k_U(tau) <= eps for tau <= tau_eps. Under the hypothesis of (e)(ii), U_n^R/R (y, tau) = T_n (u^r/r)(r_n y', z_n + r_n y_3, t_n + T_n tau) (by the scalings of Theorem 2), so (U_n^R/R)^-(y, tau) <= T_n k(t_n + T_n tau) <= C_a/(tau_n + |tau|) for large n, and the pointwise limit gives (U^R/R)^-(y, tau) <= C_a/(tau_* + |tau|).

Remark. (1) The maximum principle for u^theta alone gives only ||u^theta(t)||_infty <= ||u^theta(t_a)||_infty exp(int_{t_a}^t k) <= S(t_a) ((T_* - t_a)/(T_* - t))^{C_a} under the hypothesis of (b); (b) improves the exponent to 1/2 when C_a > 1/2; for C_a <= 1/2 it replaces the dependence on ||u^theta(t_a)||_infty by a bound in terms of G and the time window, and at C_a = 1/2 it also gives a logarithmic gain. (2) Relation to Theorem 9 and Proposition 29. Since k <= D, the conclusion of (d) concerns one component of the gradient; Theorem 9 gives limsup (T_* - t) D(t) = infinity under (A). Under Proposition 29(b)(i), the Type II statement limsup (T_* - t) k(t) = infinity also follows qualitatively from (c): a Type I swirl bound would give, with M <= C_S S, a Type I velocity bound, excluded by [CSTY2, Theorem 1.1] with the far-field argument of Theorem 9 (remark after Proposition 29); (d) is quantitative and uses Proposition 31(d) instead of [CSTY2]. Without Proposition 29(b)(i), and in particular under (A), (K) and (TAIL) alone, nothing in this report excludes Type I swirl on a Case-1 trajectory; the dichotomy (c) and the conditional conclusions of (e) and (f) do not exclude Case 1. (3) Relation to Proposition 23(d). A one-sided bound u^r >= -C_a r/(T_* - t) is the pointwise form of the hypothesis of (b); for C_a, c > 0 it is stronger than Q. S. Zhang's u^r >= -c (T_* - t)^{-1/2} [QZ] where r <= (c/C_a) (T_* - t)^{1/2}, and weaker beyond that radius, so neither global hypothesis implies the other (for C_a = 0 it is u^r >= 0); the record consequence T_* - t_n <= C_a r_n^2 of (e)(ii) is the analogue of Proposition 23(d). (4) Sharpness of (33.1). For the Burgers drift u^r = -beta r/2, u^z = beta z (beta > 0), k = beta/2, Gamma = G (1 - exp(-beta r^2/4)) is a steady solution of the circulation equation, and w = beta/(4 (1 - e^{-beta h})) -> beta/4 as h -> infinity. With the same drift, Gamma_B(r, t) := G (1 - exp(-w_B(t) r^2)) with 1/w_B(t) := e^{-beta t}/B + (4/beta) (1 - e^{-beta t}) solves the circulation equation with initial value G (1 - exp(-B r^2)), and w_B(h) -> w as B -> infinity. So (33.1) is sharp, for every window length h, within the scalar comparison class of circulation equations with linear meridional drift and given k; this drift is unbounded and has infinite energy, so the example does not show optimality in the class of sec. 1.1. The factor 1 in ||u^theta||_infty^2 <= G^2 w can be lowered to mu_0 = max_{x > 0} (1 - e^{-x})^2/x < 0.41, since |Gamma| <= G (1 - e^{-r^2 w}); this improvement is not needed for the present proposition and is used in Proposition 35 to prove (35.3). (5) Case 1. Parts (e) and (f) do not exclude Case 1. Under Type I swirl (in particular under Type I strain) the Case-1 limit satisfies ||U^theta(tau)||_infty = O(|tau|^{-1/2}) as tau -> -infinity; the physical singular time lies at bounded normalized distance tau_n -> tau_* after the records, but no singularity of U at tau_*, nor its continuation up to tau_*, is asserted. Every limit of axial and backward time translates of U is a constant axial field, and grad U tends to 0 uniformly on each cylinder {|y'| <= R_0} as tau -> -infinity; convergence to one common constant is not proved. No global decay of the meridional velocity has been established, and the additional hypotheses of the known Liouville theorems for bounded ancient axisymmetric solutions (a bound |U| <= C/R [KNSS, Theorem 5.3], a uniformly BMO stream potential [LZ, Theorem 1.2], circulation in L^infty_tau L^p_y for some finite p or uniformly decaying at large R [LZZ, Theorem 1.3 and Remark 1.4], axial periodicity with bounded circulation [LRZ1, Theorem 1], uniform large-R saturation of the circulation [LRZ2, Theorem 1.2]) have not been derived; no Liouville theorem that applies to this class is known to us. The quantity tau_n is the normalized remaining time called sigma_n in sec. 3.12; (e) bounds it above under Type I swirl, and sec. 3.12 discusses lower bounds from mild restart estimates and, under its stated spatial hypotheses, from localized smoothing; no uniform positive lower bound is obtained in general. By (f)(iv) the backward cumulative strain int_{-v}^0 k_U of a Case-1 limit exceeds (1/2) log v by an amount tending to infinity; under Type I swirl k_U(tau) -> 0, which allows this, and under Type I strain int_{-v}^{-1} k_U <= C_a log v for v >= 1, which allows it because C_a > 1/2 there. So (f) does not exclude Case 1 either. The other alternative of (c), which is not asserted to be disjoint from Type I swirl, is Type II near-axis strain, limsup (T_* - t) k(t) = infinity; without Proposition 29(b)(i) no quantitative Type II limsup rate of the kind in (d) is proved here, and (f) gives only cumulative lower bounds; under Proposition 29(b)(i), (d) gives such a rate. (6) Literature. The qualitative continuation criterion (f)(i) is not new: by the swirl maximum principle ||u^theta(t)||_infty <= ||u^theta(t_0)||_infty exp(int_{t_0}^t k), so a finite integral of k gives bounded swirl, which excludes a singularity by [CFZ, Theorem 1.1(1)] (with d = 0 and p = q = infinity, after a restart at a positive time) or by [LZ2, Corollary 1.3] (bounded swirl gives |Gamma| <= C r); the signed-compression criterion [Sh, Corollary 3.9] contains it as a special case. The new element of (f) is the quantitative form (33.5) at the records and the transfer to ancient solutions in (iii) and (iv); the exact criterion (iii) was not found in the references checked, and no priority claim is made.
Status: proved here. (a) uses the barrier of Proposition 30, Step 1; it was also derived independently and refereed separately, with the comparison justified by a Phragmen-Lindelof maximum principle; (b) and the qualitative dichotomy of (c) were also derived independently; (33.3), (d), (e) and (f) are own derivations, the qualitative criterion (f)(i) being a consequence of known results (Remark (6)); the exact prior occurrence of (33.1) has not been identified, and the literature search is not complete. (d) depends on Proposition 31(d) as stated there, and (e), (f)(iv) on Theorems 1 and 2. Verification: two hostile reviews (reviews 10 and 11 in sec. 5). The first rederived (a) to (e), found no wrong constant and required the repairs listed there; the second rederived (f), including the transfer of the comparison to ancient solutions with viscosity nu, the monotonicity argument for the divergent excess and the application to Case-1 limits, found it correct and required two corrections of wording in Remark (5), one in the proof of (iii), and the literature qualification of Remark (6); it also proposed the slightly stronger lower bound in (33.6) and the gap bound in (iv). All were applied. The author checked the Riccati equations and closed forms by hand and the constant 0.41 numerically.

Proposition 34 (strain from vorticity, superlevel absorption, and the structure of the Type I swirl branch). Notation of sec. 1.1: eta = omega^theta/r, q = u^theta/r, Delta_5 = d_rr + 3 r^{-1} d_r + d_zz, L = d_RR - R^{-1} d_R + d_ZZ, and the circulation operator L_nu := d_tau + V^R d_R + V^Z d_Z - nu L (viscosity nu; nu = 1 for the physical solution). Functions of (r, z) are identified with functions on R^5 = R^4 x R through y = (y', y_5), r = |y'|, z = y_5.

(a) (Strain from vorticity.) Let b = u^r e_r + u^z e_z be a divergence-free axisymmetric meridional field on R^3 whose derivatives up to order three are bounded (b in C^3_b), put K_r := ||u^r||_infty and eta := omega^theta/r with omega^theta = d_z u^r - d_r u^z. Then
 ||u^r/r||_infty <= (2 K_r ||eta||_infty)^{1/2}.   (34.1)
(b) (Superlevel absorption.) Let V be a smooth axisymmetric solution of NS with viscosity nu > 0 on R^3 x [sigma - h, sigma] (h > 0) whose derivatives of order <= 3 are bounded there (for the physical solution: 0 < sigma - h < sigma < T_*), let G_V >= sup |Gamma_V| over the window and 0 <= lambda < G_V. Put
 kappa_lambda(tau) := sup{ (V^R/R)^-(R, Z, tau) : R > 0, Z in R, |Gamma_V(R, Z, tau)| > lambda }   (sup of the empty set := 0),
 J_lambda := int_0^h exp(-2 int_{sigma - v}^{sigma} kappa_lambda(tau) d tau) dv.
Then kappa_lambda is lower semicontinuous with 0 <= kappa_lambda <= ||(V^R/R)^-||_infty, and
 |Gamma_V(R, Z, sigma)| <= lambda + (G_V - lambda) (1 - exp(-R^2/(4 nu J_lambda)))  for all R >= 0, Z in R.   (34.2)
For lambda = 0 and kappa_0 replaced by its majorant ||(V^R/R)^-(tau)||_infty this is (33.1).
(c) (Ancient criteria.) Let V be a bounded mild ancient axisymmetric solution of NS on R^3 x (-infinity, 0] with viscosity nu > 0, G_V := ||Gamma_V||_infty < infinity, K_V(tau) := ||V^R(tau)||_infty, kappa_lambda as in (b) for tau <= 0, and Pi_lambda := int_0^infinity exp(-2 int_{-v}^0 kappa_lambda) dv in (0, infinity]. If G_V = 0, V is a constant multiple of e_3.
 (i) For 0 <= lambda < G_V, |Gamma_V(R, Z, 0)| <= lambda + (G_V - lambda)(1 - exp(-R^2/(4 nu Pi_lambda))). If Pi_lambda = infinity, then |Gamma_V| <= lambda on R^3 x (-infinity, 0]. If Pi_lambda < infinity, then int_{-v}^0 kappa_lambda - (1/2) log v -> infinity as v -> infinity. Hence sup |Gamma_V| <= lambda whenever liminf_{v -> infinity} (int_{-v}^0 kappa_lambda - (1/2) log v) < infinity; for lambda = 0, V is then a constant multiple of e_3.
 (ii) If there is s_0 > 0 with s^2 K_V(-s) ||eta_V(-s)||_infty <= 1/8 for all s >= s_0, then V is a constant multiple of e_3. More generally V is a constant multiple of e_3 if liminf_{v -> infinity} (int_{-v}^0 (2 K_V ||eta_V||_infty)^{1/2} d tau - (1/2) log v) < infinity.
(d) (Case-1 limits.) Assume (K) and (TAIL) and let U be a limit of Theorem 2 (viscosity nu_* = 1/gamma_*, |Gamma_U| <= G/gamma_*, Gamma_U(e_1, 0) = 1, gamma_* < G by Proposition 33(f)(iv)); kappa_lambda refers to U, and K_U := ||U^R||_{L^infty(R^3 x (-infinity, 0])}, so 1/gamma_* <= K_U <= K.
 (i) For every lambda in [0, 1) and every tau <= 0, sup_y |Gamma_U(y, tau)| >= 1, and, with l_lambda := log((G - lambda gamma_*)/(G - gamma_*)) >= (1 - lambda) gamma_*/(G - lambda gamma_*) >= (1 - lambda) gamma_*/G,
  Pi_lambda <= gamma_*/(4 l_lambda),  int_{-v}^0 kappa_lambda d tau >= (1/2) log(4 v l_lambda/gamma_*) >= (1/2) log(4 (1 - lambda) v/G)  (v > 0),   (34.3)
 and int_{-v}^0 kappa_lambda d tau - (1/2) log v -> infinity as v -> infinity; in particular int_{-infinity}^{-1} (kappa_lambda(tau) - 1/(2 |tau|))^+ d tau = infinity.
 (ii) There is no s_0 with s^2 ||eta_U(-s)||_infty <= 1/(8 K_U) for all s >= s_0, and int_{-v}^0 (2 K_U ||eta_U||_infty)^{1/2} d tau - (1/2) log v -> infinity; in particular int_1^infinity ((2 K_U ||eta_U(-s)||_infty)^{1/2} - 1/(2 s))^+ ds = infinity.
 (iii) (Type I swirl branch.) Assume the hypothesis of Proposition 33(e)(i), so that |U^theta(y, tau)|^2 <= C_I/(gamma_* (tau_* + |tau|)) for tau < 0. Then, for lambda in (0, 1) and tau < 0, the superlevel set {|Gamma_U(., tau)| > lambda} is contained in {R > rho_lambda(tau)}, rho_lambda(tau) := lambda (gamma_* (tau_* + |tau|)/C_I)^{1/2}, so
  kappa_lambda(tau) <= sup{ (U^R)^-(y, tau)/R : R > rho_lambda(tau) },   (34.4)
 and the conclusions of (i) hold with this majorant. Consequently there are no lambda in (0, 1), A >= 0 and tau_0 > 0 with A C_I <= lambda^2 gamma_*/2 and R (U^R)^-(y, tau) <= A whenever R > rho_lambda(tau) and tau <= -tau_0. Moreover ||eta_U(tau)||_infty -> 0 as tau -> -infinity, and for every tau <= 0
  ||eta_U(tau)||_infty <= int_{-infinity}^{tau} ||d_Z(q_U^2)(sigma)||_infty d sigma  (q_U := U^theta/R; the right side may be infinite),   (34.5)
 so a bound ||d_Z(q_U^2)(-s)||_infty <= A_p s^{-p} for s >= s_0 (p > 1) gives ||eta_U(-s)||_infty <= A_p s^{1-p}/(p - 1) for s >= s_0, and (ii) excludes p = 3 with A_p <= 1/(4 K_U) and every p > 3. Finally there are C and s_1, depending on U, such that
  ||eta_U(-s)||_infty <= C/log s  for s >= s_1.   (34.6)

Proof. (a) Write b_1 = x_1 a with a := u^r/r. The vorticity of the meridional field b is omega^theta e_theta, so omega = (-x_2 eta, x_1 eta, 0). On the half-plane {x_2 = 0, x_1 > 0}, u^r = b_1 and omega^theta = omega_2, and b_1, omega_2 are odd in x_1 there; hence a(r, z) = int_0^1 d_1 b_1(theta r e_1 + z e_3) d theta and eta(r, z) = int_0^1 d_1 omega_2(theta r e_1 + z e_3) d theta. These formulas show that a and eta are even in r, with a_r(0, z) = eta_r(0, z) = 0, and, lifted to R^5 through y -> (|y'|, y_5), a is in C^2_b(R^5) and eta in C^1_b(R^5) (b in C^3_b, omega in C^2_b; the Cartesian second derivatives of a(|y'|, y_5) are a_rr y_i y_j/r^2 + (a_r/r)(delta_ij - y_i y_j/r^2) and their mixed analogues, bounded and continuous across the axis since a_r/r -> a_rr(0, z)). Since div b = 0, Delta_3 b = -curl omega, so Delta_3 b_1 = d_3 omega_2 - d_2 omega_3 = x_1 d_z eta; and Delta_3 (x_1 a) = x_1 (a_rr + a_r/r + a_zz) + 2 (x_1/r) a_r = x_1 Delta_5 a. Hence Delta_5 a = d_z eta for x_1 != 0, and everywhere by continuity (equivalently, with the 5D stream potential phi of sec. 1.1, a = -phi_z and -Delta_5 phi = eta; the identity was also checked by a symbolic computation). Let H_l denote the heat semigroup of R^5, H_l f = g_l * f with g_l(y) = (4 pi l)^{-5/2} exp(-|y|^2/(4 l)). For f in C^2_b(R^5), d_l H_l f = H_l Delta_5 f and H_l f -> f uniformly as l -> 0, so for h > 0
 H_h a - a = int_0^h H_l Delta_5 a dl = int_0^h H_l d_z eta dl = int_0^h (d_z g_l) * eta dl.
Since |a(y)| <= K_r/|y'| and the convolution of the symmetric decreasing functions g_h and |y'|^{-1} (in the variables y', after integrating out y_5) is maximal at y' = 0,
 |H_h a(y)| <= K_r E|(2 h)^{1/2} N|^{-1} = K_r (2 h)^{-1/2} Gamma(3/2)/(2^{1/2} Gamma(2)) = K_r pi^{1/2}/(4 h^{1/2}),
where N is a standard Gaussian vector in R^4 (E|N|^{-1} = Gamma(3/2)/(2^{1/2} Gamma(2))). The kernel d_z g_l has L^1(R^5) norm equal to the L^1(R) norm of the derivative of the one-dimensional heat kernel, 2 (4 pi l)^{-1/2} = (pi l)^{-1/2}. Hence
 ||a||_infty <= K_r pi^{1/2}/(4 h^{1/2}) + ||eta||_infty int_0^h (pi l)^{-1/2} dl = K_r pi^{1/2}/(4 h^{1/2}) + 2 (h/pi)^{1/2} ||eta||_infty.
If eta = 0, let h -> infinity: a = 0. If K_r = 0, a = 0. Otherwise take h = pi K_r/(8 ||eta||_infty): both terms equal (K_r ||eta||_infty/2)^{1/2}, and the sum is (2 K_r ||eta||_infty)^{1/2}. This is (34.1).

(b) Lower semicontinuity: if kappa_lambda(tau_0) > c >= 0, there is (R, Z) with R > 0, |Gamma_V(R, Z, tau_0)| > lambda and (V^R/R)^-(R, Z, tau_0) > c; both strict inequalities persist at (R, Z, tau) for tau near tau_0 by continuity, so kappa_lambda > c near tau_0; for c < 0 there is nothing to prove. The upper bound is clear. In particular kappa_lambda is Borel and bounded. We follow Proposition 33, Step 1 and Step 6(iii). Fix s_1 in (sigma - h, sigma) and put, for s in [s_1, sigma], phi(s) := 4 nu int_{s_1}^s exp(-2 int_t^s kappa_lambda) dt. Then phi is Lipschitz, phi(s_1) = 0, phi > 0 on (s_1, sigma] and phi(s) - phi(s') = int_{s'}^{s} (4 nu - 2 kappa_lambda phi) for s' < s; w_1 := 1/phi is locally Lipschitz on (s_1, sigma] with
 w_1(s) - w_1(s') = int_{s'}^{s} (2 kappa_lambda w_1 - 4 nu w_1^2) dt  (s_1 < s' < s <= sigma),   (*)
and w_1(s) -> infinity as s decreases to s_1. Put Psi(R, s) := lambda + (G_V - lambda)(1 - E), E := exp(-R^2 w_1(s)). As in Proposition 33, Step 1, V^R d_R Psi = 2 (G_V - lambda) R^2 (V^R/R) w_1 E and -nu L Psi = 4 nu (G_V - lambda) R^2 w_1^2 E. Let B := sup ||grad V||_infty over the window, so |Gamma_V| <= min{G_V, B R^2}. Fix eps' in (0, 1), Lambda := log(1/eps'), and s_0 in (s_1, sigma) with w_1(s_0) >= B/((G_V - lambda) eps'). Then |Gamma_V(R, Z, s_0)| <= Psi(R, s_0) + G_V eps': if x := R^2 w_1(s_0) >= Lambda, Psi + G_V eps' >= G_V - (G_V - lambda) eps' + G_V eps' >= G_V; otherwise 1 - e^{-x} = int_0^x e^{-t} dt >= eps' x, so Psi(R, s_0) >= (G_V - lambda) eps' R^2 w_1(s_0) >= B R^2. Fix eta_0 > 0 and epsilon_0 in {-1, 1}, let psi := eta_0 e^{mu (s - s_0)} rho be the barrier of Proposition 33, Step 6(iii) (rho = (1 + R^2 + Z^2)^{1/2}, mu := ||V||_infty + nu + 1, so L_nu psi > 0), and put Phi := epsilon_0 Gamma_V - Psi - G_V eps' - psi on [0, infinity) x R x [s_0, sigma]. Phi is continuous, negative on {R = 0} (Gamma_V = 0 there, Psi >= lambda >= 0) and on {s = s_0}, and tends to -infinity at spatial infinity uniformly in s. Suppose sup Phi > 0; it is attained at some (R_*, Z_*, s_*) with R_* > 0 and s_0 < s_* <= sigma. There epsilon_0 Gamma_V = Phi + Psi + G_V eps' + psi > Psi >= lambda, so |Gamma_V| > lambda at (R_*, Z_*, s_*) and, by continuity, at the same spatial point (R_*, Z_*) for s in some interval (s_* - d, s_*]; for these s, kappa_lambda(s) >= -(V^R/R)(R_*, Z_*, s). For s in (s_* - d, s_*), Phi(R_*, Z_*, s) <= Phi(R_*, Z_*, s_*), so
 epsilon_0 [Gamma_V(s_*) - Gamma_V(s)]/(s_* - s) >= [Psi(s_*) - Psi(s)]/(s_* - s) + [psi(s_*) - psi(s)]/(s_* - s)   (all at (R_*, Z_*)).
By the mean value theorem in the variable w_1 and (*), [Psi(s_*) - Psi(s)]/(s_* - s) = (G_V - lambda) R_*^2 e^{-R_*^2 xi_s} (s_* - s)^{-1} int_s^{s_*} (2 kappa_lambda w_1 - 4 nu w_1^2) dt with xi_s between w_1(s) and w_1(s_*); as s increases to s_*, xi_s -> w_1(s_*), w_1 is continuous, and kappa_lambda(t) >= -(V^R/R)(R_*, Z_*, t) with the right side continuous in t, so the liminf of the quotient is >= (G_V - lambda) R_*^2 E_* (-2 (V^R/R) w_1 - 4 nu w_1^2) evaluated at (R_*, Z_*, s_*), E_* := exp(-R_*^2 w_1(s_*)). Hence epsilon_0 d_s Gamma_V >= (G_V - lambda) R_*^2 E_* (-2 (V^R/R) w_1 - 4 nu w_1^2) + d_s psi at the point. At the maximum, grad_{R,Z} Phi = 0 and d_RR Phi, d_ZZ Phi <= 0, so -nu L(epsilon_0 Gamma_V) >= -nu L Psi - nu L psi and V.grad(epsilon_0 Gamma_V) = V.grad Psi + V.grad psi. Adding, and using L_nu Gamma_V = 0,
 0 = epsilon_0 L_nu Gamma_V >= (G_V - lambda) R_*^2 E_* [-2 (V^R/R) w_1 - 4 nu w_1^2 + 2 (V^R/R) w_1 + 4 nu w_1^2] + L_nu psi = L_nu psi > 0,
a contradiction. No bound on V^R/R at points where |Gamma_V| <= lambda is used. So |Gamma_V| <= Psi + G_V eps' + psi on [s_0, sigma]; let eta_0 -> 0 and eps' -> 0 (Psi(R, sigma) does not depend on s_0), and then s_1 -> sigma - h: 1/w_1(sigma) = 4 nu int_{s_1}^{sigma} exp(-2 int_t^sigma kappa_lambda) dt -> 4 nu J_lambda (substitute t = sigma - v). This is (34.2). If kappa_0 is replaced by its majorant k_V(tau) := ||(V^R/R)^-(tau)||_infty, J_0 decreases and the bound becomes (33.1) at viscosity nu.

(c) If G_V = 0 then V^theta = 0 and V is constant by [KNSS, Theorem 5.2 and Remark 6.1], a multiple of e_3 by axisymmetry; let G_V > 0. (i) As in Proposition 33, Step 6(iii), V and all its derivatives are bounded on R^3 x (-infinity, 0] (smoothing estimate), so (b) applies on [-h, 0] for every h, and h -> infinity gives the bound at tau = 0 by monotone convergence. At a time -a < 0, (b) on [-a - h, -a] and h -> infinity give the same bound with Pi_lambda replaced by int_0^infinity exp(-2 int_{-a-v}^{-a} kappa_lambda) dv = e^{2 int_{-a}^0 kappa_lambda} int_a^infinity exp(-2 int_{-u}^0 kappa_lambda) du, which is infinite if Pi_lambda is. So Pi_lambda = infinity gives |Gamma_V| <= lambda on R^3 x (-infinity, 0]. If Pi_lambda < infinity, E(v) := exp(-2 int_{-v}^0 kappa_lambda) is nonincreasing and (v/2) E(v) <= int_{v/2}^v E -> 0, i.e. 2 int_{-v}^0 kappa_lambda - log v -> infinity. For lambda = 0, |Gamma_V| <= 0 gives V^theta = 0, and V is a constant multiple of e_3 as above.
(ii) V(tau) satisfies the hypotheses of (a) for each tau (smoothing estimate), so k_V(tau) <= ||V^R/R(tau)||_infty <= (2 K_V(tau) ||eta_V(tau)||_infty)^{1/2}. Since kappa_0 <= k_V, the liminf hypothesis of (ii) implies that of (i) with lambda = 0. Under the first hypothesis, k_V(-s) <= (2/(8 s^2))^{1/2} = 1/(2 s) for s >= s_0, so int_{-v}^0 k_V <= c_0 + (1/2) log(v/s_0) for v >= s_0 with c_0 := int_{-s_0}^0 k_V, and the liminf is finite.

(d) By Theorem 2, K_U >= -U^R(e_1, 0) >= 1/gamma_* > 0. (i) If sup_y |Gamma_U(y, tau_0)| <= lambda for some tau_0 <= 0 and lambda < 1, the maximum principle for the circulation equation (the argument of (b) with the constant barrier lambda + eps' + psi) gives |Gamma_U| <= lambda on [tau_0, 0], contradicting Gamma_U(e_1, 0) = 1; hence sup_y |Gamma_U(y, tau)| >= 1 for every tau <= 0, and G_U := ||Gamma_U||_infty satisfies 1 <= G_U <= G/gamma_*. By (c)(i) with nu = 1/gamma_*, at (e_1, 0), 1 <= lambda + (G_U - lambda)(1 - exp(-gamma_*/(4 Pi_lambda))); the right side is nondecreasing in G_U, so
 1 <= lambda + (G/gamma_* - lambda)(1 - exp(-gamma_*/(4 Pi_lambda))).
Since G/gamma_* > 1 (gamma_* < G), Pi_lambda < infinity and exp(-gamma_*/(4 Pi_lambda)) <= (G/gamma_* - 1)/(G/gamma_* - lambda) = (G - gamma_*)/(G - lambda gamma_*), i.e. gamma_*/(4 Pi_lambda) >= l_lambda. Since log(1 + x) >= x/(1 + x) with x = (1 - lambda) gamma_*/(G - gamma_*), l_lambda >= (1 - lambda) gamma_*/(G - lambda gamma_*) >= (1 - lambda) gamma_*/G. As in Proposition 33, Step 6(iv), Pi_lambda >= v exp(-2 int_{-v}^0 kappa_lambda) for every v > 0 (kappa_lambda >= 0), which with Pi_lambda <= gamma_*/(4 l_lambda) gives (34.3). The divergence of the excess is (c)(i). Finally, int_{-v}^{-1} kappa_lambda <= int_{-v}^{-1} (kappa_lambda - 1/(2|tau|))^+ d tau + (1/2) log v, and int_{-1}^0 kappa_lambda <= ||grad U||_infty, so the excess can diverge only if the integral of the positive part diverges.
(ii) U(tau) satisfies the hypotheses of (a) (smoothing estimate), so k_U <= (2 K_U ||eta_U||_infty)^{1/2}, and kappa_0 <= k_U. By (i) with lambda = 0, int_{-v}^0 kappa_0 - (1/2) log v -> infinity, hence also the larger quantity in (ii), and therefore int_1^v ((2 K_U ||eta_U(-s)||_infty)^{1/2} - 1/(2 s)) ds -> infinity, which gives the positive-part statement. If s^2 ||eta_U(-s)||_infty <= 1/(8 K_U) for s >= s_0, then k_U(-s) <= 1/(2 s) there and the excess stays bounded above, as in (c)(ii); a contradiction.
(iii) If |Gamma_U(y, tau)| > lambda with tau < 0, then R |U^theta(y, tau)| > lambda and R > lambda |U^theta(y, tau)|^{-1} >= rho_lambda(tau). This gives (34.4), since (U^R/R)^- = (U^R)^-/R. Under the stated bound, for tau <= -tau_0 and R > rho_lambda(tau), (U^R)^-/R <= A/R^2 <= A/rho_lambda(tau)^2 = A C_I/(lambda^2 gamma_* (tau_* + |tau|)) <= 1/(2 |tau|), so kappa_lambda(tau) <= 1/(2 |tau|) for tau <= -tau_0, and the excess in (i) stays bounded above (the computation of (c)(ii)); a contradiction.
Vorticity decay. For every R_0, the supremum of |grad^2 U(y, tau)| over {|y'| <= R_0} tends to 0 as tau -> -infinity: otherwise there are eps > 0, points y_n with |y_n'| <= R_0 and times tau_n -> -infinity with |grad^2 U(y_n, tau_n)| >= eps; the translates U(. + (y_n)_3 e_3, . + tau_n) have, by Proposition 33(e)(i) and its proof, a subsequence converging in C^infinity_loc to a constant, and along a further subsequence y_n' converges, which contradicts |grad^2 U| >= eps at the limit point. On {R <= R_0}, |eta_U| = |omega_2|/R <= sup |d_1 omega_2| <= 2 sup_{|y'| <= R_0} |grad^2 U| (omega_2 = omega^theta on {x_2 = 0} vanishes on the axis); on {R > R_0}, |eta_U| <= |omega|/R_0 <= 2 ||grad U||_infty/R_0. Hence limsup_{tau -> -infinity} ||eta_U(tau)||_infty <= 2 ||grad U||_infty/R_0 for every R_0, and the limit is 0.
Estimate (34.5). With omega^theta = d_Z U^R - d_R U^Z, eta_U is a bounded smooth solution, as a function on R^5, of P eta := d_tau eta + beta.grad_5 eta - nu_* Delta_5 eta = F, F := d_Z(q_U^2), with the bounded smooth drift beta(y) := (U^R y'/|y'|, U^Z) (this is the equation of eta = omega^theta/r for axisymmetric NS with swirl; it has no stretching term, and U^R y'/|y'| = (U^R/R) y' is smooth since U^R/R is an even smooth function of R). The barrier on R^5 is eta_0 e^{mu (s - t)} (1 + |y|^2)^{1/2} with mu := ||beta||_infty + 5 nu_* + 1 (since |grad_5 (1 + |y|^2)^{1/2}| <= 1 and Delta_5 (1 + |y|^2)^{1/2} <= 5). For t < tau, the maximum principle with this barrier and the comparison function f(s) := ||eta_U(t)||_infty + int_t^s ||F(sigma)||_infty d sigma (Lipschitz; s -> ||F(s)||_infty is lower semicontinuous and bounded, and the one-sided difference quotient argument of (b) applies, using that the liminf of the averages of a lower semicontinuous function over [s, s_*] is >= its value at s_*) gives |eta_U(tau)| <= f(tau). Letting t -> -infinity and using ||eta_U(t)||_infty -> 0 gives (34.5), and the rate statement follows by integration. For p = 3 with A_p <= 1/(4 K_U), s^2 ||eta_U(-s)||_infty <= A_p/2 <= 1/(8 K_U), and for p > 3, s^2 ||eta_U(-s)||_infty <= A_p s^{3 - p}/(p - 1) <= 1/(8 K_U) for large s; both are excluded by (ii).
Estimate (34.6). Write W := U^theta e_theta, b := U^R e_R + U^Z e_Z (Cartesian fields with bounded derivatives of all orders) and a := U^R/R. Since (b.grad) e_theta = 0 and Delta_3 (U^theta e_theta) = ((Delta - R^{-2}) U^theta) e_theta, the swirl equation reads P_3 W := (d_tau + b.grad - nu_* Delta_3) W = -a W. Differentiating, P_3 |W|^2 = -2 a |W|^2 - 2 nu_* |grad W|^2, and P_3 |grad W|^2 <= -2 nu_* |grad^2 W|^2 + C (|grad W|^2 + |W|^2), P_3 |grad^2 W|^2 <= -2 nu_* |grad^3 W|^2 + C (|grad^2 W|^2 + |grad W|^2 + |W|^2), with C depending on the bounds of a, b and their first two derivatives. On a window [t_0, t_0 + 1] with eps := sup_{[t_0, t_0 + 1]} ||W||_infty, the function Q_1 := (t - t_0) |grad W|^2 + A |W|^2 satisfies P_3 Q_1 <= C_A eps^2 when A is so large that 1 + C - 2 nu_* A <= 0, and Q_1(t_0) <= A eps^2; the maximum principle (with a positive barrier growing at spatial infinity, whose coefficient is then sent to zero) gives |grad W| <= C eps on [t_0 + 1/2, t_0 + 1], and the same argument with Q_2 := (t - t_0 - 1/2) |grad^2 W|^2 + A_2 |grad W|^2 on [t_0 + 1/2, t_0 + 1] gives ||grad W(t_0 + 1)||_infty + ||grad^2 W(t_0 + 1)||_infty <= C eps. On {x_2 = 0, x_1 > 0}, q_U = W_2/R with W_2 odd in x_1, so q_U(R, Z) = int_0^1 d_1 W_2(theta R e_1 + Z e_3) d theta and d_Z q_U = int_0^1 d_1 d_Z W_2(theta R e_1 + Z e_3) d theta; hence |F| = 2 |q_U d_Z q_U| <= 2 ||grad W||_infty ||grad^2 W||_infty, and the window [-s - 1, -s] with eps^2 <= C_I/(gamma_* s) gives ||F(-s)||_infty <= C_F/s for s >= 1. Let M := sup |eta_U| and B_0 := sup |omega^theta_U|, finite, and for L > 0 put
 phi_L(r) := nu_*^{-1} int_r^L x^{-3} e^{K_U x/nu_*} (int_0^x y^3 e^{-K_U y/nu_*} dy) dx  (0 <= r <= L).
Then (r^3 e^{-K_U r/nu_*} phi_L')' = -nu_*^{-1} r^3 e^{-K_U r/nu_*}, i.e. -nu_* (phi_L'' + 3 phi_L'/r) + K_U phi_L' = 1, phi_L' <= 0, phi_L'(r) = -r/(4 nu_*) + O(r^2), so phi_L is a C^2 radial function on {|y'| < L} in R^5, and 0 <= phi_L <= T_L := phi_L(0) <= L^2 e^{K_U L/nu_*}/(8 nu_*) (since int_0^x y^3 e^{-K_U y/nu_*} dy <= x^4/4). As |U^R| <= K_U, beta.grad_5 phi_L - nu_* Delta_5 phi_L = 1 + (U^R - K_U) phi_L' >= 1. Put D_L := 1 + T_L and, on {|y'| < L} x [-2 s, -s],
 H := B_0/L + (C_F/s) phi_L + M (1 + phi_L) e^{-(tau + 2 s)/D_L}.
Then P H >= C_F/s + M e^{-(tau + 2 s)/D_L} (1 - (1 + phi_L)/D_L) >= C_F/s >= |F|, H >= M >= |eta_U| at tau = -2 s, and H >= B_0/L >= |omega^theta_U|/L = |eta_U| on |y'| = L. The maximum principle on the cylinder (unbounded in y_5; the same growing barrier, with its coefficient then sent to zero), applied to H - eta_U and H + eta_U, gives |eta_U(y, -s)| <= B_0/L + C_F T_L/s + M D_L e^{-s/D_L} for |y'| < L, and |eta_U| <= B_0/L for |y'| >= L. With L := (nu_*/(2 K_U)) log s, e^{K_U L/nu_*} = s^{1/2}, so T_L/s = O(s^{-1/2} log^2 s), s/D_L is at least a positive constant times s^{1/2}/log^2 s and D_L e^{-s/D_L} = o(1/log s), while B_0/L = 2 K_U B_0/(nu_* log s). This is (34.6).

Remark. (1) Scaling. Under V -> lambda V(lambda ., lambda^2 .), eta scales like lambda^3 and K like lambda, so s^2 K ||eta|| and the constant 1/8 in (c)(ii) are dimensionless and independent of nu. Inequality (34.1) uses only the bound |u^r| <= K_r and the heat kernel of R^5; no sign of eta is used. It is not localized: kappa_lambda(tau) is bounded by (34.1) through the global norm of eta. No sharpness of 2^{1/2} is claimed. (2) What (d) says about Case 1. By (d)(i), a Case-1 limit requires, for every lambda in [0, 1), a meridional compression (U^R/R)^- exceeding 1/(2 |tau|) on the circulation superlevel set {|Gamma_U| > lambda}, in the integrated sense int (kappa_lambda - 1/(2 |tau|))^+ = infinity. On the Type I swirl branch, for 0 < lambda < 1, this superlevel set lies beyond rho_lambda(tau), comparable to |tau|^{1/2} as tau -> -infinity; at a point of it where the compression exceeds 1/(2 s) (s = |tau|) the inflow satisfies -U^R > R/(2 s) >= lambda (gamma_*/C_I)^{1/2}/(2 s^{1/2}), and the velocity bound only gives R < 2 K s there, not R = O(s^{1/2}). (d)(iii) excludes this only below the explicit threshold A C_I <= lambda^2 gamma_*/2 for R (U^R)^- on the exterior of the parabolic radius; the immediate bound (U^R)^-/R <= K/rho_lambda = O(s^{-1/2}) is far from the critical size 1/(2 s). Spatial bounds at a single time cannot supply the missing estimate: for a smooth divergence-free meridional field b_0 supported in {1 < r < 2} with inflow somewhere and a circulation profile chi supported there, the fields c b_0(x/L) with circulation delta chi(x/L), delta > lambda, L comparable to s^{1/2}, satisfy the Type I swirl bound, bounded circulation and velocity and uniform derivative bounds, while r (u^r)^- is comparable to L and eta to s^{-1} (a kinematic example, not a Navier-Stokes solution). So (d) does not exclude Case 1. (3) What (d)(ii), (34.5) and (34.6) say. A Case-1 limit on the Type I swirl branch has ||eta_U(-s)||_infty -> 0, at least at the rate 1/log s by (34.6), but int_1^infinity ((2 K_U ||eta_U(-s)||_infty)^{1/2} - 1/(2 s))^+ ds = infinity by (d)(ii); no eventual pointwise lower bound on eta_U follows. The amplitude-sensitive estimate in the proof of (34.6) gives ||d_Z(q_U^2)(-s)||_infty <= C/s, whose time integral diverges, so (34.5) is inconclusive with this bound; the finite-window comparison of (34.6) uses instead the lateral bound |eta_U| <= ||omega^theta_U||_infty/L and loses all but a logarithm. The closing rate s^{-2} (or a source bound A s^{-3} with A <= 1/(4 K_U)) has not been derived. (4) Physical solution. Combined with Proposition 33(c), (34.1) shows that Type II near-axis strain, limsup (T_* - t) k(t) = infinity, implies limsup (T_* - t)^2 ||u^r(t)||_infty ||eta(t)||_infty = infinity; this is not used. (5) Literature. A representation of u^r/r through omega^theta/r with L^p derivative estimates is in [CFZ, Lemma 2.3] (this pinpoint was not rechecked by the independent review); (34.1) in this form, with the constant 2^{1/2}, the superlevel form (34.2) of the circulation absorption and (34.6) were not found in the references checked, and the literature search is not complete; no priority claim is made. (6) Exactly self-similar Euler-scale structures. The borderline rate ||eta_U(-s)||_infty ~ s^{-2} is that of the hyperbolic scaling U(y, tau) = V(y/|tau|), eta_U(y, tau) = |tau|^{-2} F(y/|tau|), at which the viscous term is formally of lower order. For a profile with swirl the source d_Z(q_U^2) has the same order |tau|^{-3} as the transport terms; but the bounded circulation forces the profile to be swirl-free (Gamma_U(s X, -s) = s Gamma_V(X) for s > 0, which is bounded only if Gamma_V = 0), so the source vanishes, and the source-free transport equation of eta then reads (y + V) . grad F = -2 F. This structure is not realized by a regular profile: let V in C^1(R^3) be bounded, axisymmetric, swirl-free and divergence-free, and let F := omega^theta_V/R be C^1 off the axis, bounded on {|y| <= K_0 + 1, R > 0} with K_0 := sup |V|, and satisfy (y + V) . grad F = -2 F off the axis. Then F = 0 and V is a constant multiple of e_Z. Proof: the flow Y(t) of the locally Lipschitz field y + V exists for all t, and Y(t) = e^t Y(0) - int_t^0 e^{t - t'} V(Y(t')) dt' for t <= 0, so |Y(t)| <= e^t |Y(0)| + K_0 (1 - e^t) and every backward trajectory enters and stays in the ball of radius K_0 + 1; off-axis trajectories stay off the axis (V^R = 0 on the axis and V^R/R is locally bounded), and F(Y(t)) = F(Y(0)) e^{-2t}, so |F(Y(0))| <= e^{2t} sup |F| -> 0 as t -> -infinity. Hence curl V = 0, each Cartesian component of V is a bounded harmonic function on R^3, so V is constant, and axisymmetry gives V = c e_Z. Boundedness of F near the axis holds, for instance, when V is C^2 and solves the profile equations classically; for a merely C^1 field it can fail (for the shear R^{1 + a} e_Z, 0 < a < 1, F is comparable to R^{a - 1}). This is a bounded-velocity variant of the characteristic argument of [CIV3, proof of Theorem 4.5 and Remark 4.6], whose case gamma = 1 is this scaling and which assumes C^2 profiles with decaying gradients. It concerns globally regular, exactly self-similar whole-space profiles only: time-dependent Euler-scale structures, profiles singular at the axis and configurations matched to a viscous core are not covered, so it does not exclude Case 1.
Status: proved here. (34.1) and the localization (34.2) were first derived in a research consultation with a second model, and (34.6) was supplied by the independent review below; all were rederived by the author, who checked the barrier computation, the two kernel integrals (also numerically), the identity Delta_5 (u^r/r) = d_z (omega^theta/r) (by hand and symbolically) and every step of the proof of (34.6). Verification: a hostile independent review (review 12 in sec. 5) rederived (a) to (d), found no counterexample and no wrong constant, and required the repairs listed there, all applied. The model statement of Remark (6) was refereed by an independent review (review 17 in sec. 5) and checked by the author by hand.

Proposition 35 (a small Type I swirl constant excludes a singularity; a lower bound for the near-axis strain rate). Let nu > 0, t_0 < T < infinity, and let u in C([t_0, T); H^2(R^3)) cap L^2_loc([t_0, T); H^3(R^3)) be an axisymmetric solution of NS with viscosity nu. If
 ||u^theta(t)||_infty <= C (T - t)^{-1/2} for almost every t in (t_0, T), with C < 3^{-1/4} nu^{1/2},   (35.1)
then u can be continued beyond T in the same class. The same holds under the weaker hypothesis
 int_{t_0}^t ||u^theta(s)||_infty^2 ds <= alpha' log((T - t_0)/(T - t)) + B for t in [t_0, T), with alpha' < 3^{-1/2} nu and B < infinity,   (35.1')
which (35.1) implies with alpha' = C^2 and B = 0. No bound on the circulation is assumed. Consequently, in the setting of sec. 1.1, for every t_1 in (0, T_*),
 limsup_{t -> T_*} (log(1/(T_* - t)))^{-1} int_{t_1}^t ||u^theta(s)||_infty^2 ds >= 3^{-1/2},   (35.2')
and in particular
 limsup_{t -> T_*} (T_* - t) ||u^theta(t)||_infty^2 >= 3^{-1/2},   (35.2)
and in the Type I swirl alternative of Proposition 33(c), every admissible constant C_I (in particular the one in Proposition 33(e)(i)) satisfies C_I >= 3^{-1/2}. Moreover, with k(t) := ||(u^r/r)^-(t)||_infty as in Proposition 33 and mu_0 := max_{x > 0} (1 - e^{-x})^2/x = 4 xi_0 e^{-2 xi_0}, where xi_0 is the positive root of e^x = 1 + 2 x (0.4072 < mu_0 < 0.4073), G > 0 and
 limsup_{t -> T_*} (T_* - t) k(t) >= 1/2 + c_G,   c_G := max{2/(3^{1/2} mu_0 G^2), (3/2) mu_0^{-1/3} G^{-4/3}};   (35.3)
so every constant C_a for which the hypothesis of Proposition 33(b) holds on an interval [t_a, T_*), in particular the constant of Proposition 33(e)(ii), satisfies C_a >= 1/2 + c_G, and, by (34.1), limsup_{t -> T_*} (T_* - t)^2 ||u^r(t)||_infty ||eta(t)||_infty >= (1/2) (1/2 + c_G)^2. Here 2/(3^{1/2} mu_0) > 2.835 and (3/2) mu_0^{-1/3} > 2.023; the first term of c_G is the larger one for G <= 1.658 and the second for G >= 1.659.

Proof. Step 0 (reductions). It suffices to prove the statement under (35.1'). The function v(x, t) := nu^{-1} u(x, t/nu) solves NS with viscosity 1 on [nu t_0, nu T), and int_{nu t_0}^{t} ||v^theta(s)||_infty^2 ds = nu^{-1} int_{t_0}^{t/nu} ||u^theta(s)||_infty^2 ds, while log((nu T - nu t_0)/(nu T - t)) = log((T - t_0)/(T - t/nu)); so v satisfies (35.1') with alpha'/nu < 3^{-1/2} and B/nu, and it suffices to treat nu = 1 and alpha' < 3^{-1/2}. By positive-time smoothing of H^2 strong solutions we may move t_0 forward and assume that u is smooth on R^3 x [t_0, T) with all derivatives in L^2 on compact subintervals; the integrations by parts below are justified with cutoffs at spatial infinity. Write s := u^theta, a := u^r/r, J := omega^r/r, Omega := omega^theta/r (= eta), W := s^2/r, D_t := d_t + b.grad, Sigma(t) := ||s(t)||_infty, and let all norms be over R^3 with dx = 2 pi r dr dz. For an axisymmetric field v = v^r e_r + v^theta e_theta + v^z e_z, |grad v|^2 = |grad v^r|^2 + |grad v^theta|^2 + |grad v^z|^2 + ((v^r)^2 + (v^theta)^2)/r^2; hence ||J(t_0)||_2^2 + ||Omega(t_0)||_2^2 <= ||grad omega(t_0)||_2^2 < infinity and ||W(t_0)||_2 <= Sigma(t_0) ||s(t_0)/r||_2 <= Sigma(t_0) ||grad u(t_0)||_2 < infinity.
Step 1 (equations). With omega^r = -s_z, omega^z = r^{-1} (r s)_r and Delta_5 = Delta + 2 r^{-1} d_r on functions of (r, z),
 (D_t - Delta_5) J = (omega^r d_r + omega^z d_z) a,   (D_t - Delta_5) Omega = d_z(q^2) = -2 (s/r) J,
the first from the equation of omega^r, (D_t - Delta + r^{-2}) omega^r = omega^r d_r u^r + omega^z d_z u^r, and (Delta - r^{-2})(r J) = r Delta_5 J; the second is the equation of eta in sec. 1.1, and 2 s s_z/r^2 = -2 (s/r) J. As in the proof of Proposition 34(a), Delta_5 a = d_z Omega.
Step 2 (energy inequality). For an axisymmetric f, int f Delta_5 f dx = -||grad f||_2^2 - B_f with B_f := 2 pi int f(0, z)^2 dz >= 0, and the transport terms vanish (div b = 0). Integrating by parts in r and z (dx = 2 pi r dr dz; the boundary term r s J a_z vanishes at r = 0) gives the determinant form
 int J (-s_z a_r + (s_r + s/r) a_z) dx = int s (a_r J_z - a_z J_r) dx,
so
 (1/2) d/dt ||J||_2^2 + ||grad J||_2^2 + B_J = int s (a_r J_z - a_z J_r) dx,   (1/2) d/dt ||Omega||_2^2 + ||grad Omega||_2^2 + B_Omega = -2 int (s/r) J Omega dx.
Multiplying Delta_5 a = d_z Omega by a and integrating gives ||grad a||_2^2 + B_a = int Omega a_z dx, hence ||grad a||_2 <= ||Omega||_2 [Wei, Lemma 2.1]. Integrating d_r (r f^2) in r gives int f^2/r dx = -2 int f f_r dx <= 2 ||f||_2 ||f_r||_2. With x_1 := ||J||_2, x_2 := ||Omega||_2, p := ||grad J||_2, q_1 := ||grad Omega||_2, the right sides are bounded by Sigma x_2 p and by 2 Sigma (int J^2/r)^{1/2} (int Omega^2/r)^{1/2} <= 4 Sigma (x_1 x_2 p q_1)^{1/2}. Put lambda := 4/3^{1/2}, E := lambda x_1^2 + x_2^2, D_lambda := lambda p^2 + q_1^2, m := lambda^{1/2} = 2 3^{-1/4}, k := 3^{3/4}, v := m x_2 p, w := m x_1 q_1. Then lambda x_2 p + 4 (x_1 x_2 p q_1)^{1/2} = m v + (4/m)(v w)^{1/2} <= k (v + w) (by (v w)^{1/2} <= (eps v + w/eps)/2 with eps := 2/(m k), using k (k - m) = 3^{3/2} - 2 3^{1/2} = 3^{1/2} = 4/m^2), and v + w <= (E D_lambda)^{1/2} (Cauchy-Schwarz). Hence
 (1/2) E' + D_lambda <= 3^{3/4} Sigma (E D_lambda)^{1/2} <= D_lambda + (3^{3/2}/4) Sigma^2 E,  so  E' <= (3^{3/2}/2) Sigma^2 E.
By Gronwall and (35.1'), E(t) <= E(t_0) exp((3^{3/2}/2) int_{t_0}^t Sigma^2) <= E(t_0) e^{(3^{3/2}/2) B} ((T - t_0)/(T - t))^{alpha} with alpha := (3^{3/2}/2) alpha', and since ||Omega||_2^{4/3} <= E^{2/3},
 int_{t_0}^T ||Omega(t)||_2^{4/3} dt <= E(t_0)^{2/3} e^{3^{1/2} B} (T - t_0)/(1 - 2 alpha/3) < infinity,
because 2 alpha/3 = 3^{1/2} alpha' < 1.
Step 3 (the swirl estimate). Multiplying the swirl equation (D_t - Delta + r^{-2}) s = -a s by s^3/r^2 and integrating gives
 (1/4) d/dt ||W||_2^2 + (3/4) ||grad W||_2^2 + (3/4) ||s/r||_4^4 = -(3/2) int a W^2 dx
(this identity is in the proof of [CFZ, Lemma 3.1]; it was rederived and also checked numerically with explicit test functions). By Hoelder (1/6 + 5/6 = 1), Sobolev, ||grad a||_2 <= ||Omega||_2, the interpolation ||W||_{12/5} <= ||W||_2^{3/4} ||W||_6^{1/4} and Young's inequality with exponents 4 and 4/3,
 (3/2) |int a W^2 dx| <= c ||a||_6 ||W||_{12/5}^2 <= c ||Omega||_2 ||W||_2^{3/2} ||grad W||_2^{1/2} <= (1/2) ||grad W||_2^2 + c' ||Omega||_2^{4/3} ||W||_2^2
with absolute constants c, c'. Gronwall and Step 2 give sup_{[t_0, T)} ||W||_2 < infinity and int_{t_0}^T ||s/r||_4^4 dt < infinity.
Step 4 (continuation). By [CFZ, Lemma 2.5] (an axisymmetric solution in C([0, T); H^2) cap L^2_loc([0, T); H^3) with H^2 data and T < infinity, for which u^theta/r is in L^4((0, T); L^4(R^3)), can be continued beyond T), applied after translating t_0 to 0, u continues beyond T.
Consequence. In the setting of sec. 1.1, changing t_1 changes the integral in (35.2') by a constant, so the left side of (35.2') does not depend on t_1. If (35.2') failed, there would be alpha' < 3^{-1/2} and t_2 in [t_1, T_*) with int_{t_2}^t ||u^theta||_infty^2 ds <= alpha' log(1/(T_* - t)) = alpha' log((T_* - t_2)/(T_* - t)) + alpha' log(1/(T_* - t_2)) for t in [t_2, T_*); after a restart at t_2 (a positive time, as in Remark (6) after Proposition 33), (35.1') would hold with t_0 = t_2 and B = alpha' |log(T_* - t_2)|, and the solution would continue beyond T_*, contradicting the definition of T_*. If (T_* - t) ||u^theta(t)||_infty^2 <= c on [t_2, T_*), then int_{t_2}^t ||u^theta||_infty^2 ds <= c log((T_* - t_2)/(T_* - t)), so the left side of (35.2') is at most c; hence (35.2') implies (35.2). If (T_* - t) S(t)^2 <= C_I on [t_1, T_*) with C_I < 3^{-1/2}, then ||u^theta(t)||_infty <= S(t) gives (35.1) with C = C_I^{1/2} < 3^{-1/4}; so C_I >= 3^{-1/2}.
Proof of (35.3). If G = 0, then u^theta = 0 and (35.2) fails; so G > 0. Let kappa be the left side of (35.3); there is nothing to prove if kappa = infinity. Otherwise let C_a > kappa; then there is t_a in (0, T_*) with k(t) <= C_a/(T_* - t) on [t_a, T_*). For sigma in (t_a, T_*) put delta := T_* - sigma and h := sigma - t_a. By Proposition 33(a), for all r > 0 and z, |u^theta(r, z, sigma)|^2 = Gamma^2/r^2 <= G^2 (1 - exp(-r^2 w))^2/r^2 = G^2 w f(r^2 w) with f(x) := (1 - e^{-x})^2/x, so ||u^theta(sigma)||_infty^2 <= mu_0 G^2 w; and since I(v) <= C_a log((delta + v)/delta) for 0 <= v <= h, the definition of w in Proposition 33(a) gives w <= 1/(4 J) with J = int_0^h (delta/(delta + v))^{2 C_a} dv = delta P(h/delta), P(X) := int_0^X (1 + b)^{-2 C_a} db. As sigma -> T_*, h -> T_* - t_a > 0 and h/delta -> infinity, so P(h/delta) -> 1/(2 C_a - 1) if C_a > 1/2 and P(h/delta) -> infinity if C_a <= 1/2. Hence limsup_{sigma -> T_*} (T_* - sigma) ||u^theta(sigma)||_infty^2 <= mu_0 G^2 (2 C_a - 1)^+/4, and (35.2) gives 3^{-1/2} <= mu_0 G^2 (2 C_a - 1)^+/4; hence C_a > 1/2, and then C_a >= 1/2 + 2/(3^{1/2} mu_0 G^2). For the second term of c_G put a_0 := (2 C_a - 1)/4 > 0. The computation above gives limsup_{sigma -> T_*} (T_* - sigma) w <= a_0, and |Gamma| <= G (1 - exp(-r^2 w)) <= G r^2 w gives Q(sigma) := ||u^theta(sigma)/r||_infty <= G w. So for eps > 0 there is t_1 in (t_a, T_*) with Sigma(t)^2 <= C_eps^2/(T_* - t) and Q(t) <= Q_eps/(T_* - t) on [t_1, T_*), where C_eps^2 := mu_0 a_0 G^2 + eps and Q_eps := a_0 G + eps. Use the notation of Steps 0 to 2 with nu = 1, T = T_* and t_0 := t_1 (a restart at a positive time). For lambda > 0 put E_lambda := lambda x_1^2 + x_2^2. The two energy identities of Step 2, B_J, B_Omega >= 0, the bound |int s (a_r J_z - a_z J_r) dx| <= Sigma x_2 p <= p^2 + Sigma^2 x_2^2/4 and the bound |2 int (s/r) J Omega dx| <= 2 Q x_1 x_2 give
 (1/2) E_lambda' <= (lambda Sigma^2/4) x_2^2 + 2 Q x_1 x_2 <= (T_* - t)^{-1} ((lambda C_eps^2/4) x_2^2 + 2 Q_eps x_1 x_2) <= (T_* - t)^{-1} mu_lambda E_lambda,
where mu_lambda := lambda C_eps^2/8 + (lambda^2 C_eps^4/64 + Q_eps^2/lambda)^{1/2}, the larger root of lambda mu^2 - (lambda^2 C_eps^2/4) mu - Q_eps^2 = 0, is the maximum of the quadratic form (lambda C_eps^2/4) x_2^2 + 2 Q_eps x_1 x_2 on {E_lambda = 1}. For lambda := 2 Q_eps^{2/3} C_eps^{-4/3} one gets mu_lambda = (C_eps Q_eps)^{2/3} (1/4 + (1/16 + 1/2)^{1/2}) = (C_eps Q_eps)^{2/3}, so with c_eps := 2 (C_eps Q_eps)^{2/3}, E_lambda(t) <= E_lambda(t_1) ((T_* - t_1)/(T_* - t))^{c_eps}. Since ||Omega||_2^{4/3} <= E_lambda^{2/3}, int_{t_1}^{T_*} ||Omega||_2^{4/3} dt < infinity if c_eps < 3/2, and then Steps 3 and 4 continue the solution beyond T_*, which is impossible. Hence c_eps >= 3/2 for every eps > 0, and letting eps -> 0, 2 (mu_0^{1/2} a_0^{3/2} G^2)^{2/3} = 2 mu_0^{1/3} a_0 G^{4/3} >= 3/2, that is C_a >= 1/2 + (3/2) mu_0^{-1/3} G^{-4/3}. Letting C_a decrease to kappa gives (35.3). On (0, infinity), f'(x) = (1 - e^{-x}) (2 x e^{-x} - 1 + e^{-x})/x^2, and g(x) := 2 x e^{-x} - 1 + e^{-x} has g(0) = 0, g'(x) = (1 - 2 x) e^{-x}, g(x) -> -1 as x -> infinity, so g has exactly one positive zero xi_0 (where e^{xi_0} = 1 + 2 xi_0), f increases on (0, xi_0] and decreases on [xi_0, infinity), and mu_0 = f(xi_0) = 4 xi_0 e^{-2 xi_0} (using 1 - e^{-xi_0} = 2 xi_0 e^{-xi_0}); numerically xi_0 = 1.25643..., mu_0 = 0.407264.... For the last inequality, (u^r/r)^- <= |u^r/r|, and (34.1) applies at each t in (0, T_*), where the derivatives of u of order <= 3 are bounded (smoothing estimate); so ((T_* - t) k(t))^2 <= 2 (T_* - t)^2 ||u^r(t)||_infty ||eta(t)||_infty.

Remark. (1) Scaling. (35.1) is invariant under the Navier-Stokes scaling, and in the self-similar scaling E is of order (T - t)^{-3/2}; the proof shows E <= C (T - t)^{-alpha} with alpha < 3/2, so the threshold is the swirl size at which this energy argument can no longer exclude self-similar growth of E. No sharpness of 3^{-1/4} is claimed; the first version of the argument gave 6^{-1/2}. (2) Case 1. (35.2) does not exclude Case 1: the circulation bound is not used, and on the Type I swirl branch of Proposition 33 nothing derived here prevents C_I >= 3^{-1/2}. At the records (T_* - t_n) S_n^2 = tau_n gamma_n with tau_n <= C_I/gamma_n (Proposition 33(e)(i)); (35.2) concerns all times near T_* and gives no lower bound for tau_n. On the Type I strain branch, (35.3) sharpens the conclusion C_a > 1/2 of Proposition 33(e)(ii) to C_a >= 1/2 + c_G; this is a quantitative lower bound and gives no contradiction. (35.3) holds for every singular solution in the setting of sec. 1.1, whereas Proposition 33(f)(i) gives only int k = infinity, which is compatible with (T_* - t) k(t) -> 0 (for instance k(t) = ((T_* - t) log(e/(T_* - t)))^{-1}). The weaker bound limsup (T_* - t) k(t) >= 1/2 also follows from known results: if (T_* - t) k(t) <= C < 1/2 on [t_a, T_*), the swirl maximum principle gives ||u^theta(t)||_infty <= ||u^theta(t_a)||_infty ((T_* - t_a)/(T_* - t))^C, so u^theta is in L^2_t L^infty_x near T_*, which excludes a singularity by [CFZ, Theorem 1.1] (after a restart at a positive time). The gain in (35.3) is the term c_G. Its first part comes from (33.1) and (35.2); its second part comes from (33.1) and the weighted energy E_lambda, in which the pointwise bound ||u^theta/r||_infty <= G w controls the term -2 int (s/r) J Omega dx without the weighted inequality of Step 2. Neither part gives a contradiction, and no claim is made that an energy argument of this kind can exclude the Type I swirl branch for large G. (3) Limits of the energy argument on the Type I strain branch. The second term of c_G uses, at each time, only the identities of Step 2 and pointwise bounds. These bounds give no contradiction for larger G with any constant weight, even if all dissipation and axis terms are kept. Normalize T_* - t = 1 at one time and let G = 50, C_a = 1, so that the limiting bounds from Proposition 33(a), (b) read ||u^theta||_infty <= G (mu_0 (2 C_a - 1)/4)^{1/2} (about 15.95), ||u^theta/r||_infty <= G (2 C_a - 1)/4 = 12.5, |r u^theta| <= G and ||(u^r/r)^-||_infty <= C_a. For lambda > 0 put Q_lambda := (lambda (T_1 - ||grad J||_2^2 - B_J) + T_2 - ||grad Omega||_2^2 - B_Omega)/E_lambda with T_1 := int s (a_r J_z - a_z J_r) dx and T_2 := -2 int (s/r) J Omega dx, the right sides of Step 2; an argument of the type used for (35.3) needs Q_lambda < 3/4 for all fields obeying these bounds. This fails for every lambda > 0. Let t := r^2/b^2, c := (k^2 b^2 + 4)/8, d := c (k^2 b^2 + 8) - 1, g := (1 + c t) e^{-t/2} and f := b^{-2} (d t - c t^2) e^{-t/2}; then -g'' - 3 g'/r + k^2 g = f and f(0) = 0. With s_0 := q_0 r e^{-r^2/(2 l^2)}, sigma in {-1, 1} and eps > 0 take s := s_0 - (eps/k) r f(r) sin kz and the meridional field u^r = -r psi_z, u^z = 2 psi + r psi_r with psi := sigma lambda^{1/2} eps g(r) cos kz; then J = eps f cos kz, eta = -Delta_5 psi = sigma lambda^{1/2} J and a = u^r/r = sigma lambda^{1/2} eps k g sin kz. Over one period in z the cubic terms have zero mean, the axis terms vanish and, exactly, Q_lambda = sigma (alpha lambda^{1/2} - beta lambda^{-1/2}) - D with alpha := k^2 A/(2 M), beta := B/M, D := H/M + k^2, M := int_0^infty r f^2 dr, H := int_0^infty r f'^2 dr, A := int_0^infty (r s_0' + s_0) f g dr and B := int_0^infty s_0 f^2 dr. For q_0 = 12, l = 2, b = 1: k = 1/10 gives alpha < 0.045, beta > 9.46, D < 2.006, so sigma = -1 gives Q_lambda > 2 for lambda <= 5; k = 2 gives alpha > 5.03, beta < 9.034, D < 5.329, so sigma = +1 gives Q_lambda > 15/8 for lambda >= 5. The background has ||s_0/r||_infty = 12, ||s_0||_infty = 24 e^{-1/2} < 14.6 and ||r s_0||_infty = 96/e < 35.4, so for small eps all the bounds hold, with |a| <= 1/2. Multiplying s and psi by a fixed smooth axial cutoff equal to 1 on n periods gives smooth, decaying, finite-energy axisymmetric fields; the end contributions, including the axis terms, do not depend on n, so Q_lambda > 29/16 for large n. The dilation x -> 2^{1/2} x with the velocity divided by 2^{1/2} gives the same for C_a = 3/4 with Q_lambda halved, still above 29/32 > 3/4. These are fields at one time, not Navier-Stokes trajectories. They show that constant-weight energy arguments with these pointwise bounds alone cannot exclude the Type I strain branch at G = 50; time-dependent weights and further properties of the flow are not covered. (4) Literature. The estimates are those of [CFZ, Section 3] and [Wei, Lemma 2.1], and the continuation is [CFZ, Lemma 2.5]; [CFZ, Theorem 1.1] needs u^theta in L^2_t L^infty_x, which (35.1) does not give, and [CFZ, Theorem 1.2] is a smallness condition on the data. The statement with the swirl Type I constant was not found in the references checked, and the literature search is not complete; no priority claim is made.
Status: proved here from [CFZ, Lemma 2.5 and the identities of Section 3] and [Wei, Lemma 2.1]; (35.3) from (35.2), the energy identities of Step 2 and Proposition 33(a), (b). The proof was supplied by a research consultation and refereed by an independent review (review 13 in sec. 5), which improved the constant from 6^{-1/2} to 3^{-1/4} by the weighted energy E. Checked step by step by the author, including the equations of Step 1, the determinant cancellation and the identity of Step 3 (by hand, and numerically with explicit test functions of the correct parity at the axis), the weighted inequality of Step 2, and the hypotheses of [CFZ, Lemma 2.5] against its text. The first term of c_G in (35.3) and its consequence are own derivations, refereed by an independent review (review 14 in sec. 5); the author checked mu_0 by hand and numerically. The second term of c_G was refereed by an independent review (review 16 in sec. 5); the author rederived it, including the largest eigenvalue of the quadratic form and the choice of lambda. The fields of Remark (3) were constructed by a research consultation (review 18 in sec. 5); the author rederived the periodic quotient formula and checked it, the six constants, the bounds of the background and the scaling to C_a = 3/4 by symbolic differentiation and by direct two-dimensional quadrature of the original functionals.

Proposition 36 (circulation decay at the axis under a Type I near-axis strain bound and a slowly growing inflow envelope). In the setting of sec. 1.1, without assuming (A), (K) or (TAIL), let k(t) := ||(u^r/r)^-(t)||_infty as in Proposition 33, g(t) := ||(u^r)^-(t)||_infty as in Proposition 30, and L_1, L_2, L_3 as in Proposition 30(d). Fix alpha > 1/2 and put a := alpha - 1/2 and rho := 1 - 1/(2 alpha). For C > 0 and y > 0 let
 psi_C(y) := int_0^y (min{C, alpha s} - s/2) ds,   H(C) := rho C^2,   W_C(y) := y^{-1} exp(psi_C(y) - H(C)),   L_C f := f'' + (min{C, alpha y} - y/2 - 1/y) f' = W_C^{-1} (W_C f')',
so that psi_C(y) = a y^2/2 for y <= C/alpha, psi_C(y) = H(C) - (y - 2C)^2/4 for y >= C/alpha, and H(C) = psi_C(2C) = max psi_C. Let lambda_1(C) := inf { int_0^infty f'^2 W_C dy / int_0^infty f^2 W_C dy : 0 != f in calD_C }, where calD_C is the closure of C_c^infty(0, infinity) in the norm (int_0^infty (f^2 + f'^2) W_C dy)^{1/2}; it is the bottom of the spectrum of -L_C with absorption at y = 0. Let 0 < t_a < T_* and 0 < h_0 <= (T_* - t_a)/2, and consider the hypotheses
 (S) k(t) <= alpha/(T_* - t) for all t in [t_a, T_*);
 (I) g(t) <= C(T_* - t) (T_* - t)^{-1/2} for all t in [T_* - 2 h_0, T_*), where C : (0, 2 h_0] -> [2, infinity) is continuous and nonincreasing.
Put Lambda(v) := int_{log v}^{log(h_0/2)} lambda_1(C(e^l)) dl for 0 < v < h_0/2, and Cbar(v) := (2 v^{1/2})^{-1} int_0^v C(w) w^{-1/2} dw (>= C(v)).
(a) (Spectral bounds.) For C >= 2: if alpha >= 1, then (P/480) e^{-H} <= lambda_1(C) <= 10 e^{5/4} P e^{-H} with P := C^3 a/(C^2 + a) and H := H(C); if 1/2 < alpha < 1, then (a^3 C/48) e^{-H} <= lambda_1(C) <= 5 e^{1/2} C e^{-H}. For every C > 0, lambda_1(C) <= 1. For 2 <= C <= C' <= C + 2/C, lambda_1(C') >= c_0 lambda_1(C), where c_0 := e^{-6}/(4800 e^{5/4}) if alpha >= 1 and c_0 := a^3 e^{-6}/(240 e^{1/2}) if 1/2 < alpha < 1.
(b) (Uniform decay.) Assume (S), (I) and
 (T') Lambda(v)/C(v)^2 -> infinity as v -> 0.
Then there is a function S^T : (0, infinity) -> [0, 1], depending only on C, h_0 and alpha, with S^T(r) -> 0 as r -> 0, such that |Gamma(r, z, sigma)| <= G S^T(r) for all r > 0, z in R and sigma in [T_* - h_0, T_*). Moreover Cbar(v)^2 = o(Lambda(v)) and L_2(v) = o(Lambda(v)) as v -> 0, and for every c_1 < c_0/4 there are K_1 and r_1 > 0 with S^T(r) <= K_1 exp(-c_1 Lambda(r)) for 0 < r < r_1.
(c) (A test without the factor C^2.) Assume (S), (I),
 (W2) the function l -> C(e^l) is continuously differentiable on (-infinity, log(2 h_0)], and int_{-infinity}^{log(h_0/2)} (d/dl C(e^l))^2 dl < infinity,
 (T'') Lambda(v) -> infinity as v -> 0.
Then there is a function S^{T'} : (0, infinity) -> [0, 1], depending only on C, h_0 and alpha, with S^{T'}(r) -> 0 as r -> 0, such that |Gamma(r, z, sigma)| <= G S^{T'}(r) for all r > 0, z in R and sigma in [T_* - h_0, T_*); for every c_1 < c_0/4 there are K_1' and r_1' > 0 with S^{T'}(r) <= K_1' exp(-c_1 Lambda(r)) for 0 < r < r_1'. (The assertions Cbar^2 = o(Lambda) and L_2 = o(Lambda) of (b) do not follow from (W2) and (T''): for C^2 = rho^{-1} (L_2 + (3/2) L_3 + B), (W2) and (T'') hold by (d), while Lambda is of order L_3 and C^2 of order L_2.)
(d) (Explicit envelopes.) Let C(v)^2 = kappa (L_2(v) + beta L_3(v) + B) with kappa > 0 and beta real, on a window (0, 2 h_0] on which L_3 > 0 and 1 + beta/L_2 >= 0, with B so large that C >= 2 there. Then C is continuous and nonincreasing, (W2) holds, and, with kappa' := kappa rho: (T') holds if and only if kappa' < 1, or kappa' = 1 and beta < 1/2, and these are also the cases in which Lambda/L_2 -> infinity; (T'') holds if and only if kappa' < 1, or kappa' = 1 and beta <= 3/2.
(e) (Records.) Assume (S), (I) and either (T'), or (W2) and (T''). Then gamma_n -> 0 along every sequence of first-crossing swirl records with S_n -> infinity. Consequently, on every Case-1 trajectory, if k(t) <= C_a/(T_* - t) on some interval [t_a, T_*) (the Type I strain alternative of Proposition 33(e)(ii); then C_a >= 1/2 + c_G > 1/2 by (35.3)), then for every continuous nonincreasing C >= 2 on some interval (0, 2 h_0] satisfying (T') with alpha := C_a (or (W2) and (T'')),
 limsup_{t -> T_*} (T_* - t)^{1/2} g(t)/C(T_* - t) >= 1,   (36.1)
and in particular limsup_{t -> T_*} (T_* - t) g(t)^2/L_2(T_* - t) >= 2 C_a/(2 C_a - 1).
(f) (Every singular solution.) By the circulation criterion [LZ2, Corollary 1.3] (as quoted in Proposition 31(f)), no solution in the setting of sec. 1.1 satisfies (S), (I) and (T') for any alpha > 1/2, t_a, h_0 and C as above, nor (S), (I), (W2) and (T'') with Lambda(v)/L_2(v) -> infinity. Hence, on every solution in the setting of sec. 1.1 satisfying k(t) <= C_a/(T_* - t) on an interval [t_a, T_*), (36.1) holds, with alpha := C_a, for every continuous nonincreasing C >= 2 on some interval (0, 2 h_0] satisfying (T'), or satisfying (W2), (T'') and Lambda(v)/L_2(v) -> infinity, and limsup_{t -> T_*} (T_* - t) g(t)^2/L_2(T_* - t) >= 2 C_a/(2 C_a - 1).

Proof (key estimates). If G = 0 everything is trivial; let G > 0. Since the derivatives of u are bounded on compact subintervals of (0, T_*), k and g are locally Lipschitz on (0, T_*).
Step 1 (comparison function). Fix sigma in [T_* - h_0, T_*) and z, and put s_0 := sigma - h_0 (>= T_* - 2 h_0 >= t_a). For delta > 0 let S_delta : R -> [0, infinity) be smooth, convex and nondecreasing with s_+ - delta <= S_delta(s) <= s_+ and 0 <= S_delta' <= 1, and put m_delta(r, t) := k(t) r - S_delta(k(t) r - g(t) - delta). Then min{g, k r} <= m_delta <= min{g + 2 delta, k r}, 0 <= d_r m_delta <= k, m_delta(0, t) = 0, and (u^r)^- <= min{g, k r} <= m_delta. Exactly as in Step 1 of the proof of Proposition 31 (corner-compatible truncations on (eps, L), ordered monotone limits, the barrier A (r^2 + kappa r) e^{B (t - s_0)} with kappa := 1/(g_1 + k_1 + 1), B := 2 (g_1 + k_1 + 1)^2 + 1, A := max{M(s_0)/kappa, G/(1 + kappa)}, where g_1, k_1 are the maxima of g, k on [s_0, sigma]; the barrier inequality holds because m_delta <= k_1 r), there is Q in [0, G], C^{2,1} on (0, infinity) x (s_0, sigma], with Q_t = Q_rr - r^{-1} Q_r + m_delta Q_r, Q(0, t) = 0, Q(., s_0) = min{G, M(s_0) r}, Q_r >= 0 (pathwise comparison of the representing diffusions started at ordered points), and Q(r, sigma) = E_r[Q(R_{h_0}, s_0); tau_0 > h_0] <= G P_r(tau_0 > h_0), where R solves dR_v = 2^{1/2} db_v + (m_delta(R_v, sigma - v) - 1/R_v) dv, R_0 = r, and tau_0 is its first zero. With calL := d_t + u^r d_r + u^z d_z - (d_rr - r^{-1} d_r + d_zz) one has calL Gamma = 0 and calL Q = (m_delta + u^r) Q_r >= 0, so the maximum principle with the growing barrier gives |Gamma| <= Q on R^3 x [s_0, sigma], and
 |Gamma(r, z, sigma)| <= G P_r(tau_0 > h_0).   (36.2)
Step 2 (two clocks). The process time v in (0, h_0] corresponds to the physical time sigma - v >= T_* - 2 h_0. Since C is nonincreasing and T_* - sigma + v >= v, (I) gives v^{1/2} g(sigma - v) <= C(T_* - sigma + v) (v/(T_* - sigma + v))^{1/2} <= C(v), and (S) gives v k(sigma - v) <= alpha v/(T_* - sigma + v) <= alpha. In the logarithmic time l := log v, Y_l := R_v/v^{1/2} solves dY = 2^{1/2} dB_l + (v^{1/2} m_delta(v^{1/2} Y, sigma - v) - Y/2 - 1/Y) dl with a Brownian motion B. Let r < min{1, h_0/4}, l_0 := log r, l_1 := log(h_0/2), and choose delta := 1/(2 h_0^{1/2} C(r)). Then, for l in [l_0, l_1], v^{1/2} m_delta <= min{alpha Y, Ctil(l)} with Ctil(l) := C(e^l) + 1/C(r), and C(e^l) <= Ctil(l) <= C(e^l) + 1/C(e^l). So, by pathwise comparison with the same noise, Y is dominated until its absorption by the diffusion Ybar with drift b_l(y) := min{Ctil(l), alpha y} - y/2 - 1/y, absorbed at 0.
Step 3 (terminal window). On process times v in [h_0/2, h_0], m_delta <= k(sigma - v) R, so R is dominated by the pure-strain process Rtil, dRtil = 2^{1/2} db + (k(sigma - v) Rtil - 1/Rtil) dv. By Ito's formula Z := Rtil^2 solves dZ = 2 (2 Z)^{1/2} db + 2 k(sigma - v) Z dv (the Bessel drift and the Ito correction cancel), and exp(-Z_v/(4 thetahat(v))) is a bounded martingale when thetahat' = 2 k(sigma - v) thetahat - 1, thetahat(h_0) = 0, that is thetahat(v) = int_v^{h_0} exp(-2 int_v^w k(sigma - w') dw') dw. Letting v -> h_0 (reverse Fatou) gives P_x(Rtil survives [h_0/2, h_0]) <= 1 - exp(-x^2/(4 theta)), theta := thetahat(h_0/2), and (S) gives int_{h_0/2}^w k(sigma - w') dw' <= alpha log 2, so theta >= (h_0/2) 4^{-alpha}. Hence the terminal survival function u_T(y) := P(survival over [h_0/2, h_0] | R_{h_0/2} = y (h_0/2)^{1/2}) satisfies u_T(y) <= min{1, K_T y^2}, K_T := 4^{alpha - 1}, uniformly in sigma and z, and, splitting (0, infinity) at 1 and at C/alpha,
 int_0^infty u_T^2 W_C dy <= N_T := K_T^2/4 + 2 pi^{1/2} + sup_{C' > 0} e^{-rho^2 C'^2} log_+(C'/alpha) < infinity for every C > 0.   (36.3)
Let ubar(l, y) := E[u_T(Ybar_{l_1}); Ybar survives [l, l_1] | Ybar_l = y]. By the Markov property at v_0 := r and the domination of Step 2, P_r(tau_0 > h_0) <= E[ubar(l_0, Y_{l_0}); tau_0 > v_0], because u_T is nondecreasing (starting-point comparison); ubar(l, .) is nondecreasing for the same reason, and ubar <= 1.
Step 4 (proof of (a)). The weighted Hardy inequality: for a positive locally bounded weight q on (0, infinity) with A(x) := int_0^x q^{-1}, M(x) := int_x^infty q and B := sup_x A(x) M(x) < infinity, one has int f^2 q <= 4 B int f'^2 q for f in C_c^infty(0, infinity) (Cauchy-Schwarz with the weight q A^{1/2} and an integration by parts, as in the proof of Proposition 31), so lambda_1 >= 1/(4B); and lambda_1 <= 1/(A(x) M(x)) for every x, by the trial function min{A/A(x), 1}, for weights comparable to 1/y near 0 and with Gaussian decay at infinity (so that the trial function lies in the form domain), which is the case here. Apply this to q = y^{-1} e^{psi_C} (lambda_1 does not depend on the normalization). For alpha >= 1, with kappa_0 := min{a, C^2}: A(2C) <= 1/a + 16/C^2 <= 17/kappa_0 (psi_C >= C y/4 on [C/alpha, 2C] by concavity of the difference); M(kappa_0^{-1/2}) <= 7 e^H/C (psi_C <= H - C^2/4 on [kappa_0^{-1/2}, C], Gaussian tail beyond); on (0, kappa_0^{-1/2}) one has 0 <= psi_C <= 1, and beyond 2C the product A M is bounded by A(2C) e^H pi^{1/2}/(2C) + 8, using the Gaussian product bound (int_0^D e^{w^2/4} dw)(int_D^infty e^{-z^2/4} dz) <= 8 for D >= 0. Altogether B <= 120 e^H/(C kappa_0), and the trial function at x = kappa_0^{-1/2} gives lambda_1 <= 5 e^{5/4} C kappa_0 e^{-H}; since C kappa_0/2 <= P <= C kappa_0, the bounds for alpha >= 1 follow. For 1/2 < alpha < 1: psi_C >= rho C y/2 on [C/alpha, 2C] and psi_C <= H - (rho/4)(y - 2C)^2 on (0, infinity), which give B <= 8 D_alpha e^H/C with D_alpha := (1/a + 1/rho^2)/rho <= 3/(2 a^3), hence the lower bound, and the trial function at x = 1 gives the upper bound. For the bound lambda_1 <= 1, the function h(y) = y^2 lies in calD_C and int h'^2 W_C = -int h L_C h W_C = int y^4 W_C - 2 int y^3 min{C, alpha y} W_C <= int h^2 W_C. For the parameter shift, H(C') - H(C) = rho (C' - C)(C' + C) <= 6 when C' <= C + 2/C, and P is increasing in C, so the lower bound at C' and the upper bound at C give lambda_1(C') >= c_0 lambda_1(C).
Step 5 (starting-state lemma). By (a), Lambda(w) <= Lambda(v) + log(v/w) for w <= v. Under (T') put eps(v) := sup_{0 < w <= v} C(w)^2/Lambda(w) -> 0. Since dw/(2 (v w)^{1/2}) is a probability measure on (0, v), Jensen's inequality gives Cbar(v)^2 <= int_0^v C(w)^2 dw/(2 (v w)^{1/2}) <= eps(v) (Lambda(v) + 2), so Cbar^2 = o(Lambda). Also, by the lower bounds of (a) and C(e^l) <= C(r) for l >= l_0, lambda_1(C(e^l)) >= k_alpha e^{-rho C(r)^2} with k_alpha := P(2)/480 (alpha >= 1) or a^3/24 (alpha < 1), so Lambda(r) >= k_alpha e^{-rho C(r)^2} (L_1(r) - log(2/h_0)) and L_2(r) <= rho C(r)^2 + log Lambda(r) + O(1) = o(Lambda(r)) under (T').
Step 6 (blocks and frozen estimates; proof of (b)). Define levels C_0 := Ctil(l_0) = C(r) + 1/C(r) and C_{j+1} := C_j - delta_j with delta_j := min{1/(2 C_j), (2 alpha - 1) C_j}, stopped at the first K with C_{K+1} < Ctil(l_1); then sum_j delta_j <= C_0, C_{K+1} > 7/4 and K + 1 <= K_* := 2 C_0^2 + C_0/(2 alpha - 1) + 1. Let l_j be the first time in [l_0, l_1] with Ctil(l) <= C_j, and l_{K+1} := l_1. On block j, C(e^l) <= C_j <= C(e^l) + 2/C(e^l), so lambda_1(C_j) >= c_0 lambda_1(C(e^l)) by (a), and the frozen drift min{C_j, alpha y} - y/2 - 1/y dominates b_l. For the frozen autonomous operator L_{C_j}, which is symmetric in L^2(W_{C_j}), the backward solution u with nonnegative terminal data satisfies d/dl int u^2 W_{C_j} = 2 int (d_y u)^2 W_{C_j} >= 2 lambda_1(C_j) int u^2 W_{C_j}; on truncations (eps, n) with zero Dirichlet data this is integrated in l, which gives int u(l)^2 W_{C_j} <= exp(-2 lambda_1(C_j)(l' - l)) int u(l')^2 W_{C_j} for l < l' when the terminal data have finite weighted L^2 norm, and this integrated inequality, which is the estimate used below, passes to the limit (eps, n) -> (0, infinity) through the killed representation and Fatou's lemma (W_{C_j} and its derivative are continuous at y = C_j/alpha, where the drift has a kink, so no interface term arises). With calN_j := int ubar(l_j, y)^2 W_{C_j}(y) dy and Delta_j := l_{j+1} - l_j, domination and monotonicity give calN_j <= e^{-2 lambda_1(C_j) Delta_j} int ubar(l_{j+1})^2 W_{C_j}. The weights compare as W_{C_j} <= W_{C_{j+1}} e^{delta_j (y - 2 C_{j+1})_+} (explicit formula for log(W_{C_1}/W_{C_2}), using delta_j <= min{1/4, (2 alpha - 1)(C_j + C_{j+1})}), so for every zeta_0 >= 2, using ubar <= 1 and the Gaussian form of W_{C_{j+1}} beyond 2 C_{j+1} + zeta_0,
 calN_j <= exp(-2 lambda_1(C_j) Delta_j + delta_j zeta_0) (calN_{j+1} + e^{-zeta_0^2/4}),   calN_{K+1} <= N_T (by (36.3)).
Iterating, with sum_j lambda_1(C_j) Delta_j >= c_0 Lambda(r) and zeta_0 := 2 (log K_* + c_0 Lambda(r))^{1/2},
 calN_0 <= (N_T + 1) exp(2 C_0 (log K_*)^{1/2} + 2 C_0 (c_0 Lambda(r))^{1/2} - c_0 Lambda(r)) = (N_T + 1) exp(-c_0 Lambda(r) + o(Lambda(r))),   (36.4)
the last step by (T') (C_0^2 = o(Lambda), log K_* = O(log C_0)). Starting state: on {tau_0 > v_0}, dropping the drift -1/R and using m_delta <= g + 2 delta and Step 2, R_{v_0} <= r + 2^{1/2} b_{v_0} + 2 v_0^{1/2} Cbar(v_0) + 2 delta v_0, so Y_{l_0} <= 2^{1/2} N_0 + 2 Cbar(r) + 2 with N_0 := b_{v_0}/v_0^{1/2} standard normal (r < 1, 2 delta v_0^{1/2} <= 1). For x_0 > 0 put y_* := 2 C_0 + 2 (Cbar(r) - C(r)) + 2^{1/2} x_0 + 2 (>= C_0/alpha); as ubar(l_0, .) is nondecreasing and W_{C_0}(y) = y^{-1} e^{-(y - 2 C_0)^2/4} for y >= C_0/alpha,
 P_r(tau_0 > h_0) <= P(N_0 > x_0) + ubar(l_0, y_*) <= P(N_0 > x_0) + ( calN_0 (y_* + 1) exp((2 (Cbar(r) - C(r)) + 2^{1/2} x_0 + 3)^2/4) )^{1/2}.   (36.5)
Define S^T(r) as the minimum of 1 and the infimum over x_0 > 0 of the right side of (36.5) with (36.4) inserted, for r < min{1, h_0/4}, and S^T(r) := 1 otherwise; it depends only on C, h_0 and alpha. By Step 5 and (36.4), for fixed x_0 the second term is exp(-c_0 Lambda(r)/2 + o(Lambda(r))) -> 0, so S^T(r) -> 0; with x_0 := (c_0 Lambda(r))^{1/2}, P(N_0 > x_0) <= e^{-c_0 Lambda/2} and the second term is exp(-c_0 Lambda/4 + o(Lambda)), which gives S^T(r) <= K_1 e^{-c_1 Lambda(r)} for every c_1 < c_0/4. With (36.2), (b) follows.
Step 7 (proof of (c)). Here no blocks are used. In the centered coordinate x := y - 2 Ctil(l) take the weight m(l, x) := 2 Ctil(l) W_{Ctil(l)}(x + 2 Ctil(l)), which equals (2 Ctil/(x + 2 Ctil)) e^{-x^2/4} for x >= 0; by (W2) the change of variables is a C^1 translation, and ubar solves ubar_l + ubar_xx + (b_l - 2 Ctil') ubar_x = 0 with (log m)_x = b_l. For calN(l) := int ubar^2 m dx and calD(l) := int ubar_x^2 m dx, computed first for the solutions of the zero Dirichlet problems on fixed y-intervals (eps, n), that is on the moving x-intervals (eps - 2 Ctil(l), n - 2 Ctil(l)), with nonnegative terminal data increasing to those of ubar (the moving-boundary terms vanish because the boundary values are zero, and the integrated inequality below passes to the limit through the killed representation and Fatou's lemma),
 calN' = 2 calD + 4 Ctil' int ubar ubar_x m dx + int ubar^2 d_l m dx,
where d_l log m >= 0 for x < 0 and d_l log m = Ctil' x/(Ctil y) >= -|Ctil'| x/(2 Ctil^2) for x >= 0, and the Gaussian moment bound int_{x > 0} x ubar^2 m <= 3 calN + 4 (calN calD)^{1/2} holds. Absorbing with h := |Ctil'| = |d_l C(e^l)| and using calD >= lambda_1(Ctil(l)) calN (variational definition at fixed l) and Ctil >= 2,
 calN' >= [lambda_1(Ctil(l)) - (81/16) h^2 - 3 h/(2 Ctil^2)] calN,   hence   calN(l) <= calN(l_1) exp(-Lambdatil(l) + (81/16) int_l^{l_1} h^2 + 3/(2 Ctil(l_1))),
with Lambdatil(l) := int_l^{l_1} lambda_1(Ctil) >= c_0 int_l^{l_1} lambda_1(C(e^s)) ds by (a), and calN(l_1) <= 2 Ctil(l_1) N_T by (36.3). The estimate for the squared weighted norm calN has the spectral factor e^{-Lambdatil(l_0)}; taking its square root gives the pointwise factor e^{-Lambdatil(l_0)/2} <= e^{-c_0 Lambda(r)/2}. Precisely, ubar(l_0, x)^2 <= calN(l_0)/j_x with j_x := int_x^{x+1} m dx' >= (4/(x + 5)) e^{-(x+1)^2/4} for x >= 0.
