Since p(s) <= p(s/2), (iv) gives (p(s/2)^2/(p(s) + eps)) (lambda_ax(s) - 8/(c_ent^2 s))_+^2 <= (4 s/e) J_ent(s) for almost every s >= 1; divide by s, integrate over [1, T] and use (iii). The weight is at least p_infinity^2/(p_infinity + eps) (x^2/(x + eps) increases), and (1/log T) int_1^T p ds/s -> p_infinity, so limsup_T (1/log T) int_1^T (lambda_ax - 8/(c_ent^2 s))_+^2 ds/s <= (4/e)(3 + 2 K/c_ent)(1 + eps/p_infinity). With lambda_ax^2 <= (1 + delta)(lambda_ax - 8/(c_ent^2 s))_+^2 + (1 + 1/delta) 64/(c_ent^4 s^2) for delta > 0, and letting delta, eps -> 0 and c_ent -> infinity after T -> infinity, the bound 12/e follows. The remaining statements follow from (c) and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality as indicated.
Scope of (e). It concerns the auxiliary strain a_eta, built from the driftless representation of eta, along the paths of a drifted killed diffusion; it does not estimate the strain a = U^R/R of the field, and for the limits a_U and eta are coupled to the same velocity (Remark (7)), so (e) does not give the hypothesis of Remark (2) for the limits. It shows that incompressibility and survival bounded below supply, in logarithmic average, the additional information on the law required at the end of (c); a bound on lambda_ax(s) uniform in s does not hold in this class (J_ent is controlled only in integral over the ages): the example of sparse peaks at the end of Remark (9)(c) has p(s) > 1/100 for every s and lambda_ax(s_n^pk) -> infinity along ages in windows of summable logarithmic length, and for the class defined by (40.5) and the mass alone the logarithmic-average form fails by (d). Without incompressibility the statement fails (Remark (9)(c)); the proof uses p_infinity > 0 only through the weight p(s/2)^2/(p(s) + eps), and for fields with p(s) -> 0 it gives only the weighted inequality of (v). For a general viscosity nu, the time change Xtilde(tau) := X(tau/nu), with the field U_mer(., -tau/nu)/nu, reduces to nu = 1 and preserves the hypotheses; since logarithmic averages are unchanged by a fixed rescaling of the age, the same bound 12/e holds for E[log_+(4 nu s/R_s^2); zeta > s]/p(s/2). The laws of the limits satisfy these hypotheses: a bounded mild ancient solution has bounded derivatives of every order, and record survival gives p_infinity >= 1/A.
(9) (Eternal paths and a pathwise absorption criterion.) Work in the setting of statement (b) of Proposition 40, with nu > 0, and put Sv := {zeta = infinity}. On Sv define
 calI_t := int_0^t R_u^{-2} du,
 calF_t := int_1^t log_+(4 nu u/R_u^2) du/u   (t >= 1).
The smoothness and boundedness assumptions on U and a = U^R/R are retained. Parts (a), (d) and (e) use no incompressibility or evolution equation. Part (f) concerns the limits and additionally uses their bounded smooth circulation, its circulation equation, its zero trace on the axis, and the normalization Gamma_U(e_1, 0) = 1. The proof of (f) does not use the source-budget hypotheses of Proposition 40. Parts (b) and (c) prescribe examples of fields; neither example is asserted to solve the Navier-Stokes equations.
(a) (Two kinds of eternal paths.) Before killing, Ito's formula and the definitions of J and Y in Step 7 give
 d log Y = (2 nu)^{1/2} R^{-1} dB - 2 nu R^{-2} du,
 log Y_t = log R_0 + (2 nu)^{1/2} calN_t - 2 nu calI_t,
 calN_t := int_0^t R_u^{-1} dB_u,   <calN>_t = calI_t.
These martingale statements are made before conditioning on Sv, with localization away from the axis. If calI_infinity < infinity, the continuous local martingale calN converges to a finite value. If calI_infinity = infinity, its Brownian clock and the Brownian strong law give calN_t/calI_t -> 0. Thus on Sv the finite limit Y_infinity exists, and, up to null sets,
 Sv_+ := Sv cap {Y_infinity > 0}
       = Sv cap {calI_infinity < infinity},
 Sv_0 := Sv cap {Y_infinity = 0}
       = Sv cap {calI_infinity = infinity}.
No conditioning of a martingale law on Sv is used here.
Since log_+ x <= x, on Sv_+ one has
 calF_infinity <= 4 nu int_1^infinity R_u^{-2} du
                <= 4 nu calI_infinity < infinity,
 int_1^infinity 1_{R_u < d u^{1/2}} du/u
                <= d^2 calI_infinity < infinity   (d > 0).
The latter conclusion means finite occupation measure du/u in each fixed parabolic tube, not eventual avoidance. In particular, the pointwise envelope of Remark (7), with nu = 1, gives for its auxiliary strain along the paths of any such field U
 limsup_{t -> infinity} (1/log t)
   int_1^t |a_eta(X_u,-u)| du
   <= (k_e C^2/4)(1 + 2 log 2)
    = 0.144353343869... C^2
on Sv_+.
If, almost surely on Sv_+, for u >= 1,
 a^-(X_u,-u) <= (c/u)(b + log_+(4 nu u/R_u^2)) + e_path(u),
where c,b >= 0, cb < 1/2 and e_path >= 0 is integrable, then
 calH_t <= cb log t + c calF_infinity
            + int_0^1 a^-(X_u,-u) du + int_1^infinity e_path(u) du
there. This contradicts calH_t - (1/2) log t -> infinity from statement (b) of Proposition 40. Hence P(Sv_+) = 0. This argument alone gives no exclusion of Sv_0.
(b) (Positive logarithmic occupation for a bounded incompressible field.) Let r_c := 1/4. Choose a smooth function g_r of R^2 with g_r = O(R^2) at zero, 0 <= g_r <= 1 and g_r = 1 for R >= r_c. Choose a smooth even chi_a equal to one on [-1,1] and zero outside (-2,2). For a constant Z_c > 0 to be chosen, put
 w_rz := Z/[Z_c(1 + R^2)],   Psi := 4 nu Z g_r(R) chi_a(w_rz),
 U^R := -Psi_Z/R
      = -(4 nu g_r/R)(chi_a(w_rz) + w_rz chi_a'(w_rz)),
 U^Z := Psi_R/R
      = (4 nu Z g_r'/R) chi_a(w_rz)
        - 8 nu Z^2 g_r chi_a'(w_rz)/[Z_c(1 + R^2)^2],
 U^theta := 0.
Mixed derivatives give (1/R) d_R(R U^R) + d_Z U^Z = 0. Near the axis Psi is R^2 times a smooth function of (R^2,Z), so the velocity extends smoothly as a Cartesian vector field. The first term of U^Z has bounded support in both R and Z. Its second term equals -8 nu Z_c g_r w_rz^2 chi_a'(w_rz). This is bounded, and derivatives of w_rz are bounded on the relevant supports away from the axis. Together with the smooth axis representation and the factor g_r/R in U^R, these observations prove boundedness of the field, all its derivatives and a = U^R/R.
On
 calD := {R > r_c, |Z| < Z_c(1 + R^2)}
the field is -4 nu e_R/R. The killed diffusion there satisfies
 dR = (2 nu)^{1/2} dB + 3 nu R^{-1} du,
 dZ = (2 nu)^{1/2} dB'.
Let W_4 be standard four-dimensional Brownian motion, let W_z be an independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motion, and set
 x_ref := (1,0,0,0),
 R_u^* := |x_ref + (2 nu)^{1/2} W_4(u)|,
 Z_u^* := (2 nu)^{1/2} W_z(u).
Ito's formula for the norm gives these reference equations with a radial Brownian driver independent of W_z.
Optional stopping of (R^*)^{-2} between radii r_lo and r_hi gives, after r_hi -> infinity,
 P_r(inf_{u >= 0} R_u^* <= r_lo) = (r_lo/r)^2
   for 0 < r_lo < r.
Exit from each bounded annulus is almost surely finite: over each unit interval an independent Brownian increment has a fixed positive probability of leaving its enclosing ball. Thus the optional stopping is justified. In particular, the reference path never hits zero and
 P(inf_{u >= 0} R_u^* <= 1/4) = 1/16.
Gaussian integration also gives
 E[(R_t^*)^{-2}] = 1 - exp(-1/(4 nu t)) <= 1/(4 nu t).
The Markov property and the hitting formula imply
 P(inf_{u >= 2^n} R_u^* <= 2^{3(n+1)/8})
   <= 2^{3(n+1)/4} E[(R_{2^n}^*)^{-2}]
   <= C_nu 2^{-n/4}.
The series is finite. Brownian reflection likewise bounds
 P(sup_{0 <= u <= 2^{n+1}} |Z_u^*| > 2^{5n/8})
   <= 4 exp(-2^{n/4}/(8 nu)).
Borel-Cantelli therefore gives R_u^* >= u^{3/8} and |Z_u^*| <= u^{5/8} for all sufficiently large u, almost surely. Consequently |Z_u^*|/[1 + (R_u^*)^2] tends to zero and has finite supremum.
Choose a deterministic Z_c so large that
 P(sup_{u >= 0} |Z_u^*|/[1 + (R_u^*)^2] >= Z_c) < 1/16.
Then the event
 calG := {inf_{u >= 0} R_u^* > 1/4,
          sup_{u >= 0} |Z_u^*|/[1 + (R_u^*)^2] < Z_c}
has probability greater than 7/8. Drive the killed diffusion from (1,0) by the radial and axial Brownian drivers of this reference process. Local pathwise uniqueness identifies the two processes until exit from calD. On calG there is no exit, so the killed diffusion survives forever and a = -4 nu/R^2 along it.
For the reference radius,
 log R_t^* = (2 nu)^{1/2} int_0^t (R_u^*)^{-1} dB_u^*
              + 2 nu int_0^t (R_u^*)^{-2} du.
If the last integral had a finite limit, martingale convergence would make log R_t^* converge to a finite real value. The radius would then converge to a positive finite value, contradicting finiteness of that integral. Hence calI_infinity = infinity on calG. Part (a) gives calG subset Sv_0, up to null sets, and P(Sv_0) > 7/8.
To compute the logarithmic axis moment, put
 O_v := exp(-v/2) W_4(exp v),   v in R,
 h_4(y) := log_+(2/|y|^2).
The centered Gaussian process O is stationary with covariance exp(-|v-v'|/2) times the identity. Cross covariances between finite collections separated by a large shift tend to zero, so Gaussian finite-dimensional distributions factor in the limit; approximation by cylinder events gives mixing and hence ergodicity. The function h_4 is integrable for the standard Gaussian law.
The starting point contributes the deterministic shift
 b_v := x_ref exp(-v/2)/(2 nu)^{1/2}.
The weak gradient of h_4 has magnitude 2/|y| on |y| < sqrt(2) and is zero outside, so it is integrable on R^4. The L^1 translation inequality and the bounded Gaussian density give
 E|h_4(O_v+b_v) - h_4(O_v)|
   <= (2 pi)^{-2} |b_v| int_{R^4} |grad h_4(y)| dy.
This is integrable over v >= 0. Tonelli gives a finite total absolute difference almost surely. The ergodic theorem, followed by u = exp v, therefore yields on calG
 calF_t/log t -> m_4
   := E[log_+(2/|N_4|^2)]
    = int_0^1 (-log x) x exp(-x) dx
    = 0.164479040468...,
where N_4 is a standard Gaussian vector in R^4 and |N_4|^2/2 has density x exp(-x). The almost-sure statement is proved for the reference process before restriction to calG.
Thus Sv_0 can carry a positive limiting weighted logarithmic occupation. Fatou's lemma gives
 liminf_{t -> infinity} E[calF_t; zeta = infinity]/log t
   >= m_4 P(calG) > (7/8) m_4 > 0.1439.
In particular, no estimate E[calF_t; zeta = infinity] <= delta log t + C_delta with finite C_delta and delta < 0.1439 holds for every smooth bounded divergence-free field.
For completeness, the same dyadic estimates with any lower radial exponent below 1/2 and any upper exponent above 1/2 give log R_t^*/log t -> 1/2. In the preceding identity for log R_t^*, the martingale divided by its infinite quadratic variation tends to zero. Hence
 calI_t/log t -> 1/(4 nu),   calH_t/log t -> 1
on calG, since calH_t = 4 nu calI_t there. This agrees with statement (b) of Proposition 40.
(c) (Divergence without incompressibility.) Fix c_d > 0. Choose a smooth h_d on the whole real line with 0 <= h_d <= c_d/16 and h_d(r) = nu/r for r >= 32 nu/c_d. Such an extension can be made constant for sufficiently small r and smoothly joined to nu/r where nu/r < c_d/16. Choose a smooth cutoff chi_r with 0 <= chi_r <= 1, equal to zero for R <= 16 nu/c_d and one for R >= 32 nu/c_d.
For positive H_d,t_d,m_d with t_d >= 16 H_d/c_d, put
 ell_d(u) := m_d + H_d log(1 + u/t_d).
Then 0 <= ell_d' <= c_d/16. On the whole line solve
 dD_d = (2 nu)^{1/2} dB + b_d(u,D_d) du,   D_d(0) = 0,
 b_d(u,x) := -c_d tanh x - h_d(ell_d(u)+x) - ell_d'(u).
The drift has magnitude at most 9 c_d/8 and points towards zero with magnitude at least c_d/2 for |x| >= 2. It is locally Lipschitz, and bounded drift gives global existence.
Fix theta_d := c_d/(16 nu) and put
 Phi_d(x) := exp(theta_d sqrt(1+x^2)).
For the generator calL_{d,u},
 (calL_{d,u} Phi_d)(x)/Phi_d(x)
   = nu theta_d/(1+x^2)^(3/2)
     + nu theta_d^2 x^2/(1+x^2)
     + theta_d x b_d(u,x)/sqrt(1+x^2).
The last term is uniformly negative for large |x|, and dominates the first two there. On the remaining compact interval the expression is uniformly bounded. Thus
 calL_{d,u} Phi_d <= -eta_d Phi_d + C_d^lyap
for positive constants depending only on c_d and nu. Stopped Ito's formula with an integrating factor gives
 E Phi_d(D_d(u))
   <= exp(-eta_d u) Phi_d(0)
      + (C_d^lyap/eta_d)(1 - exp(-eta_d u)).
Stopping can be removed because bounded drift and Brownian maxima give finite exponential moments on each bounded time interval.
For n <= u <= n+1,
 |D_d(u)| <= |D_d(n)| + 9 c_d/8
             + (2 nu)^{1/2} sup_{n <= v <= n+1}|B_v-B_n|.
The preceding exponential moment and Brownian reflection therefore give constants C_d^tail,lambda_d > 0, depending only on c_d and nu, such that
 P(sup_{n <= u <= n+1}|D_d(u)| > r_tail)
   <= C_d^tail exp(-lambda_d r_tail)   (r_tail >= 0).
Indeed, for r_tail >= 4(9 c_d/8), split at |D_d(n)| = r_tail/2 and at a Brownian contribution r_tail/4; enlarge the constant for smaller r_tail.
Choose H_d so that lambda_d H_d/2 > 1, set t_d := 16 H_d/c_d, and then choose m_d >= 64 nu/c_d so large that
 C_d^tail exp(-lambda_d m_d/2)
   sum_{n >= 0}(1+n/t_d)^{-lambda_d H_d/2} < 1.
The series is finite and its parameters have already been fixed. Since ell_d is increasing, the union bound gives positive probability to
 calG_d := {|D_d(u)| <= ell_d(u)/2 for every u >= 0}.
Now prescribe
 U^R(R,Z,-u) := c_d chi_r(R) tanh(R-ell_d(u)),
 U^Z := 0,   U^theta := 0.
It vanishes near the axis, is smooth and bounded with bounded spatial and age derivatives, and has bounded a. It is not divergence-free: for large R its radial divergence is positive while its axial divergence is zero. The killed diffusion from (m_d,0), driven by the same B, agrees with R_u = ell_d(u)+D_d(u) while this radius is above 32 nu/c_d. On calG_d it stays in that region for all ages, so
 ell_d(u)/2 <= R_u <= 3 ell_d(u)/2,
 p_infinity >= P(calG_d) > 0.
Since ell_d(u) = H_d log u + O(1), uniformly over calG_d,
 log_+(4 nu u/R_u^2) = log u - 2 log log u + O(1).
In particular, for one deterministic finite constant C_d^mom and all sufficiently large s,
 E[log_+(4 nu s/R_s^2); zeta > s]
   >= P(calG_d)(log s - 2 log log s - C_d^mom).
As p(s/2) <= 1, this proves
 E[log_+(4 nu s/R_s^2); zeta > s]/p(s/2) -> infinity.
Thus positive eternal survival and the bounds on U and a alone do not bound this normalized moment. For nu = 1, Remark (8)(e) bounds the logarithmic time average of this normalized moment by (12/e)^{1/2} for the prescribed incompressible fields specified there. The same bound applies to a start (r_0, 0), r_0 > 0: the rescaling U_new(r, z, -u) := r_0 U(r_0 r, r_0 z, -r_0^2 u) gives a start (1, 0), preserves the viscosity and the required field bounds, and makes the normalized moment at the age u equal to the original normalized moment at the age r_0^2 u. Its limiting logarithmic average is unchanged. Part (b) shows that incompressibility does not force calF_t/log t to vanish on the eternal event. The logarithmic average in Remark (8)(e) cannot be replaced by a bound at every large age, as the following example shows.
Sparse peaks for incompressible fields. Let nu = 1. There is a prescribed meridional field U_mer satisfying all hypotheses of Remark (8)(e), with |U_mer| <= 24992, for which the killed diffusion from (1, 0) has p(s) > 1/100 for every s >= 0 and
 lambda_ax(s_n^pk) >= (log 2/100)(4n - 57/8)_+,   s_n^pk := 2^{32n} + 2^{26n}   (n >= 1);
moreover |U^R(R, Z, -s)| <= 14 R/s^{1/2} for s >= 1, so a two-sided bound on the radial velocity, linear in R with the coefficient 14/s^{1/2}, does not restore a bound at every large age.
Construction. Let phi_pk(x) := exp(1 - 1/(1 - (x - 1)^2)) for 0 < x < 2 and phi_pk(x) := 0 otherwise. It is smooth, 0 <= phi_pk <= 1 and phi_pk(1) = 1; with y := x - 1 and w := (1 - y^2)^{-1} >= 1, |phi_pk'(x)| = 2|y| w^2 e^{1-w} <= 2e max_{w >= 1} w^2 e^{-w} = 8/e. Put I_pk := int_0^2 phi_pk(x) dx and let chi_pk be the even function equal to 1 on [-1, 1], to 1 - I_pk^{-1} int_0^{2(|x|-1)} phi_pk(y) dy for 1 < |x| < 2, and to 0 for |x| >= 2. It is smooth with 0 <= chi_pk <= 1, and |chi_pk'| <= 2/I_pk <= 2 e^{1/3} < 3 because phi_pk >= e^{-1/3} on [1/2, 3/2]. For n >= 1 put
 t_n^pk := 2^{32n},   d_n^pk := 2^{26n} = (t_n^pk)^{13/16},   b_n^pk := (1/8) log(1 + t_n^pk),   I_n^pk := [t_n^pk, t_n^pk + 2 d_n^pk];
these intervals are disjoint, since 2 d_n^pk/t_n^pk = 2^{1-6n} and t_{n+1}^pk = 2^{32} t_n^pk. For s >= 0 let
 a_pk(s) := (1 + s)^{9/16} exp(-sum_{n >= 1} b_n^pk phi_pk((s - t_n^pk)/d_n^pk)),
 beta_pk := a_pk'/a_pk,   h_pk(s) := (1 + s)^{53/32}/a_pk(s)^2,   r_pk := 16 a_pk,   z_pk := 128 h_pk,
and define U_s through the stream function Psi_pk(R, Z, s) := beta_pk(s) R^2 Z chi_pk(R/r_pk(s)) chi_pk(Z/z_pk(s)) by U_s^R := -R^{-1} d_Z Psi_pk and U_s^Z := R^{-1} d_R Psi_pk. With u := R/r_pk(s) and v := Z/z_pk(s),
 U_s^R = -beta_pk R chi_pk(u)(chi_pk(v) + v chi_pk'(v)),
 U_s^Z = beta_pk Z chi_pk(v)(2 chi_pk(u) + u chi_pk'(u)).
In the cylinder C_pk(s) := {R < r_pk(s), |Z| < z_pk(s)} this is the stagnation field U_s^R = -beta_pk R, U_s^Z = 2 beta_pk Z. Only the ages s >= 0 enter the diffusion. To define the field at all times, put theta_pk(w) := chi_pk(-4w) for w <= 0 and theta_pk(w) := 1 for w >= 0, and q_pk(s) := 1 + int_0^s theta_pk(w) dw. Then q_pk is smooth, q_pk >= 1/2, 0 <= q_pk' <= 1, q_pk(s) = 1 + s for s >= -1/4, and q_pk is constant for s <= -1/2. For s < 0 put a_pk := q_pk^{9/16}, h_pk := q_pk^{53/32}/a_pk^2 and beta_pk := a_pk'/a_pk, and define U_s by the same stream function, without pulses; for -1/4 <= s < 0 this agrees with the formulas above. For s < 0, |beta_pk| a_pk = (9/16) q_pk' q_pk^{-7/16} <= (9/16) 2^{7/16} < 1 and |beta_pk| h_pk = (9/16) q_pk' q_pk^{-15/32} <= (9/16) 2^{15/32} < 1, so the velocity bound 24992 of (i) persists; r_pk >= 16 2^{-9/16} and z_pk >= 128 2^{-17/32} stay bounded away from zero, and all mixed space-age derivatives are bounded for s < 0, because U_s = 0 for s <= -1/2 (beta_pk = 0 there) and U_s is smooth in (x, s) with support in a fixed compact set for -1/2 <= s <= 0.
(i) Bounds. On I_n^pk one has a_pk^2 >= (1 + s)^{9/8}(1 + t_n^pk)^{-1/4} >= (1 + s)^{7/8}, and a_pk = (1 + s)^{9/16} off these intervals; hence
 (1 + s)^{7/16} <= a_pk <= (1 + s)^{9/16},   (1 + s)^{17/32} <= h_pk <= (1 + s)^{25/32},   r_pk >= 16,   z_pk >= 128.
Put beta_0(s) := 9/(16(1 + s)), so that beta_0 a_pk <= 9/16 and beta_0 h_pk <= 9/16. On I_n^pk, with x := t_n^pk, one has 1 + s <= 2x and |beta_pk - beta_0| = b_n^pk |phi_pk'|/d_n^pk <= (3/8) log(1 + x) x^{-13/16}; with log(1 + x) <= 1 + log x and sup_{x >= 1} x^{-delta} log x = 1/(e delta) this gives
 |beta_pk - beta_0| a_pk <= (3/4)(1 + log x) x^{-1/4} <= (3/4)(1 + 4/e),
 |beta_pk - beta_0| h_pk <= (3/4)(1 + log x) x^{-1/32} <= (3/4)(1 + 32/e).
Hence |beta_pk| a_pk <= 11 and |beta_pk| h_pk <= 11 for all s >= 0. The support of U_s lies in {R <= 2 r_pk, |Z| <= 2 z_pk}, so |U_s^R| <= 7 |beta_pk| R <= 14 |beta_pk| r_pk <= 2464 and |U_s^Z| <= 8 |beta_pk| |Z| <= 16 |beta_pk| z_pk <= 22528, which gives |U_mer| <= 24992. Near the axis chi_pk(u) = 1, so U^R e_R is -beta_pk (chi_pk(v) + v chi_pk'(v)) times the Cartesian vector (x_1, x_2), and U^Z = 2 beta_pk Z chi_pk(v) does not depend on R; thus the field is smooth across the axis, and for R > 0 its divergence R^{-1} d_R(R U^R) + d_Z U^Z = R^{-1}(-d_R d_Z Psi_pk + d_Z d_R Psi_pk) vanishes. For the derivatives write U_s^R = -16 beta_pk a_pk G_R(u, v) and U_s^Z = 128 beta_pk h_pk G_Z(u, v), where G_R(u, v) := u chi_pk(u)(chi_pk(v) + v chi_pk'(v)) and G_Z(u, v) := v chi_pk(v)(2 chi_pk(u) + u chi_pk'(u)) are smooth and supported in [-2, 2]^2. Each derivative in R or Z produces a factor 1/r_pk <= 1/16 or 1/z_pk <= 1/128; each derivative in s acts on u and v through d_s log r_pk = beta_pk and d_s log z_pk = 53/(32(1 + s)) - 2 beta_pk, and on the prefactors through beta_pk and its derivatives. On I_n^pk the j-th derivative of beta_pk - beta_0 is at most b_n^pk ||phi_pk^{(j+1)}||_infinity (d_n^pk)^{-j-1} in absolute value, and with the bounds above this shows that beta_pk^{(j)}, a_pk beta_pk^{(j)} and h_pk beta_pk^{(j)} are bounded for every j. Hence all derivatives of U_mer are bounded.
(ii) Survival of an auxiliary diffusion. Let (Rhat, Zhat) solve, from (1, 0) and with Rhat killed at zero,
 dRhat = (beta_pk Rhat - 1/Rhat) ds + 2^{1/2} dW^1,   dZhat = -2 beta_pk Zhat ds + 2^{1/2} dW^2,
which is the backward diffusion of the proposition at nu = 1 for the stagnation field without cutoffs. Put T_pk(s) := int_0^s a_pk^{-2} and M_pk(s) := 2^{1/2} int_0^s a_pk^2 dW^2. Ito's formula gives Zhat_s = a_pk(s)^{-2} M_pk(s), and Y_pk(T_pk(s)) := Rhat_s/a_pk(s) solves dY_pk = -Y_pk^{-1} dv + 2^{1/2} dB in the clock v = T_pk(s), for the Brownian motion B(T_pk(s)) := int_0^s a_pk^{-1} dW^1; beyond v = T_pk(infinity), continue Y_pk by the same equation with an independent Brownian motion. Then Y_pk starts at 1 and is absorbed at zero, and S := Y_pk^2 satisfies dS = 2(2S)^{1/2} dB: it is a squared Bessel process of dimension zero at the time 2v, hence a nonnegative local martingale, so that P(sup_v S_v >= 256) <= 1/256, and E exp(-theta S_v) = exp(-theta/(1 + 4 theta v)), whence P(Y_pk(v) > 0) = 1 - exp(-1/(4v)). Since a_pk^{-2} <= (1 + t_n^pk)^{-7/8} on I_n^pk and d_n^pk (1 + t_n^pk)^{-7/8} <= 2^{-2n},
 T_pk(infinity) <= int_0^infinity (1 + s)^{-9/8} ds + sum_{n >= 1} 2 d_n^pk (1 + t_n^pk)^{-7/8} <= 8 + 2/3 = 26/3 < 9.
Let E_R^pk := {Y_pk(T_pk(infinity)) > 0, sup_{v <= T_pk(infinity)} Y_pk(v) < 16}. By 1 - e^{-y} >= y/(1 + y), P(E_R^pk) >= 1 - exp(-1/36) - 1/256 >= 1/37 - 1/256, and on E_R^pk, 0 < Rhat_s < r_pk(s) for every s >= 0. By the Ito isometry and a_pk(w) <= (1 + w)^{9/16}, E M_pk(s)^2 = 2 int_0^s a_pk(w)^4 dw <= (8/13)((1 + s)^{13/4} - 1). Let E_Z^pk := {|M_pk(s)| < 128 (1 + s)^{53/32} for every s >= 0}. A violation at some s in [2^j - 1, 2^{j+1} - 1], j >= 0, forces sup_{s' <= 2^{j+1} - 1} |M_pk(s')| >= 128 2^{53j/32}, so Doob's inequality for M_pk^2 and summation over j give
 P((E_Z^pk)^c) <= 128^{-2} (8/13) 2^{13/4} sum_{j >= 0} 2^{-j/16} = 128^{-2} (8/13) 2^{13/4} (1 - 2^{-1/16})^{-1} < 150/16384,
by 2^{1/4} < 6/5 and 1 - 2^{-1/16} > 1/25 (from log 2 > 2/3). On E_Z^pk, |Zhat_s| < 128 h_pk(s) = z_pk(s) for every s. Without any independence, E_pk := E_R^pk cap E_Z^pk satisfies
 P(E_pk) >= 1/37 - 1/256 - 150/16384 = 4233/303104 > 1/100.
(iii) Coupling. Let X be the diffusion of the proposition for U_mer, from (1, 0) and driven by the same W^1, W^2. The two systems have locally Lipschitz coefficients on {R > 0}, and these coincide on the open set {(s, R, Z): s >= 0, 0 < R < r_pk(s), |Z| < z_pk(s)}. On E_pk the auxiliary path stays in this set for all s >= 0, hence on each interval [0, m] in a compact subset of it, and pathwise uniqueness up to the exit from such compact sets gives X_s = (Rhat_s, Zhat_s) on [0, m] for every m. Therefore X is never killed on E_pk, and p(s) >= P(zeta = infinity) >= P(E_pk) > 1/100 for every s >= 0.
(iv) Peaks. At s_n^pk = t_n^pk + d_n^pk only the n-th term of the sum is nonzero, and phi_pk = 1 there, so
 a_pk(s_n^pk)^2 = (1 + s_n^pk)^{9/8} (1 + t_n^pk)^{-1/4} <= 2^{9/8} (t_n^pk)^{7/8}.
On E_pk, R_{s_n^pk}^2 < 256 a_pk(s_n^pk)^2, hence 4 s_n^pk/R_{s_n^pk}^2 > 2^{-57/8} (t_n^pk)^{1/8} = 2^{4n - 57/8}. Since log_+ >= 0 and p(s_n^pk/2) <= 1, lambda_ax(s_n^pk) >= N_ax(s_n^pk) >= P(E_pk)(4n - 57/8)_+ log 2, which proves the claim.
(v) Radial bound. |U_s^R| <= 7 |beta_pk| R. For s >= 1, s^{1/2} beta_0(s) <= 9/32, and on I_n^pk, with x := t_n^pk and s <= 2x, s^{1/2} |beta_pk - beta_0| <= (3 2^{1/2}/8)(1 + log x) x^{-5/16} <= (3 2^{1/2}/8)(1 + 16/(5e)) < 3/2. Hence s^{1/2} |beta_pk(s)| < 2 and |U_s^R| <= 14 R/s^{1/2} for s >= 1.
Mechanism and scope of the example. Outside the windows I_n^pk, the field in C_pk(s) is U^R = -(9/16) R/(1 + s), U^Z = (9/8) Z/(1 + s). The baseline makes the radial clock finite, and the total additional clock cost of the pulses is finite by (ii). On the common event E_pk, R_s/a_pk(s) = Y_pk(T_pk(s)) tends to the positive value Y_pk(T_pk(infinity)); hence R_s/s^{9/16} tends to that value as s tends to infinity outside the windows, while R_{s_n^pk}/(s_n^pk)^{7/16} tends to the same value. Moreover, continuity and absorption give inf_{v <= T_pk(infinity)} Y_pk(v) > 0 on E_pk, so these paths stay a positive distance from the axis. These assertions concern E_pk, not every surviving path. Remark (8)(e) applies to this prescribed field, so its normalized moment has logarithmic mean square at most 12/e. The demonstrated peaks occur at s_n^pk in I_n^pk, whose logarithmic lengths log(1 + 2^{1-6n}) are summable; no assertion is made that every large value of lambda_ax lies in these windows. On E_pk, outside the windows, s a^-(X_s, -s) = 9s/(16(1 + s)) tends to 9/16 > 1/2. Since p_infinity > 0, the field cannot satisfy (40.6) with all the profile and remainder hypotheses of (d). The example rules out a finite bound on lambda_ax uniform over all sufficiently large ages, even if that bound may depend on this field; it makes no claim of failure for a Navier-Stokes limit.
(d) (A pathwise criterion.) Let f_pr be a nonincreasing function from (0,infinity) to [0,infinity) with
 int_0^1 f_pr(x) dx < infinity,   f_inf := lim_{x -> infinity} f_pr(x) < 1/2,
and let e_path be a deterministic nonnegative measurable function with int_1^infinity e_path(u) du < infinity. Assume that, almost surely, for every age u >= 1 before killing,
 a^-(X_u,-u) <= u^{-1} f_pr(R_u^2/(nu u)) + e_path(u).   (40.6)
Then P(zeta = infinity) = 0. For constants c,b >= 0 the profile f_pr(x) = c(b + log_+(4/x)) satisfies these conditions if and only if cb < 1/2, since int_0^1 log_+(4/x) dx = 1 + log 4 and f_inf = cb; there is no additional restriction on the coefficient c of the logarithmic term.
Proof. On {zeta > 1}, put v := log u, xi_v := exp(-v/2) R_{exp v} and alpha_u := a(X_u,-u). Deterministic Brownian time change gives
 d xi = (2 nu)^{1/2} dW_c^0
        - ((1/2 + u alpha_u) xi + nu/xi) dv.
The Brownian motion is constructed in the filtration after age one; its future increments are independent of the information at age one. Set
 eps_c(v) := exp(v) e_path(exp v),
 calE_c(v) := int_0^v eps_c(w) dw,
 M_c := int_1^infinity e_path(u) du,
 delta_c := 1/2 - f_inf > 0.
Then 0 <= calE_c <= M_c, and, since -alpha_u <= a^-(X_u,-u) and R_u^2/u = xi_v^2, (40.6) implies
 -u alpha_u <= f_pr(xi_v^2/nu) + eps_c(v).
Put
 fbar_pr(x) := 2 int_{1/2}^1 f_pr(x t) dt = (2/x) int_{x/2}^x f_pr(y) dy.
Since f_pr is nonincreasing, f_pr <= fbar_pr <= f_pr(./2), and fbar_pr is nonincreasing with fbar_pr - f_inf >= 0 and fbar_pr(x) - f_inf -> 0 as x -> infinity. Since f_pr is bounded on compact subintervals of (0,infinity), the second expression shows that fbar_pr is Lipschitz on each of them. Monotonicity also gives x f_pr(x) <= int_0^x f_pr(y) dy -> 0 as x -> 0, hence x fbar_pr(x) <= 2 (x/2) f_pr(x/2) -> 0, and Tonelli's theorem gives int_0^1 fbar_pr(x) dx <= 2 log 2 int_0^1 f_pr(x) dx < infinity; fbar_pr is integrable on every bounded subinterval of (0,infinity).
Put V_c := exp(-calE_c) xi and use the clock
 sigma_c(v) := int_0^v exp(-2 calE_c(w)) dw.
Its derivative lies in [exp(-2M_c),1], so it tends to infinity. In this clock V_c has diffusion coefficient (2 nu)^{1/2}, and its drift equals
 -nu/V_c - exp(2 calE_c) (1/2 + u alpha_u + eps_c) V_c.
By the preceding inequality for -u alpha_u, this drift is at most
 -nu/V_c - delta_c exp(2 calE_c) V_c
   + exp(2 calE_c) V_c (f_pr(xi^2/nu) - f_inf).
Since xi >= V_c, f_pr is nonincreasing, f_pr <= fbar_pr, f_pr - f_inf >= 0 and 1 <= exp(2 calE_c) <= exp(2 M_c), this is at most d_c(V_c), where
 d_c(r) := -nu/r - delta_c r
             + exp(2M_c) r (fbar_pr(r^2/nu) - f_inf).
The first transformation cancels eps_c; the clock divides the drift by exp(-2 calE_c). The displayed upper bound uses calE_c >= 0 in the negative linear term and calE_c <= M_c in the nonnegative profile term.
The function d_c is locally Lipschitz on (0,infinity) and has a finite upper bound. Indeed, r fbar_pr(r^2/nu) = (nu/r) x fbar_pr(x) with x = r^2/nu is o(1/r) as r -> 0, so d_c(r) -> -infinity there; there is r_1 >= 1 such that exp(2M_c)(fbar_pr(r^2/nu) - f_inf) <= delta_c/2 for r >= r_1, so d_c(r) <= -delta_c r/2 there; and d_c is continuous in between.
With the same Brownian motion in the sigma_c clock, let
 dQ_c = (2 nu)^{1/2} dW_c + d_c(Q_c) d sigma_c,
 Q_c(0) = V_c(0),
and kill Q_c at zero. The finite upper bound of d_c gives a Brownian upper bound for Q_c and excludes finite explosion to infinity. Until either process is killed, localize both radii to a compact subinterval of (0,infinity). Their difference has no martingale part, and its positive part is bounded by a local Lipschitz constant times the integral of that positive part. Gronwall's inequality and removal of the localization give V_c <= Q_c until killing.
To prove that Q_c reaches zero, define its scale density and scale function by
 p_c(r) := exp(-int_1^r d_c(y) dy/nu),
 calS_c(r) := int_0^r p_c(y) dy.
Explicitly,
 p_c(r) = r exp(delta_c (r^2 - 1)/(2 nu))
          exp(-(exp(2M_c)/nu) int_1^r y (fbar_pr(y^2/nu) - f_inf) dy).
Since int_0^1 y fbar_pr(y^2/nu) dy = (nu/2) int_0^{1/nu} fbar_pr(x) dx < infinity,
 p_c(r) = C_{c,0} r(1+o(1))   as r -> 0,
with C_{c,0} > 0. For r >= r_1 the last exponent is at least -C_sc - delta_c r^2/(4 nu) for a finite constant C_sc, so
 p_c(r) >= C_{c,1} r exp(delta_c r^2/(4 nu))   (r >= r_1)
with C_{c,1} > 0. Hence calS_c(0) = 0 and calS_c(infinity) = infinity.
Accessibility of zero is checked as follows. For 0 < x < r_hi put
 g_{c,r_hi}(x) :=
   int_0^{r_hi}
    [calS_c(min{x,y})
      (calS_c(r_hi)-calS_c(max{x,y}))/calS_c(r_hi)]
      dy/[nu p_c(y)].
For fixed x the integrand is O(y) near zero and integrable near r_hi. The resulting function is nonnegative, continuous with value zero at both endpoints, and satisfies
 nu g_{c,r_hi}'' + d_c g_{c,r_hi}' = -1
on (0,r_hi), as follows by differentiating the two integrals split at x. Stopped Ito's formula on (epsilon,r_hi), first with a finite time cutoff, gives expected exit time at most g_{c,r_hi}(x). Letting the time cutoff and then epsilon tend to their limits proves that exit from (0,r_hi) is finite almost surely.
Applying the harmonic function calS_c on (epsilon,r_hi) and taking epsilon -> 0 now gives
 P_x(Q_c reaches r_hi before zero)
   = calS_c(x)/calS_c(r_hi).
An eternal positive path must exit every such interval through its upper endpoint. The displayed probability tends to zero as r_hi -> infinity. Thus Q_c reaches zero at a finite clock time almost surely. This argument applies conditionally on the finite starting radius at age one, and hence also for its random value.
The comparison forces V_c to reach zero no later. Since sigma_c(v) >= exp(-2M_c) v, a finite clock time corresponds to finite v and finite age exp v. The factors relating R and V_c are finite and positive there. Therefore the original radius reaches the axis at finite age. This proves P(zeta = infinity) = 0.
The two profile conditions have different counterexamples. The proof of (d) does not use |U| <= K; its argument also applies to the nonexplosive linear field in statement (b) of Proposition 40, although that field is outside the bounded-field class. For any k_* > 1/2 choose k with 1/2 < k < k_*. For this field u a^-(X_u,-u) = k u/(1+u) <= k, so (40.6) holds with f_pr = k and e_path = 0, while eternal survival has positive probability. Thus the threshold f_inf < 1/2 cannot be replaced by f_inf < k_* in the larger class admitting these linear fields. Part (h) proves that the threshold also cannot be raised among bounded smooth fields; its construction does not settle the general endpoint f_inf = 1/2. In part (b) of this remark, |a| <= C_b nu/R^2 for R > 0, where C_b := 4(sup|chi_a| + 2 sup|chi_a'|): indeed a = -(4 nu g_r/R^2)(chi_a(w_rz) + w_rz chi_a'(w_rz)), 0 <= g_r <= 1, and |w_rz| <= 2 on the support of chi_a'. Hence (40.6) holds there with f_pr(x) = C_b/x and e_path = 0. This profile is nonincreasing with f_inf = 0 but is not integrable at zero, and eternal survival has probability greater than 7/8. Thus the integrability assumption cannot simply be omitted, even in the bounded incompressible class.
(e) (A split criterion.) Suppose alpha_o,beta_i >= 0, alpha_o+beta_i < 1/2, and
 limsup_{t -> infinity} (1/log t)
   int_1^t a^-(X_u,-u) 1_{R_u < 2 (nu u)^{1/2}} du
   <= beta_i   almost surely on Sv,
 limsup_{t -> infinity} (1/log t)
   E[int_1^t a^-(X_u,-u) 1_{R_u >= 2 (nu u)^{1/2}} du;
     zeta = infinity]
   <= alpha_o p_infinity.
Statement (b) of Proposition 40 and the first inequality give a lower limit at least 1/2-beta_i for the normalized outer integral on Sv. Fatou's lemma gives
 (1/2-beta_i) p_infinity <= alpha_o p_infinity,
so p_infinity = 0. Fatou can first be applied along integer t; monotonicity of the integrals and log(n+1)/log n -> 1 give the same conclusion for real t.
By (a), the inner hypothesis holds with beta_i = 0 on Sv_+ if, in the tube along those paths,
 a^-(X_u,-u) <= M_in/u + e_in(u)
with a finite constant M_in >= 0 and nonnegative integrable e_in. Its integral is finite there by the occupation inequality. To apply the split criterion on all of Sv, Sv_0 must additionally be controlled or excluded.
(f) (A criterion on circulation superlevel sets.) Let U be a limit as in the proposition, and start X at the record point e_1 at time zero, so that Gamma_U(e_1, 0) = 1. Keep A := sup Gamma_U >= 1, and put B_Gamma := sup |Gamma_U| < infinity. The argument uses positive viscosity, the boundedness and smoothness of U and a, the bounded circulation and its equation, and the record normalization. These properties also hold for the Case-1 limits on either branch. No source-budget hypothesis is used. The generator of X at the age u is
 calL_u = nu (d_RR - R^{-1} d_R + d_ZZ) - U^R d_R - U^Z d_Z,
with coefficients evaluated at the time -u, and the circulation equation is
 d_tau Gamma_U + U^R d_R Gamma_U + U^Z d_Z Gamma_U = nu (d_RR - R^{-1} d_R + d_ZZ) Gamma_U.
Local C^{2,1} regularity away from the axis permits Ito's formula after localization, and the drift of Gamma_U(X_u, -u) is zero. Moreover |Gamma_U| <= K R gives the limit zero at every finite killing time. Consequently
 calC_u := Gamma_U(X_u, -u) for u < zeta,   calC_u := 0 for u >= zeta,
is a continuous bounded martingale, with calC_0 = 1 and |calC_u| <= B_Gamma. It converges almost surely and in L^1 to a limit calC_infinity with
 E calC_infinity = 1,   calC_infinity <= A,   calC_infinity = 0 on {zeta < infinity}.
For 0 <= ell < 1 this gives
 P(zeta = infinity, calC_infinity > ell) = P(calC_infinity > ell) >= (1 - ell)/(A - ell) > 0,
since 1 <= ell P(calC_infinity <= ell) + A P(calC_infinity > ell). The martingale is signed; no nonnegativity of Gamma_U is assumed. At finite ages its expectation is the representation 1 = E[Gamma_U(X_u, -u) 1_{zeta > u}] of Proposition 26.
Suppose that, for some ell in [0, 1), there are f_pr and e_path as in (d) such that, almost surely, at every age u >= 1 before killing with Gamma_U(X_u, -u) > ell, the inequality (40.6) holds. For each integer n >= 1 put
 F_{ell,n} := {zeta = infinity and Gamma_U(X_u, -u) > ell for every u >= n}.
On this event (40.6) holds at every age u >= n. Restart the comparison proof of (d) at the age n: set
 u = n exp v,   xi_n(v) := R_{n exp v}/(n exp v)^{1/2},   eps_{c,n}(v) := n exp(v) e_path(n exp v),
 calE_{c,n}(v) := int_0^v eps_{c,n}(w) dw = int_n^{n exp v} e_path(u) du,
so that 0 <= calE_{c,n} <= M_c, where M_c := int_1^infinity e_path(u) du. With alpha_u := a(X_u, -u),
 d xi_n = (2 nu)^{1/2} dW_{c,n}^0 - ((1/2 + u alpha_u) xi_n + nu/xi_n) dv,
where W_{c,n}^0(v) := int_n^{n exp v} u^{-1/2} dB_u is a Brownian motion in the filtration after the age n. Put
 V_{c,n} := exp(-calE_{c,n}) xi_n,   sigma_{c,n}(v) := int_0^v exp(-2 calE_{c,n}(w)) dw,
so that exp(-2 M_c) v <= sigma_{c,n}(v) <= v. With fbar_pr, delta_c and d_c as in (d), in the clock sigma_{c,n} the diffusion coefficient of V_{c,n} is (2 nu)^{1/2}, and on every path on which (40.6) holds after the age n its drift is at most d_c(V_{c,n}), by the inequalities of (d). The normalization uses R_u/u^{1/2}, so the profile argument remains R_u^2/(nu u); no translation of the absolute age in (40.6) is made. Construct, with the same Brownian motion in this clock,
 dQ_{c,n} = (2 nu)^{1/2} dW_{c,n} + d_c(Q_{c,n}) d sigma,   Q_{c,n}(0) = R_n/n^{1/2} on {zeta > n},
killed at zero, with any fixed positive starting value on {zeta <= n}. This construction is made on the whole probability space, before any restriction to F_{ell,n}. Conditionally on the information at the age n, the argument of (d) for a finite starting radius shows that Q_{c,n} reaches zero at a finite clock time almost surely. The comparison V_{c,n} <= Q_{c,n} is pathwise: after localization away from zero the difference has no martingale part, and the positive-part estimate and Gronwall's inequality apply. Hence it holds on F_{ell,n} until killing. The finite zero time of Q_{c,n} forces the radius R to reach zero at a finite age, because the clock has the displayed lower bound and the factors relating V_{c,n} to R are finite and positive at finite v. This contradicts zeta = infinity, so P(F_{ell,n}) = 0. No Brownian law is conditioned on the future event F_{ell,n}. The events F_{ell,n} increase with n, and by the convergence of calC_u their union contains {calC_infinity > ell} up to a null set, which contradicts the positive probability of this event. Hence no limit as in the proposition satisfies the stated superlevel-set hypothesis.
The same argument works if Gamma_U > ell is replaced by |Gamma_U| > ell in the hypothesis, and a bound for Lebesgue-almost every age on almost every relevant path suffices. More precisely, for fixed f_pr and e_path as in (d), the restarted comparison shows that eternal survival together with eventual validity of (40.6) for almost every age has probability zero. For the exclusion of a limit it is therefore enough to obtain that eventual bound on a subset of {calC_infinity > ell} of positive probability.
An averaged form of this criterion holds as well. Let 0 <= ell < 1 and put q_ell(s) := P(calC_s > ell); since calC_s = 0 for s >= zeta, the event {calC_s > ell} lies in {zeta > s}, so q_ell <= p. Suppose that P(calC_infinity = ell) = 0, which holds for all but countably many ell, and that for some c in [0, 1/2), s_0 >= 1 and e integrable on [s_0, infinity)
 E[a^-(X_s, -s); calC_s > ell] <= c q_ell(s)/s + e(s)   for s >= s_0.
Then the limit is excluded. Proof. Put F := {calC_infinity > ell}, so that P(F) > 0 by the bound above, and let calH_t, D_t := calH_t - (1/2) log^+(t wedge zeta) and T_infinity be as in Remark (2), where D_t >= -(1/2) log^+ T_infinity and E[log^+ T_infinity] < infinity were shown on the whole probability space. The events F_{ell,n} increase, they are contained in {calC_infinity >= ell} up to a null set, and their union contains F up to a null set; hence P(F_{ell,n}) -> P(F). A path that lies in {calC_s > ell} for arbitrarily large s has calC_infinity >= ell, so the reverse Fatou lemma along sequences gives limsup_{s -> infinity} q_ell(s) <= P(calC_infinity >= ell) = P(F); Fatou's lemma gives liminf_{s -> infinity} q_ell(s) >= P(F) in the same way, so q_ell(s) -> P(F). Put delta := (1/2 - c) P(F)/3, choose n with P(F_{ell,n}) >= P(F) - 2 delta, which is positive, and then s_1 >= max{n, s_0} with c q_ell(s) <= c P(F) + delta for s >= s_1. On F_{ell,n} one has zeta = infinity, so D_m -> infinity by (b), and Fatou's lemma applied to the nonnegative variables (D_m + (1/2) log^+ T_infinity) 1_{F_{ell,n}} gives E[D_m 1_{F_{ell,n}}] -> infinity as m -> infinity through the integers. On the other hand, let t >= s_1. On F_{ell,n} one has calC_s > ell for s >= s_1 and t wedge zeta = t, so calH_t <= ||a||_infty s_1 + int_{s_1}^t a^-(X_s, -s) 1_{calC_s > ell} ds and log^+(t wedge zeta) = log s_1 + int_{s_1}^t ds/s. By Tonelli's theorem
 E[D_t 1_{F_{ell,n}}] <= ||a||_infty s_1 + int_{s_0}^infinity |e(s)| ds + int_{s_1}^t (c q_ell(s) - (1/2) P(F_{ell,n})) ds/s,
and the integrand is at most c P(F) + delta - (1/2) P(F) + delta = -delta. Hence E[D_t 1_{F_{ell,n}}] -> -infinity, a contradiction. Without the condition on the atom the same argument applies when c P(calC_infinity >= ell) < (1/2) P(calC_infinity > ell). The left side of the hypothesis is at most E[a^-(X_s, -s); zeta > s], while q_ell(s) <= p(s) <= p(s/2); these comparisons alone do not show that either averaged hypothesis implies the other. On the Type I swirl branch with 0 < ell < 1 the set {Gamma_U(., -s) > ell} lies in {R > ell (gamma_* s/C_I)^{1/2}} (Proposition 34(d)(iii), as in the paragraph on this branch below), so there the hypothesis concerns the compression only at distances from the axis at least of the parabolic order s^{1/2}. The preceding argument using F_{ell,n} requires c < 1/2. At c = 1/2, the convergence of q_ell(s) to P(F) gives no bound on the accumulated error int_{s_1}^t (q_ell(s) - P(F_{ell,n})) ds/s, which tends to infinity as t -> infinity whenever P(F_{ell,n}) < P(F). The cancellation itself is available when the restriction to the superlevel set is kept in both terms. For t >= 1 put
 Psi_t := int_0^t a^-(X_s, -s) 1_{calC_s > ell} ds - (1/2) int_1^t 1_{calC_s > ell} ds/s,
with the compression integrand understood to be zero after killing. By Tonelli's theorem, E[int_1^t 1_{calC_s > ell} ds/s] = int_1^t q_ell(s) ds/s, so the hypothesis with c = 1/2 gives E[Psi_t] <= ||a||_infty s_0 + int_{s_0}^infinity |e(s)| ds for t >= s_0. Define the complementary contributions by
 H'_t := int_0^t a^-(X_s, -s) 1_{s < zeta, calC_s <= ell} ds,   L'_t := int_1^t 1_{s < zeta, calC_s <= ell} ds/s.
These are the parts of calH_t and of log^+(t wedge zeta) = int_1^t 1_{s < zeta} ds/s (t >= 1) contributed by the alive ages outside the superlevel set. Since {calC_s > ell} lies in {zeta > s}, Psi_t = D_t - (H'_t - (1/2) L'_t). On F one has zeta = infinity and calC_s > ell at all ages after some finite age, after which H'_t and L'_t are constant; hence Psi_t -> infinity on F by (b). Consequently the endpoint c = 1/2 holds under the additional condition sup_{t >= 1} E[Psi_t^-] < infinity: by Fatou's lemma, liminf_{t -> infinity} E[min{Psi_t^+, k}] >= k P(F) for every k > 0, and E[Psi_t] >= E[min{Psi_t^+, k}] - sup_{t' >= 1} E[Psi_{t'}^-] contradicts the upper bound for E[Psi_t] once k is large. Since D_t >= -(1/2) log^+ T_infinity and E[log^+ T_infinity] < infinity, the additional condition follows from sup_{t >= 1} E[(H'_t - (1/2) L'_t)^+] < infinity, which concerns the compression at the ages at which the path is alive and outside the superlevel set. The displayed hypothesis gives no direct estimate for this complementary term, and neither additional condition has been derived here. If {calC_s > ell} is replaced by {zeta > s}, the terms H'_t and L'_t vanish and the argument gives the endpoint of Remark (2) with p(s) in place of p(s/2); the two forms of that hypothesis are equivalent, since 0 <= (p(s/2) - p(s))/(2s) has integral at most (1/2) log 2 over [s_0, infinity) and can be absorbed into e. This averaged bound has not been derived for the limits. Returning to the superlevel set, in the abstract setting the displayed hypothesis with c = 1/2, the radial equation, the clock bounds and (b) do not by themselves give the contradiction or imply either additional condition. For nu = 1 and ell = 1/2 there is a construction satisfying the radial equation of Step 7 with a bounded progressively measurable strain, the clock bounds, the divergence (b) and the assumptions on calC (a bounded continuous martingale with calC_0 = 1 that vanishes after killing), in which the hypothesis holds with c = 1/2, s_0 = 4 and e = 0, while calC_infinity takes only the values 0 and A, where 32/17 < A < 8/3, so that P(F) = 1/A and there is no atom at ell; by the statement just proved, sup_{t >= 1} E[Psi_t^-] = infinity there. Use the usual augmented natural filtration of independent Brownian motions B and W, with R the strong killed solution driven by B. Put w_n := 2^{-n-1}, g_n := 2^{-n-7}, S_n := 4 exp(128 (2^n - 2)) and U_n := S_n - 1 for n >= 1, so that log(S_{n+1}/S_n) = 1/g_n, and let g := g_1 on [1, 4) and g := g_n on [S_n, S_{n+1}). A type N, with P(N = 0) = 1/2 and P(N = n) = w_n, is a measurable function of W(1), and a(s) := -h_N(s) with the compression schedules h_k := 128 on [0, 1) for every k, h_0(s) := (1/2 + g(s))/s for s >= 1, and, for n >= 1, h_n := 128 on [1, U_n), h_n := 0 on [U_n, S_{n+1}) and h_n(s) := (1/2 + g(s))/s for s >= S_{n+1}. For each type k the total unstopped clock tau_k := int_0^infinity exp(-2 int_0^s h_k) ds is less than 1/128, and T_infinity <= tau_N; by the dimension-zero law the path of type k survives forever with conditional probability rho_k = 1 - exp(-1/(4 tau_k)) > 1 - e^{-32}. Let calC be the continuous version of A E[xi | F_s], where xi := 1_{zeta = infinity}(1_{N = 0} + sum_{n >= 1} 1_{N = n} 1_{L_n}), L_n := {W(S_n) - W(U_n) > z_0} with P(L_n) = 1/16, and A := 1/P(xi = 1). On {N = n} and for s >= 1, calC_s = A P(L_n | F_s) f_n(s, R_s), where f_n(s, R_s) is the conditional probability of eternal survival; hence calC_s <= A/16 < 1/2 for 1 <= s <= U_n, so the compression of size 128 on [1, U_n) is incurred outside the superlevel set. For s in [S_n, S_{n+1}) one has calC_s = A 1_{L_n} f_n(s, R_s) on {N = n}, where L_n is independent of R given N; since E[f_n(s, R_s) | N = n] = rho_n > 1 - e^{-32} and f_n <= 1, P(f_n(s, R_s) > 1/(2A) | N = n) > 1/2. Thus at such ages the event {N = n, calC_s > 1/2} has probability above w_n/32 and carries no compression, which lowers E[a^-(s); calC_s > 1/2] - q_{1/2}(s)/(2s) by more than w_n/(64 s) = g_n/s; the type 0 and the types k < n follow the schedule (1/2 + g_n)/s and raise it by at most g_n/s, the type n + 1 has no compression or lies outside the superlevel set, and the types k > n + 1 lie outside it. Hence E[a^-(s); calC_s > 1/2] <= q_{1/2}(s)/(2s) for every s >= 4. The construction uses the auxiliary Brownian motion W to select the type and to conduct the lotteries; it gives a radial process and a martingale, but no record path X along which the strain and calC are functions of the position and the age, as they are for the limits, and no velocity field whose circulation is calC. It gives no conclusion about the limits.
To compare with Proposition 38, suppose that its inflow bound holds on {|Gamma_U| > ell}, with tau_* > 0, C >= 0 and 0 <= theta < 1/2. At the time -u one has tau_* + u >= u, so on {Gamma_U(X_u, -u) > ell}
 a^-(X_u, -u) <= C/(R_u (tau_* + u)^{1/2}) + theta/(tau_* + u) <= C/(R_u u^{1/2}) + theta/u = u^{-1} f_pr(R_u^2/(nu u)),   f_pr(x) := C (nu x)^{-1/2} + theta.
This profile is nonincreasing, int_0^1 f_pr(x) dx = 2 C nu^{-1/2} + theta < infinity and f_inf = theta < 1/2, so e_path = 0 is admissible. Thus part (f) recovers the qualitative exclusion of such a limit by Proposition 38(a), and restarting at an arbitrary sufficiently large age also gives the arbitrarily late violations of Proposition 38(c). It does not give the finite-window estimates, the lower bounds in logarithmic average or the space-time localization of Proposition 38. The admissible profiles are more general than this Type I profile, and an integrable deterministic remainder is allowed. The bound is required on the positive superlevel set, whereas Proposition 38 uses the absolute superlevel set. For a fixed deterministic profile and remainder, requiring the bound almost surely along all record paths gives no further spatial weakening: at each positive age the killed diffusion has full support in {R > 0}, and a strict spatial failure in the positive superlevel set persists on an open set, by the continuity of Gamma_U and a^- and the monotonicity of f_pr, so it would occur along a record path with positive probability. The eventual formulation restricted to an event, given above, requires less than a bound along all paths.
On the Type I swirl branch, for 0 < ell < 1 and u > 0, Proposition 34(d)(iii) gives {|Gamma_U(., -u)| > ell} subset {R > rho_ell(-u)}, where rho_ell(-u) = ell (gamma_* (tau_* + u)/C_I)^{1/2} >= ell (gamma_* u/C_I)^{1/2}. Thus x := R^2/(nu u) > x_ell := ell^2 gamma_*/(nu C_I) on either the positive or the absolute superlevel set. Given an admissible profile f_pr, choose theta in (f_inf, 1/2) and x_theta >= x_ell so that f_pr <= theta on [x_theta, infinity), and put C_ell := f_pr(x_ell) (nu x_theta)^{1/2}. Then f_pr(x) <= C_ell (nu x)^{-1/2} + theta for every x >= x_ell: on [x_ell, x_theta] the first term alone dominates f_pr(x), and beyond x_theta the second term does. Consequently (40.6), wherever assumed on either superlevel set, implies a^-(X_u, -u) <= C_ell/(R_u u^{1/2}) + theta/u + e_path(u) on that same set and at those same ages. Conversely, a bound of this latter form with any finite coefficient D >= 0 in place of C_ell and 0 <= theta < 1/2 is (40.6) with the admissible profile f_pr(x) := D (nu x)^{-1/2} + theta. The equivalence is therefore between existence of bounds in these two profile classes, allowing a change of profile and constants while retaining the chosen superlevel set, age range, event restriction and deterministic integrable remainder. It is not an equivalence for a previously fixed profile. The bound contradicted by Proposition 38(c) is spatial, uses {|Gamma_U| > ell}, holds for all sufficiently large ages and has no remainder. It implies the positive-superlevel hypothesis of (f) after adjusting the finite initial age interval: if it holds for u >= s_0, enlarge D to max{D, K max{1, s_0}^{1/2}}, using a^- <= K/R for 1 <= u < s_0. A bound on {Gamma_U > ell} does not by this argument control {Gamma_U < -ell}, and an integrable remainder cannot simply be omitted. For the absolute-superlevel version with zero remainder, the two existential profile conditions agree after this adjustment of the initial age interval. Thus, for 0 < ell < 1 on this branch, the general profile does not enlarge the existential class on a fixed superlevel set and with a fixed allowance for the remainder; at ell = 0 or off this branch the positive lower cutoff x_ell used in this argument is unavailable. None of these bounds for the actual strain has been derived for the limits.
For nu = 1, Remark (7) gives a scale-invariant profile for the auxiliary strain. Its majorant (iv), the identity (ii) and the substitution t = s y give, for R > 0,
 s |a_eta(R,Z,-s)| <= k_e C^2 g_eta(R^2/s),
 g_eta(x) := x^{-1} int_0^infinity y^{-1} log(1+y) (1 - exp(-x/(4y))) dy.
Writing the integrand as y^{-1} log(1+y) (4y)^{-1} phi_e(x/(4y)) with the decreasing function phi_e(z) := (1 - exp(-z))/z shows that g_eta is nonincreasing. The computation behind the envelope of Remark (7) gives g_eta(x) <= (1/4)(1 + 2 log 2 + log_+(4/x)), so g_eta is integrable at zero. For x >= 4, the inequality 1 - exp(-z) <= min{1,z}, the split at y = x/4, log(1+y) <= y for y <= 1, log(1+y) <= log(2y) for y >= 1 and int_A^infinity y^{-2} log(1+y) dy = A^{-1} log(1+A) + log(1 + 1/A) give
 g_eta(x) <= x^{-1}(2 + log 2 log(x/4) + (1/2) log^2(x/4) + log(1 + x/4)),
so g_eta(x) -> 0 as x -> infinity. Hence f_pr := k_e C^2 g_eta satisfies the hypotheses of (d) with f_inf = 0 for every finite C >= 0. Thus, if the actual strain satisfies a^-(X_u,-u) <= u^{-1} k_e C^2 g_eta(R_u^2/u) + e_path(u) almost surely for every u >= 1 before killing, with e_path deterministic, nonnegative and integrable on [1,infinity), part (d) gives almost-sure absorption without any smallness of C. For the exclusion of a limit, part (f) requires the bound only at the ages where Gamma_U(X_u,-u) > ell, for some 0 <= ell < 1; eventual control on a positive-probability set of surviving paths already suffices. The coarser envelope of Remark (7) is the profile f_pr(x) = (k_e C^2/4)(1 + 2 log 2 + log_+(4/x)), for which (d) needs
 (k_e C^2/4)(1 + 2 log 2) = 0.144353343869... C^2 < 1/2;
a sufficient rounded condition is 0.14436 C^2 < 1/2. In the averaged criteria the whole profile enters through its average against the surviving law: Remark (8)(c) gives a sufficient averaged criterion using a uniform bound int log_+(4 s/R^2) d mu_s <= L p(s/2), and Remark (8)(e) gives, for prescribed incompressible fields with p_infinity > 0, the logarithmic average bound (k_e C^2/4)(1 + 2 log 2 + (12/e)^{1/2}) <= 0.2715 C^2, which is below 1/2 when C^2 < 1.84. The displayed sufficient upper bounds for these auxiliary averaged coefficients are proportional to C^2. Requiring these upper bounds to be below 1/2 imposes smallness of C; no necessity of that smallness for absorption or for a sharper averaged estimate is proved. In (d) only f_inf and the integrability at zero matter, and f_inf = 0 for g_eta. The pathwise criterion requires no separate bound on logarithmic occupation.
The profile g_eta and the envelope of Remark (7) concern the auxiliary strain a_eta, which is not identified with U^R/R. A bound for another quantity gives no radial drift comparison. Neither (40.6), its superlevel-set hypothesis in (f), nor the hypotheses of (e) have been derived for the limits. The probabilistic Steps 7 and 8 use boundedness of U and a together with the averaged estimate (40.2); the derivation of that estimate retains the structural and source-budget hypotheses of Proposition 40. The bound |a| <= K/R gives on R >= 2 (nu u)^{1/2} only a time integral of order t^{1/2}, and in the variables of (d) only u a^- <= K u^{1/2} (nu x)^{-1/2}, with x = R^2/(nu u), which does not give an admissible fixed profile. The first missing estimate for the actual strain therefore remains unproved. Remark (9) adds sufficient conditions: (d) gives absorption from a pathwise profile bound, and (f) excludes a limit when the same bound is required only on a positive circulation superlevel set. In fact, the comparison already excludes a positive-probability set of surviving paths on which a fixed admissible bound holds eventually. For the profile of the auxiliary strain, these criteria require no smallness of C if the bound can be established for the actual strain. Part (a) and the examples also show why the finite clock of Step 7 alone does not exclude Sv_0.
(g) (A sufficient condition through the axial stretching.) For a bounded smooth axisymmetric divergence-free field, (1/R) d_R(R U^R) + d_Z U^Z = 0 and R U^R -> 0 at the axis give
  a(R, Z, tau) = -R^{-2} int_0^R r d_Z U^Z(r, Z, tau) dr,
hence
  a^-(R, Z, tau) <= R^{-2} int_0^R r (d_Z U^Z)^+(r, Z, tau) dr <= (1/2) sup_{0 < r < R} (d_Z U^Z)^+(r, Z, tau),
and a = -(1/2) d_Z U^Z on the axis. Consequently, if almost surely, at every age u >= 1 before killing, (d_Z U^Z)^+(r, Z_u, -u) <= D_+/u for 0 < r < R_u, with a constant D_+ < 1, then (40.6) holds with the constant profile f_pr := D_+/2 and e_path := 0, and (d) gives P(zeta = infinity) = 0; when U is a limit as in the proposition, this contradicts the record survival of Proposition 26(l). By the eventual form of the comparison in (f), it suffices that this bound hold, almost surely on an event of positive probability contained in {zeta = infinity}, for some finite age N, which may depend on the path, and Lebesgue-almost every u >= N. Separately, for some fixed ell in [0, 1), it suffices that this bound hold on almost every path for Lebesgue-almost every age u >= 1 before killing at which Gamma_U(X_u, -u) > ell. To combine these weakenings, it is enough to obtain the eventual bound at these superlevel ages on a positive-probability subset of {calC_infinity > ell}; on this subset the superlevel condition holds at every sufficiently large age. In particular no limit satisfies (d_Z U^Z)^+(., -beta) <= D_+/beta for all beta >= 1 with D_+ < 1, and the same holds when this bound is required only on the Euler cones {max(R, |Z|) <= E beta} with a slope E > K. Indeed, the age drift of R_u is -U^R - nu/R_u <= K and that of Z_u has absolute value at most K, so comparison gives max(R_u, |Z_u|) <= max(R_1, |Z_1|) + K(u - 1) + (2 nu)^{1/2} max(|B_u - B_1|, |B'_u - B'_1|), with the Brownian motions B, B' of the path equations in Proposition 40; by the strong law of large numbers, almost surely on {zeta = infinity} the point X_u and the segment {(r, Z_u): 0 < r <= R_u} lie in the cone of slope E at age u for all large u. The global form is also a case of Remark (2) with c = D_+/2. The threshold D_+ < 1 is twice the threshold for the compression because of the factor 1/2 in the radial average. It cannot be replaced by D_+ < D_* for any D_* > 1 in the larger class admitting the linear fields of statement (b): for U^R = -k R/(1 + s), U^Z = 2 k Z/(1 + s) with 1/2 < k < D_*/2, d_Z U^Z = 2 k/(1 + u) <= 2 k/u at the age u, while eternal survival has positive probability; by (h) the same holds among bounded smooth fields. This condition is sufficient for (40.6), not equivalent to it; it uses neither the Type I swirl bound nor an outflow hypothesis, and it has not been derived for the limits.
(h) (A bounded version of the linear strain, and a sufficient condition through the pressure.) (i) Let 1/2 < k < 1, and let chi be a smooth even function on the line with values in [0, 1], nonincreasing on [0, infinity), with chi = 1 on [0, 1], chi = 0 on [3, infinity) and |y chi'(y)| <= 1 for all y; such a function exists because int_1^3 dy/y = log 3 > 1. For M >= 1 and the age s >= 0 put rho := R/(M(1 + s)), xi_h := Z/(M(1 + s)) and define the meridional field by
  Psi(R, Z, -s) := (k/(1 + s)) R^2 Z chi(rho) chi(xi_h),   U^R := -R^{-1} d_Z Psi,   U^Z := R^{-1} d_R Psi.
With f := 2 chi(rho) + rho chi'(rho) and g := chi(xi_h) + xi_h chi'(xi_h),
  a = U^R/R = -(k/(1 + s)) chi(rho) g,   U^Z = (k/(1 + s)) Z chi(xi_h) f,   d_Z U^Z = (k/(1 + s)) f g.
Here U denotes U^R e_R + U^Z e_Z. This field is smooth (chi(rho) = 1 near the axis), divergence-free, with |U| <= 7 k M, ||a||_infty <= k and |grad U(., -s)| <= C_chi k/(1 + s), where C_chi depends only on chi; it is prescribed, and it is not claimed to solve the momentum equation. Since -1 <= f <= 2 and -1 <= g <= 1,
  a^- <= k/(1 + s)   and   (d_Z U^Z)^+ <= 2k/(1 + s)   everywhere,
and on the core {R <= M(1 + s), |Z| <= M(1 + s)} the field is the linear strain of statement (b). Run the killed diffusion of the proposition for this field from e_1 at the age 0, and let (R^lin, Z^lin) be the diffusion of the linear strain driven by the same Brownian motions B, B'. Then R^lin_s = (1 + s)^k Y(theta(s)) with theta(s) := (1 - (1 + s)^{1 - 2k})/(2k - 1) < 1/(2k - 1), where Y is a Bessel process of dimension zero with generator nu(d_yy - y^{-1} d_y) and Y(0) = 1, and (1 + s)^{2k} Z^lin_s = (2 nu)^{1/2} int_0^s (1 + v)^{2k} dB'_v. The process Y^2 is a nonnegative martingale, absorbed at zero before the clock time theta with probability exp(-1/(4 nu theta)); so R^lin survives forever with probability p_* := 1 - exp(-(2k - 1)/(4 nu)), as in (b). Doob's inequality for Y^2 gives P(sup Y^2 >= M^2) <= M^{-2}, and R^lin_s < M(1 + s)^k <= M(1 + s) on the complement; Doob's inequality for the axial martingale on the blocks 2^j <= 1 + s <= 2^{j+1}, j >= 0, gives
  P(|Z^lin_s| > M(1 + s) for some s) <= sum_{j >= 0} 2 nu 2^{(j+1)(4k+1)}/((4k + 1) M^2 2^{j(4k+2)}) = 2^{4k+3} nu/((4k + 1) M^2).
Choose M with M^2 >= 2(1 + 2^{4k+3} nu/(4k + 1))/p_*. With probability at least p_*/2 the linear path survives forever inside the core; it then solves the equations of the field, so it is the path X, and along it u a^-(X_u, -u) = k u/(1 + u) and d_Z U^Z(r, Z_u, -u) = 2k/(1 + u) for 0 <= r <= R_u. Let Gamma(R, Z, -s) be the probability that the diffusion of this field started at (R, Z) at the age s survives forever. For a fixed terminal age N, the probability of survival to age N is a bounded classical solution of the backward equation in R > 0 at ages s < N. These probabilities decrease to Gamma as N -> infinity. Interior parabolic estimates, on each compact subset away from the axis and with N sufficiently large, give convergence of derivatives and show that Gamma is a classical solution of the circulation equation there. The process equal to Gamma(X_s, -s) before killing and to zero afterwards is P(zeta = infinity | X up to the age s). Since the event {zeta = infinity} is measurable with respect to the whole path, conditional-expectation convergence gives Gamma(X_s, -s) -> 1 almost surely on {zeta = infinity}. The radial drift (k/(1 + s)) R chi(rho) g - nu/R is at most kR/(1 + s) - nu/R, the radial drift of the linear strain; the difference of the two radial components driven by the same Brownian motion has bounded variation and the larger drift is locally Lipschitz in R > 0, so the radius of the field stays below that of the linear strain started at the same point and age, and
  0 <= Gamma(R, Z, -s) <= 1 - exp(-(2k - 1) R^2/(4 nu (1 + s))) <= min{1, (2k - 1) R^2/(4 nu (1 + s))}.
Hence Gamma/R <= ((2k - 1)/(4 nu (1 + s)))^{1/2}, a Type I bound for the swirl Gamma/R. Lift q := Gamma/R^2 to R^4 x R, with R = |y'|. Off the axis it satisfies
  d_tau q + b_5.grad_5 q = nu Delta_5 q - 2 a q,   b_5 := (a y', U^Z).
The lifted coefficients are smooth, and incompressibility gives div_5 b_5 = 2a. Thus the equation is d_tau q + div_5(b_5 q) = nu Delta_5 q. The comparison bound makes q locally bounded, including near the axis. Test this conservative equation with a smooth spatial cutoff that vanishes for |y'| <= epsilon and equals one for |y'| >= 2 epsilon. On compact space-time sets the tube has volume O(epsilon^4), while the largest cutoff derivatives are O(epsilon^{-2}); boundedness of q makes every cutoff error tend to zero, with the largest error O(epsilon^2). The equation therefore extends distributionally across the axis, and interior parabolic regularity gives a smooth extension.
The added Cartesian swirl V_sw := q(-x_2, x_1, 0) is consequently smooth and satisfies
  (d_tau + U.grad - nu Delta_3) V_sw = -a V_sw.
It also has the required gradient decay. To see this, fix s >= 0, put L := 1 + s and tau_0 := -s - L, and work on [tau_0, -s]. The explicit meridional field gives |grad U| + |a| <= C_cut/L and |grad a| <= C_cut/L^2, while |V_sw| <= C_cut/L^{1/2}; constants C_cut here depend only on nu, k, M and chi. For a sufficiently large constant B_cut, differentiation of the last equation gives
  (d_tau + U.grad - nu Delta_3)
    [(tau - tau_0)|grad V_sw|^2 + B_cut |V_sw|^2]
    <= (C_cut/L) sup_slab |V_sw|^2.
The maximum principle gives |grad V_sw(., -s)| <= C_cut/L. Bounded spatial derivatives on each finite slab, needed for this application, follow first from parabolic regularity on a larger past slab, since the solution and all coefficient derivatives are bounded there. Thus U_full := U + V_sw is a smooth divergence-free field with actual circulation Gamma, the same circulation diffusion, |U_full| <= 7 k M + ((2k - 1)/(4 nu))^{1/2}, ||U_full^R/R||_infty <= k, and (1 + s)|grad U_full(., -s)| bounded. Consequently, among smooth fields with |U|, ||a||_infty and (1 + s)|grad U| bounded, even together with a bounded circulation that solves the circulation equation with a Type I swirl bound, none of the following thresholds can be raised: the constant 1/2 in (b) (on an event of positive probability inside {zeta = infinity}, calH_t = k log(1 + t)); f_inf < 1/2 in (d) (the constant profile f_pr = k with e_path = 0 holds globally); c < 1/2 in Remark (2) (E[a^-(X_s, -s); zeta > s] <= k p(s)/(1 + s) <= k p(s/2)/s); and D_+ < 1 in (g) (the bound holds globally with D_+ = 2k), where the restriction of (f) to {Gamma > ell} does not help, since Gamma(X_s, -s) -> 1 on eternal paths. This construction does not settle the general endpoint f_inf = 1/2 in (d); the averaged endpoint c = 1/2 of Remark (2) is excluded there by a separate argument. The constant-profile endpoint a^- <= 1/(2u) + e_path(u), with integrable e_path, is excluded by (b) itself: if it holds for Lebesgue-almost every u >= N, with N finite and possibly depending on the path, on an event of positive probability contained in {zeta = infinity}, then calH_t <= (1/2) log t plus a finite path-dependent constant on that event, contrary to (b). In particular the endpoint D_+ = 1 in (g) is also excluded, in its global form (the event is {zeta = infinity}, of positive probability by Proposition 26(l)), in its eventual form, and in its superlevel form (on {calC_infinity > ell}, of positive probability by (f), the superlevel condition holds at every sufficiently large age). The example establishes no sharpness assertion for Navier-Stokes limits. It shows that the listed norm bounds and the circulation equation alone do not imply the sufficient compression or stretching hypotheses; a derivation for the limits must use further information, but the example does not show that the momentum equation, or any other particular property of the limits, is indispensable.
(ii) For a limit, with U its full velocity, sigma := d_Z U^Z is the derivative d_3 u_3 of the Cartesian component and satisfies
  d_tau sigma + U.grad sigma = nu Delta sigma - sigma^2 - C_ax - d_ZZ P,   C_ax := d_Z U^R d_R U^Z.
Indeed, differentiation of the third momentum equation gives the quadratic term sum_j (d_3 u_j)(d_j u_3) = sigma^2 + C_ax. There is no explicit swirl term because grad u_3 has no azimuthal component. Here P is a pressure satisfying the momentum equation for U: grad P = nu Delta U - d_tau U - (U.grad)U. Thus d_ZZ P is well defined and is unaffected by a time-only addition to P; any spatially constant term in a pressure-gradient representation also disappears after differentiation in Z. Suppose that C_ax + d_ZZ P >= -alpha/tau^2 on R^3 x (-infinity, -1] for a constant alpha in [0, 2], and put d_alpha := ((1 + 4 alpha)^{1/2} - 1)/2, so that d_alpha^2 + d_alpha = alpha and d_alpha <= 1, with equality only for alpha = 2. For T > 1 the function v_T(tau) := d_alpha/(-tau) + 1/(tau + T) on (-T, -1] satisfies
  v_T' + v_T^2 - alpha/tau^2 = 2 d_alpha/((-tau)(tau + T)) >= 0,
so w := sigma - v_T satisfies d_tau w + U.grad w - nu Delta w <= -(sigma + v_T) w, which is nonpositive where w > 0 (there sigma > v_T > 0). Since sigma is bounded and v_T -> infinity as tau -> -T, choose delta > 0 sufficiently small that w(., -T + delta) < 0 uniformly in x. On the finite slab [-T + delta, -1], w is bounded. The maximum principle used here says that a bounded C^{2,1} function with nonpositive initial data and (d_tau + U.grad - nu Delta)w <= 0 wherever w > 0 is nonpositive when U is bounded. To prove it on R^3, subtract epsilon exp(lambda(tau + T - delta))(1 + |x|^2), with lambda > ||U||_infty + 6 nu, apply the interior maximum test, and let epsilon decrease to zero. Applying this principle for arbitrarily small delta gives w <= 0 on (-T, -1]. Letting T -> infinity at each fixed tau <= -1 gives sigma^+(., tau) <= d_alpha/(-tau). With beta := -tau this is exactly the global form of (g), for every beta >= 1, with D_+ = d_alpha, which (g) excludes when alpha < 2. For alpha = 2, d_alpha = 1, and the endpoint D_+ = 1 is excluded at the end of (i): the radial average of (g) gives a^-(X_u, -u) <= 1/(2u) at every age u >= 1 before killing, so calH_t - (1/2) log t <= ||a||_infty on {zeta = infinity}, contrary to (b), while P(zeta = infinity) > 0 by Proposition 26(l). Hence no limit satisfies C_ax + d_ZZ P >= -alpha/tau^2 on R^3 x (-infinity, -1] with alpha in [0, 2]. A negative alpha implies the already excluded condition with alpha = 0. For the linear strain of (b), C_ax = 0 and its quadratic pressure has d_ZZ P = -2k(2k + 1)/(1 + s)^2. For k > 0 the coefficient 2k(2k + 1) is at most 2 exactly when 2k <= 1. Since s^2/(1 + s)^2 increases to one on [1, infinity), a constant alpha in [0, 2] with d_ZZ P >= -alpha/s^2 at every s >= 1 exists exactly when 2k <= 1, while for 2k > 1 statement (b) gives eternal survival with positive probability. That field is unbounded, and the maximum principle above is not applied to it. On the axis C_ax = 0 and the assumed condition reads d_ZZ P >= -alpha/tau^2. This condition has not been derived for the limits. The example of (i) does not impose the momentum equation and therefore does not test this pressure condition for limits.

### 1.3 What was not proved

The exclusion of Case 1 was not proved, and no fixed-datum counterexample was found. Theorems 4 and 5 are conditional Liouville theorems whose hypotheses were not derived. Theorem 9 removes Type I gradient growth under (A) but does not reach the swirl records: it gives a limsup statement for the global gradient, does not locate the large gradients, and does not relate them to (r_n, z_n, t_n). Proposition 12 is a rigidity statement under a backward-decay hypothesis that was not derived. Theorem 13 splits the remaining scenario into two branches and excludes neither; Proposition 14 proves a necessary condition for branch (II); no incompatible upper bound was established; and Proposition 15 refines the limits without excluding them. Propositions 16 to 18 are exact identities and necessary conditions; the absorption criteria of Proposition 16 are conditional on a global inflow bound or a stream-function smallness that was not derived (the stream-function smallness is false at inviscid gradient records by Proposition 17). Proposition 19(b) is a conditional exclusion whose hypothesis (for some constant c_0, sup_{tau <= 0} ||(psi_U - c_0 R/2) e_theta||_{BMO(R^3)} < infinity for the meridional vector potential of the limit) fails for every member of LL and was not derived from the fixed trajectory; Proposition 19(c), (d) and Proposition 20 are necessary conditions. Proposition 21(a), (b) are necessary conditions. Proposition 21(c) is a conditional exclusion whose compression hypothesis was not derived; its physical threshold 2 - beta_0 is strictly below 2 and approaches the exterior-comparison endpoint of Theorem 5 as beta_0 decreases to 0. Proposition 22 consists of identities and necessary conditions. Its part (d) gives an exact local Navier-Stokes model that satisfies the weak normalized terminal-maximum conditions, bounded circulation and derivatives, and the velocity bound on the ellipsoid of part (d), for compatible constants; it does not realize first crossings of increasing levels or the global Case-1 hypotheses, so an exclusion needs some information not shared by this local model (examples are the velocity bound elsewhere, finite energy, the canonical pressure, the tail or the growth of the records, with compatible constants). Proposition 23(a) is a saturation estimate, 23(b) a conditional Liouville statement together with an inflow witness, and 23(c) a physical necessary condition; the inflow bound that would exclude Case 1 was not derived. Proposition 24 consists of identities, necessary conditions and conditional residence or growth statements; it shows that the local material phenomena at a record are consistent with the local identities, and that one proposed target (small unweighted window dissipation) is false. Proposition 25 refines the far-field inflow witness, gives a flux bound and a stronger sufficient weighted Biot-Savart criterion, gives explicit scalar models indicating that the listed scalar information is consistent with strong far-field inflow (for the whole-space model the elliptic estimates behind its exhaustion are not reproduced), shows that the far-field bound, posed for the whole class LL, is equivalent to the Liouville problem for LL, and gives an exact exterior solution with strong far-field inflow; apart from the steady slender profiles of (f), it excludes nothing, and in particular it does not exclude Case 1. Proposition 26 consists of identities, explicit lower bounds for the averaged circulation deficit, an averaged threshold theorem at the critical value 2 nu whose conclusion is only vanishing of weighted box means, and a conditional exclusion (averaged saturation together with a critical one-sided outflow bound) whose hypotheses were not derived. The work of the first research period was done in five work periods. The third added necessary conditions, tests and reformulations (Proposition 23(f), (g), the later entries of sec. 3.12 and the whole-line structure of the eternal limits and the necessary conditions of the uniformly viscous scenario in sec. 3.7) but no new viable route. The fourth added Proposition 11(iv)-(viii), the L^infty budget of Proposition 14 and Proposition 18(f)-(h), which localize and quantify, under the hypotheses and at the scales stated there, what branch (II) requires (a high-level potential-vorticity source near the axis, a q^4 cost on a level band, and a weighted inflow), again without a new viable route. The fifth added a literature update (sec. 3.9) and the tests of fixed-trajectory information in branch (I) and of the time-integrated inflow in branch (II) described in sec. 4(6)(xix) and 4(7), and first-step tests of mechanisms of other types (sec. 4(9)), again without a new viable route. None of the last three periods produced an estimate excluding either branch of Theorem 13 or a qualifying counterexample; the first missing implication stated at the beginning of this report is unchanged in kind and sharper in branch (II). Later work added Propositions 27 to 36: a conditional finite-window approximation, a shape constant for axisymmetric fields with swirl with the location of the gradient records it implies, the identification of the uniform gradient-scale sub-case of branch (I) with historical swirl domination, whose exclusion is the regularity criterion (SD), and lower bounds of iterated-logarithm type for the inward radial speed on every Case-1 trajectory (Propositions 30 and 31) and on every singular solution (Proposition 31(f), using [LZ2, Corollary 1.3]), and a pointwise lower bound near the axis for the scale-invariant inflow -r u^r, at the critical value 2 up to a logarithmic gap, on every singular solution and on every Case-1 trajectory (Proposition 32), and a bound of the circulation by the cumulative near-axis strain, which splits Case 1 into Type II near-axis strain and Type I swirl (Proposition 33), a bound of the near-axis strain by the potential vorticity together with a form of that circulation bound localized to superlevel sets (Proposition 34), a continuation criterion for a small swirl Type I constant, with a lower bound for the near-axis strain rate as a consequence (Proposition 35), and a decay of the circulation at the axis under a Type I near-axis strain bound and a slowly growing inflow envelope, which gives a necessary growth rate for the inflow on the Type I strain branch (Proposition 36). None of them excludes either branch, and (SD) was not proved. Propositions 30 and 31 are necessary conditions on the growth rate: cumulative inward displacement above every dimension-zero envelope is not excluded, and divergence of the Kolmogorov-Petrovskii integral (KP_0) of Proposition 31 is not necessary for decay of the radial survival function at the axis when F = 0, while for nonzero envelopes with C(t) -> infinity as t -> -infinity it is not proved here that convergence of (KP_0) implies a positive limiting survival (Proposition 31, Remark (1)). Proposition 32 is of the same kind: its hypothesis, a pointwise bound -r u^r <= 2 - eps(r) on the set where |Gamma| exceeds the comparison function, fails on every Case-1 trajectory (by Proposition 32(c) and the bound liminf_n gamma_n > 0 of Theorem 1), so Proposition 32 does not exclude Case 1 from (A), (K) and (TAIL) alone. Proposition 33 excludes neither alternative of its dichotomy on a Case-1 trajectory; under Type I swirl, a Liouville theorem for bounded ancient axisymmetric solutions with bounded circulation, swirl O(|tau|^{-1/2}) backward in time and gradients tending to 0 near the axis backward in time would exclude Case 1, and none was proved. Proposition 34 consists of an inequality, a comparison bound, conditional ancient criteria and necessary conditions; on the Type I swirl branch it requires inflow -U^R > R/(2|tau|), in a time-integrated sense, on each set {|Gamma_U| > lambda} with 0 < lambda < 1, which lies beyond a positive multiple of the parabolic radius, and no bound on the meridional field there strong enough to exclude this inflow was derived; its logarithmic decay (34.6) of the potential vorticity is far from the bound 1/(8 K_U s^2) that would exclude the limit. Proposition 35 excludes the Type I swirl branch only for a constant C_I < 3^{-1/2}, and no upper bound for C_I was derived. Its consequence (35.3) is a lower bound for the near-axis strain rate on every singular solution; on the Type I strain branch it is a necessary condition, C_a >= 1/2 + c_G, and gives no contradiction. Proposition 36 leaves the Type II strain branch untouched; on the Type I strain branch its conclusion (36.1) is a necessary growth condition for the inflow, of the iterated-logarithm type of Propositions 30 and 31 with a larger coefficient, and gives no contradiction. Proposition 37 decides neither branch: the strain records and the pressure inequality (37.1) are necessary conditions on the Type II strain branch (the pressure inequality is saturated by the infinite-energy Burgers local model, which does not realize the Type II history), and on the Type I swirl branch the barrier rates for U^theta/R do not reach the decay of the potential vorticity that Proposition 34(d)(ii) excludes; an expanding-radius compression bound would reach it (Proposition 37, Remark (3)), and it is not known. Proposition 38 is a Liouville theorem under a one-sided Type I inflow bound on the circulation superlevel sets; for the Case-1 limits it gives the necessary conditions 38(c) and its time-integrated form 38(d), which the kinematic family of Proposition 37, Remark (3), satisfies (38(d) in its asymptotic logarithmic-average form), together with the localization of 38(c) in 38(e) to an Euler cone and to late polynomial time windows (38.6); the inflow bound that would exclude the Type I swirl branch was not derived. Proposition 39 reduces that inflow bound, through a Feynman-Kac representation of eta = omega^theta/r along the backward five-dimensional diffusion and the localized Biot-Savart formula, to bounds for the source d_Z(q_U^2) of the potential vorticity, and excludes the Type I swirl branch under hypotheses on the limit: forward inflow (U^R <= 0) outside the moving parabolic cylinders {R < M |tau|^{1/2}} and the self-similar bound C |tau|^{-5/2} for the source inside them (the forward inflow can be weakened to U^R <= C/R if M^2 >= (1 + 2^{1/2}) C); the exterior source is controlled by the circulation equation itself, through the circulation energy collected along the backward paths, so no bound for the exterior source is needed. Under the Type I compression bound A_* < infinity of Proposition 37(d), which holds on the Type I strain branch of Proposition 33(e)(ii), or under its time-integrated form (CW) (Proposition 37(e), Proposition 39(f)(xi)), an energy along the backward paths joining q^2 inside the cylinders with |tau|^{-2} Gamma^2 outside them (the circulation equation has no compression term) replaces the core source bound, and the exclusion holds under the exterior hypothesis alone, even in the weaker form U^R <= kappa R/|tau| with kappa < 1 outside the cylinders (physically, u^r <= kappa r/(T_* - t), or u^r <= C/r, for r >= M_0 (T_* - t)^{1/2}). None of these hypotheses was derived; when A_* < infinity the missing estimate is an outflow bound between the parabolic radius and the radii K |tau|/kappa, beyond which |U| <= K gives it. Without A_* < infinity or (CW), the global energy estimate for q is not available (the compression enters the equation of q inside the cylinders), and the global argument uses instead the core source bound (H3), which is not shown to be necessary. A bounded dyadic window integral of the compression on the part of the cylinders inside an Euler cone suffices for the outflow form, required only on the cone, and for the vorticity, mass and source forms (Proposition 39(f)(xiii)), and the axial regularity (39.21) of the strain needs no compression hypothesis, since it bounds the compression on the cone (Proposition 39(f)(x)).
