When A_* < infinity, under (CW) or (CW_loc), or when the core source bound (H3) holds, the exterior outflow bound may be replaced by a bound for the vorticity alone, |omega^theta_U| <= |tau|^{-1} w(R/|tau|^{1/2}) outside the cylinders with w -> 0 and int^infinity w(xi) dxi/xi < infinity (Proposition 39(f)(vi), (xiii)). If (CW_loc) fails, the potential vorticity on every larger Euler cone has unbounded dyadic window integrals of (K E'(s))^{1/2} + s^{1/2} E'(s), E'(s) its supremum there (Proposition 37, Remark (5)(c)(8)); this is not excluded. Without a compression hypothesis, (39.19) gives the bound C_A (1 + log t) for the dyadic window integrals of the compression on the parabolic cylinders inside the cones of slope A < A_3; the same source bound on the boxes of a slope H > A_c, together with the pointwise source rate |d_Z(q_U^2)| <= F |tau|^{-5/2} on that cone, excludes the limit (Proposition 39(f)(xiv)). A uniform dyadic window bound for the reconstructed strain cannot be deduced from the source budget, the nonnegativity of phi in the source d_Z phi, and the boundedness, incompressibility and smoothness of an independently prescribed drift: Proposition 39(f)(xiv)(5)(d) gives logarithmic growth in that class, with critical radial outflow. For the limits themselves, the coupling Delta_5 a_U = d_Z eta and the source budget bound the vorticity mass of the parabolic cylinders and the signed height averages of the strain, which excludes that critical outflow across a diffusive height at radii o(|tau|^{1/2}) (Proposition 39(f)(xiv)(6)); the window bound holds in the zero-budget case, and for a positive budget the dyadic outflow count, the averaged radial flux and survival under a pointwise gap do not give it (Proposition 39(f)(xiv)(7)), nor does the time-integrated bound for the pointwise strain implied by the budget, since prescribed drifts that obey that bound but violate the vorticity mass bound for their own vorticity have packet windows growing like log log T (Proposition 39(f)(xiv)(8)). It remains open whether the additional structure of the Navier-Stokes limits removes this logarithm. For a small budget the logarithm does no harm: the compression averaged over the surviving law of the backward circulation paths has no logarithm, and Proposition 40 excludes the limits when 3 pi K/(8 (H - K)) + C_abs B/nu < 1/2 (C_abs = 7.636, or 2.80 by its Remarks (3) and (4), or 0.81 with the sharp Nash constant, or 0.735 with the heat value of the kernel constant by its Remark (5)); neither (39.19_H) nor this smallness was derived. An explicit bounded divergence-free field with exact vorticity, bounded circulation, Type I swirl, compression at most 1/(2 |tau|), vanishing source, outflow U^R = R/|tau| on {R <= |tau|, |Z| <= |tau|} for |tau| >= 1 and vorticity of the critical size 1/|tau| out to R ~ |tau| satisfies the bounds, the elliptic relation and the unsigned budgets used, but not the evolution equations (Proposition 39, Remark (7)); so this particular vorticity-decay route, a decay of |tau| |omega^theta_U| from the parabolic to the Euler scale, needs information beyond the listed bounds and the elliptic relation; neither this decay estimate nor either evolution equation is shown to be indispensable. The open task remains to exclude the swirl-record limit on both swirl branches. Without Type I swirl, a Liouville theorem for LL would suffice. With Type I swirl, sufficient alternatives, which do not need (39.19_H), include a bound on the actual strain U^R/R along the backward circulation paths: the averaged criterion of Proposition 40, Remark (2), with a coefficient c <= 1/2 and an integrable error, or its form on a positive circulation superlevel set in Remark (9)(f), with c < 1/2 and a level at which the terminal killed circulation has no atom; the pathwise or eventual criterion of Remarks (9)(d) and (9)(f); or the one-sided axial stretching criterion of Remarks (9)(g) and (9)(h), with D_+ <= 1. For a limit, the global pressure condition C_ax + d_ZZ P >= -alpha/tau^2 on R^3 x (-infinity, -1] with alpha in [0, 2] (C_ax := d_Z U^R d_R U^Z, P the pressure) of Remark (9)(h)(ii) is one sufficient route to the last criterion. None of these bounds has been derived for the limits. By the bounded kinematic example of Remark (9)(h)(i), the compression and axial stretching bounds do not follow, for prescribed fields, from the velocity, gradient and circulation bounds and the circulation equation alone; the example does not test the pressure condition for limits, since the construction does not impose the momentum equation.

## 2. Method

1. Re-derivation. The coupled system for Gamma, q = u^theta/r, eta = omega^theta/r and the 5D stream potential phi, the record identity, and the scaling identities were re-derived and checked symbolically (sympy). The 5D divergence div_5 b = 2u^r/r (not zero) was retained throughout.
2. Extraction. Mild formulation with Oseen kernel bounds |grad e^{nu h Delta} P|(y) <= C(|y| + sqrt(nu h))^{-4}, near/far splitting of the pressure with the far part controlled by (TAIL), a restart-time bootstrap for higher derivatives, and Arzela-Ascoli in the order C_tau C^m_y, then pressure gradients, then time derivatives, to pass through tau = 0.
3. Reduction. Translation-scaling compactness of bounded ancient solutions, a reflection and the maximum-point calculation of Theorem 1 at an attained swirl supremum, to identify exactly what the listed limit properties can give.
4. Route A. Five-dimensional Newton potential of eta with an axial-integration kernel bound, a Liouville theorem for bounded harmonic remainders, and the KNSS theorem for solutions with |u| <= C/r.
5. Route B. Feller scale function for the radial part of the circulation operator L = d_rr - (1/r) d_r + d_zz with a Lipschitz envelope of the inward radial velocity, and a two-step strong maximum principle argument with translated limits.
6. Pressure and (A). Calderon-Zygmund kernel splitting for grad^2 p with inner radius a = min{D/H, M/D} and outer radius b = M/D, using the near ball, the annulus and the exterior region (the annulus is empty when a = b), and only historical norms evaluated at the same time t; the Riccati inequality for the running maximum of |grad u|.
7. Theorem 9. Selection of running minima of the length l = (T_* - t) M and of gradient record times; rescaling at the Euler length; transport of the potential vorticity omega^theta/r along characteristics with backward decay and a harmonic terminal field, following Constantin, Ignatova and Vicol; in the complementary case an excursion lemma for monotone histories gives global Type I velocity, which is excluded by Chen, Strain, Tsai and Yau together with far-field epsilon-regularity.
8. Obstructions. Explicit model histories and explicit steady Euler and drift fields, used only to test whether an implication can hold in the generality in which it was attempted; none is a fixed-datum NS counterexample.
9. Computations. python3 (sympy, numpy, scipy), single-threaded: symbolic verification of identities and of the explicit examples and numerical sanity checks. No computation is part of a proof.
10. Literature. Statements of cited theorems were read in the original sources where retrievable; items only known through summaries are marked as such.
11. Inviscid rigidity (Proposition 12). Backward transport of a set where the potential vorticity is bounded below, by a flow that preserves three-dimensional volume, against the pointwise bound |omega^theta| <= sqrt2 |grad V| and the linear growth of the axial extent.
12. Scale dichotomy (Theorem 13). Taylor expansion of the swirl component along a line through the axis (where it is odd) at the point where the historical swirl maximum is attained, combined with (A) and the circulation bound; a compactness-contradiction argument at viscous gradient records using [KNSS, Theorem 5.2 and Remark 6.1] for swirl-free limits and [KNSS, Theorem 5.1] for receding-axis limits.
13. Critical mass (Proposition 14). A heat-semigroup argument gives a lower bound c_0(C_*) for the vorticity of the rescaled field at a gradient record s >= t_A (the gradient equals 1 and the Hessian is at most C_*); the swirl part (U - P U(P .))/2, P the reflection x_2 -> -x_2, has small vorticity by the Landau inequality when S/M is small; the odd meridional extension f of the azimuthal vorticity has supremum norm m >= c_0/2 and Lipschitz constant at most sqrt2 C_*. For 0 < a < m, a point with |f| >= a gives |f| >= a/2 on a disc of radius a/(2 sqrt2 C_*); the identity int_{R^2} |f| dR dZ = kappa N/pi and passage to a -> m give the critical mass bound.
14. Level selection (Proposition 15). An exact identity for (T_* - tau_k) L_k along first hitting times of geometric levels L_k shows that the normalized forward durations are unbounded when (T_* - t) D(t) is; the forward bounds come from the Landau inequality at s_n and (A) at b_n. The swirl-level version of the selection is from a research consultation (sec. 5).
15. Critical weighted energies (Propositions 16 to 18). For p > 3/2 with Y_p finite, multiplication of the q equation by p |q|^{p-2} q r^{2p-3}, integration in the 3D measure with the adjoint relation between the circulation operator and the 5D Laplacian, the weighted Hardy inequality on (0, infinity) with weight r^{2p-2}, and integration by parts of the inflow term through the stream function; symbolic check of the density identity and numerical evaluation of the stream-function threshold. The stream-function lower bound uses one-dimensional Landau inequalities along axial lines and the relation r psi^theta = int_0^r rho u^z d rho. The divergence of the inflow integral uses the C^{2,1} convergence of Theorem 2 on disjoint record cylinders.
16. Stream-function BMO form (Proposition 19). Superposition of circular ring potentials (all dilates and translates of one), a direct estimate of the mean oscillation of the unit ring potential near the ring (logarithmic), at intermediate distance (gradient bound) and at large scales (dipole decay), identification with the stream function through the Hardy-Littlewood-Sobolev inequality and a harmonic Liouville argument, lower semicontinuity of BMO under local uniform convergence, a Galilean change of frame, and the scale-invariant Hoelder estimate of Lei and Zhang applied on cylinders of every size.
17. Shrinking cylinders (Proposition 20). Seregin's exclusion of Type I singular points for axisymmetric suitable weak solutions and his local BMO criterion [Se20], applied at the singular point after a rescaling chosen from the assumed local bound; a near/far dyadic estimate for the BMO norm of the swirl potential using |u^theta| <= G/r; a cutoff decomposition of the meridional potential with the far part estimated from the energy; at the limit level and at the record tops, the Lei-Zhang Hoelder estimate for the circulation with the meridional field as the hollowed-energy part, applied at every scale (limit) or at the regular tops (records), and nesting of cylinders for the many-scale statement.
18. Circulation escape (Proposition 21). The one-sided form of the circulation barrier, applied with the local circulation supremum at the singular point. A Krylov-Safonov Harnack chain for sup Gamma - Gamma, running from a point near the axis to the point considered. First-crossing records of weighted circulations, with the zero-order coefficient of their equation. Flux identities using that the dx-adjoint of L is the 5D Laplacian Delta_5, and the 5D fundamental solution |X|^{-3}.
19. Localized pressure and strain (Proposition 22). The axisymmetric pressure Poisson equation with its swirl source in divergence form and the Newton kernel restricted to the axis; second-order conditions at the swirl maximum; the incompressibility identity for the disk {r < r_n, z = z_n} bounded by the record circle; the radial and axial momentum equations expanded at the axis; the Burgers vortex as an exact local model.
20. Ancient Liouville hypotheses (Proposition 23). In the proof, a comparison on a moving disk with an explicit quartic subsolution for the circulation deficit; a two-dimensional radial heat barrier on annuli with a smooth ramp, the maximum principle for its radial derivative, and a cosh barrier in Z; and the exterior line sink as an exact sharpness example for the exterior comparison. Separately, sec. 3.16 compares the published hypothesis classes with the available bounds, sec. 3.9 records a search of arXiv listings on 2026-10-16, and the Status line records computer checks.
21. Material lines and vorticity creation (Proposition 24). Integration of the particle and circulation equations along backward paths with C^{2,1} convergence on a short window; Stokes' theorem on instantaneous flat disks; the meridional Jacobian; Taylor expansion on the axis; the adjoint identity between L and Delta_5 with its axis term; Z-averaging of the angular equation for the nonvanishing of the source; scaling of the dissipation.
22. Far-field inflow (Proposition 25). The comparison of Proposition 23(b) with the sign of the radial derivative at the maximum; the axial integral of the incompressibility relation; the Biot-Savart kernel averaged over the angle; explicit exterior and whole-space drift models with sub- and supersolution barriers and monotone exhaustion; asymptotic evaluation of the vorticity equation for the drift model; the reduction of the limit-level statement to Theorem 3; the exact slender residual, and symbolic verification of the Landau flow with potential swirl.
23. Averaged circulation flux (Proposition 26). Integration of the circulation equation over cylinders, box averages with explicit errors, a Banach limit, and a first-order radial equation for the averaged profile, integrating factors, and the same for convex functions of the circulation, and explicit scalar and kinematic models with symbolic and high-precision numerical evaluation of the equation residuals, and the level-set form of the convex hierarchy with an explicit two-level solution, the Wirtinger bound for periodic fields and the averaged momentum balances, and the critical axial-flux iteration, its fixed-data scalings and the averaged supersolution identity and vorticity residual of the first saturating construction of Proposition 26(i), and the stated leading-order steady vorticity equation for the maximal axially long pattern, and the first integral and reciprocal-variable form of the long-pattern equation used in the rigidity proof, and the averaged energy budgets and the kinematic field of Proposition 26(k), the kinematic stationary field of Proposition 26(l), the exponent bookkeeping of the pre-limit tests in sec. 4, and the vorticity identity behind the steady head equation and the steady test field of sec. 4.
24. Finite-window realization (Proposition 27). Cutoff of the Stokes stream function and of the circulation of a member of LL at a large radius; under the uniform boundedness hypothesis of Proposition 27(a), a weighted L^infinity stability estimate for bounded mild solutions with weight (1 + |x|/(nu T)^{1/2})^{-a}, 0 < a < 1, a singular Gronwall inequality, interior smoothing and interpolation for C^2 convergence, and, under the boundary-gap hypothesis, the swirl equation at an interior window maximum.
25. Shape bound for axisymmetric fields (Proposition 28). Rotation equivariance of the gradient at axis points, the singular-value inequalities of Proposition 11(v) for k = 1, 2, 3 with weak majorization, a Landau inequality for d_3 U_3 on axial lines from the differentiated divergence identity, and maximization of a convex function over a polygon; averaging of the gradient over the rotations about the axis (an orthogonal projection onto the axis-compatible matrices) with a cylindrical formula for the Frobenius norm of the Hessian with swirl; a vector Landau inequality relating the largest singular value of the gradient to |U|, and the bound of the smallest singular value by |U|/r from the angular derivative.
26. Historical swirl domination (Proposition 29). Restarting the bounded-data local theory for the historical bounds D <= C_D M^2 and H <= C_H M^3 at sufficiently late times; the swirl bound S^2 <= G D; the comparison of Theorem 13(e) and the compactness alternative of Theorem 13(b) at the last maximizing times of the gradient.
27. Inflow envelopes (Proposition 30). A z-independent supersolution of the circulation equation built from the heat equation in a domain with the moving boundary x = int g (after [Sh, Lemma 5.1]); the maximum principle with a growing barrier; the killed Brownian representation and its shift monotonicity; Kolmogorov's integral test at small times by time inversion, the integral form of Petrovskii's regularity criterion (that form was not checked against [Pet]); dominated convergence for terminal windows; first-attainment times of the swirl as first-crossing records; an integration by parts for the iterated-logarithm envelope; and, for the localized form, the heat equation on a moving strip with a reflection bound.
28. Dimension-zero envelopes (Proposition 31). The comparison function for the exact radial operator, obtained from corner-compatible truncations by monotone limits and represented by a Bessel process of dimension zero with an outward drift; pathwise monotonicity in the starting point and a Gronwall comparison of displacements; a logarithmic time change in which the derivative of the self-similar inflow cancels; Muckenhoupt's weighted Hardy inequality for a spectral gap at least C^3 e^{-C^2}/128 for C >= 2; a backward energy estimate with a time-dependent weight; and, for part (f), the explicit form of the resulting decay together with the circulation criterion of Lei and Zhang [LZ2, Corollary 1.3].
29. Critical inflow at the axis (Proposition 32). A stationary supersolution built from the scale function of the radial comparison diffusion with drift (1 - eps(r))/r; the maximum principle with a growing barrier, using the inflow bound only where the circulation exceeds the supersolution; closed forms of the scale function for iterated-logarithm profiles; the continuation criteria [LZ2, Corollary 1.3] and [Wei, Corollary 1.1] after a restart at a positive time; and, for the remarks only, Feller's boundary classification and exit-time bounds from Ito's formula.
30. Circulation absorption by the near-axis strain (Proposition 33). The Burgers-type supersolution G (1 - exp(-r^2 w(t))) of the circulation equation, with w solving the Riccati equation w' = 2 k w - 4 w^2 started at w = infinity, compared with the circulation by the maximum principle with a growing barrier after matching through the quadratic vanishing of the circulation at the axis; closed forms under a Type I strain bound; the record identity of Theorem 1; the compactness of bounded mild ancient solutions and the Liouville theorem for swirl-free ones [KNSS, Theorem 5.2 and Remark 6.1]; and the same comparison for ancient solutions.
31. Strain from potential vorticity and superlevel absorption (Proposition 34). The identity Delta_5 (u^r/r) = d_z (omega^theta/r) and the heat semigroup of R^5 for (34.1); the comparison of Proposition 33 with a lower semicontinuous strain coefficient restricted to a superlevel set of the circulation, with the contact argument at a fixed spatial point; the swirl bound of Proposition 33(e)(i), which places {|Gamma_U| > lambda} beyond a positive multiple of the parabolic radius for 0 < lambda < 1; the maximum principle for the potential vorticity in R^5; Bernstein-type derivative bounds for the swirl equation and a radial barrier on a cylinder for the logarithmic rate (34.6).
32. A small swirl Type I constant (Proposition 35). The energy identities for omega^r/r and omega^theta/r and the swirl estimate of Chen, Fang and Zhang [CFZ], the elliptic bound of [Wei, Lemma 2.1], a weighted energy E satisfying E' <= (3^{3/2}/2) ||u^theta||_infty^2 E after normalization to nu = 1, and the continuation lemma [CFZ, Lemma 2.5]. The lower bound (35.3) for the strain rate combines (35.2) with the pointwise circulation bound (33.1), the elementary maximum mu_0 = max_{x > 0} (1 - e^{-x})^2/x, and the comparison of Proposition 33(b); its second term uses the weighted energy lambda ||omega^r/r||_2^2 + ||omega^theta/r||_2^2 with lambda chosen against the bounds for ||u^theta||_infty^2 and ||u^theta/r||_infty supplied by (33.1).
33. Circulation decay under Type I strain and a slowly growing inflow (Proposition 36). A comparison for the circulation with the smoothed state-dependent drift min{||(u^r)^-||_infty, ||(u^r/r)^-||_infty r}, the logarithmic clock l = log v and the self-similar variable y = R_v/v^{1/2} for the comparison diffusion, spectral bounds for the frozen one-dimensional operators by a weighted Hardy inequality [Mu], a block decomposition in logarithmic time with frozen energy estimates, and, for envelopes C such that l -> C(e^l) is continuously differentiable with d C(e^l)/dl square-integrable in the logarithmic time l (condition (W2)), an energy estimate in a moving centered coordinate.
34. Strain records and a swirl barrier (Proposition 37). The equation (d_t + b.grad - Delta_5)(u^r/r) = -(u^r/r)^2 + (u^theta/r)^2 - p_r/r at a running minimum of u^r/r, the axis pressure identity of Proposition 22(a), the circulation bound (33.1) with the strain replaced by its running maximum, and, for the Type I swirl limits, the comparison functions f(R^2/L^2), f(x) = (1 - e^{-beta x})/((1 - e^{-beta}) x) (the profile of the swirl ratio of a Burgers vortex), for the equation of U^theta/R, supersolutions when U^R/R >= -A/L^2 on the cylinder {R < L} throughout the earlier history with beta > 0 and a fixed A satisfying 0 <= A < 2 nu beta, with f(0) = F(beta) = beta/(1 - e^{-beta}); and, in Remark (3), a Bernstein estimate for the five-dimensional gradient of U^theta/R on unit time windows.
35. A circulation barrier in similarity variables (Proposition 38). The circulation equation in backward self-similar variables, a radial supersolution growing like a logarithm of the normalized radius under a one-sided Type I inflow bound, the weak maximum principle on the circulation superlevel sets with axial penalization, and the unbounded logarithmic time of an ancient solution; [KNSS, Theorem 5.2] and mildness for the swirl-free case.
36. Feynman-Kac representation of the potential vorticity (Proposition 39). A cutoff Bernstein estimate for U^theta/R, the backward five-dimensional diffusion with the meridional drift, a supermartingale for R^{-2} and a reflection bound for the first entrance into the moving parabolic cylinders under exterior inflow, the circulation-energy identity d(Gamma^2) = [2 nu |grad_5 Gamma|^2 + 8 nu Gamma Gamma_R/R] du + martingale along the backward paths, the energy identity d(q^2) = [4 a_U q^2 + 2 nu |grad_5 q|^2] du + martingale, joined at the boundary of the parabolic cylinders with the circulation energy (a convex kink, so the local-time term has a favorable sign) and with an increasing weight, under Type I compression on the cylinders or under (CW) (the compression loss summed over dyadic windows), and on nested cones with the paths stopped at the exit under (CW_loc) (the exit term retained), supermartingales R^{-beta} (a + u)^gamma for the arrival into the cylinders and the occupation before it under a Type I exterior outflow bound, and the localized Biot-Savart formula with the mass functional int |x - y|^{-4} |eta| dy. Under (39.21) the axial derivative bound and the signed axial flux first give the compression bound on the cone, so no compression hypothesis is assumed there.
37. Absorption of the backward circulation paths (Proposition 40). The backward diffusion of the circulation equation from the record point, killed at the axis, whose survival probability is at least 1/A by the record (Proposition 26(l)); a two-sided Green-function bound on balls of R^5 for the strain a = U^R/R by the potential vorticity; the envelope of Proposition 39(f)(xiv)(6) on arbitrary subsets of the cone and a splitting of |eta| into a part of bounded mass and a bounded part; a bound for the density of the surviving law from the positivity, contraction and smoothing of the source-free evolution in three-dimensional measure; for eternal paths, the change of variables Y = e^J R by the cumulative strain J, which in the clock int e^{2J} du turns the radius into a Bessel process of dimension zero, so that eternal survival costs a cumulative compression exceeding (1/2) log t by an amount tending to infinity; Tonelli's theorem and Fatou's lemma to compare the averaged compression with this cost. In the Remarks: comparison of pathwise compression profiles with restarts at deterministic ages, the killed circulation martingale along the paths, the identity a = -R^{-2} int_0^R r d_Z U^Z dr, a Riccati comparison for d_Z U^Z under a lower bound for C_ax + d_ZZ P, and a bounded kinematic field with a Type I swirl bound and core compression k/(1 + s), 1/2 < k < 1, showing that the thresholds of the compression and axial stretching criteria cannot be raised for prescribed fields; the example does not attain the constant-profile endpoint a^- <= 1/(2u), which the compression cost of Proposition 40(b) excludes.


## 3. Findings

Proof status. The findings below have the status of the results they cite, as recorded in the Status lines of section 1. In particular, Theorems 2 and 9 and Propositions 8, 15, 20, 21, 22 and 36 have proofs with key estimates; Propositions 16, 18, 19 and 25 have proof sketches with key estimates; Proposition 26 is a proof sketch with key estimates apart from the parts stated as proved in its Status line; Proposition 27 is a proof sketch with key estimates for its conditional statement; and some later propositions have parts that depend on cited results, as stated in their Status lines.

### 3.1 The limit problem is the bounded-circulation Liouville problem

The record identity is a pointwise statement at a space-time maximum of u^theta: d_t u^theta >= 0, vanishing first derivatives and nonpositive Laplacian give u^r S_n/r_n <= -S_n/r_n^2. Under (K) and (TAIL), after fixing the sign of the record swirl (reflecting if necessary), a subsequence of the normalized fields converges in C^{2,1}_loc through the terminal time to a bounded ancient mild solution with viscosity nu_* in [1/G, (K^2 - 1)^{1/2}] that retains the record (Theorems 1 and 2). (TAIL) is used only for the approximants; for the limit it is automatic, since sup_tau int_{|y| > L} |U|^2 |y|^{-4} dy <= 4 pi K^2/L. Finite physical energy gives int |U_n(tau)|^2 dy <= E_0/(gamma_n^2 r_n), which tends to infinity, so it gives no uniform global L^2 bound on U.

Theorem 3 shows that every extracted limit gives an LL solution after normalization and that, conversely, every LL solution has a member of its closure under axial translations, time translations into the past, parabolic scalings and the reflection x_2 -> -x_2 that has, after a rescaling of the viscosity, the listed normalized properties for some admissible parameters (this is not a realization theorem for the fixed physical datum; Proposition 27 gives, under a uniform-bound hypothesis, finite-energy solutions regular on a finite interval that approximate a member of LL on a fixed window). The swirl maximum of any W in LL can be moved, by translation compactness (a limit of translates attains the supremum), a reflection if needed and a parabolic rescaling, to a normalized point where the maximum-point calculation of Theorem 1 gives the record conditions. Hence an exclusion argument that uses only the listed limit properties, for all admissible parameters, would establish that LL is empty. Information that is not visibly retained by the abstract limit class includes (A) with its constant C_*, finite energy of the fixed trajectory, and the approximants themselves.

### 3.2 Two conditional Liouville theorems for LL

Theorem 4 (Route A). The proof writes eta_W as a bounded function on R^5 with |eta| <= min(C, A_eta |y'|^{-3}). Its 5D Newton potential phi_0 = N_5 * eta is bounded with |phi_0| <= C/R and |grad phi_0| <= C/R^2 for R >= 2 (axial integration of the kernel, int (d^2 + s^2)^{-3/2} ds = 2/d^2, reduces to R^4 integrals that converge thanks to the R^{-3} decay). The field b_0 = curl(r phi_0 e_theta) has the same vorticity as the meridional velocity V, so V - b_0 is bounded, divergence free and curl free, hence c(tau) e_3. Translates to radial infinity converge to spatially constant mild solutions, so c is constant; after the Galilean change of frame by c_0 the solution satisfies |W'| <= C/R and [KNSS, Theorem 5.3] gives W' = 0. This is unconditional apart from sup R^3 |eta| < infinity, and Corollary: every member of LL violates that bound. A derivation of the bound from properties shared by all of LL would settle the Liouville problem. The local physical target limsup_n sup_{Q_n(L)} r^3 |eta|/gamma_n <= A, uniform in L, where Q_n(L) := (z_n e_3 + r_n B_L) x [t_n - L^2 T_n, t_n] is the physical region of the normalized cylinder B_L x [-L^2, 0], is sufficient and weaker than the global criterion of Li and Pan. The weighted maximum-principle argument that needs -R V^R >= nu on vertical segments longer than K R^2/nu is ruled out (Theorem 4, last part); other weighted arguments are not excluded.

Theorem 5 (Route B). Its hypothesis is -W^R <= b(R) for R >= R_0, all Z and tau <= 0, with b locally integrable on [R_0, infinity) and int_{R_0}^infinity R exp(-(1/nu) int_{R_0}^R b) dR = infinity. The circulation solves d_tau Gamma + V.grad Gamma = nu L Gamma, with V the meridional part of W and L = d_RR - (1/R) d_R + d_ZZ, the generator of a diffusion that hits the axis. Replacing the given b by the envelope B(R) = sup_{Z, tau} (-V^R), which is bounded and Lipschitz by the smoothing estimate for bounded mild ancient solutions (sec. 1.1) and satisfies B <= b on [R_0, infinity), the scale function sigma(R) = int_{R_0}^R rho exp(-(1/nu) int_{R_0}^rho B) d rho satisfies nu(sigma'' - sigma'/R) = -B sigma' and tends to infinity. Comparison with Gamma - m(R_1) - eps sigma on {R > R_1}, for R_1 >= R_0, and translated limits show that sup_{R >= R_1} Gamma = sup_{R = R_1} Gamma, so a positive supremum would be approached at bounded radius, which the strong maximum principle and Gamma = 0 on the axis exclude. An upward mollification of b is not safe (for b = 2 nu/R the integral diverges, for b + eps it converges); the envelope avoids this. The record identity gives compression -R V^R >= nu only at the record point (R, Z, tau) = (1, 0, 0); the vertical-flux identity (Proposition 25(b)) shows that the vertical mean of rho V^R over long segments is O(rho^2/h), so an averaged envelope holds trivially but does not feed the comparison argument. O1 (Proposition 8(d)) shows that bounded smooth divergence-free drift alone allows a bounded nonconstant circulation with sup approached at radial infinity.

### 3.3 What (A) gives

Theorem 7 bounds the pressure Hessian at every earlier time s <= t by historical norms at time t only. Under (A) this yields the Riccati inequality for the running maximum D and the lower blow-up rate D(t) >= 1/(C_2 (T_* - t)) for late t. It gives magnitude information only: no sign of u^r and no upper bound on D.

At the swirl record, (A) becomes m_n h_n <= C_* d_n^2 between global historical numbers (Proposition 8(a)). If d_n is bounded, then along a further subsequence on which (m_n, d_n, h_n) converges to (m, d, h) the limit U satisfies sup|U| <= m, sup|grad U| <= d, sup|grad^2 U| <= h with m h <= C_* d^2, but the actual sup|grad U| may be strictly smaller than d because the gradient maxima of the approximants can escape. So the denominator of (A) need not be retained in the limit, and passing (A) with its constant to U has not been justified. Proposition 8(b) shows that a prescribed constant would be a genuine restriction on LL if LL is nonempty, so a quantitative use of C_* is not excluded by the reduction; we did not find one.

Rescaling at gradient records instead of swirl records (Proposition 8(c)) keeps (A) as a global bound, |grad^2 V| <= C_*, but in general loses the swirl record. Theorem 13 shows what (A) gives about the relation between the two kinds of records; see sec. 3.6.

### 3.4 Theorem 9: (A) excludes Type I gradient growth

Assume (A) and the Type I hypothesis (TI): D(t) <= C_I/(T_* - t) on [t_I, T_*). Let l(t) = (T_* - t) M(t), f(t) = l(t)^2/(T_* - t) and nu(t) = 1/f(t).
 Basic facts. Leray's lower bound gives f >= c_L^2. The interpolation ||u||_infty <= c ||u||_2^{2/5} ||grad u||_infty^{3/5} with the energy bound gives l(t) <= c (T_* - t)^{2/5} -> 0, so the last minimum point of l on [t_0, t] is a running-minimum time tending to T_*. Combining (TI) with the Riccati bound of Theorem 7, every running-minimum time tau has a gradient record time s <= tau with T_* - s <= A_0 (T_* - tau), A_0 = C_2 C_I.
 Case (E): f(tau_n) -> infinity along running minima. At the associated gradient record times s_n, rescale at the Euler length l_n = (T_* - s_n) M(s_n) and time T_n = T_* - s_n, with viscosity nu_n = T_n/l_n^2 (local notation: these T_n, nu_n differ from the record quantities of sec. 1.1). The rescaled fields satisfy, on all of R^3 and all rescaled times sigma <= -1 back to t_0: |V_n| <= 1, |grad V_n| <= C_I/|sigma|, |grad^2 V_n| <= A_0 C_* C_I^2/|sigma| (by (A) at each earlier time and the running-minimum property l(t) >= l_n/A_0), R_n |Z_n| <= G nu_n, where R_n is the rescaled distance to the original symmetry axis and Z_n := V_n^theta e_theta the swirl part of V_n with respect to that axis, and |grad V_n(y*_n, -1)| >= 1/C_2, with nu_n -> 0. The swirl gradient at sigma = -1 is O(nu_n^{1/3}), so the meridional gradient stays of size 1/C_2. Adapting the scheme of [CIV, Lemmas 3.2-3.3] with these global bounds (the estimates are given after Theorem 9), the potential vorticity (for a receding axis, the planar vorticity) converges off the axis along a subsequence and is weakly transported by the limiting meridional field; characteristics starting off the axis stay off it on finite backward intervals, and the backward decay along them forces the azimuthal vorticity to vanish at sigma = -1, so the limit meridional field at sigma = -1 is bounded, divergence free and curl free, hence constant, contradicting the lower bound on its gradient.
 Case (P): f <= F at all late running minima. The excursion lemma (between consecutive returns of l to its running minimum, monotonicity of M and f >= c_L^2 give f <= F^2/c_L^2 at all late times) yields ||u(t)||_infty <= (F/c_L)(T_* - t)^{-1/2}. [CSTY2, Theorem 1.1] (data in H^{1/2}, r v^theta(0) bounded, pressure in L^{5/3}) gives local boundedness, and the far field is bounded by the epsilon-regularity criterion [ESS, Lemma 2.2], because the energy class gives vanishing scaled L^3 and L^{3/2} norms of u and p at spatial infinity. So u stays bounded up to T_*, a contradiction.
Remarks. The theorem uses (A) twice: in the Riccati lower bound, which makes gradient records dense in logarithmic time, and in the bound H(t) <= C_* D(t)^2/M(t) at every earlier time t, which gives the backward decay of the transported potential vorticity. No historical quantity is replaced by an instantaneous one. Theorem 9 is an adaptation of [CIV, Theorem 1.2]: there the Euler length is prescribed, nonincreasing, with (T_* - t)/l(t)^2 -> 0 at all late times; here l is built from historical norms, is not monotone, and case (E) gives nu -> 0 only along selected times. This adaptation uses the historical-norm selection and the excursion lemma.

### 3.5 Why Theorem 9 does not reach the Case-1 limit

Write g = 1/D and theta(t) = (T_* - t) D(t). Theorem 9 gives limsup theta = infinity. The backward decay used in Case (E) of the proof of Theorem 9 is, on the gradient time scale 1/D(s), supplied by backward windows W(c, A, s). A window is exactly the historical ratio bound D(s + sigma/D(s))/D(s) <= [c(1 + |sigma|)]^{-1}; it implies an upper bound for the rescaled gradient, but it is not equivalent to actual decay of the rescaled gradient, nor to decay of the transported potential vorticity. Type I implies windows (Proposition 11(i)). Proposition 11(ii) constructs admissible scalar histories (levels 2^{-k} on flats of length k 2^{-k}, joined by drops of slope -C_2) for which every window W(c, A, s) with c(1 + A) > 2 fails at all late s (windows with c(1 + A) <= 1 hold there, since the rescaled history is at least 1); there theta(s) is unbounded and the rescaled history is between 1 and 2 on [-A, 0], so the scalar information gives no backward decay of the historical gradient bound. Under (A) the two lengths M/D (gradient scale) and (T_* - t) M (Euler length) have ratio theta, which is unbounded along a sequence; the running-minimum control of Theorem 9 is for the second, while (A) gives Hessian control in the first.

Windows W(c, A_j, s_j) with one fixed c > 0 and A_j -> infinity along the gradient records are a sufficient condition for excluding inviscid gradient-scale limits (Proposition 12); they are not shown to be necessary. The proof of Proposition 12 is a volume argument: a set E of positive volume on which |Omega| >= delta is transported back to time -sigma_n, where it lies in {R <= sqrt2 ||grad V(-sigma_n)||_infty/delta} and in a slab of height O(sigma_n), so its volume tends to 0 under the stated decay. In the inviscid branch the steady example e^{-|y'|^2} e_3, after the rescaling y -> V(b y) with b = sqrt(e/2) and a translation of a gradient maximum point to the origin, satisfies every normalized bound when C_* >= sqrt2 e (Proposition 11(iii)). In the viscous branch the limits are in LL, which returns to sec. 3.1. Thus under (A) the remaining scenario is Type II gradient growth (in the limsup sense of Theorem 9) whose gradient-scale ancient limits are either finite-axis viscous limits in LL after viscosity normalization, or finite-axis or planar inviscid limits for which no sufficient backward-decay estimate has been established.

### 3.6 Scale dichotomy (Theorem 13)

Theorem 13(a) is elementary. Along the line through the point where the historical swirl maximum S is attained and perpendicular to the axis, the swirl component is odd, vanishes on the axis, and has a critical point at distance r_0 <= G/S; Taylor's formula gives S <= (1/2) r_0^2 H, hence 2 S^3 <= G^2 H, and, for t >= t_A, (A) turns this into 2 M S^3 <= C_* G^2 D^2.

Theorem 13(b) is a quantitative form of Proposition 8(c). If a sequence of uniformly viscous gradient records (kappa >= c for a fixed c > 0) had S/M -> 0 or the gradient maximizer at unbounded rescaled distance from the axis, the gradient-scale limit would be either a swirl-free axisymmetric NS solution with positive viscosity, constant by [KNSS, Theorem 5.2 and Remark 6.1], or planar and constant by [KNSS, Theorem 5.1]; both contradict |grad V(0, 0)| = 1. So at uniformly viscous gradient records the historical norms M, D, H are comparable to powers of the historical swirl maximum: M ~ S, D ~ S^2, H ~ S^3, and the gradient maximizer lies within O(1/S) of the axis.

Theorem 13(c) identifies the two branches of Proposition 8(c) with the swirl ratio, and Theorem 13(d) transfers this to the swirl records of Case 1. In branch (I) the normalized global numbers m_n, d_n, h_n are bounded, so (K) and (TAIL) follow from (A) together with the branch condition and the record estimates, and, after viscosity normalization, the swirl-record limits belong to LL, and so do the gradient-record limits after a horizontal translation taking their axis to the x_3 axis. Every member of LL has finite Q. Consequently, an exclusion of branch (I) using only the ancient limit properties of Theorem 2 and finiteness of Q, uniformly over all finite shape constants, would settle the bounded-circulation Liouville problem; an exclusion for one fixed C_* is not covered by this reduction, and none is known to us. This reduction does not apply to an argument using the additional eternal selection of Proposition 15 or information from the fixed physical trajectory.

Branch (II) is a high-Reynolds-number regime: the local Reynolds number at a gradient record is 1/kappa -> infinity, the swirl is small relative to M, and the gradient maximizers escape every swirl-record observation cylinder. The gradient-scale limits are swirl-free Euler flows, so Proposition 12 applies once a backward decay o(sigma_n^{-1/2}) of ||grad V(-sigma_n)||_infty is known along one sequence. In the rescaled variables the swirl forcing d_Z(q^2) of the potential vorticity is pointwise O(kappa^{1/3}), so it tends to zero on fixed Euler-time intervals; a pointwise estimate for the full material derivative is unavailable because the viscous term is uncontrolled, and transport is asserted for the weak Euler limit; over an interval of length A the forcing integrates to O(A kappa^{1/3}), which is not small for A of order 1/kappa, and the viscous term kappa Delta_5 Omega is not controlled by the available Hessian bound. The following is therefore heuristic, and only the displayed estimates are claimed. An exact unidirectional jet f(R, sigma) e_3 evolves by the heat equation d_sigma f = kappa Delta f (the Gaussian terminal profile e^{-b^2 R^2} has the backward continuation (1 + 4 b^2 kappa sigma)^{-1} exp(-b^2 R^2/(1 + 4 b^2 kappa sigma)) for -1/(4 b^2 kappa) < sigma <= 0, whose gradient supremum is the terminal one times (1 + 4 b^2 kappa sigma)^{-3/2}, a factor larger than 1 for sigma < 0), so an exact jet cannot sit at a terminal historical gradient record. Quantitatively, Duhamel's formula shows that the nonlinear and pressure acceleration F = -V.grad V - grad P satisfies sup ||F||_infty >= kappa/(8 C_h^2) on [-4 C_h^2/kappa, 0], C_h the heat-gradient constant; but an acceleration of order kappa vanishes in the Euler limit, so convergence on compact sets to a steady jet is not excluded. Also int_0^infinity q_V^2 R dR = O(kappa^{4/3}) at every height and time.

A single-profile field lambda(t) W(lambda(t) x, tau(t)) with W in LL and tau' = lambda^2 is not a model of branch (I): it leaves the residual lambda'(t)(W + X.grad_X W), X = lambda(t) x, in the NS equations, which does not vanish in general.

### 3.7 Critical mass and eternal limits (Propositions 14 and 15)

The critical-mass lower bound in Proposition 14 is a single-time statement. At a gradient record s >= t_A the rescaled field U has |U| <= 1, |grad U| <= 1 attained at the origin and |grad^2 U| <= C_*. If the vorticity of U were uniformly small, heat-semigroup smoothing would make its gradient small, so ||curl U||_infty >= c_0(C_*). If S/M is small, the swirl part of U has small vorticity by the Landau inequality, so the azimuthal vorticity is at least c_0/2 somewhere, hence on a disc of radius of order c_0/C_*, which gives a lower bound for its meridional L^1 norm; in physical variables this is N(s) >= c_1 M(s)^2/D(s). The quantity N is critical, and in branch (II) M^2/D = 1/kappa -> infinity, so this branch forces the global potential-vorticity mass to diverge at the gradient records. The lower bound comes from a disc of physical radius comparable to M/D centred at a point where the heat-semigroup argument finds substantial azimuthal vorticity (not necessarily the gradient maximizer), and |omega^theta| <= sqrt2 D there, so the mass on such a disc is of order M^2/D. A global bound N(s_n) = o(M(s_n)^2/D(s_n)) would suffice; the strict deficit of Proposition 14 would already suffice. When N(a) < infinity, the balances give N = o(D^{1/2}) and N = o(S); neither contradicts the established lower bound. A truncated balance (Proposition 18(f)) removes the assumption N(a) < infinity from the consequence kappa_n S(s_n) -> infinity and, when M^5/D^3 >= epsilon_0, shows that the source, integrated over [a, s_n] and over the superlevel set {|eta| > lambda_n} at distance at least c M(s_n)/D(s_n) from the axis, is o(1/kappa_n) for every fixed a and c > 0. The swirl source d_z(q^2) of the eta equation is critical in L^1_t L^1_x but was not controlled critically under (A). The supremum of eta obeys a pointwise budget instead: the maximum principle for eta and the swirl-part bound ||d_z(q^2)||_infty <= 2 sqrt6 S^{1/2} H^{3/2} give, along branch-(II) records s_n with M(s_n)^5/D(s_n)^3 >= epsilon_0 > 0 uniformly in n, D^2/M <= C (1 + int (D^2/M)^{5/3} dt) (Proposition 14, L^infty budget). Since (D^2/M)^{5/3} = kappa^{1/3} D (D^2/M), this is a budget with rate kappa^alpha D (D^2/M), alpha = 1/3. If D(t) and M(t) are comparable to (T_* - t)^{-beta} and (T_* - t)^{-3 beta/5} throughout a fixed late interval, a budget with rate kappa^alpha D (D^2/M), a fixed alpha < 5 and a constant independent of n requires beta >= 5/(5 - alpha), by comparison of exponents; for alpha = 1/3 this is beta >= 15/14, and in the case of equality the conclusion also depends on the constants. These are necessary conditions only, and such a budget does not exclude sufficiently fast power-law growth. Two further proved facts locate the difficulty. The point where the budget finds |eta| of order D^2/M lies at r >= c_0 M/(4 sqrt2 C_* D), and at r >= c M/D the source is at most C kappa D (D^2/M) (Proposition 14, endpoint remark), so saturation of the source bound with rate kappa^{1/3}, if it occurs, requires r = o(M/D). And an energy atom of mass m has a concentration radius rho_m(t) with int^{T_*} rho_m^{-2} dt < infinity (Proposition 11(vii)). For the power laws above, a budget with rate kappa D (D^2/M) (alpha = 1) would need beta >= 5/4, while a core that stays at the gradient scale, rho_m(t) <= C M(t)/D(t) for all late t, needs int (D/M)^2 dt < infinity, that is beta < 5/4. Under these power-law assumptions and the persistent-core assumption, for every fixed c > 0 the source from r >= c M(t)/D(t) contributes o(X(s_n)) to the parabolic (backward-diffusion) representation of eta at the budget point, so a contribution of order X(s_n) must come from r < c M(t)/D(t); no corresponding statement about deterministic particle paths has been proved. A research consultation gives formal power-law orders of this kind (beta = 6/5, S ~ (T_* - t)^{-14/25}, eta generated in an axial tube of radius 1/S and length (T_* - t)^{11/25}, cores of size M/D at axial distance (T_* - t)^{7/25} from the singular point) that satisfy the scalar budgets it checks; it is not a Navier-Stokes solution, the author checked its exponents but not its profiles, and it does not verify every necessary condition of this report (Proposition 18(c) in particular). Neither an o(X(s_n)) bound on this inner-region contribution nor the all-late-time bound rho_m(t) <= C M(t)/D(t) has been derived from the Case-1 hypotheses.

Proposition 15 adds eternality and an attained spacetime gradient maximum to the limits. Its forward bounds use only (A) and the Landau inequality: if s <= b < T_*, b >= t_A, D(b) <= lambda D(s) and s is a gradient record, then M(b) <= 18 C_* lambda^2 M(s). It does not exclude either branch; an appropriate Liouville theorem for eternal members of LL with a shape bound would exclude an eternal limit selected by Proposition 15 if its viscosity is positive, but not an arbitrary prescribed viscous subsequence (steady members would be eternal, and we know of no theorem excluding bounded steady axisymmetric solutions with bounded circulation and nonzero swirl on R^3 without further decay). In the scenario in which all late gradient records are uniformly viscous (kappa >= c for one c > 0 and all sufficiently late gradient records; a viscous subsequence does not suffice), the solution is single-scale at all late times (M(t) <= 18 C_* C_c S(t)), so limsup (T_* - t) S(t)^2 = infinity by Theorem 9, and along suitable swirl records ||(u^r)^-|| >= S/G and ||grad^2 u|| >= 2 S^3/G^2; hence the global hypotheses of Zhang's one-sided Type I criterion, of the paired Euler-length bounds of [CIV] (their product would bound (T_* - t)^2 ||u|| ||grad^2 u||, which is at least (2/G^2)((T_* - t) S^2)^2 along these records) and of the radial bound in [CIV2] fail there. No application of the local versions of these criteria is obtained from these estimates. For the eternal swirl-record limits W of this scenario (velocity bound C_0 := 18 C_* C_c, circulation bound G/gamma_*, viscosity nu_* = 1/gamma_*, |W^theta| <= 1 = W^theta(e_1, 0) on R^3 x R) the circulation structure of Proposition 23(f), (g) extends to the whole time line: a(tau) = sup_x Gamma_W(x, tau) is nonincreasing and Lipschitz on R with limits A_- >= A_+ >= max{B, 0} as tau -> -infinity and tau -> +infinity, where the tail supremum B is time independent; a(tau_0) = A_- for one finite tau_0 holds if and only if B = A_-, and then a = A_- identically; a(s) > a(t) whenever s < t and a(t) > max{B, 0}; and ess sup |a'| over tau >= T and over tau <= -T tends to 0 as T -> infinity (a + C tau^2/2 is convex, C = sup |d_tau^2 Gamma_W|). Whether A_+ = max{B, 0} is not known (B >= 0 is not established either): one approach would interchange tau -> +infinity with radial infinity, but the available estimate |sup_{R >= rho} Gamma_W(., t) - sup_{R >= rho} Gamma_W(., s)| <= |t - s| sup_{R >= rho} |d_tau Gamma_W| does not permit it. The attained normalization adds nothing at the level of Liouville theorems: if W is any eternal bounded mild axisymmetric solution with |Gamma_W| <= G' and m := sup |W^theta| > 0 over space and time, then near-maximizers of |W^theta| have radii in [m/(2 ||grad W||_infty), 2 G'/m] (since |W^theta| <= ||grad W||_infty R and |W^theta| <= G'/R), so a subsequence of axial and temporal translates converges to an eternal mild solution V attaining |V^theta| = m at some radius r_* > 0; after the reflection V(x, t) -> P V(P x, t), P = diag(1, -1, 1), if needed (it reverses the swirl and preserves the class and the bounds), the rescaled field Wt(y, tau) := m^{-1} V(r_* y, (r_*/m) tau) is a solution with viscosity nu/(m r_*), velocity bound K/m, circulation bound G'/(m r_*) and |Wt^theta| <= 1 = Wt^theta(e_1, 0); a Liouville theorem for eternal solutions with an attained swirl maximum, uniform over all finite constants and positive viscosities, is therefore equivalent to one for all eternal bounded mild axisymmetric solutions with bounded circulation and nonzero swirl, the steady ones included. (The equivalence does not preserve prescribed constants and says nothing about realizability by one physical trajectory. These statements are from a research consultation; they were checked by the author and in adversarial audit round 26.)

In the same uniformly viscous scenario the following necessary conditions hold; none of them excludes either branch of Theorem 13, although they exclude certain growth histories and exact shrinking copies of steady profiles. Fix C_1 with D(t) <= C_1 S(t)^2 at late times (the restart bound D(t) <= C M(t)^2 of sec. 3.9 and M(t) <= C_0 S(t)). The field u(t) is Lipschitz with finite energy, hence tends to 0 at infinity, so a nonzero extremum of u^theta(t) is attained off the axis; at a positive spatial maximum of u^theta (or of -u^theta) the transport term of the swirl equation vanishes and (Delta - r^{-2}) u^theta <= 0 (respectively >= 0); moreover ||d_t u^theta||_infty <= sqrt(3) H + M D, the axisymmetric pressure having no angular gradient, so ||u^theta(t)||_infty is locally Lipschitz in time and its upper Dini derivative is at most ||u^r/r||_infty ||u^theta||_infty <= D S; as the running maximum S grows only where it is attained, S' <= C_1 S^3 almost everywhere, and integration of (S^{-2})' >= -2 C_1 gives (T_* - t) S(t)^2 >= 1/(2 C_1) for late t. In the normalized variables of the swirl records, int over t_n + T_n I of int over z_n e_3 + r_n Omega of |grad u|^2 dx dt equals gamma_n r_n times the normalized Dirichlet integral of U_n over Omega x I; with eps(t) := int_t^{T_*} ||grad u(s)||_2^2 ds, lower semicontinuity gives liminf_n eps(t_n)/(gamma_n r_n) >= int_0^A int_{B_L} |grad W|^2 for all fixed A, L, so a steady nonconstant eternal limit W forces eps(t_n)/(gamma_n r_n) -> infinity, which is compatible with eps(t_n) -> 0. With m(t) := ||u(t)||_infty and C_S the constant in ||f||_6 <= C_S ||grad f||_2, the bound |u| >= m/2 on the ball of radius m/(2 D) about a maximizer gives ||grad u(t)||_2^2 >= c_S m(t)^3/D(t), c_S = (4 pi/3)^{1/3}/(8 C_S^2); hence, for 0 < eta <= 1, the integral of S dt over {t >= t_0 : ||u^theta(t)||_infty >= eta S(t)} is at most C_1 eps(t_0)/(c_S eta^3). Conversely, ||d_t u^theta||_infty <= C_2 S^3 at late times with C_2 = sqrt(3) C_* C_1^2 + C_0 C_1 (by (A), H <= C_* D^2/M <= C_* C_1^2 S^3); with c_2 = min{(4 C_1)^{-1}, (16 C_2)^{-1}} and a first crossing t_n of a level S_n, the interval [t_n, t_n + c_2 S_n^{-2}] lies before T_*, carries S <= 2 S_n and ||u^theta(t)||_infty >= S_n/2 >= S(t)/4, so it lies in the set with eta = 1/4 and contributes between c_2/S_n and 2 c_2/S_n to the integral; for a fixed geometric ladder S_n = S_0 lambda^n, lambda > 1, these contributions have a finite sum, so the occupation bound is consistent with such records (this interval estimate, with its constants, was supplied in adversarial audit round 27 and checked by the author). On the counterexample side, write u = (gamma/rho) V(y, s) and p = (gamma^2/rho^2) P(y, s) (up to a function of time), y = (x - z e_3)/rho, ds/dt = gamma/rho^2, with C^1 functions rho, gamma > 0 and z; then V_s + V.grad V + grad P = gamma^{-1} Delta V + a (V + y.grad V) - b V + c d_Z V with a = rho rho'/gamma, b = rho^2 gamma'/gamma^2, c = rho z'/gamma, and the integral of a ds equals log(rho(t)/rho(t_0)), which tends to -infinity as rho -> 0. An exactly shrinking copy of a bounded steady profile (W smooth, bounded, divergence-free and steady with viscosity 1/gamma on R^3, gamma and z constant, rho' not identically 0) is impossible unless the profile is constant: taking the curl of grad(P - P_W) = a (W + y.grad W) at a time where a is not 0 gives 2 omega + y.grad omega = 0, so lambda^2 omega(lambda y) does not depend on lambda > 0 and omega = 0 by continuity at the origin; a bounded divergence-free and curl-free field is constant, and an axisymmetric constant has no swirl. This excludes exact shrinking copies, not steady subsequential limits or approximate modulations. A qualifying counterexample in the uniformly viscous scenario would, by Proposition 15, yield a bounded eternal mild axisymmetric solution with bounded circulation and nonzero swirl; no such solution is supplied here or known to us (constant axial fields are bounded eternal solutions without swirl). A construction around a chosen profile would further need a modulation law with rho -> 0 in finite time, stability under the secular dilation term and matching to finite energy with (A) for one fixed datum; the change of variables alone does not make V an eternal solution or prove convergence to a profile. (These statements are from a research consultation, except the interval estimate noted above; they were checked by the author and in adversarial audit round 27, and the precision repairs requested there were made afterwards.)

### 3.8 Energy-type identities

At positive classical times, with the integrability needed for the integrations by parts, Proposition 10 gives exact identities for |q|^p, p >= 2, in the 5D measure dmu = r^3 dr dz and for eta^2 in the three-dimensional measure dx. The q^p identity shows that the compression term 2(1 - 1/p) int |q|^p phi_z dmu is the only possible source; by the Hardy inequality in R^4 it is dominated by the dissipation when -r u^r <= 2/p. At the critical exponent 5/2 the threshold 4/5 is below the value 1 forced at every swirl record, so this particular global absorption criterion cannot exclude the records; this does not show that every refinement of the energy method fails. The eta^2 identity contains the absorbing axis term -2 pi int eta(0, z)^2 dz, but its source int eta d_z(q^2) dx is controlled by ||q||_{L^4(dx)}^2 ||grad eta||_{L^2(dx)}. The norm ||q||_{L^4(dx)} is subcritical (it scales like lambda^{5/4}); it satisfies ||q(t)||_{L^4(dx)}^4 <= 4 E_0 H(t)^2 <= 4 E_0 C_*^2 D(t)^4/M(t)^2 under (A), which may diverge as t -> T_*. No adequate uniform or time-integrated bound was obtained.

### 3.9 Literature relevant to the remaining regime

 Q. S. Zhang [QZ, Theorem 1.1]: v_r >= -c (T - t)^{-1/2} implies regularity, so at T_* the inward radial velocity is not Type I in the sense limsup (T_* - t)^{1/2} ||(u^r)^-(t)||_infty = infinity. The swirl records give -u^r(r_n, z_n, t_n) >= 1/r_n, which is consistent with this. The proof uses a one-dimensional auxiliary equation and a circulation barrier with a time-only drift g(t) >= ||(u^r)^-(t)||_infty; the published time envelope g = c (T - t)^{-1/2} has the interval-integral consequence int_a^b g dt <= 2c (b - a)^{1/2}, and that consequence alone, on a late time interval, already excludes a singularity: it implies (31.0) with beta = 0 and B = c^2, so Proposition 31(f) applies. We have ||(u^r)^-(t)||_infty <= M(t) <= c E_0^{1/5} D(t)^{3/5}, but no bound of the required temporal strength.
 Pan [Pan] and Zujin Zhang [ZZ], as summarized in [QZ]: r u^r >= -1 (respectively -M with M in (1, 2)) everywhere implies regularity. The record identity -r_n u^r >= 1 at the record point does not contradict these global hypotheses, which were not established here. These papers were not retrieved.
 Constantin, Ignatova and Vicol [CIV2, Theorem 1.3]: local regularity under anisotropic Type II pointwise bounds on u and its derivatives up to order 2 near the singular point; these bounds were not derived from (A), (K), (TAIL).
 Seregin [SeII]: reductions and exclusions of Type II scenarios (in the sense of those papers) under additional quantitative hypotheses, including bounds on second spatial and time derivatives and spatial envelopes; these were not derived from (A), (K), (TAIL).
 Lei, Ren and Zhang [LRZ2, Theorem 1.2] prove triviality for bounded ancient solutions when Gamma^2 approaches L = limsup_{r -> infinity} sup_{z, t} Gamma^2 (which the source identifies with the global supremum) at the quantitative rate eps_0 L/r, uniformly in z and t for sufficiently large r, with eps_0 depending on the velocity bound in viscosity-one units; the z-periodic case is in [LRZ1]; Lei, Zhang and Zhao [LZZ] treat Gamma in L^infty_t L^p_x for some finite p, and, separately, Gamma -> 0 uniformly at radial infinity. None of these hypotheses was derived for the Case-1 limit.
 Shahmurov [Sh] proves critical signed-action continuation criteria: with Y_q = r^{1-3/q} u^theta and Ubar_q = int (u^r/r) |Y_q|^q dx / int |Y_q|^q dx, defined as zero when the denominator vanishes, the integrating factor is exp(3 int Ubar_q dt), and a hypothetical singularity with smooth H^2 data and bounded circulation must have unbounded signed compression action for every finite q >= 2. The paper also proves continuation under the sliding condition int_{sigma-h}^{sigma} ||(u^r)_-||_infty dt <= 2 sqrt(nu h l_{h_0}(h)), where l_{h_0}(h) = log log(e^e h_0/h), on all sufficiently small windows specified in its Theorem 5.3, and proves non-amplification of the instantaneous source-only meridional response for the weighted functionals of its Theorem 6.1. These are regularity criteria and necessary conditions, not a Liouville theorem; neither their signed-action nor sliding-compression hypotheses have been derived here from (A), (K), (TAIL) and the fixed data. The last step of that regularity argument uses the near-axis logarithmic circulation criterion [Wei, Corollary 1.1]. For axis regularity, [LZ2, Corollary 1.3] uses a bound |Gamma| <= C_1 |log r|^{-2} near the axis, uniform up to the terminal time; the improvement in [Wei, Corollary 1.1] has order |log r|^{-3/2}. Smoothness of each normalized limit at its own axis does not supply a uniform physical modulus as t -> T_*. Further papers of the same author [Sh2], [Sh3], [Sh4] give a conditional reduction of axis regularity to scale-uniform closure statements in a five-dimensional framework, the sharp coercivity range of power-weighted swirl energies, and structural obstructions. Among the latter is the elementary bound S_R <= 2 pi G^2 log(1 + R D_{theta, R}/(2 pi G^2)) for the scaled swirl energy S_R = R^{-1} int_{B_R} |u^theta|^2 dx in terms of the swirl dissipation D_{theta, R} = int_{B_R} |u^theta|^2 r^{-2} dx [Sh4, Proposition 10.1], which with the energy inequality controls the time spent at large scaled swirl energy [Sh4, Theorem 10.2]. At the swirl records the scaled swirl energy at scale L r_n is at most of order gamma_n^2 + G^2 log L (from |u^theta| <= S_n and |Gamma| <= G), which is consistent with that bound. A further paper [Sh5] compares record-selection frameworks for the general and the axisymmetric problem and states that it claims no unconditional regularity theorem and no singularity construction. These papers state that they do not prove regularity for arbitrary swirl, and none of them is a Liouville theorem for LL.
 Hou [Hou1] reports numerical evidence of potentially singular, nearly self-similar behaviour, at a point of the symmetry axis, of axisymmetric Navier-Stokes solutions with swirl and smooth data, driven by a potential Euler singularity in the interior reported in [Hou2]; no singularity is proved there. The computation is posed in the periodic cylinder {r < 1}, with a no-slip, no-flow condition at r = 1, period 1 in z, and a viscosity that is increased once at an early time and is fixed on the late fitted interval; because of the bounded domain it is not a finite-energy solution on R^3. The tracked point (R(t), Z(t)) maximizes u_1 = u^theta/r (other maxima are also tracked), not u^theta (these points were read in the text of [Hou1]). Whether such a scenario, transplanted to R^3, would satisfy (A), (K) and (TAIL) is not known to us. [Hou3] studies generalized axisymmetric equations with a dynamically varied space dimension and a rescaled model with two viscosity coefficients, which are different equations. Chen and Hou [CH] prove finite-time, nearly self-similar blowup of the 2D Boussinesq and the 3D axisymmetric Euler equations with smooth initial data of finite energy in the presence of a boundary; it does not concern the Navier-Stokes equations on R^3. Hou, Wang and Yang [HWY, Theorem 1] give a computer-assisted proof of nonuniqueness of suitable Leray-Hopf solutions on R^3 with compactly supported initial data in C^infinity(R^3 \ {0}) intersected with L^q, q < 3, which are singular at the origin; this is not singularity formation from smooth data. Petrillo and Glimm [PG] report that a forced Navier-Stokes singularity was produced in September 2026 and state that the unforced problem remains open; a forced solution does not solve the equations considered here. These works bear only on the counterexample alternative and supply no fixed-datum Navier-Stokes singularity.

Two elementary consequences bear on power-law fits of numerical data; the first uses Proposition 20(a), a proof with key estimates, and the second is proved here. First, a finite-energy axisymmetric solution with singular time T_* cannot satisfy ||grad u(t)||_2^2 <= C (T_* - t)^{-1/2} for t near T_*: at every point of the singular time this gives E(rho) <= rho^{-1} int_{T_* - rho^2}^{T_*} ||grad u(t)||_2^2 dt <= 2C, so every singular point would be of Type I, contradicting [Se20, Theorem 2.1], while a singular point exists (Proposition 20(a)). Second, suppose M, S, D, H (running maxima) and the record radii satisfy two-sided power laws M ~ delta^{-a}, S ~ delta^{-s}, D ~ delta^{-d}, H ~ delta^{-h} and r_n ~ delta_n^b, with delta = T_* - t and constants independent of time. Then M >= S gives a >= s; at a swirl record, |u^theta|/r <= |grad u| gives D(t_n) >= S_n/r_n, and the swirl on the radial segment through the record vanishes on the axis and has a critical point at the record, so S_n <= H(t_n) r_n^2/2; hence d >= s + b and h >= s + 2b. Since gamma_n = r_n S_n is at most G and, for large n, at least a positive constant (by (K) and the record inflow), b = s. Hypothesis (A) gives a + h <= 2d, and ||grad u||_infty^2 <= C ||u||_infty ||grad^2 u||_infty gives a + h >= 2d, so a + h = 2d. Fix an early time t_0 > 0; for late t put h_0 := c M(t)^{-2} < t_0/2 and restart the mild solution at q - h_0 for every q in [t_0, t]; the smoothing estimate gives ||grad u(q)||_infty <= C M(t) h_0^{-1/2} <= C' M(t)^2, and D(t_0) is absorbed as M(t) -> infinity, so D(t) <= C M(t)^2 at fixed viscosity and d <= 2a. Finally a > 1/2, since a velocity bound M <= C delta^{-1/2} excludes a singularity [CSTY2]. These are necessary tests on exponents, not criteria: genuine two-sided power bounds with a + h = 2d give some finite shape constant, but exponent fits alone establish neither those bounds nor a prescribed value of C_*, and (K) and (TAIL) concern whole rescaled fields on backward intervals. A ratio bound M(t_n)/S_n <= C would give both witnesses (it bounds the rescaled velocity by C, so the rescaled tail integral over |y| > L is at most 4 pi C^2/L), but (K) does not imply it.
 A further search of arXiv listings on 2026-10-16 (abstracts read) found nothing that applies here: Liouville theorems for stationary D-solutions under additional decay conditions [WY] and related stationary results; a regularity criterion for axisymmetric solutions in a finite cylinder with boundary conditions, which requires ||u^theta||_{L^infty_t L^p_x}/||u^theta||_{L^infty_t L^infty_x} to stay bounded below for some p in (6, infinity) [OZ] (on R^3 finite energy gives ||u^theta(t)||_p <= E_0^{1/p} S(t)^{1-2/p}, so this ratio tends to zero whenever S -> infinity, as in Case 1, and the criterion gives no information); and a revised version of a global regularity claim whose current version states that no unconditional global regularity claim is made [GZ]. A second search on 2026-10-18 (arXiv, mathematics, submissions from 2026-01-01 matching 'axisymmetric Navier-Stokes', and from 2023-06-01 matching 'ancient solutions Navier-Stokes'; abstracts read) found no Liouville theorem for bounded ancient axisymmetric solutions with bounded circulation, with or without the backward swirl decay of the Type I swirl branch of Proposition 33(c); the Liouville theorems found there concern stationary solutions (for example [WY], and a rigidity theorem for the Landau solutions within a class of rotated self-similar stationary solutions), and the time-dependent results are regularity criteria already discussed above ([CIV], [CIV2], [SeII], [Sh] to [Sh5]). A third search on 2026-10-19 (arXiv, abstracts matching both 'axisymmetric' and 'Navier', and both 'ancient' and 'Navier', newest submissions first) found no relevant paper beyond those cited here.
 The papers above exclude particular classes. We know no theorem excluding the unrestricted remaining regime under the assumptions stated here, and to our knowledge the bounded-circulation case of the ancient Liouville conjecture is open on R^3. This is based on the cited sources and an arXiv search, not on an exhaustive survey.

### 3.10 Critical weighted energies and the inflow integral (Propositions 16 to 18)

The circulation Gamma is dimensionless in viscous units, so the critical weighted norms of Gamma are int |Gamma|^p r^{-3} dx. In the variable q = Gamma/r^2 these are the functionals Y_p (p > 3/2) of Proposition 16. Whenever Y_p is finite, their evolution (Proposition 16, a proof sketch with key estimates) has a single term without sign, -3 int (u^r/r)|q|^p r^{2p-3} dx, which is an inflow term: it is harmful exactly where u^r < 0. Every way we found to absorb it requires a global hypothesis on the solution. One option is a bound -r u^r <= 2 - 3/p, which, for p >= 5/2, interpolates between the Hardy threshold 4/5 of Proposition 10 (p = 5/2) and the value 2 as p -> infinity (for 3/2 < p < 5/2 it lies below 4/5); the latter matches the critical value 2 nu of Route B. The other is smallness of the angular stream function: for a chosen finite p, ||psi^theta||_infty <= P_p (P_2 = 3^{-1/2}; P_p increases to (8/3)^{1/2} = 1.632993...). Neither hypothesis was derived. Proposition 17 shows that the second is false at the gradient records of branch (II), where ||psi^theta|| is at least of order 1/kappa. Weights centered at a point of the axis, including the self-similar Gaussian weight, have an analogous inflow term toward the chosen point, and other functionals leave additional unsigned terms. At a swirl record with S_n > S(0) the record identity gives -U_n^R(e_1, 0) >= 1/gamma_n in the record normalization, and for the limit -U^R(e_1, 0) >= nu_* = 1/gamma_* (1 in viscosity-one units), a lower bound that does not reach the threshold 2 nu_* of the self-similar weight. In Case 1 the time-integrated inflow is infinite (Proposition 18(a)), because each record contributes a fixed amount of critical dissipation of q in its own cylinder. No compatible bound on the total has been obtained; spatial or temporal localization is another possible approach. When N(a) and Y_2(a) are finite for some a < T_*, branch (II) needs the inflow integral I_in(a, s_n) to be at least of order 1/kappa_n before the gradient record (Proposition 18(b)). A separate necessary condition, from the exact backward adjoint identity, is that the adjoint test functions develop axial gradients of total size at least of order kappa_n^{-4/3} (Proposition 18(c); the existence and maximum principle for the adjoint and the construction of the terminal test are not reproduced). When M^5/D^3 >= epsilon_0, the truncated balance of Proposition 18(f) places the high-level part of the source that branch (II) needs, integrated over [a, s_n] on {|eta| > lambda_n}, within distance c_n M(s_n)/D(s_n) of the axis for some sequence c_n -> 0 (not for an arbitrary prescribed sequence).

### 3.11 The stream-function BMO form (Proposition 19)

Lei and Zhang [LZ, Theorem 1.1] prove that for an axisymmetric Navier-Stokes solution on a parabolic cylinder Q_L of radius L whose meridional field is curl B_2 + b_3 with B_2 bounded in BMO and r|b_3| bounded, the circulation is Hoelder continuous at the axis with constants depending only on these two norms. Both norms are invariant under the Navier-Stokes scaling, so for an ancient solution with bounded circulation whose meridional field has such a decomposition with bounds uniform in tau (Proposition 19(b)) the estimate holds on every Q_L with the same constants, and letting L -> infinity gives Gamma = Gamma(0, 0) = 0. We apply this to the Case-1 limit after the Galilean change of frame that removes a uniform axial flow c_0 e_Z. Since curl((c_0 R/2) e_theta) = c_0 e_Z, the natural choice is B_2 = (psi_U - c_0 R/2) e_theta. This contains Route A (under the hypothesis sup R^3 |eta| < infinity of Theorem 4, that theorem gives R|V - c_0 e_Z| bounded, which is the b_3 part) and replaces the smallness of Proposition 16 by a bound, in a weaker norm, and only for the limit. Like the hypotheses of Theorems 4 and 5, it fails for every member of LL. Deriving the BMO condition from the abstract LL properties would itself prove a Liouville theorem. The fixed trajectory may supply additional information, but its use is not proved necessary.

On the physical side, the stream function is a superposition of ring potentials weighted by omega^theta dr dz, and all ring potentials are dilates and translates of one, so the BMO norm of B(t) is at most an absolute constant times N(t) = 2 pi int int |omega^theta| dr dz. The BMO norm of the normalized stream function equals the physical one divided by gamma_n, and BMO is lower semicontinuous at the limit, so a bound sup_tau liminf_n N(t_n + T_n tau) < infinity along the subsequence of Theorem 2 would give the hypothesis of Proposition 19(b) (Proposition 19(b) uses bounds uniform in the cylinder size, as the Lei-Zhang constants must be; bounds depending on the window length or on the radius of the balls would need further quantitative control). Proposition 19(c) shows that no such bound holds. The global statement limsup N = infinity is a known consequence of [LZ, Theorem 1.4]; what is specific here is that large N appears at fixed normalized phases of the record windows. The balance of N has the source ||d_z(q^2)||_{L^1(dx)}, whose integral over each normalized swirl window has a positive lower bound (Proposition 19(d)), so the integrated absolute source diverges, like the inflow integral. This does not show that a bound on N would need a cancellation between the signed source and eta: the diffusion loss in the balance of N can absorb a same-signed source, as a stationary scalar example in 5D radial variables shows. But no estimate controlling either the diffusion term or the signed source was found. A kinematic family (not an NS solution: a record-scale swirl core plus a meridional field at the intermediate scale S^{-2/3}) is reported to satisfy the listed energy, circulation and shape inequalities and the instantaneous record conditions while the normalized BMO norm and N diverge. The family and its estimates are not given in this report, so the conclusion that these instantaneous constraints do not by themselves give a bound is not checkable from the report alone.

bounded drift rigidity (false by O1, Proposition 8(d)); Hardy-threshold energy criterion (threshold 4/5 below the record value 1); Euler-length transport without windows (no backward decay from the scalar information); Zhang's time-only drift mechanism combined with (A) (no bound of the required temporal strength on the inward velocity); the scale dichotomy as an exclusion (both branches survive); the L^1 balance for the critical mass N (when N(a) < infinity it gives N = o(D^{1/2}) and N = o(S), neither of which contradicts the lower bound); For g > 0, 1/2 < alpha < 1, h = (T - t)^{2 alpha} and a = (4 - h')/h = 4/h + 2 alpha/(T - t), the field u^r = -a r/2, u^z = a z, u^theta = (g/r)(1 - e^{-r^2/h}) with pressure (a'/4 - a^2/8) r^2 - (a' + a^2) z^2/2 + int_0^r (u^theta(s, t))^2 s^{-1} ds is an exact smooth solution of infinite energy; its swirl maximum is at r = (xi h)^{1/2}, where xi is the unique positive root of e^xi = 1 + 2 xi (xi lies in (1, 2)), so the records are genuine, increasing, with gamma_n = gamma := g(1 - e^{-xi}) and (T - t_n) S_n^2 -> infinity. A finite-energy modification that keeps these records and the affine meridional field on balls B_{l_n} with l_n/r_n -> infinity violates (K) (the normalized axial velocity at (0, 0, L) is A_n L with A_n = a(t_n) r_n^2/gamma -> 4 xi/gamma) and (TAIL) (the weighted shell integral of |U_n|^2 over L < |y| < l_n/r_n is at least that of the meridional part, which equals 2 pi A_n^2 (l_n/r_n - L)), and (A) with D(t_n) <= C_1 S_n^2 alone gives limsup l_n/r_n <= C_* C_1^2 gamma^3/(8 xi), from H(t_n) >= 2 S_n/r_n^2 and M(t_n) >= a(t_n) l_n. Matching within O(r_n) is not excluded, and no modification that solves the equations is known. A third test comes from a research consultation (checked by the author by hand; audited in round 29, with the repairs requested there made afterwards): the Gaussian frequency of q = u^theta/r in the five-dimensional lift, where q_t + b.grad q = Delta_5 q - c q with c = 2 u^r/r = div_5 b. For N = tau int |grad q|^2 G_tau dy / int q^2 G_tau dy, with G_tau the five-dimensional backward heat kernel of tau = T_* - t centred at an axis point, completing the square in the exact identity gives N_t <= M^2 N + 4 (T_* - t) D^2, whose majorants int M^2 dt and int (T_* - t) D^2 dt diverge for the power histories S = (T_* - t)^{-alpha}, 1/2 < alpha < 1 (this concerns the majorants, not the signed errors). More decisively, a frequency bound has nothing to contradict: in the uniformly viscous scenario, with the kernel of scale r_n centred at (0, z_n) at time t_n, the rescaled Q_n(x) = (r_n/S_n) q(r_n x', z_n + r_n x_3, t_n) has |Q_n(e_1)| = 1 (Q_n(e_1) = 1 with the sign convention of the records; the lifted coordinates are (x', x_3) in R^4 x R) and |grad Q_n| <= r_n^2 H(t_n)/S_n <= L_0 := C_* C_1^2 G^2 (because q = -d_2 u_1 on {x_2 = 0}), so N <= L_0^2/kappa with kappa = mu(B_eps(e_1))/4, eps = min{1/2, 1/(2 L_0)}, mu the Gaussian probability measure (4 pi)^{-5/2} e^{-|x|^2/4} dx on R^5 (this record-scale frequency differs from the frequency with pole T_* unless the two radii coincide); q need not vanish on the axis.

Five further mechanisms were tested; none currently supplies an exclusion, and none is used elsewhere in this report. (a) Generalized helicity Casimirs (the author's; the identity R^2 Delta_5(R^{-2} g) = L g was checked by a computer calculation). For F in C^2 with F(0) = 0 and enough decay, the critical functional C_F(t) = int eta F(Gamma) dx has no swirl source (int d_z(q^2) F(Gamma) dx = -int r^{-4} Gamma^2 F'(Gamma) d_z Gamma dx = 0) and, by the integration by parts of sec. 1.1 (the axis term vanishes since F(0) = 0), dC_F/dt = int eta [2 F'(Gamma) L Gamma + F''(Gamma) |grad Gamma|^2] dx. The right side has no sign, and C_F = 0 at every time for data with u(Qx) = Q u(x), Q = diag(1, 1, -1), for which eta is odd and Gamma even in z. (b) Product barriers for the eta equation (the author's; checked by the same computer calculation). For the operator calL = d_t + b.grad - Delta_5 of the eta equation, calL(r^{-alpha} g(Gamma)) = r^{-alpha-2} { -g''(Gamma) r^2 |grad Gamma|^2 + (2 alpha - 4) g'(Gamma) r d_r Gamma + g(Gamma) [ -alpha r u^r - alpha (alpha - 2) ] } for r > 0. For g > 0 and alpha >= 2 (the critical weight is alpha = 3) the zero-order coefficient is negative wherever r u^r > 2 - alpha, in particular on every outflow region, and at points where grad Gamma = 0 the whole expression is then negative. So this ansatz supplies no supersolution for arbitrary data; where grad Gamma != 0 the derivative terms can compensate (example: alpha = 3, g(c) = e^{-4 c^2}, u^r = r, u^z = -2z, Gamma = r^2 (r^2 - 1)/2 near (r, z) = (1, 0) give the value 8 - 6 = 2 > 0 in the braces), and compensation along a particular trajectory is not excluded; a barrier for the forced eta equation must also dominate the source d_z(q^2). For alpha < 2 the weight is subcritical. (c) A swirl-normalized dynamically rescaled trajectory (from a research consultation, checked by the author by hand and, for the test field, with a computer calculation). With V(y, s) = S^{-1} u(y/S, t), P(y, s) = S^{-2} p(y/S, t) and ds = S^2 dt, V_s + V.grad V + grad P = Delta V - a (V + y.grad V), where a = S'/S^3 >= 0 (S is locally Lipschitz with S' <= D S a.e.) is supported on the contact set {||u^theta(t)||_infty = S(t)}, a <= C_1 in the uniformly viscous scenario of sec. 3.7, and int_{s_0}^{s} a = log(S(t(s))/S(t(s_0))), which diverges as s -> infinity. At an active record (a contact time at which S is differentiable) the angular equation gives -R V^R >= 1 + a R^2. The normalized energy E = ||V||_2^2 obeys E_s + 2 ||grad V||_2^2 = a E, every dilation-invariant functional receives no contribution from a, and J_4 = int (V^theta/R)^2 dy receives -a J_4 but has a positive rate from the equation itself at an attained record of a Gaussian test field: for V^theta/R = e^{(1 - R^2 - Z^2)/2} and the Stokes stream function (b^R = -Psi_Z/R, b^Z = Psi_R/R) Psi = beta R^2 Z chi((R^2 + Z^2)/9) with beta > 4, 0 <= chi <= 1, chi = 1 on [0, 1], chi = 0 on [4, infinity) and |chi'| <= 1, one has a = beta - 4 and (J_4)_s >= (66 beta/25 - 3) J_4 > 0 (with zero meridional velocity the rate would be -7 J_4).
