A finite-dimensional example (w_s = w x - a w, x_s = (2 - 1/k) x^2 - 2 a x with the exact solution w = 1, x = a = k/(s + s_0), k > 1) shows that scaling neutrality, compactness and O(a) proximity to an equilibrium do not give a bounded adjoint mode with a positive projection on the dilation direction (at W = (1, 0) the adjoint solutions are (A, B - A s), bounded only for A = 0; the unbounded (1, -s) has projection one). (d) A localized axial impulse in branch (II) (from a research consultation, checked as in (c)). For I_chi = (1/2) int chi r omega^theta dx = int u.Xi_chi dx with Xi_chi = curl(chi e_3 x (x - a)/2), a fixed smooth compactly supported axisymmetric cutoff chi and a fixed point a on the axis, the balance dI_chi/dt = int u_i u_j d_j (Xi_chi)_i dx + int u.Delta Xi_chi dx contains no pressure. The resulting exclusion of finite-axis branch-(II) limits assumes that, in the units of the gradient scale, the flux integrated from a fixed smooth time to s_n tends to 0 for every axisymmetric chi; by the balance itself and the smallness of the initial impulse in these units, this is equivalent to omega^theta = 0 for the terminal limit, so the balance supplies no estimate. (e) Circulation-level multipliers for the potential vorticity on the Type I swirl branch. Since Gamma and eta are carried by the same meridional drift, the weighted mass int chi psi(Gamma) |eta| dmu_5 (psi nondecreasing and C^2, psi = 0 for Gamma <= lambda, chi a smooth nonnegative compactly supported spatial cutoff) has no advective flux through circulation levels; it satisfies d/dtau int chi psi(Gamma) |eta| dmu_5 <= int chi psi(Gamma) |d_Z(q^2)| dmu_5 + 2 int chi psi(Gamma) a |eta| dmu_5 + nu int chi |eta| [2 psi'(Gamma) Delta_3 Gamma + psi''(Gamma) |grad Gamma|^2] dmu_5 + (cutoff terms), with Delta_3 = d_RR + R^{-1} d_R + d_ZZ (checked by a symbolic computer calculation for generic smooth fields). It does not give the compression bound of Proposition 37: the compression of Proposition 34(d)(i) is a supremum over the superlevel set and is not a damping coefficient for the weighted mass, and a^+ enters with the unfavourable sign; for a backward self-similar profile with finite nonzero profile integral the full five-dimensional mass is proportional to the age s, so this scaling gives no uniform initial-mass bound for a forward budget started at tau_0 -> -infinity (it need not hold for the mass with a fixed spatial cutoff); and the diffusion exchange has no sign for any nontrivial psi. For the last point there is an exact local Navier-Stokes solution, U^R = a_0 R, U^Z = -2 a_0 Z + V(tau, R) with V_R = -R eta, a_0 < 0 constant, and Z-independent swirl and eta (so d_Z(q^2) = 0 and Delta_5 a = 0), in which oscillating circulation profiles with N oscillations make the diffusion exchange exceed the compression term by a factor of order nu N^2/|a_0| at the critical scaling (from a research consultation; incompressibility, the three scalar equations and the integration by parts were checked independently). Finally, the elliptic step still needs the vorticity outside the superlevel set: with the heat-truncated Biot-Savart representation a = e^{L^2 Delta_5} a + T_L * eta, where ||e^{L^2 Delta_5} a||_infty <= pi^{1/2} ||U^R||_infty/(4L), |T_L(v)| <= (3/(8 pi^2)) |v|^{-4} and ||T_L||_{L^1(R^5)} = 2L/pi^{1/2} (constants checked independently), the contribution of eta outside {Gamma > lambda/2} is not controlled by the budget, and the kinematic family of Remark (3) after Proposition 37 (whose circulation does not depend on Z, so its superlevel sets also meet the vorticity shell) shows only that the kinematic bounds listed there do not imply the expanding-radius compression bound; it violates both the eta equation and the circulation equation.

### 3.13 Shrinking physical cylinders (Proposition 20)

This section uses the fixed solution near its singular point, where the finite energy, the circulation bound and (A) are all available at once, instead of the limit U. Seregin [Se20] proved that axisymmetric suitable weak solutions have no Type I singular points: at a singular point the scale-invariant energy quantities A, E and C are all unbounded as the radius tends to 0. He also proved that a stream function bounded in local BMO gives regularity. Since the swirl part has a potential of BMO norm C G for every bounded circulation (Proposition 20(b)), the BMO criterion reduces to the meridional potential, whose local part is controlled by the local critical mass and whose far part is controlled by the energy at the chosen scale. This gives Proposition 20(c): the local critical mass is unbounded near every singular point, at every scale. These are fixed-data necessary conditions. The first unproved arrow is an upper bound, uniform as t -> T_*, for int_{C_rho(z_*)} |eta| on one cylinder, or for the local BMO norm of the meridional vector potential B = psi^theta e_theta. For a fixed smooth, nonnegative, compactly supported axisymmetric cutoff chi, the local balance of this mass, d/dt int chi |eta| + 4 pi int chi(0, z) |eta(0, z)| dz <= int |eta| (b.grad chi + L chi) + int chi |d_z(q^2)|, has an axis drain, and its uncontrolled terms are the source and the cutoff transport. The local energy inequality bounds A + E at scale rho/2 by C and the pressure quantity D at scale rho; C is a Type II quantity and D is not controlled. (A) relates global sup norms that all diverge and does not enter these inequalities; this does not show that (A) cannot be useful in combination with other estimates. At the record scale, the scale-invariant quantities A, E, C and the mean-subtracted pressure quantity on cylinders of radius L r_n around the records are bounded for each fixed L. Proposition 20(e) shows where the unbounded quantities sit (after an extraction with the record tops converging to a singular axis point): the scaled energy of the meridional field alone, centered at the record tops, exceeds any M on scales between a multiple of r_n that depends on M and a scale tending to 0, with explicit heights and dyadic counts; the same holds for the scaled dissipation. This is again a necessary condition. The physical dissipation of disjoint record cylinders is summable, nested cylinders cannot be summed (a finite measure can have divergent scaled mass at every scale), and no universal instantaneous bound on the local mass, for this kinematic class, can depend only on E_0, G, C_* and rho (the dilates eps^{-3/2} b_0(x/eps) of one swirl-free field keep energy and shape ratio fixed while the local mass grows like eps^{-1/2}). The example does not rule out an estimate using the evolution of the fixed solution and all Case-1 hypotheses.

### 3.14 Circulation escape (Proposition 21)

This section tests whether the circulation must leave the neighbourhood of the singular point by diffusion into the axis, where Gamma = 0 and the radial part of L is absorbing, against the inflow. The local spacetime limsup G_0 of the circulation at the singular point at which the swirl records concentrate (after a subsequence) exceeds gamma_* (Proposition 21(a); the circulation vanishes on the axis at every regular time), so the swirl records do not carry the local circulation supremum. Near the points that do, the Harnack chain of Proposition 21(b) shows that the normalized meridional speed is unbounded, or the circulation reaches deeper toward the axis than every fixed fraction of the radius. In the ancient limit the circulation supremum is approached only at infinite normalized radius; this does not by itself locate large meridional speeds there. For 0 < beta < 2 and 0 <= Gamma_0 < G_0, the first-crossing records of (Gamma - Gamma_0) r^{-beta} exist, converge to the axis and carry compression -r u^r >= 2 - beta (Proposition 21(c)). In the frame normalized at such a record this is -R V^R >= (2 - beta) nu at normalized radius 1, just below the threshold 2 nu of Theorem 5, whose hypothesis holds if the opposite inequality -R V^R <= 2 nu holds uniformly at large radius. No fixed radial weight e^{-w(r)} with w' > 0 certifies -r u^r >= 2 at all small scales in the first-crossing argument (other uses of fixed weights are not excluded), and the weights depending on time or height that do improve it locally do so only where records are not known to occur. For a nonlinear function Phi(Gamma) in place of Gamma, with Phi' > 0, Phi(Gamma_0) = 0 and Phi/Phi' -> 0 at Gamma_0, put calR = Phi Phi''/Phi'^2. The certificate exceeds 2 only where calR > 1, and int_{Gamma_0}^{Gamma} (calR - 1) d xi = -Phi(Gamma)/Phi'(Gamma) < 0, so calR averages below 1 from the zero of Phi (a positive calR < 1 can still improve 2 - beta). The flux identity for scale averages of Gamma allows a change of order G over a time of order rho^2 at radius rho, even under bounded scale-invariant meridional energy, and by Proposition 20(e) that energy is unbounded on intermediate scales at the record tops. A proposed further estimate here is critical control of the meridional field at scales at and above the record scale, related to, but not shown equivalent to, the estimates proposed in Route B and Propositions 19 and 20. Here it appears as a near-axis compression bound -r u^r <= 2 - beta_0 at late times on {Gamma > Gamma_0}, for some beta_0 > 0 and some Gamma_0 in [0, G_0) (Proposition 21(c)); or as the joint validity, infinitely often along points approaching the singular point at which Gamma -> G_0, of both hypotheses of Proposition 21(b) for some fixed delta in (0, 1/2] and B >= 1 (a bound on the normalized meridional speed on the annuli, and a drop of the circulation to at most half its value at the fraction delta of the radius in the earlier time window); or (not yet a precise sufficient condition) as smallness of the circulation fluxes. None was derived from (A), (K), (TAIL), finite energy or the circulation bound.

### 3.15 Localized pressure and strain (Proposition 22)

This section tests whether the pressure field near a swirl record, or the axial strain that the record forces, is incompatible with the bounds of Case 1. For S_n > S(0) the record forces inflow -u^r >= 1/r_n and therefore, by incompressibility, a mean axial strain at least 2/r_n^2 on the disk {r < r_n, z = z_n} bounded by the record circle (Proposition 22(b)). The record also forces d_n^2 >= 2 + 6 beta_n^2/gamma_n^2 for the normalized gradient, where beta_n = -r_n u^r >= 1. The swirl lowers the pressure on the axis, by at most G D(t), but the sign of its axial curvature is not fixed (the curvature formula contains a local term 2c^2/5 and has no sign). On the axis the strain obeys a Riccati equation forced by the axial pressure curvature. Its long-time average along an axial trajectory says that strain of size sigma is accompanied, up to viscous terms, by an averaged axial pressure curvature: in an ancient limit, along a common subsequence of the averages, <p_zz> = -<sigma^2> + nu <d_z(Delta u^z)> (Proposition 22(c)). For Burgers, the displayed axial stagnation pressure is meridional. The general identity does not separate the origins of p_zz, and the swirl contribution has no fixed sign. For t_n >= t_A, the radial momentum balance at the record fixes the material radial acceleration only up to the pressure Hessian bound and the viscous term sqrt3 H(t_n) (Proposition 22(b)), so it gives no sign. The Burgers vortex satisfies these local identities and the weak record conditions exactly, for compatible constants, with bounded circulation and derivatives and the velocity bound on an ellipsoid around the axis (Proposition 22(d)). It is not a Case-1 solution (no finite energy, unbounded velocity, divergent tail), so an exclusion needs some information not shared by this local model (examples are the velocity bound outside the ellipsoid, finite energy, the canonical pressure or the tail). Here two proposed targets are a signed bound on the meridional part of the radial momentum balance and a lower bound on the averaged axial pressure curvature near the record height; they are not shown to be necessary or equivalent. Neither was derived. The averaged identity converts the second into a lower bound on a third-order viscous term, and no contradiction from that bound alone was found.

### 3.16 Ancient Liouville hypotheses (Proposition 23)

This section checks whether a published Liouville theorem for bounded ancient axisymmetric solutions with swirl has a hypothesis that every Case-1 limit satisfies, and compares conditional rate packages, which concern the physical solution near T_*. The hypotheses fall into five classes: critical pointwise bounds on the velocity or vorticity (Koch, Nadirashvili, Seregin and Sverak; Chen, Strain, Tsai and Yau; Li and Pan; Q. S. Zhang), critical integral bounds on the meridional drift (Lei and Zhang; Seregin), integrability of the circulation (Lei, Zhang and Zhao) or a near-axis modulus of the circulation (Lei and Zhang), tail or periodicity conditions (Lei, Zhang and Zhao; Lei, Ren and Zhang), and conditional rate packages (Seregin; Constantin, Ignatova and Vicol). Saturation of the circulation at large normalized radius (Proposition 23(a)) rules out uniform tail decay for every Case-1 limit, and the integrability, periodicity and rate hypotheses of the third and fourth classes fail as well, by the corresponding Liouville theorems and the nonzero terminal swirl; a modulus for the physical circulation near the axis is violated by the trajectory itself, while a modulus for the limit near its own axis holds trivially and is no obstruction. This shows only that those theorems do not apply to U directly. The fifth class consists of hypothesis packages that include upper rates in T_* - t, which (A) does not supply. The ancient theorems of the first two classes need their stated bounds (on the velocity or vorticity, or on the meridional drift) on the whole ancient domain; uniform critical bounds for the physical solution on expanding normalized cylinders would be one sufficient way to obtain them for a Case-1 limit, and none was derived. Proposition 23(b) localizes the inflow hypothesis of Theorem 5 to the near-maximal circulation set. Saturation of the circulation at large radius forces, by two-dimensional recurrence, inflow stronger than 2 nu/R somewhere in the near-maximal circulation set, and the threshold is critical for the exterior comparison. In physical variables (Proposition 23(c)) the near-maximal circulation at radii R_0 r_n < r <= L r_n must coexist with -r u^r > 2 somewhere near every sufficiently late record of the subsequence defining U. Compare Proposition 21(c): for some Gamma_0 in [0, G_0), G_0 the local circulation supremum at the singular point, and some beta_0 > 0, a bound -r u^r <= 2 - beta_0 at late times near the axis on {Gamma > Gamma_0} would exclude Case 1; in Proposition 23(c) the threshold rises to 2 and the region moves outward in normalized radius (beyond R_0 r_n, at physical radii still tending to zero). On the near-maximal set the circulation is nearly flat (Proposition 23(e)), so the instantaneous source of the meridional vorticity equation is small there, at most 2 A (4 m (R h + 2 d))^{1/2}/R^3 where m < A/2 bounds the deficit A - Gamma_U and d, h bound the first and second derivatives of U on the meridional ball of radius R/2 around the point (on the near-maximal set of Proposition 23(b), m = (A/2) e^{-lambda_{R_0}}, and d, h are bounded uniformly for a Case-1 limit by the smoothing estimate for bounded mild ancient solutions, so for R_0 >= 1 the bound is exponentially small in lambda_{R_0}); this does not control the accumulated vorticity or the inflow it induces. The global energy bound alone does not exclude the inflow (if inflow of size 1/r occupied a region with all relevant lengths comparable to r, its scaled energy would be of order one against an allowance E_0/r), but a pointwise violation gives no such region, so this does not show that every energy argument fails. For prescribed fields, a local smallness condition on omega^theta does not by itself give the bound: with alpha > 0 and a smooth compactly supported axisymmetric cutoff chi, the vector potential (alpha/2) R Z chi e_theta gives b^R = -alpha R/2 and b^Z = alpha Z with zero vorticity on the region where chi = 1 (the vorticity is supported where chi is not constant), so an argument from the vorticity must also control its contribution from elsewhere; this kinematic example does not exclude a bound derived from the ancient Navier-Stokes dynamics. Proposition 25(c) gives one specified sufficient form, the weighted critical bound calQ_omega <= 4 (viscosity-one units) through the Biot-Savart law, which controls local and far contributions for a field given by the Biot-Savart integral. That hypothesis was not derived.

### 3.17 Material lines and vorticity creation (Proposition 24)

This section tests whether following the fluid from the record, or the creation of meridional vorticity by the swirl, gives a quantity that must blow up or a residence time that must be infinite. Backward from the record the particle comes from a slightly larger radius with more circulation (Proposition 24(a)), but only on a short normalized window: the maximum principle controls the extrema of Gamma, not its monotonicity along particle paths. Proposition 24(b) gives omega.grad Gamma = 0, so instantaneous vortex lines lie in circulation level sets; this identity gives no quantitative estimate for the coherence of the vorticity direction above the record scale, and none was derived. The record forces a positive mean axial strain on the disk {r < r_n, z = z_n} bounded by the record circle, not a pointwise strain at the record particle. On the axis, stretching competes with the radial diffusion term 8 d, which balances it exactly in the Burgers vortex. In the weighted vorticity balances the source pairing of q^2 with the derivative of the weight is unsigned; nonlinear or coupled choices can leave additional unsigned terms. The source cannot vanish on any window ending at the record time of a Case-1 limit (Proposition 24(e)), so the accumulated absolute source of the physical solution diverges, but this is a necessary condition and signs nothing. Small window dissipation, o(r_n), would make the pairing small against record-scale weights. That estimate is false in Case 1: by scaling, the window dissipation is at least a constant times r_n. This unweighted dissipation-smallness criterion is impossible in Case 1; signed cancellation, localization or a different weighted estimate is not excluded. Proposed further estimates are the propagation of a signed circulation loss along paths beyond the record window, and a sign or gain for a weighted vorticity quantity whose unsigned pairing is controlled at intermediate scales. They have not been proved sufficient as complete strategies, and no equivalence with the other proposed meridional estimates is established.

### 3.18 The far-field inflow arrow (Proposition 25)

This section tests whether the one-sided far-field bound of Proposition 23(c) follows from the structure of the equations. Proposition 25(a) sharpens the witness: strong inflow is needed only at near-maximal points where the circulation still increases outward. The vertical-flux identity (b) limits each connected strong-inflow interval to axial length K R^2/(2 nu), but bounds neither their number nor their duration. The scalar models (d) concern the scalar circulation equation, incompressibility and the record conditions. The exterior model (d)(i) is exact but has no smooth axis. The whole-space model (d)(ii), a smooth bounded divergence-free drift with the largest axial flux allowed by (b), is proposed to carry a bounded steady circulation with the record normalization and inflow above 2 nu on a near-maximal region of axial extent comparable to R^2 at every large radius; the existence and regularity of its exhaustion limit and the axis removability are not reproduced, so this consistency with strong far-field inflow has proof-sketch status. The model fails the vorticity equation at large radius, so even if completed it would show only that the listed scalar and kinematic properties are insufficient; further physical or drift estimates might exclude it. The Biot-Savart estimate (c), for the physical field, which is the Biot-Savart integral of its vorticity, gives the weighted critical vorticity bound calQ <= 4 in viscosity-one units as a stronger sufficient condition, and the kernel weight r R/(d D) cannot be replaced by the critical Morrey norm alone. (e) shows that the near-maximal far-field bound -R W^R <= 2, asserted for every W in LL with sup Gamma_W > 0 with a radius R_0(W) chosen for each W, is equivalent to LL being empty; the equivalence is not automatic for the subclass of physical limits, and information that distinguishes physically obtainable limits from unrestricted members of LL is one possible route. Candidates are finite energy, (A) at the intermediate scales R_0 r_n < r <= L r_n, or a fixed-data bound on calQ. Part (f) tests the far field directly. The slender reduction is exact up to explicit lower-order terms but not uniform near Z ~ R, and its global steady odd profiles with bounded axial velocity and nonzero vorticity violate the whole-space flux bound (Proposition 25(f), through the long-pattern rigidity of Proposition 26(i)); the finer classification of these profiles is not reproduced, was rechecked only for alpha = 2 and alpha = 3, is not proved in this report and is not used. The Landau flow with potential swirl satisfies the exterior equations exactly, with bounded velocity and bounded signed inner flux, and has -R U^R = 20 nu/9 along a ray, so an exclusion must use information beyond these exterior conditions, such as the strict deficit A - Gamma > 0 with d_R Gamma > 0 at the witnesses, or the axis. Finite energy bounds the normalized energy only by E_0/(gamma_n^2 r_n), which diverges, (A) gives no small normalized derivatives, and (TAIL) controls a velocity-square tail rather than vorticity concentration. None of these gave the bound.

### 3.19 Averaged circulation flux (Proposition 26)

This section tests whether the conservation form of the circulation equation, together with ancientness and the flux bound, constrains the far field. Integrating over a cylinder of radius rho gives an exact flux identity in which the axis contributes nothing. Averaging over long boxes in Z and in the past kills the time derivative, the axial flux and the mean of the inflow, and a Banach limit MM (Proposition 26(c)) gives the averaged radial equation 2 nu a(rho) - nu rho a'(rho) = F(rho) for the averaged circulation a(rho) := MM[Gamma_U(rho)], where F(rho) := MM[Q_rho Gamma_U(rho)] and Q_rho = -rho U^R(rho). Its bounded solution is a(rho) = (rho^2/nu) int_rho^infinity F(s) s^{-3} ds. In the exterior line sink the flux through every cylinder is the same nonzero constant, which is possible only because there is no axis. Two consequences follow (Proposition 26(d), proof sketch with key estimates). The averaged deficit cannot decay faster than order nu A/(K rho), which gives an explicit constant 2 nu/K in a box-averaged form of the rate theorem of Lei, Ren and Zhang. Averaged saturation and a critical one-sided outflow bound R U^R <= C at large radii cannot hold together for any C. Proposition 23(b) constrains the inflow on the near-maximal set; this constrains the outflow on the deficit set. Neither averaged saturation nor the outflow bound was derived for Case-1 limits. Proposition 23 gives saturation only along some points, and the box averages can stay below the supremum. In fact they must: an integrating factor in the radial equation shows that at each fixed radius rho the mean deficit in all sufficiently long boxes is at least 2 nu A/(K rho + 3 nu) minus any prescribed epsilon, and an outflow bound C would raise this to 2 nu A/(C + 2 nu) at all large radii. The same averaging applied to convex C^2 weights f of the circulation with f(0) = 0 and f >= 0 (Proposition 26(e), with the same Banach limit MM at every radius, a_f = MM[f(Gamma_U)] and F_f = MM[Q_rho f(Gamma_U)]) recovers the critical value 2 nu for the weighted box means of the inflow, but its conclusion, under the flux bound F_f <= 2 nu a_f at all large radii, is only that a_f vanishes at every radius; for the cubic weight f(gamma) = (gamma - theta)_+^3 with 0 < theta < A, positivity and f(Gamma_U) >= delta^3 1_{Gamma_U > theta + delta} give MM[1_{Gamma_U > theta + delta}] = 0 at every radius for every delta > 0 (separated superlevel sets), and nothing is asserted about MM[1_{Gamma_U > theta}] or about ordinary box densities. At the endpoint, a weighted mean inflow at most 2 nu at all large radii forces the weighted mass to vanish at every radius, and nonzero weighted mass at one radius forces the weighted mean inflow strictly above 2 nu at arbitrarily large radii. One sufficient contradiction would therefore follow from nonzero weighted mass at one radius, for some level below A, together with weighted mean inflow at most 2 nu at all large radii, for the same box family. Two models (Proposition 26(f)) locate the obstruction. In the first, a bounded drift with finite vertical flux carries a steady circulation that approaches its supremum at large radius with strong inflow and unbounded outflow, yet its averaged circulation vanishes at every radius for every box family; near-maximal plateaux at growing radii do not produce saturation at a fixed radius. The elliptic exhaustion and the axis removability behind this model are not reproduced, so it has proof-sketch status. In the second, an explicit periodic kinematic field, the circulation saturates and the linear averaged identities hold, but the unaveraged circulation equation fails, and so does the convex identity for the square of the circulation. Subject to that qualification, the scalar example prevents deriving averaged saturation from the scalar hypotheses alone, and the periodic example prevents a contradiction from the linear averaged identities alone; neither rules out nonlinear averaged estimates. All convex identities together form a balance, at each deficit level, between the inflow and the averaged Dirichlet energy carried by that level (Proposition 26(h)). In logarithmic means this hierarchy is consistent with saturation, by explicit two-level data (an inflow distribution over the deficit levels and a level measure satisfying all the relations; no field realizing them is constructed); these logarithmic-mean constraints alone give no contradiction, and additional information could be a flux-energy estimate or information retained at finite radii. For steady fields of fixed axial period the hierarchy forces the logarithmic mean of R d(R) to diverge under saturation, and Proposition 26(i) excludes nonzero steady periodic circulation altogether, which is why the periodic example fails. The averaged momentum and pressure balances retain unsigned terms: a periodic kinematic field is reported to satisfy them, the full pressure Poisson equation with bounded pressure, and saturation (Proposition 26(h); its pressure bounds were checked only by the computer calculation that accompanied the field and are not reproduced). Nonzero weighted mass at a fixed radius is a positive upper density of a separated superlevel set in a sampled-translate family (it does not establish recurrence of the particular record configuration), and at scale R the needed flux bound is first order in the effective viscosity nu/R. One sufficient target is positive mass and the critical flux bound for the same box family, potentially obtained from the coupled dynamics or compatible fixed-data estimates (the coupled equations are not claimed to be the only possible source). A critical bound on the oscillation of the axial flux through disks suffices (Proposition 26(i), proved); the available bound is one power of the radius short. A scalar solution with slowly increasing axial wavelength is reported to saturate, which would show that the scalar equation alone does not supply the bound (its corrector error bounds are not reproduced). For steady long patterns of the maximal form psi = nu beta R^2 f(Z/R^2), every bounded C^4 profile f that solves the leading-order steady vorticity equation of Proposition 26(i) on either half-line is constant, so such patterns carry no leading-order inflow (proved; the expansion that yields this leading-order equation is not reproduced); this excludes one mechanism for violating the bound but does not prove it. The bound may grow with the radius, as C(rho) with int^infinity d rho/(rho (1 + C(rho)^2)) = infinity (Proposition 26(i), proved), so C(rho) = (log rho)^p with p <= 1/2 still excludes positive mass. For p in (1/2, 1] exact scalar solutions with bounded drift are reported to saturate uniformly, which would make this growth condition sharp at the scalar level on that scale; the corrector error bounds of that construction are not reproduced. On the physical solution the window errors can be made to vanish at every fixed normalized radius along a slow diagonal, but this gives no relation between the box sizes and the radii where the circulation is nearly maximal. Circulation-weighted long-box means also vanish identically for axially localized fields, those with Gamma_U -> 0 as |Z| -> infinity uniformly in time at every radius (velocity moments need not; Proposition 26(g)); such localization was not established for Case-1 limits, although a blow-up of a finite-energy solution might produce it. For those, under the mass, trace and integrability assumptions of Proposition 26(g), Z-integrated time means obey the same radial equation with an added dissipation term, and the critical value 2 nu degrades to (2 - alpha) nu (one constant kappa < (2 - alpha) nu at all large radii is needed, 0 <= alpha < 2) when the Z-integrated weighted mass is at most a constant times the radius to the power alpha, as it is when the axial extent of the superlevel sets grows at most at that rate (Proposition 26(g), whose hypothesis is this upper bound). Three further items reformulate the averaged target. A critical decay, at large radii, of the averaged fluctuation of the axial velocity about an axially uniform flow implies the flux bound (Proposition 26(j)). The averaged meridional and swirl energy budgets close exactly, the total centrifugal work satisfies W(infinity) = -nu D_theta(infinity) <= 0 and the averaged swirl dissipation is finite, but the pressure work and the meridional transport have no sign, and an explicit kinematic field, with the pressure set to zero and the averages taken over symmetric axial boxes centred at Z = 0, satisfies these averaged budget identities while violating the flux bound (Proposition 26(k)). Long-box means are expectations under invariant measures on the hull of the limit, so positive mass means that some invariant measure charges nonconstant fields; for an ergodic such measure the flux bound becomes a bound on the negative second moment int_{k != 0} k^{-2} d sigma_{Q,R}(k) of the axial spectral measure of Q_R = d_Z Phi_R, after projecting Phi_R off its axially invariant component (a condition at low axial frequency), and limits on whose hull every invariant measure is trivial, which include uniformly axially localized structures, are outside the averaged route altogether (Proposition 26(l)).

### 3.20 Finite-window realization (Proposition 27)

Theorem 3 says that an exclusion using only the properties of the limit, for all admissible parameters, would prove that LL is empty. Proposition 27 moves this one level down, conditionally. If LL is nonempty, let W be the normalized ancient solution supplied by Theorem 3(b), with viscosity nu. Fix L >= 2 and T >= L^2 + 1, cut off its stream function and circulation at radius rho at time -T, and solve the Navier-Stokes equations at viscosity nu from these compactly supported data. If the resulting solutions stay bounded on [0, T] uniformly in rho, their translates w^rho(x, tau) = v^rho(x, tau + T) converge to W in spatial C^2 on closure(B_L), uniformly for tau in [-L^2, 0], keep the circulation bound, satisfy the window bounds of (K) and (TAIL), have finite energy and, when the swirl maximum set of W in the window does not meet its parabolic boundary (a sufficient condition), carry an exact record inequality at the window maximum. If the uniform bound fails for every sufficiently large cutoff range, either loss of regularity occurs at or before T for arbitrarily large cutoff radii, or all sufficiently large cutoffs remain regular through T and their supremum norms diverge along a sequence of radii tending to infinity; neither alternative is excluded by anything known to us. The result does not give a global first crossing (the swirl in the cutoff shell is uncontrolled after time 0), an energy bound uniform in rho, or a bound for all later times (under the hypothesis of part (a) it gives T_rho > T and, by the local existence theory for bounded data, a bound uniform in rho on a short interval beyond T). It is a conditional compatibility result, not a classification of exclusion arguments: under its hypotheses the listed properties of one record window are compatible with finite-energy solutions regular on [0, T], but the proposition does not reproduce a global first-crossing record, several ordered records of one trajectory with common physical constants, or (A) across those records.

### 3.21 Shape bound for axisymmetric fields (Proposition 28)

At an axis point the singular values of the gradient have the form t, t, v; the repeated pair need not be the two largest values. Combining the two- and three-singular-value inequalities with the axial Landau bound gives B_ax = 3.860749266... < B_3 = 3.928931.... Away from the axis two further facts enter. The average G_0 of the gradient over the rotations about the axis has the axis form and satisfies the same singular-value inequalities, so |G_0|^2 <= B_ax M H, while the cylindrical Hessian formula of Proposition 28(e) bounds the remainder |grad U - G_0| by r |grad^2 U|; this gives |grad U|^2 <= (B_ax + rho^2) M H with rho = r (H/M)^{1/2}. At larger radius, the angular derivative (u e_theta - v e_r)/r bounds the smallest singular value by |U|/r, and the scalar Landau inequality applied to n.U in suitable directions n couples the largest singular value to |U|; together with the singular-value inequalities this gives the third bound of Proposition 28(b). The two regimes overlap and give the global constant 3.9184 < B_3. Under (A) this raises the exclusion of C_* < 0.25452... to C_* < 0.25520..., bounds the quantity a of Proposition 11(viii) at the late gradient records when C_* < 0.3234..., and for C_* < 0.2590... confines the late gradient records to a shell (1 - B_ax C_*)^{1/2}/C_* <= r D/M <= (1 - B_2 C_*)^{-1/2}; this is consistent with, and does not decide, the branches of Theorem 13. The route cannot be decisive: the columnar vortex bounds every constant of this kind below by 8/sqrt7, so no inequality of this type excludes C_* > sqrt7/8 = 0.3307.... The divergence-free form of the singular-value inequality, obtained later (Proposition 11(v)), supersedes Proposition 28(a), (c) and the first statement of (d): averaging over all rotations and pairing the Hessian with the orthogonal projection of the test tensor onto the tensors allowed by div U = 0, it gives |grad U|^2 <= B_div M H = 3.830187... M H at every point of every bounded divergence-free field. Under (A) with D(t) > 0 it excludes C_* < 1/B_div = 0.261083... and leaves no admissible C_* in the shell range C_* < 1/B_ax. The sharp inequality of Proposition 11(v), obtained after that, projects onto the spherical harmonics of degree one instead of averaging over rotations and gives |grad U|^2 <= (12/sqrt10) M H = 3.794733... M H for every bounded C^{1,1} field, so under (A) with D(t) > 0 it excludes C_* < sqrt10/12 = 0.263523...; no smaller constant holds for all bounded fields. For divergence-free fields, testing the Hessian against the Hessian of |x| B x projected onto the tensors with vanishing divergence contraction, with an explicit bound for the amplitude <|B omega|>, gives |grad U|^2 <= B_div'' M H = 3.702534... M H (Proposition 11(v)), so under (A) with D(t) > 0 the constants C_* < 1/B_div'' = 0.270085... are excluded. The radius-dependent estimates in Proposition 28(b) remain valid; their large-radius bound still gives the upper bound on a for C_* < c_2 = 0.3234..., which is not superseded (with the sharp planar inequality of Proposition 11(v) in step (1) of the proof of Proposition 28(b) it holds for C_* < sqrt7/8; remark after Proposition 28). An explicit axisymmetric field with swirl (Proposition 11(v)) shows that no such inequality excludes C_* > 0.313019...; so over nonconstant bounded divergence-free C^{1,1} fields, and over their axisymmetric subclass with swirl, the infimum of Q lies between 0.270085... and 0.313019... and is not determined.

### 3.22 Historical swirl domination (Proposition 29)

Theorem 13(b) shows that at uniformly viscous gradient records the swirl is comparable to the velocity. Proposition 29 turns this into an equivalence for the whole late history: D/M^2 bounded below at all late times, (A) together with D/M^2 bounded below at the late gradient records, and historical swirl domination M <= C_S S are the same condition, and under it (A), (K) and (TAIL) follow, with (K) and (TAIL) on the whole normalized past of every sufficiently late first-crossing swirl record. The exclusion of this sub-case of branch (I) is therefore exactly the regularity criterion (SD). The criteria checked here do not establish (SD): under historical swirl domination a singularity must be of Type II in the swirl itself, and this report derives no upper bound on the swirl growth rate from bounded M/S alone. A counterexample to the exclusion of Case 1 within this sub-case would be a Type II singularity in which the swirl carries a fixed fraction of the historical velocity maximum at all late times. The remaining parts of branch (I), in which D/M^2 is bounded below only along some record sequences, and branch (II) are unaffected.

### 3.23 Inflow envelopes at the axis (Proposition 30)

At a first-crossing swirl record the circulation equals gamma_n at radius r_n = gamma_n/S_n, and on a Case-1 trajectory gamma_n is bounded below (Theorem 1) while r_n -> 0. So the circulation does not vanish at the axis in the joint limit (r, t) -> (0, T_*). The circulation vanishes on the axis, and the comparison of [Sh, Lemma 5.1] makes the relevant transport obstruction precise. It dominates |Gamma| by a function of r and t alone that solves a heat equation in a half-line whose boundary moves inward at the speed g(t) = ||(u^r(t))^-||_infty, so that a lower-class bound on the cumulative inward radial displacement, the time integral of g, forces the circulation to vanish uniformly in z as (r, t) -> (0, T_*). This heat comparison function has a killed Brownian representation and is bounded by G times the probability that a Brownian path survives above a moving barrier; the decay of that probability at the axis is decided by Kolmogorov's integral test, equivalently, in a form that was not checked against [Pet], Petrovskii's criterion for the regularity of the tip of the moving domain. Proposition 30 uses this only qualitatively. The record argument needs only that the circulation tends to 0 at the axis, not a rate, so the full integral test applies, terminal windows suffice, and the conclusion holds without the criterion [Wei]. [Sh, Corollary 5.4] uses a quantitative rate in order to invoke [Wei], which limits it to a coefficient below 1/2 in front of log log log; here the coefficient is 3/2, with any number of further iterated logarithms. The same conclusion holds under historical swirl domination, through first-attainment times of the swirl. The proposition does not decide Case 1. It says that on a Case-1 trajectory the cumulative inward radial displacement exceeds any given lower-class envelope on arbitrarily short terminal windows; no estimate of this report shows that such displacements are incompatible with the energy bound, with (A) or with the records. The comparison discards the term -r^{-1} d_r, which for the exact operator is the drift of a Bessel process of dimension 0 towards the axis; Proposition 31 (sec. 3.24) keeps it. Two further limits of the route were identified. A localization to a bounded neighbourhood of an axis point needs, in addition to the local inflow, control of the axial displacement. And no swirl-only version follows, since no bound of the meridional inflow by the swirl is available except under historical swirl domination.

### 3.24 Dimension-zero envelopes (Proposition 31)

Proposition 31 keeps the term -r^{-1} d_r of the radial operator. The comparison diffusion is then a Bessel process of dimension zero, run backward in time, with the outward drift g. In self-similar variables, for an inflow C (T_* - t)^{-1/2}, its killing rate is of order C^3 e^{-C^2} instead of the rate C e^{-C^2} of the one-dimensional comparison; the proof makes this precise by a weighted Hardy inequality and a backward energy estimate and turns it into the integral test (KP_0), which allows the coefficient 5/2 of log log log in place of 3/2. Along records the test is used qualitatively, as in Proposition 30. Part (f) uses the explicit form of the decay instead: under a sliding bound with coefficient beta, the circulation is at most C G exp(-c (log log(1/r))^{5/2 - beta}) near the axis, which is below the threshold |log r|^{-2} of [LZ2, Corollary 1.3] (and Wei's threshold |log r|^{-3/2}) when beta < 3/2. So, by [LZ2, Corollary 1.3], every singular solution violates such a sliding bound for every beta < 3/2; the corresponding statement of [Sh, Corollary 5.4] has beta < 1/2. The statement of [LZ2, Corollary 1.3] was checked in the arXiv version, and it is used as in step (a) of the proof of Theorem 1. Part (f) concerns all singular solutions and does not use the Case-1 hypotheses. Like Proposition 30, the proposition restricts the growth rate of the inflow and decides neither branch. For envelopes whose self-similar inflow C tends to infinity, whether convergence of (KP_0) allows the radial comparison function to stay positive at the axis was not examined, so it is not claimed that 5/2 is the limit of the method.

### 3.25 Critical inflow at the axis (Proposition 32)

Propositions 30 and 31 bound the time integral of the inward speed and allow any spatial profile. Proposition 32 bounds instead the scale-invariant quantity -r u^r pointwise near the axis and allows any growth in time. Its comparison function is time-independent: Q = G s(r)/s(r_1), where s is the scale function of the radial diffusion with generator d_rr + ((1 - eps(r))/r) d_r, and Q is a supersolution of the circulation equation wherever -r u^r <= 2 - eps(r). Decay at the axis is obtained exactly when s is finite at 0, the condition (F_0); for eps = kappa/log(1/r) this is kappa > 1, and (32.2), with m = 1, gives the upper bound |Gamma(r, z, t)| <= G (log(1/r_1)/log(1/r))^{kappa - 1} for 0 < r <= r_1, z in R and t in [t_0, T_*), with r_1 and t_0 as in Proposition 32(a) (an upper bound, not an asymptotic rate). Since the maximum principle only sees points where |Gamma| exceeds Q, the inflow bound is needed only on that superlevel set. Along records the decay is used qualitatively, as in Proposition 30, and gives the joint liminf as (r, t) -> (0, T_*), liminf log(1/r) (2 - Lambda(r, t)) <= 1, on every Case-1 trajectory (and under historical swirl domination); for all singular solutions it is combined with the continuation criteria of [LZ2] (decay |log r|^{-2}, reached for kappa >= 3) and, conditionally on [Wei, Corollary 1.1], of [Wei] (decay |log r|^{-3/2}, reached for kappa > 5/2). For constant eps in (0, 1) the same comparison gives power decay and recovers, in a near-axis terminal form, the fixed-gap condition attributed to [ZZ] in [QZ]; for eps = 1 it gives the condition r u^r >= -1 of [Pan]. When (F_0) fails the radial comparison cannot give decay at the axis; this is a limit of the method, not a Navier-Stokes counterexample. On the Case-1 subsequence, Proposition 23(c) already gives points with -r u^r > 2 and Gamma > gamma_n (A - m) in windows at distances between R_0 r_n and L r_n from the axis, consistently with (c). The proposition does not exclude Case 1 from (A), (K) and (TAIL) alone.

### 3.26 Circulation absorption by the near-axis strain (Proposition 33)

Propositions 30 to 32 control the circulation through the inflow (u^r)^- or -r u^r. Proposition 33 uses instead the radial strain rate k = ||(u^r/r)^-||_infty, which is bounded by the velocity gradient. The circulation equation has the Burgers-type supersolution G (1 - exp(-r^2 w(t))) whenever w' >= 2 k w - 4 w^2, and starting w at infinity, which is possible because the circulation vanishes quadratically at the axis, gives (33.1) without any information on earlier data. The resulting bound ||u^theta||_infty^2 <= G^2 w is of Type I whenever k is of Type I, and the quantitative form (33.3) gives the dichotomy between Type II near-axis strain and Type I swirl. For the Burgers drift the supersolution is an exact solution, so (33.1) is the best bound in terms of k within the scalar comparison. Along the records the identity -r_n u^r >= 1 gives k(t_n) >= r_n^{-2}; a Type I strain bound k <= C_a/(T_* - t) therefore places the records within C_a r_n^2 of T_*, and the Case-1 normalization forces C_a > 1/2, since for C_a <= 1/2 the comparison removes all circulation of the limit before the record. Under Type I swirl the Case-1 limit has |U^theta|^2 <= C/|tau| backward in time, so all limits of its backward translates are swirl-free and hence constant by the Liouville theorem of [KNSS]; its meridional part need not decay away from the axis, and the Liouville theorems for ancient solutions with additional decay, integrability or periodicity do not apply. The same comparison for ancient solutions shows that a bounded mild ancient axisymmetric solution with viscosity nu > 0 and bounded circulation whose cumulative backward strain over [-v, 0] is at most (1/2) log v + C along some sequence v_j -> infinity is a constant multiple of e_3 (mildness is needed: V = sin(tau) e_3 with pressure -cos(tau) x_3 is a bounded smooth ancient solution with zero circulation and zero strain; the circulation bound is (1 - exp(-R^2/(4 nu Pi_V))) times its supremum, and Pi_V < infinity forces the cumulative strain to exceed (1/2) log v by an amount tending to infinity, since the integrand of Pi_V is monotone), while every Case-1 limit has Pi_U <= G/4. Under historical swirl domination, (33.3) and Proposition 31(d) give a lower bound of iterated-logarithm type for (T_* - t) k(t). None of this excludes Case 1 from (A), (K) and (TAIL) alone.

### 3.27 Strain from potential vorticity (Proposition 34)

The near-axis strain of Proposition 33 is the quotient u^r/r, which satisfies Delta_5 (u^r/r) = d_z (omega^theta/r) in R^5. The heat semigroup of R^5 then gives ||u^r/r||_infty <= (2 ||u^r||_infty ||eta||_infty)^{1/2}, a scale-invariant inequality that uses, besides the potential vorticity, only the bound of u^r. The circulation comparison of Proposition 33 needs the strain only where |Gamma| exceeds a level lambda, at the cost of replacing G by G - lambda above that level. For a Case-1 limit and 0 <= lambda < 1, define kappa_lambda(tau) as the spatial supremum of (U^R/R)^- on {|Gamma_U(., tau)| > lambda}, with supremum 0 for the empty set. Proposition 34(d)(i) gives int_{-v}^0 kappa_lambda(tau) d tau - (1/2) log v -> infinity as v -> infinity. On the Type I swirl branch, for 0 < lambda < 1, the swirl bound places that set beyond the radius rho_lambda(tau) = lambda (gamma_* (tau_* + |tau|)/C_I)^{1/2}, of the order of the parabolic radius |tau|^{1/2}, so the limit needs, in the same time-integrated sense, inflow -U^R > R/(2|tau|) at points beyond rho_lambda(tau); a bound R (U^R)^- <= A on that region with A C_I <= lambda^2 gamma_*/2 would exclude it. The potential vorticity of these limits tends to 0 backward in time, at least like 1/log |tau|, and cannot be bounded by 1/(8 K_U tau^2) at all large |tau|. The logarithmic rate comes from a barrier on a cylinder around the axis of radius proportional to log |tau|, on whose boundary the potential vorticity is controlled by the bounded vorticity; the available bound for the swirl source d_Z(q^2) of the equation of the potential vorticity is O(1/|tau|), which is not integrable in time, so it does not give a time-integrable source. A kinematic scaling example shows that spatial bounds at a single time cannot give the missing critical estimate for the meridional field.

### 3.28 A small swirl Type I constant (Proposition 35)

For viscosity 1, the energy identities of Chen, Fang and Zhang for J = omega^r/r and Omega = omega^theta/r have swirl terms bounded by ||u^theta||_infty times products of the energies and dissipations, after a determinant cancellation and Wei's elliptic bound ||grad(u^r/r)||_2 <= ||Omega||_2. With the weighted energy (4/3^{1/2}) ||J||_2^2 + ||Omega||_2^2 the growth rate is at most (3^{3/2}/2) ||u^theta||_infty^2, so a swirl Type I bound with constant C gives growth at most like (T - t)^{-alpha}, alpha = (3^{3/2}/2) C^2, and alpha < 3/2 when C < 3^{-1/4}. Then ||Omega||_2^{4/3} is integrable in time, which the swirl estimate of [CFZ] turns into u^theta/r in L^4_t L^4_x, the continuation criterion [CFZ, Lemma 2.5]. The circulation bound is not used. The result does not exclude the Type I swirl branch of Case 1; it gives the lower bound 3^{-1/2} for its constant. Combining (35.2) with the circulation bound gives a lower bound for the near-axis strain rate. The pointwise bound (33.1) gives ||u^theta||_infty^2 <= mu_0 G^2 w with mu_0 = max_{x > 0} (1 - e^{-x})^2/x = 0.4072..., where w is the quantity of Proposition 33(a); if k(t) <= C_a/(T_* - t) near T_*, the comparison of Proposition 33(b) gives limsup (T_* - t) w <= (2 C_a - 1)^+/4, and (35.2) then forces C_a >= 1/2 + 2/(3^{1/2} mu_0 G^2). The same bound (33.1) gives ||u^theta/r||_infty <= G w, so the term -2 int (u^theta/r) J Omega dx of the energy identity for Omega is at most 2 ||u^theta/r||_infty ||J||_2 ||Omega||_2. For the weighted energy lambda ||J||_2^2 + ||Omega||_2^2 the growth exponent is then the largest value of a quadratic form, and the optimal lambda gives the exponent 2 mu_0^{1/3} a_0 G^{4/3} in the limit, with a_0 = (2 C_a - 1)/4; it is below 3/2 unless C_a >= 1/2 + (3/2) mu_0^{-1/3} G^{-4/3}. The two bounds together are (35.3), which holds for every singular solution. The weaker bound 1/2 already follows from the swirl maximum principle and the L^2_t L^infty_x swirl criterion of [CFZ, Theorem 1.1]; the gain is the term c_G. Remark (3) after Proposition 35 shows by explicit fields that, at G = 50, energy arguments with a constant weight and these pointwise bounds alone cannot exclude the Type I strain branch.

### 3.29 Circulation decay under Type I strain and a slowly growing inflow (Proposition 36)

Proposition 36 gives a proof with key estimates: its Status says that the numerical-constant verifications in (a), the level bookkeeping in Step 6 and the truncation limits in Steps 6 and 7 are summarized rather than reproduced in full. The following conclusions have that qualification. For viscosity 1, the comparison of Proposition 31 bounds the circulation by the survival probability of a radial diffusion with drift -1/R plus the inflow. Put g(t) = ||(u^r)^-(t)||_infty and k(t) = ||(u^r/r)^-(t)||_infty. Under (S) and (I) of Proposition 36, alpha > 1/2, k(t) <= alpha/(T_* - t), and g(t) <= C(T_* - t) (T_* - t)^{-1/2}, where C : (0, 2 h_0] -> [2, infinity) is continuous and nonincreasing, on the respective time intervals specified there. The inflow part of the comparison drift is capped by min{g, k R}. In the logarithmic clock l = log v and variable y = R_v/v^{1/2}, the resulting drift is at most min{C, alpha y} - y/2 - 1/y. For fixed C >= 2 the symmetrizing weight is W_C(y) = y^{-1} exp(psi_C(y) - rho C^2), with rho = 1 - 1/(2 alpha) and psi_C(y) = int_0^y (min{C, alpha s} - s/2) ds; psi_C is maximal at y = 2C with value rho C^2. The bottom lambda_1(C) of the absorbed spectrum is comparable to C exp(-rho C^2), with constants depending on alpha. Define Lambda(v) = int_{log v}^{log(h_0/2)} lambda_1(C(e^l)) dl. Test (T'), Lambda(v)/C(v)^2 -> infinity, gives a circulation bound K G exp(-c Lambda(r)) near the axis. The same decay follows from (W2) and (T''), where (W2) requires that l -> C(e^l) be continuously differentiable with int_{-infinity}^{log(h_0/2)} |d C(e^l)/dl|^2 dl < infinity, and (T'') requires Lambda(v) -> infinity. For C^2 = kappa (L_2 + beta L_3 + B), on the admissible window of Proposition 36(d), (T') holds exactly when kappa rho < 1, or kappa rho = 1 and beta < 1/2; (W2) holds, and (T'') holds exactly when kappa rho < 1, or kappa rho = 1 and beta <= 3/2. At Case-1 swirl records gamma_n is bounded below, so either admissible test forces failure of the inflow bound on every sufficiently short terminal window of the Type I strain branch. This gives (36.1) and the leading coefficient 2 C_a/(2 C_a - 1). Proposition 36(f), using [LZ2, Corollary 1.3], gives the same leading coefficient for every singular physical solution in sec. 1.1 whose near-axis strain satisfies k(t) <= C_a/(T_* - t) on some terminal interval [t_a, T_*); its extension of (W2), (T'') to all such solutions additionally requires Lambda(v)/L_2(v) -> infinity. For constant C, the conclusion is already [QZ, Theorem 1.1], without the strain hypothesis. The Type II strain branch is untouched, and (36.1) is a necessary condition, not a contradiction.

### 3.30 Strain records and a swirl barrier (Proposition 37)

Proposition 37 adds one piece of information to each branch of Proposition 33(c) and excludes neither. On the Type II strain branch the near-axis strain k has records in the historical sense, and at a record the minimum of u^r/r gives the strain analogue of the record inequality of Proposition 22(b): p_r/r >= q^2 - K_j^2 at the minimum point, and p_zz <= -4 K_j^2 if that point lies on the axis. The infinite-energy Burgers vortex with z-independent swirl attains equality; this shows that the local pressure inequality is sharp for flows with its linear strain, and it does not realize the Type II record history. The circulation bound evaluated with the running maximum of k gives S(sigma_j)^2 <= (mu_0 G^2/2 + o(1)) K_j, which improves Theorem 13(a), at leading order, when mu_0 G K_j/2 < D(sigma_j). Normalized by the velocity scale M and the strain K_j, the solutions at the records converge either to viscous ancient solutions in LL (after normalization of the viscosity) with nonzero swirl and the extra normalization a_W >= -1 on the past, a_W = -1 at a point, or, under (A) and a gradient bound D <= C K_j, along subsequences to swirl-free ancient Euler flows; the bounded-gradient and compression normalizations of the latter are shared by steady vortex rings seen in their moving frame (the bounded second derivatives require a ring of more than Hoelder regularity), so this information does not exclude the Euler regime. When the Type II strain alternative occurs together with Type I swirl, a positive limiting viscosity is excluded: the Type I swirl bound gives S(sigma_j) = o(M(sigma_j)) and K_j = o(M(sigma_j)^2) at the records, so a viscous limit would be swirl-free and hence constant; the normalized viscosity tends to 0, and an Euler limit is extracted only under (A) and D <= C K_j. On the Type I swirl branch the function q_U = U^theta/R of a limit solves a drift-diffusion equation on R^5 with zero-order term 2 U^R/R. The Burgers profile f(R^2/L^2) with parameter beta is a supersolution when U^R/R >= -A/L^2 on {R < L} over the whole earlier history with A < 2 nu beta, and since grad U tends to 0 on cylinders backward in time, q_U = o(|tau|^{-1/2}), improving the bound O(|tau|^{-1/2}) contained in the proof of (34.6). Unless |tau| times the compression on the parabolic cylinder {R < |tau|^{1/2}} is unbounded as tau -> -infinity, the rate improves to O(1/|tau|). A time-integrated form of the barrier, with the integrating factor exp(2 int (compression)), gives the same rate when only the integrals of this compression over the dyadic windows [t, 2 t] of backward time stay bounded (the condition (CW)); a smooth bounded test field with zero potential vorticity in the parabolic cylinders fails (CW); it violates the evolution equations and the normalization of the limits, so it shows only that (CW) does not follow from the kinematic properties checked for it. On the boundary of a wider cylinder {R < L} the bounded circulation gives |q_U| <= G/(gamma_* L^2), so a compression bound U^R/R >= -A/L(sigma)^2 on {R < L(sigma)} for all sufficiently negative sigma, with L(sigma) nondecreasing in |sigma| and L(tau)/|tau|^{3/4} -> infinity, gives q_U = o(|tau|^{-3/2}), which through (34.5) and the derivative estimate (D) of Proposition 37, Remark (3) contradicts Proposition 34(d)(ii); nothing is known about the compression at these radii. Through (34.5) and (D), the first rate gives no decay of eta_U beyond (34.6), since its integrand o(1/s) need not be integrable, and the second only ||eta_U(-s)||_infty = O(1/s), short of the bound 1/(8 K_U s^2) that Proposition 34(d)(ii) excludes (the joined energy of Proposition 39 gives the stronger ||eta_U(-s)||_infty = O(s^{-3/2}) under (CW), Proposition 39(f)(xi), also short of it); for 0 < lambda < 1, the compression required by Proposition 34(d) occurs on {|Gamma_U| > lambda} beyond rho_lambda, possibly outside the parabolic cylinder. On the Type I swirl branch Remark (5)(c) of Proposition 37 also bounds the compression on the part of the parabolic cylinder inside an Euler cone by the axis compression and the potential vorticity of a larger cone, with a harmonic remainder, and the axis compression by that potential vorticity (the envelope m_{A,c}(s) <= C (K E'(s))^{1/2} + C K/(delta s), sharp for bounded fields). If (CW_loc) fails, Proposition 37, Remark (5)(c)(8) shows that limsup_t int_t^{2t} [(K E'(s))^{1/2} + s^{1/2} E'(s)] ds = infinity for every larger cone C_{A'}, A' > A_c, E'(s) the supremum of |eta_U(-s)| over C_{A'}(-s); the axis identities, the reduction of the cone compression to the axis and the width bound for compressed axis intervals do not prove (CW_loc). Combined, [AB, Theorem 1.1] and [Se20, Theorem 2.1] exclude non-trivial axisymmetric mild bounded ancient solutions with I < infinity, where I is the supremum over all parabolic balls of the scale-invariant energy, dissipation and pressure quantities (Proposition 37, Remark (4)); this requires bounds on the whole velocity at all scales. For the limits of Proposition 33(e)(i) the meridional field at large scales is not controlled, and a circulation bounded below across many intermediate annuli would make the scale-invariant energy grow at least like log R; the supremum saturation of Proposition 23(a) does not establish that distribution.

### 3.31 A circulation barrier in similarity variables (Proposition 38)

In the variables rho = R/(tau_* - tau)^{1/2}, zeta = Z/(tau_* - tau)^{1/2}, sigma = -log(tau_* - tau), the circulation equation acquires the drift -(rho/2) d_rho - (zeta/2) d_zeta towards the origin, and the radial operator d_rhorho - rho^{-1} d_rho is that of a Bessel process of dimension zero, absorbed at the axis, where the circulation vanishes. A Type I inflow bound -U^R <= C (tau_* - tau)^{-1/2} + theta R/(tau_* - tau) with theta < 1/2 caps the outward part of the drift by C + theta rho, which the drift -rho/2 dominates at large rho; the radial function F with nu F'' + (C + theta rho - rho/2 - nu/rho) F' = -1, F(0) = 0, grows like (1/2 - theta)^{-1} log rho, and (G - lambda)(F + sigma_0 - sigma)/S is a supersolution on a logarithmic window of length S. Since an ancient solution has windows of every length, the circulation above any level lambda at which the inflow bound holds vanishes. The comparison needs the bound only where |Gamma| > lambda, and the quantitative form (38.2) bounds the circulation at a point by its normalized radius and the logarithmic length of the window on which the inflow bound holds. This is the ancient form of the constant-envelope criterion [QZ, Theorem 1.1] for singular solutions. It improves Proposition 34(b)-(d) on the Type I swirl branch in one respect: there the test was the divergence of Pi_lambda, a condition on the time-integrated compression at the critical rate 1/(2|tau|), while (38.1) allows any compression C/(R |tau|^{1/2}) near the parabolic radius and compression theta/|tau|, theta < 1/2, beyond it (Proposition 34 in turn allows a logarithmic excess over the critical rate, which (38.1) does not). It also corrects the discussion of Type I Liouville theorems: for axisymmetric solutions with bounded circulation the condition I < infinity of [AB] is not needed, and a full Type I velocity bound (indeed its one-sided radial part) would exclude the Type I swirl limits. For the Case-1 limits it gives the necessary condition 38(c), with its time-integrated form (d) and its localization (e) described below: on circulation superlevel sets, at arbitrarily late backward times, inflow above C s^{-1/2} together with compression above theta/s. The kinematic family of Proposition 37, Remark (3), with compression alpha/(1 + |tau|) on the ball of radius (1 + |tau|)^{3/4}, satisfies it for alpha > 1/2; an exclusion using Proposition 38(a) would require establishing its inflow hypothesis, which the bounds used in this report do not give. The time-integrated form 38(d) bounds the circulation by the logarithmic-time integral of the excess compression (k - theta)^+, so for the Case-1 limits the spatial supremum of the normalized excess has a positive lower average in logarithmic time (38.4); for C = 0 a bound of the same form already follows from Proposition 34(d), and the new content relative to it is the allowance C near the parabolic radius. It is again a necessary condition. If the boundedness of the velocity is dropped, allowances theta > 1/2 admit nontrivial examples: for every theta > 1/2 the collapsing Burgers vortex, a linear strain of rate theta/(tau_* - tau) with the circulation A (1 - exp(-(2 theta - 1) R^2/(4 nu (tau_* - tau)))), is an exact solution on R^3 x (-infinity, 0] with bounded circulation and bounded velocity gradient, and with these constants it realizes the circulation bound (33.4), the Type I swirl bound and the global compression bound of the Type I strain sub-branch, together with the normalization of the Case-1 limits for suitable A and tau_* (Remark (4) after Proposition 38). Its velocity is unbounded. So the equations and the bounds it shares with that sub-branch do not alone exclude the sub-branch; an exclusion must use a property the example lacks, such as the bound |U| <= K. The comparison also localizes (Proposition 38(e)): up to an error exponentially small in the distance, the circulation at a point depends only on the inflow inside a backward cone of speed K + nu, so for the Case-1 limits the inflow points of (c) exist inside the Euler cone max{R, |Z|} < 2 (K + nu_*) s at times s in every window [T_0, T_0^p], for every p > 1 + (G/gamma_* - lambda)/((1 - 2 theta)(1 - lambda)) and T_0 large (38.6).

### 3.32 The vorticity behind the compression (Proposition 39)

On the Type I swirl branch the potential vorticity eta = omega^theta/r of a limit has no stretching term: it is transported by the meridional field, diffuses in five dimensions and is created only by the source d_Z(q_U^2), the axial derivative of the squared swirl ratio. Hence eta at a point is the limit, as the horizon v tends to infinity, of the expected source collected up to time v along the backward five-dimensional diffusion paths from it (39.2), and the compression at a point is bounded by the harmonic part of the localized Biot-Savart formula, at most (3 pi/8) K/L, plus a weighted integral of |eta| over the ball of radius L. A cutoff Bernstein estimate bounds the source by 2 C_loc Q_1^2, and by 162 C_loc G'^2 R^{-4} for R >= 3, the second bound from the bounded circulation. If the forward radial velocity is nonpositive outside the moving parabolic cylinders, the backward paths that start at radius r enter the cylinders before a time of order r^2/M^2 only with small probability, with a weight controlled by a supermartingale, and, with the bound Q_1 = O(1/|tau|) available when A_* < infinity, eta is O(r^{-2}); this gives a Type I vorticity bound only at radii beyond a multiple of |tau|. With the self-similar size |tau|^{-5/2} of the source inside the cylinders (no bound for the source outside them is needed, see below), the potential vorticity eta is O(|tau|^{-3/2}) everywhere and O(r^{-3}) outside, the Biot-Savart estimate then gives compression O(1/|tau|) at all points and below any theta_0/|tau| beyond a fixed multiple of the parabolic radius, and Proposition 38(c) is contradicted. The exterior estimate rests on an identity of the circulation along the backward paths: Gamma^2 increases on average by 2 nu |grad Gamma|^2 per unit time, up to a lower-order term, and is bounded, so the expected gradient energy collected along the stopped paths is bounded (39.9), and by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality the expected time integral of |grad Gamma| over the stopped stretch, of length at most r^2/(4 M^2), is O(r) rather than O(r^2); this lowers the expected exterior source budget from r^{-2} to r^{-3}. The hypotheses are consistent with the collapsing Burgers vortex, whose compression is carried entirely by the harmonic part and which is excluded only by its unbounded velocity; none of them was derived for the limits. The missing estimates are the exterior inflow and the self-similar size of the core source, that is, (H3): |d_Z(q_U^2)| <= C |tau|^{-5/2} on the parabolic cylinders (when q_U = O(1/|tau|) is available, an axial derivative of q_U of order |tau|^{-3/2} suffices). Under Type I compression on the parabolic cylinders (A_* < infinity), in particular on the Type I strain branch, and more generally under its time-integrated form (CW) of Proposition 37(e), the second is not needed: then q_U = O(1/|tau|), and along a backward path the energy that equals q^2 inside the cylinders and |tau|^{-2} Gamma^2 outside them has a drift at least a positive multiple of its gradient energy minus C |tau|^{-3} - 4 C_q |tau|^{-2} m_P(|tau|), since the compression enters only inside, where it is at most m_P(|tau|) (at most A/|tau| when A > A_*), and the circulation equation has no compression term; under (CW) the dyadic bound int_t^infinity s^{-3/2} m_P(s) ds <= W t^{-3/2}/(1 - 2^{-3/2}) makes the integrated loss of the same order as under A_* < infinity, and no pointwise bound on m_P is used; as this energy is O(|tau|^{-2}), with the increasing weight |tau|^{1/2} the gradient energy, and with it the source, collected after any backward time u_0 is O((a + u_0)^{-3/2}) in expectation. Under exterior inflow the bounds on early entrance into the cylinders give eta = O(r^{-3}) outside; under an exterior outflow bound U^R <= kappa R/|tau| with kappa < 1, supermartingales of the form R^{-beta} |tau|^gamma control the arrival and the occupation before it, and the potential vorticity eta is O(r^{-p_1} |tau|^{-(3 - p_1)/2}) outside with some p_1 > 1, which suffices for the Biot-Savart step. Since |U| <= K gives U^R <= kappa R/|tau| at R >= K |tau|/kappa (kappa > 0), the missing estimate when A_* < infinity is an outflow bound on the intermediate region M |tau|^{1/2} <= R < K |tau|/kappa; every limit on the Type I swirl branch violates (CW) (in particular has A_* = infinity) or violates that bound at arbitrarily late times, and the same holds with the cone-local window bound (CW_loc) in place of (CW), the violation then occurring in the Euler cone max{R, |Z|} < A_c |tau| (Proposition 39(f)(xiii)). With no compression hypothesis, (39.19_H) of Proposition 39(f)(xiv), for H > K, gives int_t^{2t} n_A(s) ds = O(log t) for 0 < A < H, where n_A(s) is the supremum of (U^R/R)^- over {R < s^{1/2}, |Z| < A s} at time -s. The proof uses ultracontractivity of the source-free equation for eta in three-dimensional measure, with an absolute constant and a dissipative axis term, and a near-field kernel bound at all radii. If H > A_c > A_3, the same source budget together with |d_Z(q_U^2)| <= F |tau|^{-5/2} on C_H gives (CW_loc) and (39.19), and hence the conditional exclusion in Proposition 39(f)(xiii), as stated in (xiv)(4). The unsigned estimate used there permits logarithmic window growth for the short source bursts that (39.19) allows (this is not a lower bound for the compression); for the linear problem with a prescribed drift V that has critical radial outflow R V^R = 2 nu the logarithm is attained, also for the reconstructed strain of a signed source, and without radial velocity, for a source with a global dyadic L^1 budget, it is absent (Proposition 39(f)(xiv)(5)(d), (e)); for limits satisfying the source budget (39.19_H), in each strictly smaller Euler cone, the coupling excludes that critical outflow across a diffusive height at radii o(|tau|^{1/2}) without removing the logarithm (Proposition 39(f)(xiv)(6)); the multiscale and time-averaged forms of these bounds, survival decay of packets under a pointwise outflow gap c <= lambda nu with lambda < 2, the zero-budget case and an exact forced expanding pair whose logarithmic compression costs a logarithmic source are in Proposition 39(f)(xiv)(7); the time-integrated strain bound C_1 + kappa log(1 + length), kappa proportional to B/nu, its survival and occupation consequences, and two prescribed drifts showing that it alone gives no uniform packet estimate are in Proposition 39(f)(xiv)(8); in the model without drift, keeping the derivative structure of the source gives a bound of order 1/|tau| for the strain it generates on the parabolic cylinder R <= |tau|^{1/2}, provided q_U^2(y, -beta) <= C (beta + R_y^2)^{-2} for beta >= |tau|. The outflow bound may be replaced by a Dini-type decay of |tau| |omega^theta_U| outside the cylinders (Proposition 39(f)(vi); there A_* < infinity may also be replaced by (H3)): if |omega^theta_U| <= |tau|^{-1} w(R/|tau|^{1/2}) there, with w -> 0 and int^infinity w(xi) dxi/xi < infinity, the weighted integral of |eta| over all of R^5 is at most (pi/2) |tau|^{-1} J(x'/|tau|^{1/2}) with J bounded and J -> 0 at infinity, which again gives compression O(1/|tau|) everywhere and below theta_0/|tau| beyond a fixed multiple of the parabolic radius. More weakly, it suffices that the masses of |omega^theta_U| in the meridional half-plane be small at the scale of the distance (Proposition 39(f)(vii)): the angular average of the five-dimensional kernel is explicit and at most min{pi^2/(r d), 2 pi^2/d^2} at meridional distance d from a point at radius r, so the weighted integral of |eta| is controlled by the mass of the disk of radius r/2 about the point weighted by 1/d, and by the masses of the dyadic annuli at distance d divided by d^2; the conditions are needed only at radii at least 2 M |tau|^{1/2}, and the inner points are reached through an auxiliary point at a fixed multiple of the parabolic radius. These masses are controlled in turn by the total unsigned source: the volume element of R^3 is subinvariant for the potential-vorticity equation without source (the axis absorbs), so the mass of |omega^theta_U| in a region at time -s is at most C_0 T^{-3/2} times the R-weighted area of the region plus the space-time L^1 norm of the source on (-T, -s), and the scale-invariant bound B_0 (1 + log(T/s)) for that norm gives the contradiction (Proposition 39(f)(viii)). The pointwise bounds (H3) and (H4) do not give it, since they allow the source to extend over the whole axis. By the localization 38(e), the same contradiction follows when the source at time -beta is integrated only over the box max{R, |Z|} < A_3 beta, a fixed multiple of the Euler scale (Proposition 39(f)(ix)); this form allows any number of Euler-scale axial cells, and for the periodic model profiles of Proposition 39(f)(ix) (a fixed profile with nonzero axial variation, at amplitude 1/beta and axial scale l(beta)) it holds when l(beta) >= c beta and fails when l(beta)/beta -> 0. So the extent of the source along the axis is no longer an obstruction to applying this criterion; for the periodic model profiles, wavelengths l(beta) = o(beta) violate the hypothesis (39.19), which controls a time integral of the inverse wavelength, and such profiles are not excluded by this criterion. The meridional condition (39.21) of Proposition 39(f)(x) gives a separate sufficient exclusion, proved with no compression hypothesis (the cone strain bound it implies takes the place of A_* < infinity and (CW)); the wavelength statements above concern the source budget of the periodic profiles and do not characterize (39.21). The condition (39.21) gives d_Z q = O(|tau|^{-2}) on the Euler box, with the radial decay and the remainder estimates needed for (39.19); in the equation for d_Z q along the backward paths the axial derivative of the strain supplies the forcing and R d_R(U^R/R) the zeroth-order coefficient, which an R-independent strain does not have. For the collapsing Burgers model, Remark (8)(b) after Proposition 39 gives sufficient wavelength conditions for the contraction of a one-unit linearized feedback map in a weighted supremum norm, not a necessary condition or a stability criterion for the full evolution; for each nonzero axial mode the homogeneous linearized coupled evolution decays in a time-dependent energy at a rate independent of the circulation, exterior modulations with the physical tail have infinite energy, and after a decomposition their forcing of the core is bounded by a multiple of the circulation (with an additional factor of the rescaled axial wavenumber under a weighted supremum bound on the tail). These model estimates imply no stability statement for Case-1 limits. The bounded kinematic family of Remark (7) after Proposition 39 shows that the bounds, the elliptic relation and the unsigned budgets do not give this decay: it has outflow R/|tau| (for |tau| >= 1), produced by an axial stream function of Euler scale with return inflow in distant axial slabs, and vorticity of size 1/|tau| on the whole range |tau|^{1/2} << R <= |tau|, produced by a Z-independent part of the stream function that carries no radial velocity, and it fails the potential-vorticity and circulation equations, with explicit residuals.

### 3.33 Absorption of the circulation paths (Proposition 40)

The record survival of Proposition 26(l), P(zeta > s) >= 1/A, says that the backward circulation path from the record survives forever with positive probability. Along a path that never reaches the axis, the radius multiplied by e^J, with J the time integral of the strain U^R/R along the path, is a Bessel process of dimension zero run with the clock int e^{2J}, and such a process reaches zero in finite clock time almost surely; so the clock stays finite, which forces the time-integrated compression up to the age t to exceed (1/2) log t eventually. On the other side, the coupling Delta_5 a = d_Z eta and the source budget bound the compression averaged over the surviving law at the age s by (kappa + C_abs B/nu) p(s/2)/s, up to an integrable error: the harmonic part gives kappa/s, a multiple of K over the distance to the boundary of a larger cone; the vorticity mass bound at the parabolic scale, which holds on arbitrary measurable sets, splits |eta(-s)| on the cone into a part of L^1 mass at most B and a part bounded by C_N B/((1 - 2^{-3/2}) (nu s)^{3/2}) + eps_s, with the remainder eps_s of Proposition 39(f)(xiv)(6) (its contribution is part of the integrable error); and the density of the surviving law is at most of order (nu s)^{-3/2} p(s/2), by the uniform smoothing bound of Proposition 39(f)(xiv)(1) for the reversed drift (proved there with Nash's inequality, and with the heat constant by the logarithmic Sobolev argument of Proposition 40, Remark (5)), which is dual to the killed backward evolution. Averaging the pathwise lower bound with Fatou's lemma gives (1/2) p_infinity <= (kappa + C_abs B/nu) p_infinity, so the survival probability tends to zero when kappa + C_abs B/nu < 1/2, which contradicts the record survival; here C_abs = 7.636 for the splitting radius (nu s)^{1/2}; 5.79 suffices for the optimal radius (Remark (3)), 2.80 with the kernel constant obtained by duality, 0.81 with the sharp Nash constant (Remark (4)), and 0.735 with the heat value (4 pi)^{-3/2} of the kernel constant, which no kernel bound uniform over the smooth bounded divergence-free axisymmetric drifts with bounded derivatives can improve (Remark (5)). This needs (39.19_H) with a slope H large compared with K and a budget B small compared with nu; neither was derived. The coefficient 1/2 is sharp for the linear strain and for a bounded kinematic version of it (Proposition 40, Remark (9)(h)), and a bound of the averaged compression by c p(s/2)/s with c <= 1/2 (the endpoint is included by Proposition 40, Remark (2)) obtained in any other way would give the same exclusion; for c < 1/2 such a bound on a positive circulation superlevel set {Gamma_U > ell}, 0 <= ell < 1, with the probability of that set along the paths in place of p(s/2), suffices as well when the terminal killed circulation has no atom at ell (Remark (9)(f)). The source budget enters only through the vorticity mass envelope and its remainder, so, keeping the other hypotheses of Proposition 40, a bound (E_M) for the critical vorticity mass of omega^theta/r on sets inside an Euler cone of slope E > K gives the same exclusion when 3 pi K/(8 (E - K)) + C_abs M/nu < 1/2 (Remark (6)); both the slope and the size of M/nu matter. The Type I swirl bound and the linear properties of the representation alone do not imply this envelope: an explicit smooth swirl field with zero meridional velocity generates, through the linear heat representation, an auxiliary scalar with unbounded mass on axisymmetric sets of volume o((nu s)^{3/2}); this scalar is not the potential vorticity of the velocity (which is zero), and the field violates the circulation equation. The strain that this scalar would induce through Delta_5 a = d_Z eta, averaged against the fixed killed paths of the example, started at (1, 0) (which have zero meridional drift), satisfies the inequality of Remark (2) for s >= 1 with c = 0.16 C^2 and e = 0 (nu = 1, C <= 1 the Type I constant of the example), and, when the average over a cone of slope E <= 2 is bounded through the density bound of the surviving law alone, with c = C^2 (0.122 E + 0.373 s^{-3/4}) < 1/2 for s >= 2; for every axisymmetric swirl with |U^theta| <= C beta^{-1/2} such that U^theta e_theta is smooth across the axis with bounded derivatives on every time slab with ages in [beta_0, beta_1], 0 < beta_0 < beta_1 < infinity (arbitrary time and axial dependence otherwise), the strain induced through the same linear representation and averaged over all space against the same driftless killed paths satisfies the inequality for s >= 1 with c = 0.0925 C^2 and e = 0 (Remark (7));
